..................................................................................................837 Page left intentionally blank Preface The world’s food hunger is widespread and growing. Billions of people suffer from severe malnutrition in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The gap in the life expectancies between rich and poor nations is nearly 20 years. Apart from the caloric needs, there is a severe shortage of food materials—fruits, vegetables, tubers, root crops, and fruit nuts—which are the most important plant foods that supply humans with many nutritive requirements including minerals, vitamins, proteins, fats, and carbohydrates, as well as fiber and a variety of flavors and aromas. According to a report published by the National Research Council of the National Academy of Sciences in Washington, DC (2005), postharvest losses of fruits and vegetables may be as high as 80–100% in some instances, particularly in developing countries. In developed countries, strongly urbanized modern living demands transportation of enormous quantities of foodstuffs of good quality from the production zones to centers for storage and distribution. The process comprises a succession of storages that are closely linked to each other. In developing countries, most of which are situated in warm regions, refrigeration is effective in preserving the hygienic quality of almost all local perishable foodstuff resources necessary for feeding the population and essential to children, the ill, and the elderly as well as for preserving certain pharmaceutical items and vaccines. It is vital that the consuming public in a much more health-conscious world be provided with products that retain their quality and characteristics for healthier living. Fruits and vegetables are highly perishable food products. Water loss and postharvest decay account for most of their losses. These losses have been estimated to be more than 40–50% in the tropics and subtropics. Postharvest biotechnology is critical in the battle to minimize waste of fruits and vegetables and to extract the maximum potential from the harvested crops. Wastage of fruits and vegetables is so high in some instances that between the field and the consumer large amounts of nutritious crops are reduced to heaps of refuse. India ranks second in world vegetable production, with annual production of 81 million tons, but because of inadequate postharvest facilities and because high crop yields result lower prices, farmers left crops unharvested, unable even to bear the cost of labor. This type of situation has led some farmers to commit suicide. xxvii xxviii Preface Lack of understanding of postharvest etiology of these crops affects both supplies and profits even in some technically advanced countries. Technological measures such as harvesting, handling and maturity, low-temperature storage and environmental control (CAS, MAS, and MAP), irradiation, packaging techniques, and processing (canning, freezing, drying, etc.) of fresh fruits and vegetables into suitable products with improved storage characters provide the ultimate road map to overcome these losses. Losses of foods, especially of perishable foods such as fruits and vegetables in transit and in storage, must be gradually reduced in order to increase the world food supply. This is an especially important consideration in developing countries where food perishes rapidly and where storage and processing facilities are virtually nonexistent. The reduction of postharvest losses of fruits and vegetables and conservation of valuable nutrients present in these products can be a positive step toward a healthy and happy world. In fact, in developing countries the steps to be taken are similar to those adopted in the industrialized countries between the two world wars. The first link is established for storage in production zones to ensure to feeding of the local population, and it is progressively developed with economic growth in these countries. The influence of storage is extended because of development in transport air conditions, construction of storage structures in consumption zones, and sometimes in exporting ports. In this way, attempts to reduce the loss of perishable produce in a developing country must generally involve using a multipurpose cell, which at the lowest limit could be simply one cold room. With the advancement of industrialization, people are living far from food production areas in highly populated urban areas. This dislocation of population requires proper means for food preservation and distribution without its spoilage. The standard of living of people has gone up with the advance of science, and people are showing interest for better and fresher food, which is now possible to provide with the use of modern methods of preservation. The uneven population and uneven production of foods of different kinds in the world demand the transport of food from food producing areas to the food consumption areas. This transportation requires proper preservation of food because the transportation period is generally greater than the natural life of food. Research institutions around the world spent millions of dollars to increase the productivity of fruits and vegetables. They take great pride in pointing to production increases up to 5%. Little attention is given to the direct losses of that production to poor storage, handling, and transportation practices. Even developed countries experience significant loss of horticultural commodities in the postharvest process. That loss is multiplied many fold in developing countries where cold storages or temperature-controlled transportation are lacking and where marketing takes place in the shade of tent or tree or thatched roof. Preface xxix In fact in order to properly maintain the quality of perishable products, it is necessary to maintain their temperature throughout the cycle of trade uninterrupted within limits sufficiently narrow to ensure that enzymatic reactions and microbial growth do not reach levels prejudicial to their nutrition and quality. The sequence of steps given here has been termed the Cold Chain. • • • • • • Multiproduct cold stores in the production zones Refrigerated vehicles for long-distance transport Refrigerated rooms in wholesale market Refrigerated distribution vehicles Refrigerated rooms and display cabinets Domestic refrigerators and freezers In controlled atmosphere (CA) storage, fruits or vegetables are cooled to temperatures of –1–2˚C and the composition of atmosphere around the product is manipulated in order to minimize the respiration of produce by maintaining a low O2 (1–3%) and higher CO2 (4–5%) atmosphere around the produce. To obtain the different ratios, specialized equipment such as gas generators and CO2 scrubbers are installed. For the purpose of CA storage, separate chambers are provided inside the cold storage itself. Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) is a technique used for prolonging the shelf life period of fresh or minimally processed foods. The shelf life of perishable products such as fruits and vegetables, meat, and fish can be prolonged with MAP, which slows the natural deterioration of the food material. Fruits and vegetables respire even after putting them in the packages by interacting with the surrounding atmosphere through the material of the package. If the permeability for O2 and CO2 of the package film is adapted to the product respiration rates, an equilibrium modified atmosphere (EMA) will be established in the package around the produce. These conditions will enhance the shelf life of the product. By reducing the O2 level and increasing the CO2 level, ripening of the fruits and vegetables can be delayed because of reduction in respiration and ethylene production rates. The result is reduced softening, a delay of various compositional changes associated with ripening, and hence prolonged shelf life. This book consists of four major parts. The first part (Chapters 1–10) deals with postharvest physiology, handling, and storage and various precooling methods of fruits and vegetables. The second part (Chapters 11–26) deals with fundamentals of the air-conditioning process, load calculation, and design of air-conditioning equipment for cold storages including spray pond and fans. The transportation of fruits and vegetables and instrumentation and control systems for cold storage are also discussed. The third part (Chapters 27–34) deals with controlled xxx Preface atmosphere storages, including unsteady-state mass balances for equilibrium conditions in CA storage, equipment for generation of different gas regimes, and design of CAS structures. The final part (Chapters 35–47) presents modified atmosphere packaging, including MAP packaging materials, deteriorative reactions, kinetic reactions, and shelf life of packaged foods. For the students of BTech (Horticultural Engineering) and BTech (Agricultural Engineering) who study a full-length course of cold storages, no single book contains all aspects of the cold storage of fruits and vegetables. The available matter for this subject is so scattered that it takes a long time for teachers and students to consolidate the subject information. It is the far flung nature of this information that motivated me to take up the task of bringing the important aspects of cold storages and controlled atmosphere storages, including that of MAP of fruits and vegetables, into a single text book. In an attempt to make each chapter reasonably complete in itself, some repetition of material became necessary. Fundamentals such as properties of moist air, psychrometric process, and so on, which students might have learned in earlier courses, are given again with the sole intention of making the book easier to use. Because the qualitative treatment of selected topics is relatively advanced, this textbook is also appropriate for mechanical engineering students doing postgraduate work in cold storages or in refrigeration and air-conditioning. This book is also useful for personnel in horticulture professions. Chandra Gopala Rao PAR T I Pre Cooling of Fruits and Vegetables and their Storage Requirement 1 Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 1 Introduction This chapter presents a brief description of traditional and modern storage methods for fruits and vegetables, with the intention of exposing the reader to the science and engineering involved in the storage of fruits and vegetables. Proper marketing of perishable commodities such as fruits and vegetables often requires some storage to balance day-to-day fluctuations between harvest and sale or for long-term storage to extend marketing beyond the end of harvest season. Storage of fresh fruits and vegetables prolongs their usefulness and in some cases, improves their quality. It also controls a market glut. The principal goal of storage is to control the rate of transpiration, respiration, disease, and insect infestation and to preserve the commodity in its most usable form for the consumer. Storage life can be prolonged by harvesting at proper maturity, control of postharvest diseases, chemical treatments, irradiation, refrigeration, controlled and modified atmospheres, and by several other treatments. The main goals of storage include the following: 1. Slow the biological activity of fruits and vegetables without chilling injury. 2. Slow the growth of microorganisms. 3. Reduce transpirational losses to avoid the following undesirable processes that may occur in certain fruits and vegetables: a. Sprouting: potatoes, onions, ginger, garlic b. Elongation: asparagus, carrots, beets, kohlrabi c. Rotting: due to increased humidity that may result in rapid decay, shriveling, and exhaustion of food reserves d. Greening: exposure of potatoes to light during storage may produce green tissue and synthesis of toxic glycoalkaloids such as solanine and chaconine e. Toughening: green beans and sweet corn due to prolonged storage at relatively high temperatures Factors need to be considered for success of produce storage: 1. Temperature: Temperature in a storage room should normally be maintained at the desired level for commodities being stored. Delay in cold storage reduces marketability of fruits and vegetables. Temperatures below the optimum range for a given fruit or a vegetable will cause freezing or chilling injuries. Temperatures above, depending upon the produce, will reduce storage life. A wide temperature fluctuation can result in rapid weight and water loss depending upon maturity of produce. The refrigeration temperature within the recommended range is a result of several important design factors. The refrigeration system must be sized to handle the maximum expected heat load. An undersized system will allow the Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00001-4 3 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 4 Chapter 1 air temperature to rise during peak heat load condition. An oversized system is unnecessarily expensive. The system should be designed so that the temperature of the air leaving the refrigeration coils is close to the desired temperature in order to prevent large temperature fluctuations as the refrigeration unit cycles on and off. Temperature variation within the room is minimized by incorporating adequate amounts of insulating material in the walls and by maintaining adequate levels of air circulation in the room. When the room is filled, the containers should be stacked to allow an air passage along at least one side of each container. Thermostats are placed at a height of 1.5 m from the floor for ease in checking locations. A calibrated thermometer should be used to periodically check the thermostat. 2. Relative humidity: For most perishable fresh fruits and vegetables, the relative humidity should be maintained between 90% and 95%. The relative humidity below this range will result in a moisture loss from the produce (Table 1.1). Thus the produce will be shriveled and limp. Refrigeration equipment must be especially designed to maintain a higher relative humidity. The environmental factors of temperature, relative humidity, and vapor pressure deficit are important in the storage life of fruits and vegetables. A 5–10% loss in weight of produce results in shriveling, which makes the produce look stale and unattractive Table 1.1: Weight losses in various fruits during storage as affected by humidity, temperature, and air movement Fruit Pears Apples Strawberries Temperature (°C) 0 0 0 5 0 0 5 0 0 3.9 3.9 3.9 0 0 0 0 0 0 Air Movement Relative Changes per Hour Humidity (%) 3–4 3–4 3–4 4 3–4 3–4 8–9 8–9 8–9 4 4 4 4 4 4 9 9 9 Source: Ryall and Pentzer (1982), used with permission 65 80 98 65 80 98 65 80 98 65 75 100 65 80 90 65 80 90 Weight Loss, Percent of Original Weight After (d = Days) 30d 60d 90d 120d 2.9 2.5 2.0 5.6 3.5 2.6 8.4 5.2 3.0 2.5 2.1 1.2 5.8 4.8 3.5 9.9 6.2 4.2 15.5 9.5 4.5 4.7 4.0 1.8 7.7 6.5 4.6 14.0 8.5 5.0 22.5 13.8 6.0 6.9 6.0 2.7 10.7 8.3 5.5 19.7 11.3 6.4 29.3 18.3 7.8 9.3 8.3 – 2d 4d 8d 10d 4.7 4.4 4.4 4.7 4.4 4.2 7.3 7.0 6.8 8.4 6.3 6.6 12.4 11.6 11.3 15.7 11.1 11.2 15.0 13.3 14.0 20.4 13.8 13.9 Introduction 5 to sell. By using high relative humidity during storage, care must be taken to prevent the growth of surface microorganisms. 3. Atmospheric composition: The atmospheric composition in a storage room is controlled by addition of gases allowing the commodity to produce or consume gases or by physically or chemically removing undesirable gases from the storage room. Gases such as carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO2), ethylene (C2H4), and nitrogen (N2) can be added to a facility from a bottled supply (or dry ice in the case of CO2) or produced by on-site generators. As the perishable fruits and vegetables undergo respiration, they consume O2 and release CO2. This effect can be successfully used to control the desired concentration of these gases in storage. High concentrations of undesirable gases are removed by scrubbing devices. For example, CO2 can be absorbed in water or lime. C2H4 and other volatiles can be removed by potassium permanganate, catalytic oxidation, or by UV light; O2 can be removed by using it in a combustion process or by a molecular sieve. In certain cases, external concentrations of gases are desirable and the accumulated gases can be adjusted by ventilation. 4. Air movement: Air movement must be sufficient to remove respiration heat. Because it is essential that all parts of the room are subject to a uniform flow of air, proper placement of blowers or ducts and stacking of fruits and vegetables will permit free air flow. The successful operation of a large refrigeration system requires an efficient control system. Microcomputers are presently used to allow precise controls for large warehouse refrigeration systems. The defrosting cycle should be set to accomplish the process automatically. 5. Light and other factors: Exposure of potato tubers to light in grocery stores can synthesize glycoalkaloids (solanine and chaconine), which are toxic to humans. Likewise, other factors such as herbicides, fungicides, pesticides, and growth regulators may affect the produce and may have harmful effects on humans. 1.1 Storage Operations The increase of fruit and vegetable production, owing to large acreage and high-yielding cultivars, requires sufficient storage space. Accordingly, efficient storage methods have evolved with a wide range of variations depending upon the existing facilities, including nature and the variety and quantity of produce to be stored. Storage operations may be either temporary, short term, or long term. Temporary storage operations are needed for highly perishable produce that requires immediate marketing. It may be installed with or without refrigeration. Temporary storage is extremely important for roadside stands, gardens, markets, railway stations, shipping yards, and retail stores. The midterm storage operation is aimed at checking the market glut without product deterioration. Storage may extend from 1 to 6 weeks, depending upon the need, kind, and maturity of the produce. Mango, banana, papaya, cabbage, eggplant, tomatoes, cauliflower, and French bean are transferred to short-term storage rooms, when their quality is still good, and held there 6 Chapter 1 until a reasonable market price is attained. Fruits and vegetables such as apples, oranges, pomelo, pears, squash, potatoes, sweet potatoes, carrots, onions, garlic, and pumpkins require long-term storage. These operations are mainly influenced by economic factors. The produce is stored during production and sold continuously during the rest of the year when producers and dealers can obtain reasonably high prices. Storage operations may be classified as either natural or artificial. The natural storage operation keeps the produce in situ without any treatment, whereas artificial storage may be further classified into four types: (1) mechanical or structural, (2) controlled atmosphere, (3) chemical, and (4) radiation. In case of natural storage, the main purpose is to let the fruits or vegetables mature and ripen on plants as long as possible; on the other hand, artificial storage operations attempt to provide conditions to prolong the produce quality. 1.1.1 Traditional Storage Methods 1. Natural storage: Vegetables such as potato, yam, sweet potato, and garlic are kept underground for several months. They are harvested prior to the rainy season for a better market price. This storage does not involve extra expenditure or buildings for storage. 2. Artificial storage: Pits or trenches are dug underground for storing beets, potatoes, onions, carrots, turnips, cabbages, parsnips, and sweet potatoes where they are covered with straw and soil until there is a market demand (Figure 1.1). Figure 1.1: Farm Storage of Potatoes. (Source: CIP, 1981) Introduction 7 3. Ventilated storage: Cellars are underground rooms with slanting roofs covered with sods and soils. The structure may be built into the hillside and covered with additional soil. Cellars are provided with heaters and dry atmospheres during winter months. Potatoes, turnips, carrots, and beets are stored with high relative humidity at 35–40°F (1.7–4.4°C). Where snow is prevalent, a good cellar will provide satisfactory storage for hard vegetables and fruits. Above ground warehouses may be used to store produce. In cold weather, the produce is covered with blankets to protect from cold temperatures. Ventilation is essential for good storage. Potatoes, onions, garlic bulbs, crucifer, leafy vegetables, and fruits are stored successfully. This storage structure has several advantages over other types. a. Special construction is not needed. b. Produce is easily handled. c. Grading, storing, and packaging of fruits and vegetables are facilitated. d. Air may be humidified. e. Fans can be controlled manually or automatically with a thermostat. 4. Storage with ice refrigeration: An advance on the above-ground warehouses was the use of ice as a refrigerant. Lower temperatures obtained enable longer storage of meat and perishable fruits and vegetables. Ice can be obtained in winter from frozen lakes and ponds and stored in ice houses. The melting of 1 kg of ice absorbs 325 kJ of heat. However, removal of melted ice water is a disadvantage. The introduction of a small ice box was a great advance on the domestic level and for small-scale commercial storage of fruits and vegetables. 1.2 Modern Storage Methods 1.2.1 Storage with Mechanical Refrigeration Refrigerated storage makes possible the marketing of perishable fruits and vegetables beyond their harvest season. Most fruits and vegetables are available year-round to consumers due to refrigerated storage. Most storage facilities use mechanical refrigeration to control the desired temperature. This system utilizes the fact that a liquid absorbs heat as it changes to gas. A common mechanical refrigeration system uses a refrigerant such as ammonia or Freon where vapor can be easily recaptured by a compressor. Heat exchange methods of heat transfer play an important part in the refrigeration of fruits and vegetables in maintaining the desired temperature in a refrigerator or refrigerated warehouse. The refrigerant passes through an expansion valve where its pressure drops and liquid evaporates at temperatures low enough to be effective in removing heat from the storage area. Heat needed for evaporation comes from the fruits and vegetables to be cooled. The evaporator is located in the storage room. The gas is repressurized by the compressor and then passed through a condenser where it is cooled to a liquid. The condenser is located outside the storage area and it rejects heat. Refrigerant is stored in the receiver and is metered out as needed to produce an essential or a desired cooling temperature. 8 Chapter 1 The capacity of a refrigeration system is based upon total heat inputs to a storage area. Heat inputs include: 1. 2. 3. 4. Heat conducted through walls, floor, and ceiling Field and respiration heat of fruits and vegetables Heat from air infiltration Heat from equipment such as lights, fans, forklifts, and personnel moving in and out The two types of mechanical refrigeration are: 1. Vapor compression 2. Vapor absorption The basic equipment for vapor compression mechanical refrigeration consists of compressor, condenser, expansion valve, and evaporator. The refrigerant (ammonia or Freon) is compressed, cooled by passing through an air- or water-cooled condenser, and then expanded through an expansion valve into evaporator coils. During evaporation and expansion phase, heat is absorbed from fruits, vegetables, and the area to be cooled. The absorbed heat is returned for eventual elimination in the condenser. All modern roomrefrigeration systems provide forced-air circulation. These systems use prefabricated units containing both evaporator coils and blowers for air circulation. They provide an excellent storage environment. Substantial heat must be removed quickly from the produce in storage; it is apparent that greater refrigeration capacity and air velocity must be available. Figures 1.2 and 1.3 show the schematic diagram of vapor compression refrigeration system and its cyclic representation on a psychrometric chart, respectively. The psychrometric chart gives the Figure 1.2: Simplified Schematic Drawing of Refrigeration Cycle. Introduction 9 Figure 1.3: Psychrometric Chart. graphical representation of various thermodynamic properties of air. If any two measurable properties of air are known, the other properties such as enthalpy, vapor pressure, and specific volume can be directly read from the chart. It facilitates a quick and easy estimation of various design parameters for air-conditioning equipment. The success of mechanical refrigeration storage depends upon controlled temperature, relative humidity, and air movement. Temperature Temperature control depends upon a tight, well-insulated structure and sufficient refrigeration capacity. It also depends on the amount and nature of the evaporator-coil surface, its freedom from condensed ice, and the rate of air flowing over the coils. These factors control the total efficiency of refrigeration. Relative humidity Relative humidity is the percentage of saturated water vapor at a given temperature. Relative humidity (%) can be determined from a psychrometric chart (Figure 1.3) on the basis of wet bulb and dry bulb temperatures. As the temperature of air increases, so does its water-holding capacity. Accordingly, air with 90% RH at 70°F (21°C) contains much more water vapor than air of the same relative humidity at 40°F (4°C). As the relative humidity of air decreases, so does its vapor pressure, and as vapor pressure decreases, the capacity of the air for removing water from moist produce increases. Thus it is important to maintain a high vapor pressure. If drying is to be avoided, a small vapor pressure differential between stored produce and storage air must be obtained. Effective ways of accomplishing this is by rapid equalization of produce and air temperature, maintenance of high relative humidity in the storage room air as the produce will tolerate and no more air movement than is required for even temperature distribution in the refrigerated room. 10 Chapter 1 1.3 Controlled Atmosphere Storage The controlled atmosphere storage (CAS) process is the most important innovation in fruit and vegetable storage since the introduction of mechanical refrigeration. To reduce fruit losses during refrigerated storage, it is important to maximize all the potentialities of this method in order to suppress the vital activity of phytopathogenic microorganisms that are always present on the fruit surfaces, to retard the processes connected with most harvest ripening of fruits, and to delay the senescence and collapse of fruit tissues. But in most cases, maintaining a definite regime of temperature and humidity alone is not sufficient for prolonging the period for which fruits can be preserved and reducing fruit losses. A definite gas composition of the atmosphere, strictly differentiated for each type of fruit and for different varieties of the same fruit, is also necessary. The first studies regarding fruit preservations in gaseous medium were carried out in an atmosphere consisting of more CO2 and less O2 than normally present in air. Carbon dioxide played the dominant role, which is why the method is also called the “carbon dioxide preservation method.” It was found that CO2 concentration in the regime not only reduces the vital activities of the fruit but also provides strong antiseptic nature. Many investigations have shown that the basic advantages of fruit preservation in a controlled atmosphere are as follows. 1. The so-called low-temperature diseases are prevented during refrigeration. 2. Infestation of fruits by other physiological diseases frequently encountered when fruits are preserved in refrigerators in conventional fruit storages is reduced. 3. The taste and aroma fruits are better preserved. 4. The consistency of fruits is maintained for longer periods. 5. The fruit losses in the controlled atmosphere are reduced by half to one third, while the period of preservation is significantly higher than when kept in an uncontrolled atmosphere. Various aspects of the controlled atmosphere storage are given in Part III of this book. 1.4 Modified Atmosphere Packaging Storage of fruits in packaging of polymer materials with selective permeability for gases is what it is called modified atmosphere storage. This technique was found to enhance the shelf life of produce stored in the polymeric pouches, bags, and containers. Such storage is done in conventional cold storage chambers and therefore does not involve large capital outlay for the construction and equipping of special hermetically sealed chambers with controlled atmosphere. Advances in the design and manufacture of polymeric films with wide range of gas permeability have stimulated interest in creating and maintaining modified atmosphere within the flexible film packages. Introduction 11 The gas composition in packaging can be changed partially by the type of material selected, capacity of the packaging, variety of fruit, and the temperature of storage. In the selection of material, their gas-vapor permeability is especially important, and depends on the type and thickness of the material. To understand this method of storage in more detail, it is necessary to know about characteristics of gas exchange during the storage of fruits in packages with selective permeability. For maintaining the desired atmosphere within a package, absorbers of O2, CO2, C2H4, and water vapor provide additional benefit. Selection of suitable packaging materials for fruits based on their selective permeability to the gases and the basic principles governing such selections are discussed in Part IV of this book. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 2 Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables Fresh fruits and vegetables are essential components of the human diet and contain a number of nutritionally important compounds such as vitamins that cannot be synthesized by the human body. A fruit or vegetable is a living, respiring, edible tissue that has been detached from the parent plant. Fruits and vegetables are perishable products with active metabolism during the postharvest period. The shelf life of fruits and vegetables can be extended by, in simple terms, retarding the physiological, pathological, and physical deteriorative processes (generally referred to as postharvest handling) or by inactivating the physiological processes (generally referred to as food preservation by climate control). Difficulties arise when trying to draw a clear line between fruits and vegetables. Fruits and vegetables cannot be described clearly either botanically or morphologically because they encompass numerous organs in vegetative or reproductive stages and belong to a large number of botanical families. Fruits tend to be restricted to reproductive organs arising from the development of floral tissues with or without fertilization. Vegetables, on the other hand, consist simply of edible plant tissues. Thus some fruits are included as vegetables, and vice versa. Table 2.1 classifies horticultural produce according to the plant organs used, based mainly on the form in which the product is handled (e.g., root, tuber, stem, leaf, etc.). 2.1 Postharvest Physiology Growth, maturation, and senescence are the three important phases through which fruits and vegetables pass, the first two terms often being referred to as fruit development. Ripening (a term reserved for fruit) generally begins during the later stages of maturation and is considered the beginning of senescence, a term defined as the period when anabolic or synthetic biochemical processes give way to catabolic or degradative processes that lead to aging and final death of the tissue. 2.2 Respiration Respiration involves the oxidation of energy-rich organic substrates normally present in cells such as starch, sugars, and organic acids, to simpler molecules (CO2 and H2O) with the concurrent production of energy and other molecules that can be used by the cell for synthetic reactions. The greatest yield of energy is obtained when the process takes place in the Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00002-6 13 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 14 Chapter 2 Table 2.1: Classification of horticultural produce according to the plant organ used Class Commodities (Examples) Root vegetables Tubers Leaf and stem vegetables Carrot, celery, garlic, horseradish, onion, parsnip, radish, turnip Potato, yam, Jerusalem artichoke Brussels sprouts, cabbage, celery, chicory, Chinese cabbage, cress, green onion, kale, lettuce, spinach Artichoke, broccoli, cauliflower Bean, cucumber, gherkin, okra, pea, pepper, squash, sweet corn Melon, tomato Most fruits Flower vegetables Immature fruit vegetables Mature fruit vegetables Reproductive seeds presence of molecular oxygen. Respiration is then said to be aerobic. If hexose sugar is used as the substrate, the overall equation can be written as follows: C6 H12 O 6 + 6O 2 → 6CO 2 + 6H 2 O + energy (2.1) This transformation actually takes place in a large number of individual stages with the participation of many different enzyme systems. The water produced remains within the tissue, but the CO2 escapes and accounts for part of the weight loss of harvested fruits and vegetables, a range of 3–5% of weight loss having been ascribed to respiration. When one mole of hexose sugar is oxidized, 36 moles of ATP (each possessing 32 kJ of useful energy) are formed. This represents about 40% of the total free energy change, the remainder being dissipated as heat. Rapid removal of this heat is usually desirable, and it is important that the atmosphere in package and cold storage assists this process. The best keeping quality is observed in fruits harvested either in preclimacteric state or in the early climacteric phase. Such fruits ripen slowly during preservation. The rate of respiration is often a good index to the storage life of horticultural products: the higher the rate, the shorter the life, and the lower the rate, the longer the life. Table 2.2 classifies vegetables according to their respiration intensities. Table 2.2: Classification of vegetables according to respiration intensity Class Respiration Intensity at 10°C mg CO2 kg/h Commodities Very low Low Moderate High Very high Extremely high Below 10 10–20 20–40 40–70 70–100 Above 100 Onion Cabbage, cucumber, melon, tomato, turnip Carrot, celery, gherkin, leek, pepper, rhubarb Asparagus (blanched), eggplant, fennel, lettuce, radish Bean, brussels sprouts, mushroom, savoy cabbage, spinach Broccoli, pea, sweet corn Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables 15 From measurements of CO2 and O2 it is possible to evaluate the nature of the respiratory process. The ratio of the volume of CO2 released to the volume of O2 absorbed in respiration is termed the respiratory quotient (RQ). Values of RQ range from 0.7 to 1.3 for aerobic respiration, depending on the substrate being oxidized: for carbohydrates, RQ = 1; for lipids, RQ < 1; for organic acids, RQ > 1. Anaerobic respiration (sometimes called fermentation) involves the incomplete oxidation of compounds in the absence of O2 and the accumulation of ethanol, acetaldehyde, and CO2. Much lower amounts of energy (2 moles of ATP) and CO2 are produced from 1 mole of hexose sugar than that produced under aerobic conditions. As well, very little heat energy (approximately 5%) is produced for a given amount of carbohydrate oxidation in anaerobic respiration compared to aerobic respiration. The oxygen concentration at which a shift from aerobic to anaerobic respiration occurs varies among tissues and is known as the extinction point. Very high RQ values (>1.3) usually indicate anaerobic respiration. 2.3 Internal Factors Affecting Respiration Variations in the rate of respiration occur during organ development; as fruit increase in size, the total amount of CO2 emitted increases, although the respiration rate calculated on a per-unit weight basis decreases continually. Three different routes are available for the exchange of gases between horticultural commodities and their surrounding atmospheres: lenticels and stomata, the cuticle, and the stem scars or floral (calyx) end. In leaves, the resistance of the epidermal layer to gas diffusion is mainly regulated through the stomatal aperture. A majority of studies on gas exchange in plant tissues indicate that the skin represents the main significant barrier to diffusion. Clearly the rate at which the three gases O2, CO2, and C2H4 diffuse through the tissue will have a significant effect on the rate of respiration. Fruits may be divided into climacteric and nonclimacteric types. Climacteric fruits are those in which ripening is associated with a distinct increase in respiration and ethylene production, the respiration rate rising up to the climacteric peak and then declining. Such an increase can occur either while the fruit is attached to or separated from the plant. A further distinguishing feature is that treatment of climacteric fruits with ethylene or propylene stimulates both respiration and autocatalytic ethylene production. Low temperatures greatly reduce the magnitude of the climacteric. The climacteric generally coincides with changes associated with ripening such as colour changes, softening, increased tissue permeability, and the development of characteristic aromas. Typical climacteric fruits include apples, pears, peaches, nectarines, bananas, mangoes, plums, tomatoes, and avocadoes. In nonclimacteric fruits, ripening is protracted and the attainment of the ripe state is not associated with a marked increase in respiration or ethylene production. Treatment of 16 Chapter 2 nonclimacteric fruits with ethylene stimulates respiration only; there is no increase in autocatalytic ethylene production. Fruits such as citrus, strawberries, and pineapples are nonclimacteric. Vegetables, in general, do not show a sudden increase in metabolic activity that parallels the onset of the climacteric in fruit, unless sprouting and regrowth is initiated. 2.4 External Factors Affecting Respiration 2.4.1 Temperature Temperature is the most important environmental factor in the postharvest life of horticultural products because of its dramatic effect on the rates of biological reactions including respiration. Typical Q10 values (the ratio of the respiration rates for a 10°C interval) for vegetables are 2.5–4.0 at 0–10°C; 2.0–2.5 at 10–20°C; 1.5–2.0 at 20–30°C, and 1.0–1.5 at 30–40°C. Mean Q10 values can be used to calculate the increase in relative velocity of respiration from 1.0 at 0°C to 3.0 at 10°C, 7.5 at 20°C, 15.0 at 30°C, and 22.5 at 40°C. These figures dramatically illustrate the need to reduce the temperature of fresh fruits and vegetables as soon as possible after harvesting in order to maximize shelf life. The rate of increase in respiration rates declines with an increase in temperature up to 40°C, with the Q10 becoming less than 1 as the tissue nears its thermal death point (about 50–55°C) when enzyme proteins are denatured and metabolism becomes disorderly. The storage life of some fruits and vegetables, primarily those of tropical or subtropical origin, can be limited by chilling injury, a disorder induced by low (0–12°C) but nonfreezing temperatures in whole plants or susceptible tissues. The extent of the chilling injury is influenced by the temperature, the duration of the exposure to a given temperature, and the chilling sensitivity of the particular fruit or vegetable. The symptoms of chilling injury may not be evident while the produce is held at chilling temperatures but only become apparent after transfer to a higher temperature. Chilling injury prevents some fruits from ripening and increases their susceptibility to fungal spoilage. Chilling injury is generally associated with necrosis of groups of cells situated either externally, leading to the formation of depressed areas, pitting and external discoloration, or internally leading to internal browning. 2.4.2 Ethylene Ethylene (C2H4) is a natural plant hormone and plays a central role in the initiation of ripening. It is physiologically active in trace amounts (less than 0.1 ppm). The capacity to produce C2H4 varies greatly among fruits as shown in Table 2.3, with those fruits exhibiting Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables 17 Table 2.3: Classification of fruits according to their maximum ethylene production rate Ethylene Production Rate mL/kg/h at 20°C Fruits Very low: 0.01–0.1 Low: 0.1–1.0 Moderate: 1.0–10.0 High: 10.0–100.0 Very high: > 100.0 Cherry, citrus, grape, pomegranate, strawberry Blueberry, kiwifruit, peppers, persimmon, pineapple, raspberry Banana, fig, honeydew melons, mango, tomato Apple, apricot, avocado, plum, cantaloupe, nectarine, papaya, peach, pear Cherimoya, mammy apple, passion fruit, sapota µL/kg/h × 0.91 = mL/ton/h Source: Ryall and Lipton (1979) moderate-to-very-high production rates being generally classified as climacteric fruits. Vegetables also produce C2H4 although data are comparatively scarce. Some typical figures in mL/kg/h at 20°C range from 0.04 for whole carrot roots, 0.02 for potato slices, 0.6 for intact cabbage head, 1.1 for summer squash, 1.7 for cauliflower head, 2.3 for brussels sprouts, to 3.3–27.0 for broccoli head. Some fruit-vegetables such as tomatoes and melons are climacteric, while other fruit-vegetables such as cucumbers are not. The production of ethylene by edible floral parts such as cauliflower and broccoli may be quite high and comparable with that of tomatoes. When climacteric fruits are exposed to ethylene during their preclimacteric stage, the time to the start of the climacteric rise in respiration is reduced. The magnitude of the final respiratory rise is controlled by the fruit’s endogenous ethylene production and is not influenced by added ethylene. A reduction in ethylene production and sensitivity associated with modified atmospheres can delay the onset of the climacteric and prolong the storage life of these fruits. When nonclimacteric tissues are exposed to ethylene, a climacteric-like rise in respiration is induced proportional to the ethylene concentration. Respiration rates return to their pretreatment level when the ethylene is removed. Nonclimacteric fruits and vegetables can benefit from reduced ethylene sensitivity and a lower respiration rate attributed to modified atmosphere. The potent effects of ethylene on plant growth, development, and senescence mean that this gas, which is commonly found in the environment, can greatly reduce the storage life of perishable commodities sensitive to it. Important effects of ethylene in hastening the deterioration of perishable commodities include accelerated senescence and loss of green color in some immature fruits (e.g., cucumbers, squash) and leafy vegetables; accelerated ripening of fruits during handling and storage; russet spotting on lettuce; formation of a bitter compound (isocoumarin) in carrots; sprouting of potatoes; abscission of leaves (e.g., in cauliflower and cabbage), and toughening (lignifications) of asparagus. 18 Chapter 2 In addition to ethylene, several other hydrocarbons such as propylene and acetylene mimic ethylene effects on respiration rates of fruits and vegetables. Ethylene production is reduced by either low O2, high CO2, or both, and the effects are additive. 2.5 Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide Concentration A simple consideration of equation (2.1) would suggest that if the CO2 in the surrounding atmosphere were augmented (or the O2 decreased), the respiration rate and the storage life would be extended. Reduction of the O2 concentration to less than 10% provides a tool for controlling the respiration rate and slowing down senescence, although an adequate O2 concentration must be available to maintain aerobic respiration. Vegetables usually require a minimum O2 content of 1–3% in the storage atmosphere. At O2 contents below 2%, most vegetables react with a sudden increase in CO2 production. Glycolysis results in the formation of acetaldehyde, CO2, and finally ethanol. Both acetaldehyde and ethanol are toxic to plant cells. Elevated CO2 levels can inhibit, promote, or have no effect on C2H4 production by fruits. However, CO2 has been shown to be a competitive inhibitor of C2H4 action, delaying fruit ripening by displacing C2H4 from its receptor site. At concentrations above 20%, a significant increase in anaerobic respiration occurs, which can irreversibly damage plant tissue. Low O2 and/or high CO2 can reduce the incidence and severity of certain physiological disorders such as those induced by ethylene (scald of apples and pears) and chilling injury of some commodities (e.g., avocado, citrus fruits, chili pepper, and okra). On the other hand, O2 and CO2 levels beyond those tolerated by the commodity can induce physiological disorders, such as brown stain on lettuce, internal browning and surface pitting of pome fruits, and blackheart of potato. 2.6 Mechanical Stresses Physical damage due to mechanical stresses such as surface injuries, impact bruising, and vibration bruising can stimulate respiration and ethylene production rates, depending on the variety of fruit or the vegetable and the severity of the damage. The extent of the increase in respiration rate is usually proportional to the severity of bruising. However, the commercial implications of the bruising (i.e., the fact the consumers prefer not to purchase bruised fruits and vegetables) is of far greater importance than its effect on the respiration rate. Water stress resulting from loss of water to the surrounding atmosphere can stimulate the respiration rate, although once the water loss exceeds 5% the respiration rate may be reduced, coinciding with noticeable wilting and shriveling of tissue. Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables 19 2.7 Respiration Rate The rate of respiration can be defined as the weight of CO2 produced per unit weight of the fruit or vegetable per unit time (i.e., mg of CO2/kg/h). The respiration rate may also be expressed in mL of CO2/kg/h or the quantity of O2 taken up rather than CO2 given out. The respiration rates of certain fruits at various temperatures are given in Table 2.4. The respiration rates given in Table 2.4 can be converted to equivalent heat produced in the following way. For example, when asparagus is held at 25°C, it respires at rate of about 50 mg CO2 per kg/h and thus produces 12,800 kJ of heat per metric ton per day (50 × 256 = 12,800). 2.8 Van’t Hoff Rule This law indicates that the rate of enzymatic reaction is controlled by temperature. The optimum temperature for most enzymatic reactions is between 30°C and 40°C, and at the temperatures of the order of 50–90°C, most enzymes are destroyed. Lowering the temperature increases the length of storage because of the reduction in rate of reactions, but at no point of time is the reaction completely stopped. This phenomenon is seen in the case of freezing of foodstuffs, where after long period of storage at temperatures from about –18°C to –20°C or even lower, certain undesirable enzymatic reactions continue to take place, resulting in change in the stored product. The concept named after the Dutch chemist Van’t Hoff states that the rate of chemical reaction approximately doubles for each 10°C rise in temperature, which is abbreviated as Q10 and written as R Q10 = 2 = a constant and is about 2 (2.2) R1 where R1 = rate of reaction at a given temperature R2 = rate of reaction at temperature 10°C higher A more general form of the Van’t Hoff equation was developed, which is applicable to temperature intervals other than 10°C. This equation is as follows. 10 R  Q10 =  2  e t2 − t1 = Constant and is about 2  R1  (2.3) where t2 and t1 are temperature in °C and R2 and R1 are respiration rates. This formula permits calculation of either Q10 or an unknown rate of respiration for any temperature difference, but the temperature difference should not exceed 10°C. The Q10 usually ranges from 1 to about 5, although higher rates may occur. The Q10 values are highest for 0–10°C. They are commonly between 2 and 3 for 10–32°C. Q10 of 1 indicates that Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables 21 the rate does not change with change in temperature, and Q10 below 1 shows that the rate is decreasing as the temperature rises. Q10 values are useful even though they change with temperature because, if the rate of respiration of crop is known at 10°C interval between 0°C and about 40°C, any intermediate rates can be calculated with sufficient accuracy for prediction of refrigeration and ventilation requirements. However, Q10 values should be based on initial respiration rates because after storage at different temperatures, the fruits and vegetables would no longer be of the same physiological age and the results would be misleading. 2.9 Calculation of Q10 Values For condition Respiration rates are known, but the temperature difference is not 10°C. These reactions also interact. Therefore, Q10 must be measured over a limited range of temperature. The optimum temperature for most enzymatic reactions is between 30°C and 40°C and at the temperatures of the order of 50–90°C, most enzymes are destroyed. Nevertheless temperatures normally used for certain chilled products of animal origin (meat, fish, eggs) lie between 1.5°C and 0°C, and these ensure sufficient inhibition of microbial growth for short- or medium-term trade, without risk of deterioration that renders the produce unfit for consumption. Finally, although the optimum temperature for growth of molds is about 25°C, they are capable of adjustment to cold conditions; when their spores find themselves on an adequate substrate, they begin to germinate, the fungi develops, provoking important losses, especially in the case of chilled fruits or vegetables between –1°C and 5°C. 2.10 Heat of Respiration All living food products respire, and during this respiration process sucrose and oxygen combine to form CO2, H2O, and heat as shown in equation (2.1). In most stored plant products, little cell development takes place, and the greater part of respiration energy is released in the form of heat, which must be taken into account when cooling and storing these living commodities (Becker and Fricke, 1996a). The rate at which this chemical reaction takes place varies with the type and temperature of the commodity. Becker and Fricke, 1996b developed correlations that relate a commodity’s rate of carbon dioxide production to its temperature. The carbon dioxide production rate can then be related to the commodity’s heat generation rate due to respiration. The resulting correlation gives the commodity’s respiratory heat generation rate W in W/kg as a function of temperature t in °C: W= 10.7 f  9t   + 32  3600 5 g (2.4) where f and g are respiration coefficients. Fruits, vegetables, flowers, bulbs, florists, greens, and nursery stock are storage commodities with significant heats of respiration. Dry plant products, such as seeds and nuts, have low respiration rates. Fast-­developing fruits, such as strawberries, raspberries, and blackberries, have much higher respiration rates than do fruits that are slow to develop, such as apples, grapes, and citrus fruits. In general, most vegetables, other than root crops, have a high initial respiration rate 1–2 days after harvest. Within a few days, the respiration rate quickly lowers to the equilibrium rate (Ryall and Lipton, 1979). Fruits, however, are different from most vegetables. Those fruits that do not ripen during storage, such as citrus fruits and grapes, have fairly constant rates of respiration. Those that ripen in storage, such as apples, peaches, and avocados, exhibit an increase in the respiration rate. At low storage temperatures, around 0°C, the rate of respiration rarely increases because no ripening takes place. However, if fruits are stored at higher temperatures (10–15°C), the respiration rate increases due to ripening and then decreases. Soft fruits, such as blueberries, figs, and strawberries, show a decrease in respiration with time at 0°C. If they become infected with decay organisms, however, respiration increases. Vegetables such as onions, garlic, and cabbage can exhibit an increase in heat production after a long storage period. 2.11 Transpiration Transpiration is the process by which fresh fruits and vegetables loose some of their water. All fruits and vegetables continue to lose water through transpiration after they are harvested, and this loss of water is one of the main processes that affect their commercial and physiological deterioration. If transpiration is not retarded, it induces wilting, shrinkage, and loss of firmness, crispness and succulence, with concomitant deterioration in appearance, texture, and flavor. Most fruits and vegetables lose their freshness when the water loss is 3–10% of their initial weight. As well as loss of weight and freshness, transpiration induces water stress, which has been shown to accelerate senescence of fruits and vegetables. 2.12 Factors Influencing Transpiration Several factors, such as the surface area to volume ratio, nature of the surface coating, relative humidity, temperature, atmospheric pressure, and extent of any mechanical damage, influence the transpiration process in fruits and vegetables. The surface area to volume ratio can range as follows: • • • • • 50–100 cm2 mL–1 for individual edible leaves 5–10 cm2 mL–1 for soft fruits such as currants 2–5 cm2 mL–1 for larger soft fruits such as strawberries 0.5–1.5 cm2 mL–1 for tubers, pomes, stone and citrus fruits, bananas, and onions 0.2–0.5 cm2 mL–1 for densely packed cabbage Other factors being equal, a leaf will lose water and weight much faster than a fruit, and small fruit or root or tuber will lose weight faster than a larger one. Although O2, CO2, and C2H4 diffuse mainly through air-filled stomata, lenticels, floral ends, and stem scars, water vapor preferentially diffuses through the liquid aqueous phase of the cuticle. In addition, significant water vapor loss can result from cut tissues such as asparagus and celery ends. Mechanical damage and physical injury in the form of bruising, scratches, surface cuts, and so on greatly accelerate the rate of water loss from fruit and vegetable tissue. Some tuber and root vegetables such as onions and potatoes retain the capacity to seal off wound areas after harvest when held at appropriate temperatures and humidity for “curing” (as it is known) to occur. Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables 27 As mentioned earlier, respiration generates heat that is dissipated through direct heat transfer to the environment and through evaporation of water. The heat of respiration raises the tissue temperature and therefore increases transpiration. The ambient relative humidity is not a reliable guide to likely water loss, and it is more useful to calculate the water vapor pressure deficit (VPD) at the particular temperature and humidity. The VPD of the air is defined as the difference between the water vapor pressure of the ambient air and that of saturated air at the same temperature. Thus the drier the air, the greater its VPD and the more rapidly any produce held in that environment will transpire. To minimize transpiration, produce should be held at low temperature, high relative humidity, and as small a VPD as possible. Acidic fruit tissue is generally attacked and rotted by fungi, while many vegetables having a tissue pH above 4.5 are more commonly attacked by bacteria. Initially only one or a few pathogens may invade and break down the tissues, followed by a broad spectrum attack of several weak pathogens resulting in complete loss of the produce. Moisture loss from a fruit or vegetable is driven by a difference in water vapor pressure between the product surface and the environment. Becker and Fricke (1996a) state that the product surface may be assumed to be saturated, and thus the water vapor pressure at the commodity surface is equal to the water vapor saturation pressure evaluated at the product’s surface temperature. However, they also reported that dissolved substances in the moisture of the commodity tend to lower the vapor pressure at the evaporating surface slightly. Evaporation that occurs at the product surface is an endothermic process that cools the surface, thus lowering the vapor pressure at the surface and reducing transpiration. Respiration within the fruit or vegetable, on the other hand, tends to increase the product’s temperature, thus raising the vapor pressure at the surface and increasing transpiration. Furthermore, the respiration rate is itself a function of the commodity’s temperature. In addition, factors such as surface structure, skin permeability, and airflow also affect the transpiration rate. Becker et al. (1996c) performed a numerical, parametric study to investigate the influence of bulk mass, airflow rate, skin mass transfer coefficient, and relative humidity on the cooling time and moisture loss of a bulk load of apples. They found that relative humidity and skin mass transfer coefficient had little effect on cooling time, whereas bulk mass and airflow rate were of primary importance to cooling time. Moisture loss was found to vary appreciably with relative humidity, airflow rate, and skin mass transfer coefficient; but bulk mass had little effect. They reported that an increase in airflow results in a decrease in moisture loss. The increased airflow reduces the cooling time, which quickly reduces the vapor pressure deficit, thus lowering the transpiration rate. The driving force for transpiration is a difference in water vapor pressure between the surface of a commodity and the surrounding air. Thus, the basic form of the transpiration model is as follows: m = kt ( ps − pa ) (2.5) 28 Chapter 2 where m is the transpiration rate expressed as the mass of moisture transpired per unit area of commodity surface per unit time. This rate may also be expressed per unit mass of commodity rather than per unit area of commodity surface. The transpiration coefficient kt is the mass of moisture transpired per unit area of commodity rather than per unit area of commodity surface. The quantity (ps – pa) is the water vapor pressure deficit. The water vapor pressure at the commodity surface ps is the water vapor saturation pressure evaluated at the commodity surface temperature; the water vapor pressure in the surrounding air pa is a function of the relative humidity of the air. In its simplest form, the transpiration coefficient kt is considered to be a constant for a particular commodity. Table 2.7 lists values for the transpiration coefficients kt of various fruits and vegetables (Sastry et al., 1978). Because of the many factors that influence transpiration rate, not all the values in Table 2.8 are reliable. They are to be used primarily as a guide or as a comparative indication of various commodity transpiration rates obtained from the literature. Fockers and Meffert, 1972 modified the simple transpiration coefficient to model variable skin permeability and to account for airflow rate. Their modified transpiration coefficient takes the following form: kt = 1 1 1 + k a ks (2.6) where ka is the air film mass transfer coefficient and ks is the skin mass transfer coefficient. The air film mass transfer coefficient ka describes the convective mass transfer that occurs at the surface of the commodity and is a function of airflow rate. The skin mass transfer coefficient ks describes the skin’s diffusional resistance to moisture migration. The air film mass transfer coefficient ka can be estimated by using the Sherwood-ReynoldsSchmidt correlations (Becker and Fricke, 1996b). The Sherwood number is defined as follows: Sh = ka′d δ (2.7) where k′a is the air film mass transfer coefficient, d is the diameter of the commodity, and d is the coefficient of diffusion of water vapor in the air. For convective mass transfer from a spherical fruit or vegetable, Becker and Fricke (1996b) recommend the following SherwoodReynolds-Schmidt correlation, which was taken from Geankoplis (1978): Sh = The skin mass transfer coefficient ks, which describes the resistance to moisture migration through the skin of a commodity, is based on the fraction of the product surface covered by pores. Note that three values of skin mass transfer coefficient are tabulated for most commodities. These values correspond to the spread of the experimental data. Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables 31 2.13 Surface Heat Transfer Coefficient Although the surface heat transfer coefficient is not a thermal property of a food, it is needed to design heat transfer equipment for the processing of foods where convection is involved. Newton’s law of cooling defines the surface heat transfer coefficient h as follows: q = hA(ts − t∞ ) (2.10) where q is the heat transfer rate, ts is the surface temperature of the food, t∞ is the surrounding fluid temperature, and A is the surface area of the food through which the heat transfer occurs. The surface heat transfer coefficient h depends on the velocity of the surrounding fluid, product geometry, orientation, surface roughness, and packaging, as well as other factors. Therefore, for most applications h must be determined experimentally. Experimentalists have generally reported their findings as correlations, which give the Nusselt number as a function of the Reynolds number and the Prandtl number. The following guidelines are important for using Table 2.9: 1. Use a Nusselt–Reynolds–Prandtl correlation or a value of surface heat transfer coefficient that applies to the Reynolds number called for in the design. 2. Avoid extrapolation. 3. Use data for the same heat transfer medium, including temperature and temperature difference, which are similar to the design conditions. The proper characteristic length and fluid velocity, either force stream velocity or interstitial velocity, should be used in calculation. 2.14 Desiccation Water loss, which causes a product to shrivel, is a physical factor related to the evaporative potential of air and can be expressed as follows: PD = p (100 – φ ) 100 where PD = vapor pressure deficit, indicating combined influence of temperature and relative humidity on evaporative potential of air p = vapor pressure of water at given temperature φ = relative humidity percent For example, comparing the evaporative potential of air in storage rooms at 0 and 10°C dry bulb, with 90% relative humidity in each room, the vapor pressure deficit at 0°C is 60 Pa, 32 Chapter 2 Table 2.9: Surface heat transfer coefficients for some important fruits Product Shape and Transfer ∆t and/or Temperature Length (mm) Medium of Medium (°C) Velocity of Medium (m/s) Apple, Red Delicious Spherical 63 72 76 57 70 75 Air Water ∆t = 22.8 ∆t = –0.6 t = 25.6 t=0 1.5 4.6 1.5 4.6 0.0 1.5 3.0 4.6 0.27 Nicholas et al. Thus, if all other factors are equal, commodities tend to lose water twice as fast at 0°C dry bulb as at 10°C at the same relative humidity values. For equal water loss at the two temperatures, the relative humidity has to be maintained at 95% at 10°C in comparison to 90% at 0°C. These comparisons are not precise because the water in fruits and vegetables contains a sufficient quantity of dissolved sugars and other chemical materials Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables 33 to cause the water to be in equilibrium with water vapor in the air at 98–99% relative humidity instead of 100% relative humidity. Lowering the vapor pressure deficit by lowering the air temperature is an excellent means of reducing water loss during storage. Other important factors in desiccation include product size, surface-to-volume ratio, the kind of protective surface on the product, and air movement. Of these factors, the storage operator can control only the last, and this control is greatly influenced by the container type, kind of packaging, and stacking arrangement (i.e., the ability of the air to move past individual fruits and vegetables). As a rule, shriveling does not become a serious market problem until fruits lose about 5% of their mass, but any loss reduces the salable amount. Moisture losses of 3–6% are enough to cause a marked loss of quality for many kinds of produce. A few kinds may lose 10% moisture and still be marketable although some trimming may be necessary, as for stored cabbage. The vapor pressure deficit cannot be kept at a zero level, but it should be maintained as low as possible. A maximum of about 60 Pa, which corresponds to 90% relative humidity at 0°C, is recommended. Some compromise is possible for short storage periods. In many instances, the refrigerated storage operator may find it desirable to add moisture or, in special cases, the owner of the produce may find it desirable to use moisture barriers such as film liners. 2.15 Determination of Water Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD) Water vapor, like all gases, exerts pressure and at a given atmospheric pressure, the amount of water vapor pressure (WVP) depends only on temperature. There are many methods for determining water vapor pressure of atmospheric air. The WVP can be ­determined by using formulae, by using Mollier diagram or by using nomograms. Determination of WVP by using the latter two methods is illustrated. The original Mollier diagram is shown in Figure 2.1. Example: In a room, the temperature of fruit surface and that of its surrounding air is 20°C. The relative humidity is 80%. Making use of the Mollier diagram allows determination of whether moisture migration occurs from fruit surface to the surrounding air or from the surrounding air to the fruit surface. Solution: It is assumed that the surface moisture of the fruit is in the state of saturation at 20°C. 1. Locate the point on the Mollier diagram at the point of intersection of 20°C on 80% relative humidity line. (Figure 2.1) From this point draw a line vertically down until it intersects the inclined line on the vapor pressure scale. From this point of intersection, draw a horizontal line and at the point of intersection of the vapor pressure scale, the value is 1.9 kPa. 34 Chapter 2 Figure 2.1: Process on Mollier Diagram. 2. The same intersection point of (80% relative humidity and 20°C) is now extended to 100% relative humidity and to the vapor pressure scale and corresponding value of VP value is 2.4 kPa on the vapor scale. The difference of vapor pressure between the two is 2.4 – 1.9 = –0.5 kPa. As the water vapor pressure of surface moisture of fruit is higher than that of the surrounding air, moisture will diffuse from the surface of the fruit to the surrounding air. Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables 35 Figure 2.2: Nomogram for Finding Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD) from Relative Humidity and Temperature. (Note: 1 mb = 0.1 kPa) Vapor Pressure Nomogram: Figure 2.2 is the nomogram for finding of vapor pressure deficit. Example: From which of the following atmosphere conditions the moisture loss from the surface of the fruits will be higher 2°C and 84% relative humidity (or) 5°C and 90% relative humidity. Solution: In the nomogram, connect 2°C on temperature scale with 84% relative humidity and read the value where the straight edge interests vapor pressure scale. In this example it is 1.1 mb = 0.11 kPa. For the second condition, in the similar way the vapor pressure difference is 0.85 mb, or 0.085 kPa. 36 Chapter 2 Result: Because the VPD is higher in the first case, water is lost at a faster rate, and is higher by 1.3 times, (0.11/0.085). Experimentally determined values of the surface heat transfer coefficients are given in Table 2.9. 2.16 Postharvest Decay Once microorganisms are established in plant tissue, they can proliferate and secrete enzymes to bring about quality deterioration. Frequently there is a lag period between infection and any manifestation of the presence of microorganisms. The most common pathogens causing rot in harvested vegetables are fungi such as Alternaria, Botrytis, Diplodia, Monilinia, Penicillium, Phomopsis, Rhizopus, and Sclerotinia and the bacteria Erwinia and Pseudomonas. The majority of these can only invade damaged tissue such as bruised structures and fractured cells. The development of postharvest decay is favored by high temperatures and high humidity, the latter often as a result of condensation that may affect spore germination and can cause tissue anaerobiosis. 2.17 Conclusions Because all fruits and vegetables are living tissues, they continue their life processes after harvest. If the storage conditions provided are not proper and adequate, certain undesirable changes may occur, which ultimately reduce quality and postharvest life. Respiration, transpiration, and ethylene production are the most important postharvest physiological aspects that are to be minimized in fruits and vegetables for prolonged storage without change in their original attributes. The moisture content of fruits and vegetables is high, and weight loss during transportation and storage can be a serious economic factor, especially if the fruits are sold by weight. In most fruits and vegetables with 5–10% loss in moisture content, the products are visibly shriveled as a result of cellular plasmolysis. The pedicels of cherva and calyx of strawberries turn brown and dry and the berries become dull and lose luster. Hence, quick cooling is necessary to preserve fresh appearance. The weight loss of fruits and vegetables in storage depends upon size, maturity, composition and structure, air composition surrounding them, storage temperature, relative humidity, velocity of air in the storage, thickness of cuticles, size and number of stomata and lenticels, and other factors. A practical way to minimize this effect is to cool the fruit quickly using suitable cooling methods such as convective air, hydro, vacuum, or evaporative cooling systems. Lettuce and other leafy vegetables are cooled by sprinkling cold water on them followed by vacuum treatment. Precooling chambers, cold storages, controlled atmosphere store, and modified atmosphere packaging are a few of the facilities that are required for long shelf life with minimum deviation from original attributes for horticultural produce. Postharvest Physiology of Fruits and Vegetables 37 Fruits and vegetables should be precooled before their storage at lower temperature. Sometimes it is essential to package the produce in semipermeable polyethylene or Mylar bags. Fruits and vegetables can be protected from lower relative humidity by using various types of permeable polyethylene bags or films or by providing moisture in the form of ice or hydro cooling. High air velocities cause rapid evaporation by continuously removing water that is saturated. Air movement should be sufficient enough to effectively remove respiratory heat from the produce after it has cooled to the temperature of the room. For providing these precooling and air movement facilities and for subsequent storage at controlled conditions and composition of atmosphere, structures (a building) and machinery fitted with refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment are necessary. Such structures are called cold storage. The same cold storage, if provided with additional facility of production and control of gas regime around the produce, is called controlled atmosphere storage. In this book the subsequent chapters deal with various aspects of precooling facilities, cold storage, controlled atmosphere storage, and modified atmosphere storage for fruits and vegetables. 2.18 Questions 1. CHAPTE R 3 Estimation of Cooling Times of Foods 3.1 Introduction Preservation of food is a significant application of refrigeration and air-conditioning. Cooling of food effectively reduces the activity of microorganisms and enzymes, thus retarding deterioration. In order for cooling operation to be cost effective, refrigeration equipment should fit the specific requirements of the particular cooling applications. Time required to cool the food is an important requirement for sizing various inputs in the design of process equipment. Numerous methods for predicting cooling times are available based on numerical, analytical, and empirical analysis. The cooling and freezing of fruits or vegetables is a complex process. The cooling and freezing of these items can be described via the Fourier heat conduction equation. 3.2 Fourier Heat Conduction Equation ∂T 1  ∂  ∂T  ∂  ∂ T  ∂  ∂ T   = + k k  k +  ∂θ ρc  ∂ x  ∂ x  ∂ y  ∂ y  ∂ z  ∂ z   (3.1) where T = temperature u = time ρ = density of the food item c = specific heat of food items k = thermal conductivity of food items x, y, z are the coordinate directions In this chapter, the estimation of cooling time for foods of a few standard shapes is given. For regular-shaped food items with constant thermophysical properties, uniform initial conditions, constant external conditions, convective boundary conditions, and prescribed surface temperature, exact analytical solutions for equation (3.1) are available. However, for practical cooling processes, the foods are generally irregularly shaped with temperaturedependent thermophysical properties. Therefore, exact analytical solutions cannot be derived for cooling times of these items. Accurate numerical estimation of the cooling and freezing times of foods can be obtained using appropriate finite element or finite difference computer Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00003-8 39 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 40 Chapter 3 programs. However, the effort required to perform this task makes it impractical for the design engineer. In addition, two-dimensional and three-dimensional simulations require time-consuming data preparation and significant computing time. Hence, most of the research effort has been in the development of semi analytical/empirical cooling time prediction methods. 3.2.1 Cooling Times of Foods The precooling removes only sensible heat and thus no phase change occurs. The cooling time of foods is influenced by the ratio of the external heat transfer resistance to the internal heat transfer resistance. This ratio, called the Biot number, is defined as Bi = hL k (3.2) where h is the convective heat transfer coefficient, L is the characteristic dimension of fruits/ vegetables, and K is the thermal conductivity of the food item. When the Biot number approaches zero (Bi < 0.1), the internal resistance to heat transfer is much less than the external resistances, and the lumped-parameter approach can be used to determine the cooling time of food item. When the Biot number is large (Bi > 40), the internal resistances to heat transfer is much greater than the external resistances, and the surface temperature of food item can be assumed to be equal to the temperature of the cooling medium. For this latter situation, series solutions of the Fourier heat conduction equation are available for simple geometric shapes. When the Biot number falls within the range (0.1 Bi < 40), both the external resistance to heat transfer and the convective heat transfer coefficient must be considered. In this case, series solutions that incorporate transcendental functions to account for the influence of the Biot number are available for simple geometric shapes. Simplified methods for predicting the cooling time of foods applicable to regularly and irregularly shaped food items over a wide range of Biot numbers are available. In this chapter, the simplified cooling time estimation methods based on f and j factors for regular-shaped food items are presented. 3.3 Estimation of Cooling Time Based on f and j Factors All cooling processes exhibit similar behavior of cooling as shown in Figure 3.1. After an initial lag of time, the temperature decreases exponentially with time. Estimation of Cooling Times of Foods 41 Figure 3.1: Typical Cooling Curve. As shown in Figure 3.1, a cooling curve depicting this behavior can be obtained by plotting on semilogarithmic axes, the fractional unaccomplished temperature difference verses time. The fractional unaccomplished temperature difference Y is defined as Y= Tm − T T − Tm = Tm − Ti Ti − Tm (3.3) where Tm = cooling medium temperature T = product temperature Ti = initial temperature of the product This semilogarithmic temperature history curve consists of one initial curvilinear portion, followed by one or more linear portions. Empirical formulae that model this cooling behavior incorporate two factors, f and j, which represent the slope and intercept, respectively, of the temperature history curve. The j factor is a measure of the lag between the onset of cooling and exponential decrease in the temperature of the food. The f factor, represent the time required to obtain 90% reduction in the nondimensional temperature difference. Graphically, the factor f corresponds to the time required for the linear portion of the temperature history curve to pass through one log cycle. The factor f is a function of the Biot number, while the j factor is a function of the Biot number and the location within the food item. 42 Chapter 3 The general form of the cooling time model is Y= Tm − T = J(e −2.303θ / f ) Tm − Ti (3.4) where u is the cooling time, this equation can be rearranged to give the cooling time explicitly as θ= Y  −f ln   2.303  j  (3.5) 3.3.1 Determination of f and j Factors for Slabs, Cylinders, and Spheres Pflug et al. Often products are cooled in bulk or packages of several layers where the surrounding materials influence the cooling response particularly in air cooling systems. Then the individual fruit approach usually gives poor estimates for cooling of bulk loads. Baird and Gaffney (1976) developed a numerical technique for calculating cooling rates in bulk loads of fruits or vegetables. This procedure, applicable to spherical products, uses finite difference solutions of the differential equation that describe heat transfer both within individual fruits and at different levels in bulk loads. The models can be used to calculate temperatures at various points within the individual products and at different depths in bulk loads at regular time intervals during cooling. Required inputs to the models include: product size and shape, thermal properties of the product, the convective coefficient, and flow rate of the cooling medium. 3.5 Questions 1.
