CHAPTE R 4 Precooling of Fruits and Vegetables by Ventilation Method 4.1 Introduction Precooling is the rapid removal of heat from freshly harvested produce. This process is typically done before the produce is transported to market or put into cold storage. The amount of heat produced is governed by the temperature around it. The temperature difference between newly harvested produce and its optimum storage temperature is an indicator of field heat. Rapidly lowering the temperature of harvested produce to near storage temperature is known as precooling or removal of field heat. Although produce may be precooled in a cold storage facility, precooling differs from cold storage. In cold storage the optimum temperature, relative humidity, and air circulation are maintained to keep the product without spoilage for long time periods. Fresh produce starts to deteriorate immediately following harvest. Respiration due to enzymatic oxidation in the growing produce continues even after harvest. This process results in the consumption of sugars, starches, and moisture without replenishment by the plant. Carbon dioxide and other gases along with heat are generated in this process. If the heat is not removed, the process is accelerated, resulting in a further rise in temperatures of the produce. Growth of molds and the loss of moisture from the produce are also accelerated. Brushing of the produce further accelerates these processes, resulting in the loss of texture, firmness, color, flavor, and appearance. In addition, the nutritional value is lost when these losses occur, and the produce is generally considered to have lost its freshness and quality. Rapid lowering of produce temperature and then maintaining it at a constant low temperature are essential. Therefore, precooling is important requirement for maintaining quality, especially for produce with naturally high respiration rates. 4.2 Factors Contributing to Spoilage A generally accepted rule of thumb is that deterioration of fresh produce doubles for every 10°C rise above the optimum storage temperature. Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00004-X 49 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 50 Chapter 4 Produce such as onion, potatoes, and winter squash spoil rapidly if not cured as soon as possible after harvest. Curing at an elevated temperature heals the cuts and bruises and forms a tight outer skin that resists further deterioration. Atmosphere in storages also affect the spoilage rate. Excess carbon dioxide and insufficient oxygen result in rapid deterioration and deter the production of flavor. Ethylene is produced by some fruits, which accelerates their ripening. It is important therefore to consider the gases that will be associated with the cold storage. 4.3 Selection of a Cooling Method Packaging house size and operating procedures, response of product to the cooling method, and market demands largely dictate the cooling method used. Other factors considered are whether the product is packaged in the field or in a packaging house, how the product mix being cooled, the length of cooling season, and the comparative costs of dry versus waterresistant cartons. In some cases, there is little question about the type of cooling to be used. For example, vacuum cooling is most effective on lettuce and other similar vegetables. Peach packers in the southeastern United States and some vegetables and citrus packers are satisfied with hydrocooling. Air (room) cooling is used for apples, pears, and citrus fruit. In other cases, choice of cooling method is not so clearly defined. Celery and sweet corn are usually hydrocooled, but they may be vacuum cooled as effectively. Cantaloupes may be satisfactorily cooled by several methods. Sweet cherries are often hydrocooled in packing houses but are air-cooled if orchard packed. When more than one method can be used cost becomes a major consideration. Although rapid forced-air cooling is more costly than hydrocooling, if the product does not require rapid cooling, a forced-air system can operate almost as economically as hydrocooling. In a study to evaluate costs of hypothetical precooling systems for citrus fruit, Gaffney and Bowman (1970) found that the cost for forced-air cooling in bulk lots was 20% more than for hydrocooling in bulk and that forced-air cooling in cartons costs 45% more than hydrocooling in bulk. In this chapter, simple and low-cost techniques that can be used for precooling of fruits and vegetables are given. 4.4 Ventilation Food processing is seasonal in nature both in the demand for its output product and in the availability of its raw materials. The food processor would prefer that raw material be continuously available in sufficient quantity and quality to enable processing plant operation in a planned year-round basis. Particularly, when the place of produce is near to the processing plant or cold storage, there is no need to remove the field heat of produce by using costly methods such as hydrocooling, vacuum cooling, or evaporative cooling. Instead, by keeping Precooling of Fruits and Vegetables by Ventilation Method 51 the produce either in the form of stacks or loose in a specially designed low-cost structures with proper ventilation, the field heat, heat of respiration, and respiration moisture can be removed efficiently without change in the freshness of the produce. Such types of structures are referred to as ventilated storage structures. 4.5 Estimation of Airflow for Moisture Removal If moisture is to be removed, the rate of airflow depends upon the following: • • The rate at which moisture has to exchanged The difference in moisture content of the incoming and outgoing air. For a given rate of moisture exchange, the rate of airflow may be expressed as M= We µ2 ws – µ1 ws 2 (4.1) 1 where M = airflow rate, kg/h We = moisture to be exchanged, kg/h m2 and m1 = degree of saturation of outgoing and incoming air, respectively. (For all practical purposes, m is usually assumed equal to the relative humidity.) Ws2 and Ws1= water in saturated air vapor mixture at temperature of outgoing and incoming air, respectively, kg/kg of dry air. These values can be obtained from a psychrometric chart. 4.6 Airflow Required in Heat Removal In ventilation for the purpose of controlling temperature, an exchange of heat is accomplished by changing the temperature of the air. Such temperature changes usually occur at constant pressure. The amount of sensible heat change in the air may be estimated by Qs = M Cpa (t 2 − t1 ) where Qs = sensible heat exchange of air, kw M = mass flow rate of air, kg/sec Cpa = specific heat of air, kJ/kg °C (t2 – t1) = temperature difference between outgoing and incoming air, °C (4.2) 52 Chapter 4 4.7 Ventilation Systems 4.7.1 Natural Ventilation System The flow of air caused naturally due to the pressure difference between the ambient air and air in an enclosed space is known as the natural ventilation system. The flow of air resulting from this phenomenon is known as wind. Because blowing wind is always uncertain, both in its direction and speed, lacks control of dust and odor carried by incoming air, and is generally a slow process, it is not preferred for large-scale produce cooling. 4.7.2 Mechanical Ventilation System In a forced ventilation system, the controlled ventilation (flow quantity and direction) caused with the use of fan is known as a mechanical ventilation system. In this system, the temperature, humidity, and air motion are controlled in a given space. Three different basic systems of mechanical ventilation are used in practice. 4.7.3 Extraction System The extraction system is the most widely used method in forced-air ventilation. The air from the stored space is withdrawn with the help of a suction fan and is accomplished either by using the propeller fans exhausting through holes in the wall or through ducts, depending upon the requirements. An exhaust fan produces a low pressure zone around it, which causes the flow of air toward the fan. The space occupied in this system of ventilation depends upon the location of inlet and exhaust fans. The desirable and undesirable location of inlet points are shown in Figures 4.1(a) and (b). The short circuit caused as shown in Figure 4.1(b) will not give the required ventilation because the amount of air drawn from the occupied space is proportionately reduced. An inlet close to exhaust reduces the ventilation in remote parts of the storage space. The effectiveness of an extraction system largely depends on the location of inlets with respect to exhaust outlets. Figure 4.1: Ventilation Inlet and Exhaust Positions. (a) Desirable position of inlet. (b) Undesirable position of inlet. Precooling of Fruits and Vegetables by Ventilation Method 53 As the air traverses an occupied space, the risk for potential contamination increases. Therefore, the distance between the inlet and exhaust point should not be excessive to ensure fresh air at all points. 4.8 Forced System In this system of air supply, the air is passed into the air-conditioned space under pressure by means of fans. The air goes out through the outlets arranged in the system. The advantages of this system over the extraction system are listed here: 1. A positive control over quantity, velocity, and its distribution can be maintained as conditioned air is introduced under positive pressure. 2. The incoming air can be cleaned wherever required. 3. The recirculation of interior air for heating systems can be achieved more conveniently. 4. The conditioned air passed under pressure maintains a positive pressure in the occupied space and removes all possibilities of creating a draft. But loss of conditioned air through cracks in the building is comparable to the extraction system due to positive pressure inside. 4.9 Combined Forced and Extraction System To ensure the uniform fresh air, a combined system is always preferred compared with individual systems. In this system, fresh air can be introduced at required or desired points, and its uniform distribution in the occupied space is achieved with the help of extraction and supply fans. In combined systems, the capacity of the supply fan should be 20% greater than the exhaust fan to keep the pressure in the air-conditioned space above atmosphere. This also helps to reduce the drafts and prevent the infiltration of dust and other airborne contaminants. Sometimes one wall inlets and opposite wall exhausts are also preferred as shown in Figure 4.2 for rooms of moderate width. If only one wall gives access to atmosphere, another practical alternative is to put an extract duct along the other sidewall as shown in Figure 4.3. Figure 4.2: Plan for Opposite Wall Inlets and Outlets. Figure 4.3: Plan for Extract Duct used for Outlet. 54 Chapter 4 Figure 4.4: Plan for Center Extracting Duct in Large Areas. If the distance between the walls is considerable, it is always desirable to put an extracting duct at the center to avoid the possibility of short-circuiting as shown in Figure 4.4. Mass flow rate of air can be calculated as follows: M= Qs C pa (ti − t o ) (4.3) where Qs = sensible heat to be removed, kw CPa = specific heat, kJ/kg °C (ti – to) = temperature difference between inside and outside air °C Note: In these processes it is assumed that there is no change of phase of moisture from liquid to vapor because the temperatures are not usually high enough to cause vaporization, and also it is a process that occurs at atmospheric pressure. 4.10 Natural Ventilation 4.10.1 Ventilation by Wind Forces The most common type of ventilation is that accomplished by wind forces. The rate of ventilation depends upon the wind speed and direction, interference of nearby obstructions such as hills or buildings, and size and location of outlet and inlet openings in the structure. 4.10.2 Rate of Ventilation The following equation based on experimental data is used for calculating ventilation rate. V = ASE where Precooling of Fruits and Vegetables by Ventilation Method 55 V = airflow rate, m3/min A = area of inlet opening, m2 (outlet openings are assumed to be equal in area) S = wind velocity, m/min E = effectiveness of opening (E may vary from 0.5–0.6 for perpendicular winds to 0.25–0.35 for diagonal winds) 4.10.3 Wind Speed and Direction Although wind speed and direction vary with season and locality, usually the seasonal average is 1.5 to 3.5 kmph. To assure on days when velocities are less than the seasonal average, the design velocity in estimating ventilation is usually taken as one-half the seasonal average. 4.11 Effectiveness of Ventilator Openings The effectiveness of an air opening depends chiefly on its orientation with respect to wind direction and its location on the structure. These relations are better understood by the Figure 4.5. Wind impinging on wall C is stopped or retarded, and a portion of its kinetic energy is converted to potential energy. A static pressure against wall C is created that is higher than in adjacent areas. Owing to deflection of the air stream, regions of relatively low pressure are created in areas E and D shown on the plan view and in area B of the elevation. From inspection of Figure 4.5 the following may be deduced. 1. Inlet openings in wall C perpendicular to wind direction have the maximum effectiveness compared to other orientations. 2. Outlet openings in the roof area B, in sidewall areas E, and in endwall area D have greater effectiveness than in areas where negative pressure does not exist. Figure 4.5: Distribution of Wind Pressure on a Storage Chamber. 56 Chapter 4 3. Outlets in regions where downward air currents or high pressure exists are less effective than outlets in other regions. 4. A wind direction inclined to wall C creates less static pressure on wall C than a perpendicular wind and consequently produces less airflow through openings in that wall. However, static pressure is developed on the other windward wall with consequent effects on the rate of ventilation, provided that the new exposure contains inlet openings. 5. In order that the inlet openings are fully effective, there must be approximately equal (or large) outlet areas. 4.11.1 Forced Draft Systems of Ventilation In temperate zone areas, ambient air temperature at night after fall harvest usually produces favorable storage temperatures for such products as potatoes, dry onions, cabbage, and mature carrots and for fruits like mango, sapota, pineapple, and apples when applied under forced draft ventilation in an insulated structure. Such structures require high-capacity fans with automatic control to draw outside air in when ambient temperatures are favorable and to circulate the air inside the structure. Thus the product stored is gradually cooled by removing the field heat and temperature is maintained at the desired level. Modern forced ventilation storage is usually contained in a frame or cinder block construction with 5 cm thick rock wool or equivalent in the walls with 7.5 or 10 cm of insulation in the ceiling. One such type of structure is shown in Figure 4.6. Figure 4.6: Natural Cooling of Potatoes. Precooling of Fruits and Vegetables by Ventilation Method 57 4.11.2 Exchange of Air Equipment is necessary for automatic control of outside air intake and exhaust air removal. Maximum use can be made of cool night air during the fall cooling period; and in the winter months just enough outside air can be drawn in to maintain product temperature. Air can be circulated around the perimeter of the storage or through the product in the stack or bins, depending on the design and mode of application of the air. A constant airflow rate of 0.023 m3/min per 45 kg of stored potatoes is recommended. Less air will permit vital heat to accumulate and stimulate decay organisms, while more air may cause excessive loss of moisture from the product. Relative humidity requirements vary with the commodity. 4.11.3 Air Circulation in the Storage The air circulation in the store may be a vertical flow type or a horizontal flow type. In the conventional type of forced-air ventilation system (i.e., in vertical flow type), air is released from supply ducts placed on or near the floor (Figure 4.6). The air travels up through the pile of product and reaches the top of the pile from where it is exhausted out. The available floor area is limited. So air released at the ducts is often of high velocity, which can result in excessive moisture loss and pressure brushing in case of potatoes. 4.11.4 Cross-Flow System This method consists of wall ducts with the air released from inner wall openings and flowing through the pile to similar opening on the opposite wall. A positive pressure at one wall and a negative pressure at the other ensure air movement without high velocity. The system can also be made reversible. Modification of a wall duct system and limiting the bin width to 4–5 m with a cross-flow system is a useful alternative to vertical flow systems. 4.12 Low-Cost Cold Room Low-cost cold rooms can be constructed using concrete for floor and polyurethane foam as an insulator. Building a storeroom in the shape of a cube will reduce the surface area per unit volume of storage space, thereby reducing construction costs and fan size and consequently the overall cost of the storage structure. 4.13 Storehouse Figure 4.7 is a cross-sectional view of a storehouse for fruits. This system was officially approved as a store model for farm-house storage by the ministry of construction in Korea in the year 1983. 58 Chapter 4 Figure 4.7: Storehouse. (Source: Seung Koo Lee, 1994. Assoc. Prof., Postharvest Technology Lab., Department of Horticulture, Seoul National University, Suwon 441-744, Korea.) In this structure, air inlets are at the base of the building and the floor is perforated, allowing for free movement of air. The air entering will pass over the surface of water where it cools and then passes into the product. The entire building is set below the ground level for taking advantage of cooling properties of the soil. 4.14 Layout of Floor Ducts for Storehouse Proper arrangement of floor ducts for air circulation will improve ventilation in the storage house (Figure 4.8). Lateral ducts should be 2 m apart when measured from center to center. Airflow velocity from the main duct should be 10–13 m/s. Lateral ducts can be constructed of a variety of materials. Portable vents can be made from wooden slats in a triangular, square, or rectangular design (Figure 4.9). A round tube of plastic or clay with 45 cm diameter can be used with holes of size 2 to 3 cm in diameter (Figure 4.10). Permanent ducts can be constructed below the ground using concrete. 4.15 Overhead Ventilation Air Distribution System In cooler regions, suitable storage temperature can be maintained by bringing outside air into the storage structure. This process is also called as the convective cooling or winter cooling of storage rooms. The schematic diagram of the system is shown in Figure 4.11. Precooling of Fruits and Vegetables by Ventilation Method 59 Figure 4.8: Arrangement of Floor Vents. (Source: Potato Marketing Board. No date. Control of Environment. Part 2. London: Sutton Bridge Experiment Station, Report No. 6.) Figure 4.9: Triangular Wooden Duct. (Source: Potato Marketing Board.) Figure 4.10: Clay Pipe Duct. (Source: Potato Marketing Board.) Figure 4.11: Convection Tube-Type Cooling System. 60 Chapter 4 Whenever the temperature rises above the set point, the exhaust fans turn on and send the inside air into the outer atmosphere. Then the pressuring fan will start and draw the cool air from outside and deliver it through holes in the convection tube into the storage structures. The air mixture then results in decreased inside temperature. This process will continue till the set point temperature is reached. Convection tubes are conventionally oriented from end to end in the structure. One convention tube placed down the center of the structure will cool 9.0 m in width. Storage structures of 9.0–18.0 m are cooled by two tubes placed equidistantly across the structure. Tubes derive cold air from a louvered air inlet fitted on one side of the tube. The pressuring fan in the inlet end of the convection tube should be larger. Sometimes two pressuring fans are needed; they should have a combined capacity equal to that of the exhaust fan capacity. 4.16 Package Icing The simplest and easiest and most economical way of preventing spoilage of fruits and vegetables is by using package icing. Finely crushed ice placed in containers can effectively cool products that are not harmed by contact with ice (Figure 4.12). Spinach, collards, kale, Brussels sprouts, broccoli, radishes, carrots, and green onions are commonly packaged with ice. Cooling a product from 35°C to 2°C requires melting ice equal to 38% of the product’s mass. Additional ice must melt to remove heat leaking into the packages and to remove heat from the container. In addition to removing field heat, package ice can keep the product cool during transit. Pumping slush ice or liquid ice into the shipping container through a hose and special nozzle that connect to the package is another method used for cooling some products. Some systems can ice an entire pallet at one time. Figure 4.12. Figure 4.12: Package Icing. Precooling of Fruits and Vegetables by Ventilation Method 61 Sometimes top icing is used occasionally to supplement another cooling method. Wax-impregnated corrugated containers, however, have allowed the use of icing and hydrocooling of products after packaging. Flaked or crushed ice can be manufactured on site and stored in an ice bunker for later use or for short season cooling requirements with low ice demands (e.g., a few tons a day). It may be more economical to buy block ice and crush it on-site. Another option is to rent liquid ice equipment for on-site production. The cooling capacity of ice is 335 kJ/kg; 1 kg of ice will reduce the temperature of 3 kg of produce by approximately 28°C. However, commercial ice injection systems require significantly more ice over and above that needed to produce cooling. For example, 10 kg of broccoli requires about 16 kg of manufactured ice. But because of losses that occur in product cooling, transport, and equipment heat gain, a remainder of ice is required in the box on delivery to the customer. 4.16.1 Disadvantages of Top Icing Top icing involves a number of potential disadvantages: 1. The high ice requirement makes liquid icing an energy-inefficient and expensive cooling method (Thompson et al., 1998). 2. The space taken up by the ice decreases the amount of space available for transporting the product. 3. Water-resistant packaging is necessary to prevent both water damage to other products and safety hazards during storage. These disadvantages can be minimized if ice used for temporary maintenance in transit rather than for cooling or by using gel-pack ice (often used for flowers), which is sealed in a leak-proof pack. Because corrugated containers have largely replaced wooden crates, the use of top icing has decreased in favor of forced-air and hydrocooling. Cut flowers are often forced-air cooled, but if the box is handled in a refrigerated environment, bags of ice may be added to the box to prevent heating. This system allows a measured amount of ice to be added and the melt water is removed preventing damage to the product and fiber board boxes. Another vegetable commonly precooled with top ice is cabbage because rapid precooling is not critical for most cabbages. It is often loaded warm and top-iced immediately after loading in mesh bags or wirebound crates. Satisfactory cooling usually occurs during first couple of days in transit. 62 Chapter 4 Figure 4.13: Ice Bunker. 4.17 Ice Bunker Ice can be used in a bunker as source of refrigeration by passing air through a bunker of ice and then passing the cooled air through the commodity or as top ice laid direct in contact with the product. Ice can cool the product only if melts so good ventilation is necessary for effective cooling. The cross-sectional view of a simple ice bunker is shown in Figure 4.13. An electric fan is commonly mounted inside the bunker and the fan capacity should at least equal the empty volume of the bunker room. 4.18 Windrowed Top-Icing Top ice applied evenly over the load in a mechanically refrigerated railcar or trailer interferes with the normal pattern of air circulation. If air is blocked from passage through the load, heat removal from the load is slowed. The method of “windrowed top-icing” provides air channels through the load (Figure 4.14). The crushed ice is applied over only lengthwise rows particularly for cooling fruits like melon in crates. Spaces between rows of crates are left essentially ice-free for air movement. Precooling of Fruits and Vegetables by Ventilation Method 63 Figure 4.14: Windrowed Top-Icing for Melons and Vegetables to Hasten Cooling. Refrigerated air moves through the channels between lengthwise rows of containers and returns under the floor racks. Recommended ice application as a supplement to mechanical precooling varies from 613 kg loaded at 21°C to 908 kg loaded at 32°C per one-ton load of melons. Wide use is made of the melting of ice in homes, storage, transportation, and so on for presentation of products at refrigerated temperatures. The main drawbacks of ice are the temperature limitation of 0°C and the spoilage caused by the melted water. These drawbacks can be avoided by the use of solid carbon dioxide, also called dry ice, which sublimates at atmosphere pressure. Dry ice is rather widely used in refrigerated air transport. In recent times, liquid nitrogen has also become quite popular in transport refrigeration. Description of these two methods is given elsewhere in this book. 4.19 Problems on Cooling Load Calculations Problem 4.1 In a cooling chamber 11,350 kg of fruits are received each day. The fruits are to be cooled from 35°C to 3°C in 3 h. What must the capacity of the refrigerating machine be if the specific heat of the fruits is 3.8 kJ/kg °C. Q1 = mi Cpi ∆t1 where mi = mass of ice, kg Cpi = specific heat of ice, kJ/kg °C ∆t1= temperature difference, °C 100 × 1.94 × [(0 – (–5)] Q1 = 100 × 1.94 × 5 = 970 kJ Heat used in fusion of ice at 0°C to water at the same temperature is given latent heat of fusion of ice and expressed as Q2 = m1Li 66 Chapter 4 where mi = mass of ice melted, kg Li = latent heat of fusion of ice, kJ/kg Q2 = 100 × 335 = 33,500 kJ Heat acquired by melted water in raising the temperature from 0°C to 10°C Q3 = mw Cpw ∆t 3 where mw = mass of water formed, kg Cpw = specific heat of water, kJ/kg °C ∆t3 = temperature difference, °C between the produce and the surrounding medium Q3 = 100 × 4.186(10 − 0) = 100 × 4.186 × 10 = 4186 kJ Total heat removed in 24 h QT = Q1 + Q2 + Q3 = 970 + 33,500 + 4,186 = 38,656 kJ Heat removed per hour = 38,656 = 1,611 kJ 24 1TR = 12,660 kJ/h, or 3.5 kW) Tons of refrigeration produced by ice TR = 1,611 = 0.127 12,660 which is also equal to 0.127 × 3.5 = 0.44 kw. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 5 Forced-Air Cooling of Fruits and Vegetables 5.1 Introduction Forced-air cooling is adaptable to a wider range of commodities than any other cooling method. It is much faster than room cooling, because it causes cold air to be in direct contact with warm product. With proper design, fast uniform cooling can be achieved through stacks of pallet bins or unitized pallet loads of containers. The heat transfer from fruit surface to the surrounding air occurs through forced convection. The film coefficient of heat transfer, the surface area, and temperature difference between the fruit surface and the surrounding air is important. Coefficients of heat transfer are sensitive to the physical conditions involved among objects and their surroundings. The physical conditions of the fluid around the fruit such as density, viscosity, thermal conductivity, specific heat at constant pressure, and coefficient of thermal expansion, which for gas is 1/T by Charles’s law, are significant. The product factors that affect convective heat transfer are the linear dimensions of the product, such as diameter and length. The temperature difference and gravitational acceleration due to density differences create circulation. For calculating heat load in forced-air cooling, the estimation of film coefficient of heat transfer is important. The rate of heat transfer is expressed by Newton’s law of cooling, which accounts for the overall effect of convection. Q = hc A (t p − t ∞ ) (5.1) where Q = heat transfer, kW hc = convective heat transfer coefficient, W/m2, °C tp = temperature of product, °C t∞ = temperature of the surrounding air, °C Numerical values of convective heat transfer coefficients for various fruits and vegetables can be found in Table 2.9. All rights reserved. 72 Chapter 5 Forced-air cooling is 4 to 10 times faster than conventional room cooling, but two to three times slower than hydrocooling or vacuum cooling. Pulling, rather than blowing, air through the containers is a better option so that cooled air first flows around the product. In circumstances where air cannot be forced directly through the voids of products in bulk, a container type and a load pattern that permits air to circulate through the container and reach a substantial part of the product surface is beneficial. Examples include the following: 1. Small products such as grapes and strawberries that offer appreciable resistance to airflow through the voids in bulk lots 2. Delicate products that cannot be handled in bulk, and 3. Products that are packed in the shipping containers before they cooled. Forced-air or pressure cooling involves definite stacking patterns and the baffling of stacks so that cooling air is forced through rather than around individual containers. Successful use of the method requires a container with vent holes placed in the direction in which the air will move and a minimum of packing materials that would block the free movement of air through the containers. Under these conditions, a relatively small pressure differential between the two sides of the containers results in good air movement and excellent heat transfer. Differential pressures in use are about 60 – 750 Pa with airflows ranging from 1 – 3 L/s per kilogram of product. Because the cooling air comes in direct contact with the product being cooled, cooling is much faster than with conventional room cooling. The advantage is more rapid product movement through the cooling plant; also, the size of the plant is one-fourth that of an equivalent cold room-type of plant. A proprietary direct-contact heat exchanger cools the air and maintains high humidity using chilled water as a secondary coolant and a continuously wound polypropylene monofilament packing. It contains about 24 km of filament per cubic meter of packing section. Air is forced up through the unit while chilled water flows downward. The dew-point temperature of air leaving the unit equals the entering water temperature. Chilled water can be supplied from coils submerged in a tank. Buildup of ice in the coils provides an extra cooling effect during peak loads. This design also allows an operator to add commercial ice during long periods of mechanical equipment outage. 5.1.1 Portable Forced-Air Cooler In one portable forced-air method, refrigeration components are mounted on flatbed trailer and the warm, packaged produce is cooled in a refrigerated transport trailer. Usually the refrigeration equipment is mounted on two trailers: one holds the forced-air evaporators and the other holds compressors, air cooling condensers, a high-pressure receiver, and electrical gear. The loaded produce trailers are moved to the evaporator trailer and the product is cooled. After cooling, the trailer is transported to its destination. Forced-Air Cooling of Fruits and Vegetables 73 5.2 Effects of Containers and Stacking Patterns The accessibility of the product to the cooling medium is essential to rapid cooling, and it may involve both access to the product in the container and to the individual container in a stack. This effect is evident in the cooling rate data of various commodities in various types of containers reported by Mitchell et al. (1972). Parsons (1972) developed a corrugated paperboard container venting pattern for palletized unit loads that produced cooling rates equal to those from conventional register stacked patterns. Fisher (1960) demonstrated that spacing apple containers on pallets reduced cooling time by 50% as compared with pallet loads stacked solidly. A minimum of 5% sidewall venting is recommended. Palletization is essential for shipment of many products and pallet stability is improved if cartons are packed closely together. Thus, cartons and packages should be designed to allow ample airflow through the stacked products. Amos et al. (1993) and Parsons (1972) showed the importance of vent sizes and location to obtain good cooling in palletized loads without reducing the strength of the container. Some operators wrap the palletized products in polyethylene to increase stability. In this case, the product may need to be cooled before it is palletized. Optimum air velocity for forced-air cooling is in the range of 1.5–2 m/s, depending on conditions and circumstances. 5.3 Commercial Methods of Forced-Air Cooling Products can be satisfactorily cooled with the following: 1. With air circulated in a refrigerated room adapted for this purpose, which is popularly called room cooling 2. In railcars using special portable cooling equipment that cools the load before it is ­transported 3. With the cool air forced through the voids of bulk products moving through a cooling ­tunnel on continuous conveyer 4. On continuous conveyer in a wind tunnel 5. By the forced-air method of passing air through the container by pressure differential Each of these methods is used commercially, and each is suitable for certain commodities when properly applied. 5.3.1 Forced-Air Room Cooling Room cooling involves placing field temperature (warm) containers of product in a cold room. Cooling is achieved by moving cool air round the containers. Containers are stacked individually so that cold air from the ceiling flows over or around the produce to contact 74 Chapter 5 Figure 5.1: Forced-Air Cooling Room Cooling. all sides of the containers. An airflow rate of 5.3–10.5 m3/min with a relative humidity of 90–95% is necessary. To cool the produce, containers should be well vented so that as much air as possible can circulate through them. Spacing between containers and walls must be 15–30 cm, and 45–60 cm between the boxes and ceiling. Room cooling is not recommended for bulk bins because they contain a much greater mass of product than do smaller containers (Figure 5.1). The refrigeration equipment must be capable of cooling down fresh product within 24 h. Normally much larger refrigeration equipment is needed for initial cooling of the product than is necessary to maintain the product at a cool temperature. The method is best suited to less perishable products such as potatoes, onions, apples, sweet potatoes, and citrus fruits. Bunched flowers in buckets can cool in 15 min; but the same flower packed in boxes and loaded on a pallet takes days to cool. After cooling is completed, airflow can be reduced to 20–40% of that needed for initial cooling. Room cooling is probably the most widely used refrigeration technique due to its versatility and low cost. However room-cooled produce must be tolerant of slow heat removal because much of the cooling is by heat conduction through the container walls. This technique is not considered to be a true precooling method. It involves placing field containers in a room cooled by a refrigeration system. The ventilation system must provide good air circulation through and around the container. Cold air from the evaporator enters the room near the ceiling and then sweeps past the produce containers in returning to the evaporator. For adequate heat removal, the airflow velocity must be 1–2 m s–1, with the moving cold air in good contact with all container surfaces. Container disposition is therefore, especially important in the handling sequence. Forced-Air Cooling of Fruits and Vegetables 75 Figure 5.2: View of Cold Wall Forced-Air Cooler. 5.3.2 Cold Wall Forced-Air Cooling The permanent false wall or air plenum contains air exhaust fans that draw cold air from the room and direct it over the cooling surface; the wall is at the same end of the cold room as the cooling surface (Figure 5.2). The wall is built with a damper system that can open when containers with openings are placed in front of it. The fan pulls cold room air through the container thus cooling the contents. This system is good for operations in which the produce arrives at various times. It is also versatile in the way that the treatment can be adjusted to each product. 5.3.3 Tunnel-Type Forced-Air Cooling This system is the most used cooling system. A row of palletized containers or boxes is placed on either side of an exhaust fan. The aisle left between the rows and the open end are then covered to create an air plenum tunnel. The exhaust fan creates a low air pressure within the tunnel. Cold air from the room moves through the openings in or between containers toward the low pressure zone, sweeping heat away from the product (Figure 5.3). The exhaust fan is typically a permanent unit that also circulates air over the refrigeration coils and returns it to the cold room. The exhaust fan can be a portable unit that is placed to direct the warm exhaust air toward refrigeration evaporators. 76 Chapter 5 Figure 5.3: Tunnel Cooler. 5.3.4 Forced-Air Serpentine Cooling The serpentine cooling in Figure 5.4 is used for forced-air cooling of product in bins. Bins must have bottom ventilated slots; ventilation on sidewalls of the bins does not aid cooling although it does not hinder it either. The system requires modification of cold-wall design to allow the forklift openings between bins to be used as air supply and return plenums. The cold air moves vertically through the product in each bin causing a slight pressure differential between plenums. Bins may be stacked up to six rows deep against the cold wall, depending upon the cooling speed desired and the available airflow. The airflow capacity of small forklift opening plenums is nearly 0.005 m3/s/kg of product. Cooling is usually slower than tunnel coolers. To achieve the desired airflow pattern, openings are placed in the cold wall to match alternate forklift openings, starting one bin up from the floor. On the room side of the bins, these same openings are then blocked. Air flows into an open slot between bins and passes up or down through one bin of product to reach the return plenum. This system does not require space between rows of bins, and bins can be stacked in even numbers as high as the cold store or forklift can reach. Forced-Air Cooling of Fruits and Vegetables 77 Figure 5.4: Serpentine Cooling. 5.3.5 Hydro Air Cooler A frequent complaint about both conventional and batch hydrocoolers is that they do not cool all containers uniformly. The chilled water may not be evenly distributed throughout the load resulting in undercooling some parts. To overcome these deficiencies, the batch hydrocoolers are fitted with a high-capacity fan to pull a fine mist of chilled water through the product packages. The forced air has the effect of making the cooling more consistent because it pulls hydro air past the product more evenly than would occur by gravity flow alone. This design in Figure 5.5 known as hydro air cooling has been successfully used with items that are difficult to air cool. Pallet loads of sweet corn or celery are effectively cooled in these types of hydro air cooler. Sweet corn in wirebound crates stacked five crates high was cooled from 32°C – 1.0°C in 1 h with overhead flow from nozzle of 380 lpm in conjunction with air circulation of 78 m3/min. 5.3.6 Air Cooling of Cut Flowers Because of their high rate of respiration and low tolerance for heat, deterioration in cut flower is rapid at field temperatures. Refrigerated highway vans do not have the capacity to remove the field heat in sufficient time to prevent some deterioration from occurring. Forced-air cooling is commonly used by the flower industry. As with most fruits and vegetables, the cooling rate of cut flowers varies substantially among the various types. The half cooling time for packed boxes of gypsophila was about 3 min compared to about 20 min for chrysanthemums 78 Chapter 5 Figure 5.5: Hydro Air Cooler. at airflows ranging from 38 to 123 lps per box. Within this range, cooling time was proportional to the reciprocal of the airflow but varied less with airflow than with flower type. 5.4 Product Moisture Loss in Forced-Air Cooling Moisture loss in forced-air cooling ranges from very little to amounts significant enough to damage product. Factors that affect moisture loss include product initial temperature, respiration coefficient, rate of cooling, humidity, exposure to airflow cooling and weather, as well as use of moisture-resistant packing. High initial temperature results in greater moisture loss. This factor can be minimized by harvesting at cooler times of day (i.e., early morning or night), and cooling or at least shading the product immediately after harvest to keep reheating during packing to a minimum. The primary advantage of high humidity during cooling is that product packing can absorb moisture, which reduces the packaging’s absorption of moisture from the product itself. A high respiration coefficient also increases moisture loss. For example, carrots with a high respiration rate can lose 0.6–1.8% of their original uncooled weight during cooling. Packing carrots in polyethylene packaging has reduced moisture loss to 0.08%, although cooling times are about five times longer. Film box liners, sometimes used for packing products with low respiration coefficient (e.g., apples, pears, kiwifruit, and grapes) are useful in reducing moisture loss, but they also increase the time required to cool products. Some film-based liners are perforated to reduce condensation. Boxes used for packaging grapes must also include SO2-generating pads to reduce decay. Forced-Air Cooling of Fruits and Vegetables 79 Figure 5.6: Produce Cooling Pattern with Forced-Air Cooling at 1.5°C. The forced-air cooler should reduce or stop airflow automatically as soon as the target product temperature is reached. Otherwise moisture loss will continue if the surrounding air is not close to saturation. One of the methods for doing this is to link the cooler fan control to the return air plenum temperature so that the fan speed can be slowed as the temperature of the return air approaches that of the supply air. 5.5 Produce Cooling Pattern with Forced-Air Cooling The product cooling pattern shown in Figure 5.6 was obtained during forced-air precooling from 24°C to 1.5°C using cool air at 1.5°C. Produce cools at different rates depending on its position in the container and in the stack. Product along the periphery of the container is more exposed to cool air and cools faster (lower line of the graph). Product in the center of a container shielded from cool air cools slower (upper line of the graph). Figure 5.6 represents temperature and cooling time for a produce in forced-air cooling. The initial temperature of the produce was 24.0°C. The cooling medium temperature was 1.5°C. This method removes the field heat quickly from horticultural produce and at the same time prevents a reduction of weight and quality due to moisture loss. This new system is used more and more in the flower and vegetable trade. The system gives excellent results when flowers or vegetables have to be transported over long distances, and it increases the shelf life of the produce. Good results are obtained, however, only when using this system in combination with a new method of air circulation called flow-through cooling. Cold air is made to flow through all the packaged produce by means of pressure difference. There are two systems: 1. Pressure cooling, in which the air is pushed through the spaces between the products. Pressure cooling was developed at the University of California in Davis. 2. Suction cooling, where the air is sucked through the space between the products. The first system can only be used for products stored in more or less closed cartons, the second for products stored in more open cartons or cases, as used for tomatoes and mushrooms. Pressure 82 Chapter 5 cooling results in a more uniform produce temperature, and because of the investment costs, it is mainly used for large plant produce and for produce to be sold at auctions, for instance. In long rows, 12, 13, or 14 pallets may be put behind one another, but when using carton boxes, only one pallet high is possible. The height of a pallet is between 1.2 and 1.65 m. When wooden or plastic boxes are used, pallets can be arranged too high. Figure 5.7 shows the rows of pallets placed on both sides of a suction channel and closed at the top by a roll-type curtain at one end; at the other end, the suction channel is connected to the space behind a separation wall. This particular system can be considered as a combination of cold wall and tunnel-type of forced-air cooling. The air leaving the air coolers is then forced through the pallets, and between all the packages, at the same time and temperature and with the same velocity of 2 m/s; the air then returns to the coolers via the suction channel and the space behind the separation wall. Two rows of pallets form one section. Between every section there should be a corridor of 60 cm. To achieve an adequate air velocity between the packages, an airflow of at least 25,000 m3/h per section is needed, and can even reach 50,000 m3/h. The air passage between the boxes on the pallets is equal to about 5% of the surface. The suction opening in the separation wall is about 60 cm wide, but the height depends on the height of the pallets. The pressure drop over the suction opening is about 100 Pa. Figure 5.7: Pressure (flow-through) Cooling System. Forced-Air Cooling of Fruits and Vegetables 83 For a refrigeration capacity up to 75 kW per section, cross-stream air coolers are used; above this capacity, counter-flow coolers are used; and above 95 kW per section, these coolers are fed with chilled water from a separate water chiller. The unit may be an ice bank machine. An ice bank can be built up during the hours when the refrigeration capacity demand is low and the price of electricity is also low. For small capacities of less than 50 kW per section, dry air coolers with a large cooling surface, small temperature differences, special suction pressure regulators, and pump-circulation can be used. Some examples of cooling times are: tomatoes 1 h, cucumbers 5 h, and peppers 2 h. These products are cooled down to +14°C and even as low as +8°C. The following products are cooled down to +4°C and sometimes down to +0.5°C: lettuce 12 h, spinach 6 h, cauliflower 8 h, and Brussels sprouts 8 h. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 6 Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 6.1 Introduction Cooling is generally considered the removal of field heat from freshly harvested products to inhibit spoilage and to reduce the rate of quality and flavor loss. The term precooling implies the removal of heat before the product is transported to a distant market, processed, or stored. Some products are slowly cooled by putting them in a shelter with good natural ventilation or with forced ventilation. Precooling is generally done in a separate facility within a few hours or even minutes of harvest. 6.2 Heat Load The refrigeration capacity needed for precooling is much greater than that required for holding a product at a constant temperature or for slow cooling of a product. Therefore, the heat load on a precooling system should be determined as accurately as possible. Even though it is imperative to have an adequate amount of refrigeration for effective precooling, it is uneconomical to have more refrigerating capacity available than is normally needed. 6.2.1 Mass Average Temperature Product temperature must be determined accurately in order to calculate heat load accurately. During rapid heat transfer, a temperature gradient develops within the product, with faster cooling causing larger gradients. This gradient is a function of product properties, surface heat transfer parameters, and cooling rate. Initially, for example, hydrocooling rapidly reduces the temperature of the exterior of a product, while the center temperature may not change at all. Most of the product mass is in the outer portion. Thus, calculations based on center temperature would show little heat removal while, in fact, substantial heat has been extracted. For this reason, the product mass average temperature must be used for product heat load calculations (Bennet et al., 1965). A mass average temperature denotes the single value from the transient temperature distribution that would become the uniform product temperature when held for a period under adiabatic conditions. All rights reserved. 86 Chapter 6 6.3 Hydrocooling Rates To design and operate hydrocooling machines effectively, it is necessary to understand how water removes heat from the produce and the factors that affect the rate of cooling for various types of produce. The basic heat transfer between the produce and the surrounding medium (i.e., cold water) is of the convection mode. The rate of heat transfer by convection mode depends on convection heat transfer coefficient, the surface area of the produce, and the temperature difference between the produce surface and the surrounding cooling medium. The basic heat transfer equation governing convection is (6.1) Q = h· a· (ts − t w ) where Q = the rate of heat transfer from produce, watts h = convective heat transfer coefficient, W/m2/°C a = surface area of produce, m2 ts = surface temperature of the produce, °C tw = cooling water temperature, °C The surface area that is exposed to the chilled water varies considerably among different types of produce. For example, the surface area of 5 kg of sweet corn is considerably less than that of 5 kg of snap beans. Therefore, if hydrocooled in water of the same temperature, the snap beans can be expected to lose heat at a much faster rate than sweet corn. In addition, the greater the difference of temperature between the water and produce, the faster the cooling. Hydrocooling rates are commonly represented in terms of cooling coefficient C and halfcooling time Z. The temperature ratio Y is defined as the unaccomplished temperature change at any time in relation to the total temperature change possible for the cooling condition. It is calculated by the following equation: where t –t Y= d w ts – t w (6.2) td = temperature to which the product is to be hydrocooled, °C tw = temperature of the coolant (water), °C ts = surface temperature of the product, °C The inverted temperature ratio times 100 denotes the percentage accomplished temperature change and is represented as 1 × 100 Y (6.3) Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 87 6.3.1 Cooling Coefficient The cooling coefficient denotes the change in product temperature per unit change of cooling time for each degree temperature difference between the product and its surrounding medium. In most cases, the relationship between temperature and time is exponential and the logarithmic transformation of the temperature ratio (Y) provides fairly an accurate straight-line fit to the data points. The typical cooling rate curve is shown in Figure 6.1. This curve is same as the curve shown in Figure 3.1. If Newtonian heat transfer occurs (a negligible temperature gradient within the product during cooling) and the straight-line asymptote intercepts the temperature ratio at unity for zero time, the cooling coefficient may be calculated by the simplified formula: C= where u = time lnY θ (6.4) When the produce is rapidly cooled, the conditions for Newton’s law are seldom satisfied because a considerable temperature gradient often develops within the product, depending on its properties and rate of surface heat transfer. Also, the zero asymptote intercepts the temperature ratio at some value either greater or less than unity. In the present case, the constant cooling coefficient is calculated by the equation, which is the slope of the cooling curve. Figure 6.1: A Typical Cooling Curve. 88 Chapter 6 C= lnY1 − lnY2 θ1 − θ 2 (6.5) where the subscripts 1 and 2 denote points along the straight-line asymptote to the cooling curve. 6.3.2 Half-Cooling Time The half-cooling time is the time required to reduce the temperature difference between the product and its surroundings by one-half. Mathematically it is expressed as Z = ln(0.5) / C (6.6) where C is a negative value 6.4 Empirical Methods for Calculating Hydrocooling Rates Field and laboratory studies have provided useful data on hydrocooling rates for many fruits and vegetable. Graphical relationships were developed summarizing the information. These graphs can be used to calculate the time required to cool the interior of a particular product to a designed temperature. The graph in Figure 6.2 shows seven ideal cooling times for various types of produce immersed in agitated chilled water. The horizontal axis is the cooling time in Figure 6.2: Time–Temperature Response of Various Fruits and Vegetables Immersed in Agitated Chilled Water. Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 89 minutes and the vertical axis is the temperature ratio (Y ). To calculate the hydrocooling time for a specific product, the Y is estimated by using equation (6.2) and the value so obtained is projected downward to the x-axis from a selected curve. This gives the time required to cool the product.
