How long will it take to reduce the center temperature to 10°C? What is the additional cooling time required for the product to be cooled to 5°C? Solution Y is calculated by using equation (6.3). Y= (10 – 1.5) = 0.30 ( 30 – 1.5) Locating the point on Figure 6.2 where curve F (for large cucumbers) intersects the Y = 0.30 line produces a cooling time of 44 min. (Note that this figure has a log scale.) For the time taken for product to be cooled to 5°C.  Y= ( 5 – 1.5 ) = 0.12 ( 30 – 1.5 ) Locating the point on Figure 6.2 where curve F intersects the Y = 0.12 line produces a cooling time of 70 min. Therefore, an extra 26 min of cooling is required for the cucumbers to be cooled to 5°C. Note: In this problem, it was assumed that the produce was completely immersed in agitated cold water. It is known that immersion is the fastest possible hydrocooling method. But when produce hydrocooled in a conventional hydrocooler are closely packed in a wirebound crate with other fruits, the cooling time would be considerably longer than with immersion 90 Chapter 6 hydrocooling. In such of the cases, the cooling rate of a conventional hydrocooler can be estimated by multiplying the immersion hydrocooling rate obtained as above with a conversion factor, the value of which is different for different types of product. For large cucumbers this value is 1.75. Therefore, the actual cooling time from 30°C to 10°C is 44 × 1.75 = 77 min, and for cooling to 5°C it is 70 × 1.75 = 122.5 min. Bennet et al., 1965 have given Figure 6.3(a) and 6.3(b) that shows the time-temperature response for hydrocooling of citrus, sweet corn, delicious apples, and peaches. From these Figure 6.3: Time–Temperature Response of Hydrocooled Produce. (a) Cooling time (min) (center), (b) Cooling time (min) (mass average) Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 91 curves we can calculate the time to cool the produce to mass average temperature (temperature at the geometric center) for different values of Y. 6.4.1 Half-Cooling Time Definition: The half-cooling time t1/2 is the time in any units, during which the temperature difference between product and coolant (air, water, ice, etc.) is halved. For example, if cantaloupe are at 33°C and water at 0°C, for a difference of 33°C, the time required to cool cantaloupe by 16.5°C is t1/2. The concept of half-cooling time lends itself admirably to calculation involving precooling, because t1/2 theoretically is independent of initial temperature of the product and remains constant during cooling. Thus, once t1/2 has been determined for a given crop and cooling condition, prediction of cooling accomplished in a certain interval is possible, regardless of the temperature of the product or coolant. Such prediction would not be possible if simple cooling rates were used, because they constantly change as the gradient between product and coolant changes. Thus, heat is removed rapidly during first half-cooling period, while the difference between product and coolant is greatest. Heat removal then becomes progressively slower during subsequent half-cooling periods and eventually becomes nil as the temperature of the product and coolant converge. This condition approaches after the third period has elapsed Figure 6.4. The theoretically valid conditions noted here do not always hold for rapid heat removal, such as occurs with hydrocooling, because heat conductivity and heat capacity of the product influence the rate of cooling. However, these difficulties were overcome by Covey who developed Figure 6.4: Heat Removal as a Function of Half-Cooling Time in Terms of Cooling Accomplished (left) and in Terms of Temperature Difference Remaining Between Product and Coolant (right). 92 Chapter 6 Table 6.1: Numerical values of half cooling times obtained in experiments Ishibashi (1969) Forced-air cooler with air at progressively declining temperature (10°C to 0°C); fruit conveyed through a cooling tunnel with air velocity 3.6 m/s; 65 mm diameter citrus fruits Delicious apples with air velocity of 2 m/s Bennett et al. (1969) Perry et al. (1968) 1. Potatoes in a bulk bin with air velocity of 1.3 m/s 2. Peaches 3. Apples Cooled from 25°C to 5°C in 1 h and half cooling time of 0.32 h Half cooling time of 0.32 h Half cooling time of 0.5 h, 0.4 h, and 0.38 h, respectively calculations that take into account these factors and yield reliable and highly practical data. These authors have determined t1/2 for hydrocooling of many vegetables. Half-cooling times however cannot be applied to vacuum cooling. Here, heat removal does not depend on a coolant, such as air or water, but on evaporation of water, a physical process that does not obey the same laws as heat removal from a surface (Table 6.1). 6.4.2 Application of the Concept of t1/2 Stewart and Couey, 1963 developed nomographs that permit ready prediction of commodity temperature with minimum calculation. The nomographs developed by Stewart and Couey, 1963 for crated asparagus, jumble-stacked contaloupes, and crated sweet corn are shown in Figures 6.5, 6.6, and 6.7, respectively, and are used to explain the method in the following numerical examples. Figure 6.5: Nomograph for Hydrocooling Exposed or Crated Asparagus. Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 93 Figure 6.6: Nomograph for Hydrocooling Jumble-Stacked Cantaloupe. Figure 6.7: Nomograph for Hydrocooling Crated Sweet Corn. Example 1: Determine how long crated asparagus at 90°F (32.2°C) must remain in the hydrocooler if a final temperature of 40°F (4.4°C) is desired and the coolant water is maintained at 34°F (1.1°C)? Solution: Figure 6.5 is the nomograph for hydrocooling of exposed and crated asparagus. Connect 90°F on the left and 34°F on the right of the nomograph with a straightedge. The 94 Chapter 6 sloped line intersects the horizontal line of 40°F at slightly under 8 min. Therefore, the answer in 8 min. Example 2: Contaloupe, jumble-stacked as on a conveyor belt (size 36) are 95°F (35°C) as they enter the hydrocooler and the coolant water is at 35°F (1.66°C). Due to high volume, the contaloupe can remain in the cooler only 10 min. How much cooling will have been accomplished? Solution: Figure 6.6 is the nomograph for jumble-stacked cantaloupe. Connect 95°F and 35°F with a straightedge. This sloping line intersects the 10 min vertical line at about 68°F (20°C). Obviously, considerably more precooling will be required in the railcar or truck trailer if the cantaloupe are to be carried satisfactorily. Incidentally, after 10 min, less than 50% (top horizontal line) of cooling has been accomplished. In this example, the half-cooling temperature value is calculated as follows. Temperature difference between product and coolant is 95 – 35 = 60°F. 60 Half of this difference in temperature is = 30°F. 2 For half-cooling, the product temperature is taken as either 95 – 30 = 65°F or as 35 + 30 = 65°F. From the nomograph corresponding to 65°F, the cooling time on the x-axis is 13 min. Therefore, t1/2 is 13 min. Example 3: Sweet corn is 85°F (29.4°C) when harvested in Florida and is packed in wirebound crates before being cooled. Can such corn be adequately cooled in 20 min when the water is held at 32°F (0°C)? Also calculate how long corn must be cooled to reach 40°F (4.4°C)? Solution: Figure 6.7 is the nomograph for hydrocooling of sweet corn. Connect 85°F and 32°F with a straightedge and corn will be cooled to 65°F (18.3°C) in 20 min. This represents an entirely unsatisfactory job of precooling. Hydrocooling should be followed by vacuum cooling and top-icing for a satisfactory precooling. How long would corn, as described here, have to be cooled to reach 40°F. The line drawn previously intersects 40°F at 75 min. 6.4.3 Universal Nomograph Stewart and Couey also provided a universal nomograph that is applicable to any commodity or method of cooling. This nomograph also can be used to solve problems such as that given for hydrocooling as long as t1/2 is known. Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 95 Figure 6.8: Universal Nomograph for Cooling or Warming. Example 4: Assume that potatoes packed in 100 lb (45 kg) bags and shipped in a railcar have a t1/2 of 1 12 days and that the air removing heat from the potatoes has average temperature of 41°F (5°C). How long would it take to cool the potatoes from 77 °F (25°C) to 50°F (10°C)? Solution: Figure 6.8 is the universal nomograph. Connect 25°C and 5°C on the nomograph with a straightedge. The horizontal 10°C line is intersected at two half-cooling periods. Because each t1/2 is equal to 1 12 days, for two half-cooling periods, the time required is 2 × 1 12 = 3days Example 5: Assume tomatoes packed in cartons are at 32°C (90°F) and cool to 15°C (59°F) by the end of the third day in transit when the air is 10°C (50°F). What is t1/2 for tomatoes under these conditions? Solution: The solution is shown in the general nomograph (Figure 6.8). Connect 32°C and 10°C with a straightedge. The 15°C line is intersected at 2 41 half-cooling periods. 3 Thus, 3 days is equivalent to 2 41 half-cooling periods and t1/2 is = 1.3 days. 2.25 Note that t1/2 can be determined only on the general nomograph; construction of the others required prior determination of t1/2 for the specific commodity. The general nomograph also can be used to solve problems such as those given for hydrocooling as long as t1/2 is known. The same procedure as given in Examples 4 and 5 applies. 96 Chapter 6 Figure 6.9: Typical Time–Temperature Pattern in Produce Cooling. Numbers along the temperature curve indicate the fraction obtained by dividing the difference between produce temperature and air temperature in the cooler by the difference between the initial produce temperature and the air temperature. 6.4.4 Half-warming Time The concept of half-cooling can also be applied with equal facility to warming except that the line drawn between product and coolant ascends rather than descends from left to right. Practical applications involve calculation of precooling that is wasted when cooled products wait in warm surroundings for loading into railcars or truck trailers or of heat that is gained during hot-water treatment for diseases control. 6.4.5 Cooling Time Curve Rate of cooling is directly related to the temperature difference between the cooling medium and the product. Initially, when the product is warm, temperature drops quite rapidly; later, the rate slows as product temperature drops. Average product temperature during cooling follows a pattern similar to Figure 6.9. The product is considered “half-cool” when its temperature drops to half the difference between its initial temperature and the cooling medium temperature. After another half-cooling period the product is “three-quarters” cool. Product is usually finished cooling at “seven-eighths” or “fifteen-sixteenths” cool. 6.5 Hydrocooling Methods Water is a better heat-transfer medium than air; consequently, hydrocoolers cool produce much faster than forced-air coolers. In well-designed shower coolers, small diameter produce, such as cherries, cool in less than 10 min. Large diameter products such as melons cool in 45 to 60 min (Stewart and Lipton, 1960; Stewart and Couey, 1963; Thompson et al., 1998). Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 97 Immersion coolers usually have longer cooling times than shower coolers because water speed past produce is slower. Packages for hydrocooled produce must allow vertical water flow and must tolerate water contact. Plastic or wood containers work well in hydrocoolers. Corrugated fiberboard must be wax-dipped to withstand water contact. Hydrocoolers cause no moisture loss in cooling. In fact, they can rehydrate slightly wilted product. Hydrocooler water spreads plant decay organisms and it must be obtained from a clean source and treated (usually with hypochlorous acid from sodium hypochlorite or gaseous chlorine) to minimize the levels of decay organisms (Thompson et al., 1998). Free stone peaches, clingstone peaches for canning, tart cherries, and cantaloupe are hydrocooled. Few apples and citrus fruits are hydrocooled. Hydrocooling is not popular for citrus fruit because it has a long marketing season and good postharvest holding ability. Citrus fruits are also susceptible to increased peel injury and to decay and loss of quality and vitality after hydrocooling. Many vegetables are successfully hydrocooled. The more important of these are sweet corn, celery, radishes, and carrots. Hydrocooling can be fairly energy efficient and is the least expensive cooling method to purchase. 6.6 Types of Hydrocoolers A typical schematic view of a hydrocooler is shown in Figure 6.10. Hydrocooling is accomplished by flooding, drenching, or immersing the product in an agitated bath of chilled water. Figure 6.10: Schematic View of a Typical Hydrocooler. 98 Chapter 6 6.6.1 Continuous-Flow Immersion Hydrocooler A continuous-flow immersion hydrocooler cools the packaged product by flooding as it is conveyed through a cooling tunnel. Adaptations consist of conveying the product through the cooling tunnel in loose bulk or in bulk bins through the use of combined immersion and flood cooling of loose fruits dumped into cold water that remain immersed for half of their travel through the cooling tunnel. An inclined conveyer gradually lifts the fruits out of the cooler and moves them through an overhead shower. A typical hydrocooler working on this principle is shown in Figure 6.10. These coolers have greater flexibility in the packaging of product than a cooler working only on a simple flooding principle. 6.6.2 Water Shower Hydrocooler Water shower hydrocoolers with conveyors are used to cool vegetables before packaging. The water is cooled by flooded refrigerated plates or pipe coils located over or adjacent to flood pans above the mesh belt conveyor. The flood pans deliver 0.6 to 1°C water evenly over the produce as it is conveyed below. The water passing through the mesh conveyors is filtered and returned by pump and piping to the chiller. In some cases, particularly where produce has a high initial temperature, it may be worthwhile to augment the basic hydrocooler with ambient water or air cooling sections prior to the refrigerated hydrocooler to reduce refrigeration and energy costs (Figure 6.11). Most vegetables are moved by fork truck in unit loads of as many as 40 packages. In one system, chilled water sprays stacks of packed vegetables placed in a refrigerated room. Water is collected in floor drains leading to a sump and recirculated over the product. One nozzle spraying approximately 5.7 l/s of water is located over each stack, which may contain 30-40 crates (Figure 6.12). Figure 6.11: Cutaway Side View of a Continuous-Flow Immersion Hydrocooler. (Source: © 1998 Univ. of California Board of Regents. In Thompson et al., op. cit. Used by permission.) Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 99 Figure 6.12: Cutaway Side View of a Continuous-Flow Shower-Type Hydrocooler. (Source: © 1998 Univ. of California Board of Regents. In Thompson et al., op. cit. Used by permission.) Other unit load systems convey the stack through cooling tunnels. Either spray nozzles or a flood pan may be used to deliver up to 25 l/s of chilled water to each stack. Most commercial hydrocoolers provide overhead showering at a rate of 14 to 17 l/s per square meter of top face area. This type of hydrocooler requires less space than the batch type but is not as flexible. With the batch system, chilled water can be sprayed on the product indefinitely depending on the season and the incoming product temperature. Also, the crates can be left in place after cooling until they are shipped. 6.6.3 Batch-Type Hydrocooler A batch-type hydrocooler uses spray nozzles for cooling the product and is shown in Figure 6.13. 6.7 Hydrocooler Design Considerations The rate of heat transfer q is directly proportional to the surface heat transfer coefficient h, the total surface area A, and the difference in temperature between the surface and its surroundings ∆L. To determine refrigeration requirements, the product mass average temperature, which was described previously, should be used. If the fluid velocity is sufficient, as in gravity flow or forced convection over fruit and vegetable products, the resistance to heat transfer at the surface is negligible. In this case, the heat is removed as fast as it comes to the surface, and the temperature difference across the surface boundary layer is small (0.5 K or less). In ideal hydrocooling, the optimum average film coefficient of heat transfer is roughly 680 W/(m2 K): the average temperature difference across the boundary layer is about 0.4 K. On this basis, the rate of heat transfer per unit surface area 100 Chapter 6 Figure 6.13: Batch-Type Hydrocooler. is = 680 × 0.4 = 270 W per square meter of product area. The value of h varies substantially, depending on many conditions. However, because of limitations in water temperature and product thermal properties and similarity among products, this is about as fast as any fruit or vegetable can be cooled in water. Flooded ammonia systems are often used to cool the water for hydrocoolers in large packing houses. Some use a secondary coolant. In packing houses with central plants, cooling coils are contained in a tank through which water is rapidly circulated. Refrigerant temperature inside the cooling coils is approximately 2°C, except in systems with ice-building coils, which may operate at a lower temperature. 6.8 Hydrocooler Operation and Maintenance Solar load, radiation from hot surface, convection from ambient air, or conduction from surroundings can affect the load. Protecting the hydrocooler from these sources of heat gain will enhance efficiency. Refrigeration capacity in excess of needs and cooling to a temperature below that required also reduces efficiency. Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 101 When hydrocooler water is recirculated, as is usually the case in mechanically refrigerated units, decay-producing organisms accumulate. Mild disinfectants such as chlorine will reduce buildup of bacteria and fungus spores, but they will not kill infections already in the products or sterilize either the water or the product surfaces. Brown rot and rhizopus decay spores on the surface and under the skin of peaches can be destroyed by soaking the fruit in water at 52°C for 2 to 3 min, or by treating the fruit with a chemical fungicide, which is usually put into the hydrocooling water. The principal problem with chemicals is maintenance of uniform concentrations, particularly in ice-refrigerated equipment because of the constant dilution from melting ice. In addition, hydrocooler shower pans and/or trash screens need regular (daily) cleaning to provide maximum efficiency. In this process, water is cooled and delivered to the produce by a simple system consisting of tanks holding thousands of liters of water, a high-capacity pump and valves, and an ice crusher. Graded and packed product, as much as 600–800 crates, are loaded from the field into a tractor trailer. Perforated pipes are then inserted into the trailer above the load to deliver a shower of chilled water from the stationary cooling system. The water flowing out of the trailer is collected, filtered, recooled, and recycled. Water flow rates of 1,000 gallons per minute are common. After an hour or more of hydrocooling, the pipes are withdrawn and a layer of crushed ice is added over the top of the crates and the product is immediately shipped. 6.8.1 Truck Hydrocooling To cool the water, blocks of ice are crushed and added to the tank. Approximately 300 pounds of block ice is required per 100 gallons of water initially. As the water warms during the cooling process, ice is added periodically. Though such type of cooling systems can be arranged by producers, it has poor thermal efficiency. 6.9 Warm–Up after Hydrocooling After hydrocooling the cooled product should be promptly loaded into a refrigerated car or truck or placed in a refrigerated room. Hydrocooled melons in ambient summer temperature warm up quite rapidly. A few hours of such exposure will result in loss of most of refrigeration gained through hydrocooling. Hydrocooled carrots packed in ventilated film bags rewarm from below 4.5°C to above 15.5°C in about 30 min when exposed to 21°C ambient. Part of the rewarming is due to heat transfer through bags and part is from respiration. A comparison of typical product effects and cost for six common cooling methods is shown in Table 6.2. 102 Chapter 6 Table 6.2: Cost comparison Forced-air Hydro Vacuum Water Spray Ice 1 – 10 0.1 – 2.0 No 0.1 – 1.0 0 – 0.5 Yes 0.3 – 2.0 2.0 – 4.0 No 0.3 – 2.0 No data Yes 0.1 – 0.3 No data 0.1 – 2.0 Yes, unless No bagged Forced-air Hydro Vacuum Water Spray Ice Room Potential for decay contamination Capital cost Energy efficiency Water-resistant packaging needed Portable Low High None High Low Low Low Low No Low High Yes Medium High No Medium Medium Yes High Low Yes Low Low No Sometimes Common Common Common No Feasibility of in-line cooling Rarely done Rarely done Yes No No Rarely done No Typical cooling time (h) Product moisture loss (%) Water contact with product Room Source: Thompson et al., 1998. 6.10 Refrigerated Storage of Flowers Refrigerated storage is the most common system for handling harvested flowers. Flowers can be held in refrigerated storage for 1 to 3 weeks, depending on the species. Refrigerated storage is more generally used as an aid for maintaining quality as flowers pass through the market channel. It involves the following sequential steps. 1. Flower stems should be cut with a sharp knife or shears to prevent crushing of stem and water-conduction cells. 2. The cut flowers should be placed in a preservative solution as soon as possible to prevent wilting. 3. The flowers should not be allowed to be out of water while waiting to be transferred to storage or grading. 4. If flowers are cut in the field, buckets containing solution can be brought out on trailers to hold the harvested flowers. 5. Flowers cut in the greenhouse should not be left in the sun or out of water for more than a few minutes. One person should be assigned to carry these flowers to the grading room or storage cooler immediately. 6. As soon as flowers arrive at the storage room, they should be placed in preservative solution inside the refrigerated storage room. 7. If wilted, they should be placed in a warm preservative solution at room temperature until turgid. They should then be placed in the cooler. Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 103 8. The temperature of the refrigerated room should be 0.5–4°C (33–40°F). The lower the temperature the better because the respiration rate falls off with diminishing temperature. Low respiration rates have an effect similar to that resulting from adding sucrose to the preservative solution in that they conserve carbohydrates within the flower. A temperature range of 35–40°F (2–4°C) is usually encountered in flower coolers. Special attention should be paid to some flowers, such as orchids and gardenias, which cannot withstand low temperatures. 9. Air should be gently circulated inside the cooler only to the extent necessary to ensure uniform temperatures in all areas. Unprotected flowers placed in a direct air stream will be desiccated. Flowers immediately adjacent to a cooling coil may freeze even though the air temperature is above freezing. Because the coil itself is below the freezing point, radiant heat is lost from the flower to the coil, and the flower can be colder than the surrounding air. 10. Potential sources of ethylene gas should be avoided by keeping fruit and vegetables out of the cooler. Discard old flowers. Wash the inside of the cooler periodically. 11. Replace the preservative solution at intervals of 2 to 7 days. The preservative should be checked periodically for bacterial growth, which is apparent when the solution becomes cloudy. Despite the bactericides in preservatives, microorganisms will develop and need to be eliminated periodically. To accomplish this, wash the buckets with a disinfectant such as bleach. 12. Refrigerated storage goes beyond this point, but from here on it becomes difficult to ensure that it is carried out properly. The flowers are sold to a wholesaler who, in turn, sells them to a retail shop. The wholesaler and retailer should also hold the flowers under refrigeration. Whenever possible, flowers should be transported under refrigeration. Needless delays at shipping terminals should be avoided. Instruct the wholesaler and retailer to cut ½ inch (1.3 cm) from the base of the steams whenever it has been necessary to leave the flowers out of water for a period of time and then to place them in warm water at a cool air temperature to avoid the ends of the stems from drying out and restricting water movement. It is the opinion of many growers and wholesalers that with the use of these procedures, floral preservatives are not necessary. 6.11 Dry Storage of Flowers Dry storage is used when flowers must be held for periods longer than 1–5 days. Roses may be held in dry storage up to 18 days, chrysanthemums and carnations for as long as 6 weeks. Gladioli do not store well. Flower prices depend to a great degree upon market demand. Prices are high at holidays but flowers cannot always be scheduled to bloom at each holiday. Most flowers freeze at 27–29°F, so it is essential that the temperature stay above this point. Flower life expectancy is lessened at 33°F (0.5°C) and drops rapidly at temperatures above this point. 104 Chapter 6 6.11.1 Advantages and Procedure of Dry Storage 1. Dry storage offers a means of holding flowers without deterioration for a high-price holiday market. 2. Only the best-quality flowers should be dry stored. 3. Poor-quality flowers have a short vase life, if any at all, when they are removed from storage. 4. Flowers should be cut packaged for storage immediately without being placed in water. 5. Standard cardboard flower boxes are suitable, but a lining of polyethylene film should be placed in them to cover the flowers and seal in moisture. 6. Desiccation can be a problem in long-term storage, especially when an absorbent container such as cardboard is used. 7. With proper handling, dry stored flowers should have reasonable quality and the same longevity as fresh flowers. 6.11.2 Disadvantages of Dry Storage 1. A common problem of dry storage is the presence of free water on the flowers, which encourages the development of disease. While flowers only freeze at temperatures below 29°F (– 1.7°C), the free water will freeze at 32°F (0°C). Resulting ice crystals on the petals can be injurious. 2. Boxes and flowers packed at warm temperature develop condensation (free water) as the plants and air inside are cooled. Because of the polyethylene barrier, the water cannot escape. 3. Disease, enhanced by this moisture, is a common cause of failure in dry storage. Boxes of flowers should be cooled open in a 38–40°F cooler (3.3–4°C) and then sealed and placed in a 31°F (– 0.6°C) cooler. 4. Flowers removed from dry storage need to be hardened. Cut ½ inch (1.3 cm) from the bottom of each stem. Place the flowers in a preservative solution inside a 38–40°F (3– 4°C) cooler. Allow the flowers to become fully turgid (12–24 h) before marketing them. 5. Poor temperature control will decrease quality and longevity. 6. Dry storage is used to a limited degree by the industry and works best with chrysanthemums. Chrysanthemums, carnations, and roses are the crops to which it is primarily applied. 6.12 Bud Harvesting Bud harvesting is a procedure that is used infrequently but is fairly well proven and has a tremendous potential. Carnations and chrysanthemums can be harvested and shipped in the bud stage, which cuts down greatly on their volume and hence lowers the cost of shipping. The wholesaler may then store the buds or open them immediately for resale. Once open, the flower has at least the same vase life potential as a mature harvested flower. Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 105 There are other advantages to this system. Buds are more immune to handling injuries and ethylene toxicity, making a higher-quality final product possible. As in the case of mature harvested flowers, buds will dry store very well, enabling one to build up inventory for higherpriced market dates. Bud harvesting is not a new concept for all crops: roses, gladioli, irises, tulips, and peonies have always been cut in the bud stage. Carnations are cut when from ½ to 1 inch (13–25 mm) of petal color is showing. Standard chrysanthemums are cut when the buds are 2 inches (51 mm) in diameter. Buds at this stage can be placed directly into dry storage, or they can first be shipped under ice or refrigeration in a box and then be put into dry storage. When needed, buds are removed from the storage box, an inch (13 mm) of stem is cut off, and they are placed in a floral preservative solution. The buckets of buds are held in an opening room at (21–24°C) until the buds are fully open. A low light intensity is provided in the opening room. Carnation buds open in 2 to 3 days and chrysanthemum buds in 7 to 9 days. The open flowers may be held under refrigeration in the preservative solution, or they may be sold directly. The quality and longevity of these flowers have been reported to be superior to that of flowers harvested at maturity. Bud harvesting is becoming important. Growers who ship flowers great distance, across North America or from other countries, recognize its value and find it necessary to use this system. Greater cooperation among growers, wholesalers, and retailers will foster it even more. 6.13 Other Approaches Hypobaric (low-pressure) storage is a much newer idea. Fruits, vegetables, or flowers are placed in a sealed chamber, and a vacuum is established in the chamber down to a pressure of about 50 mm of mercury (6.7 kPa). The chamber is constructed to maintain a vacuum, yet allow fresh air to be swept through it. The chamber is also cooled to a low temperature. As the chamber is evacuated, the oxygen content is reduced to a level that sharply reduces respiration. Ethylene gas evolved by the plant tissue is quickly removed by the flowing air. Tentative evidence indicates that these systems will play a role in the future of floriculture. More testing is needed before low-pressure storage is realized. 6.14 Nursery Stock and Cut Flowers Low temperature (0°C + 0.5°C) and dry packaging prevent, or at least greatly retard, flower disintegration and extend the storage life. The temperature and storage life given in Table 6.3 for cut flowers allow for a reasonable shelf life after removal from storage; however, the storage period may be extended beyond that listed. These conditions, while not widely used commercially, are recommended. Proper dry packing requires a moisture-vapor-proof container in which flowers can be sealed. No free water is added because the package prevents almost all water loss. 106 Chapter 6 Table 6.3: Storage conditions for cut flowers and nursery stock Commodity Storage Temp (°C) Relative Humidity (%) Approx. Flowers held in water should not be crowded in the containers and should be arranged on shelves or racks to allow good air circulation. Forced air circulation should be provided, but flowers must be kept out of a direct draft. Use clean water and clean containers. Many kinds of nursery stock can also be stored at temperatures of 0.5 to 2°C. Open packages and freshen flowers before marketing if the blooms have been stored for long periods. Many kinds of cut flowers and greens are injured if stored in the same room with certain fruits, principally apples and pears, which give off gases (such as ethylene) during ripening. These gases cause premature aging of blooms and may defoliate greens. Greens should not be stored in the same room with cut flowers because the greens, acting in the same way as fruit, can hasten bloom deterioration. Greens, bulbs, and certain nursery stock are usually packaged or rated when stored. Some bulbs and nursery stock are packed in damp moss or similar material, and low temperatures are required to keep them dormant. Polyethylene wraps or box liners are effective for maintaining quality of strawberry plants, bare-root rose bushes, and certain cuttings and other nursery stock in storage. Strawberry plants can be stored up to 10 months in polyethylenelined crates at –1 to 0°C. 6.15 Storage Aspects of Few More Horticultural Products 6.15.1 Maple Syrup Maple syrup keeps indefinitely at room temperature without darkening or losing flavor, if packed hot (at or within a few degrees of its boiling point) and in clean containers, which are promptly closed airtight and laid on their sides or inverted to self-sterilize the closure, 108 Chapter 6 and then cooled. Refrigerated storage is not necessary. However, once opened, the syrup in a bottle, can, or drum may become contaminated by organisms in the air. Mold or yeast spores, which may be present in improperly pasteurized syrup, though unable to germinate in fulldensity syrup, may grow in the thin syrup on the surface caused by condensed water. Small packages not completely sterile, containing spores, can be kept free of vegetative growth by periodically inverting the containers to redisperse any thin syrup on the surface caused by condensed water. Maple syrup should never be packaged at temperatures below 82°C. After pasteurizing, cool the syrup as quickly as possible to prevent stack burn, which darkens the syrup and causes a lowering of its grade. 6.15.2 Honey Both extracted (liquid) and comb honey can be held satisfactorily in common dry storage for about a year. The slow darkening and flavor deterioration at ordinary room temperatures become objectionable after this time. Although cold storage is not necessary, temperatures below 10°C will maintain original quality for several years and retard or prevent fermentation. The range between 10 and 18°C should be avoided, because it promotes granulation; this increases the probability of fermentation of raw (unheated) honey. As storage temperature increases in the 27–38°C range, deterioration is accelerated; temperatures constantly above 30°C are unsuitable and above 32°C, quite damaging. Honey for export is best kept in cold storage, because the half-life for honey diastase at 25°C is about 17 mon. Raw honey of greater than 20% moisture is always in danger of fermentation; the likelihood is much less at or below 18.6% moisture. Below 17% moisture, raw honey will not ordinarily ferment. Granulation increases the possibility of fermentation of raw honey by increasing the moisture content of the liquid portion. Properly pasteurized honey will not ferment at any moisture content. Granulated honey can be reliquified by warming to 50–60°C. Comb honey should not be stored above 60% relative humidity to avoid moisture absorption through the wax, which leads to fermentation. Finely granulated honey (honey spread, Dyce process honey, and honey cream) must not be stored above about 25°C. Higher temperatures will, in time, cause partial liquefaction and destroy the texture. Any subsequent regranulation by lower temperatures will produce an undesirable coarse texture. For holding more than 4 months, cold storage is required. 6.15.3 Vegetable Seeds Seeds generally benefit from low temperatures and low humidity storage. High temperatures and high humidity favor loss of viability. Most vegetable seeds undergo no significant Hydrocooling of Fruits, Vegetables, and Cut Flowers 109 decrease in germination during one season when stored at 10°C and 50% relative humidity. Full viability is retained far longer than 1 year as temperature and humidity are reduced. A temperature of –7°C and 15–25% relative humidity are considered ideal but rarely necessary unless seed viability must be maintained for many years. Aster, pepper, tomato, and lettuce seeds stored under these conditions had equal or better viability after 13 years than did the fresh seed. Low moisture content of the seed is important for germination. Hemp seed containing 9.5% moisture was mostly dead after 12 years storage at 10°C, but lost only 12% viability when moisture content was 5.7%. If stored at about –20°C, moisture percentage should not exceed 10% for many species. Seed with higher moisture content, when stored at –20°C, eventually equilibrates at a lower moisture level but may initially suffer frost damage. At higher temperatures, if it is impossible to keep humidity low enough, seeds must be stored in moisture-proof containers. 6.16 Questions 1. CHAPTE R 7 Evaporative Cooling Systems for Fruits and Vegetables 7.1 Introduction In an evaporative cooling (EC) system, dry air is drawn through moist padding or a fine mist of water. The dry air gets cooled by giving its heat to the moisture of the pad. This method is inexpensive and effective for lowering the product temperature. The air thus cooled is drawn through the vents between the product containers. This method would be suitable for warm season crops such as tomato, cucumbers, eggplant, and peppers. The minimum outdoor air temperature required for successful evaporating cooling is above 32°C; another requirement is relatively low wet bulb temperature (WBT) preferably less than 21°C. High dry bulb temperature and low WBT provide better conditions for EC of outdoor air. 7.2 Thermodynamics of EC The EC is considered an adiabatic process; therefore, the process occurs at constant enthalpy. The cooling of air occurs while passing through a wet padding material or through mist or fog of water because the transforming of sensible heat (SH) of incoming air into latent heat (LH) is actually used in evaporating moisture from the wet pad or from the fog or mist. This ultimately results in a decrease in dry bulb temperature and increase in the relative humidity (RH) of the air entering into the cooling chamber. The WBT and enthalpy remain unchanged. The schematic diagram of EC is shown in Figure 7.1. 7.3 Psychrometry of EC Process The adiabatic EC system is represented on psychrometric chart as shown in Figure 7.2 and Figure 7.3. t di < t do = Decrease in dry bulb temperature t wi < t wo = No changes in WBT RHi < RHo = Increase in RH hi = ho = No change in enthalpy In Figure 7.2, Point 1 represents the condition of the ambient air entering into the wet pad of the evaporative cooler, and Point 2 is the condition of the air leaving the evaporative cooler. Cp (t1 − t 2 ) = hfg (W2 − W1 ) (7.1) where Cp = specific heat of air, kJ/kg oC t1, t2 = dry bulb temperatures of the entering and leaving air °C respectively hfg = LH of evaporation of water at temperature t2, kJ/kg W1, W2 = specific humidity of air entering and leaving the evaporative cooler, kg/kg of dry air A higher drop in dry bulb temperature is possible with greater increase in specific humidity. The maximum outlet air specific humidity is limited to W2′ as shown at Point 3 in Figure 7.2. From Figure 7.3 it can be seen that for the same dry bulb temperature of outdoor air, the EC will be more effective if the RH of the incoming air is lower. This point is clear as (t1 – t2) > (t1 – t 2′ ). Therefore, low RH of the incoming air is preferable for EC. 7.3.2 Efficiency of EC System The efficiency of EC system is defined as the ratio of the actual drop in dry bulb temperature of air passing through the cooler to the wet bulb depression of the cooling air. η= (t1 – t 2 ) × 100 (t1 – t 3 ) (7.2) Evaporative Cooling Systems for Fruits and Vegetables 113 Figure 7.3: Psychrometric Chart with Lower Relative Humidity. where t1 = temperature of the outdoor air, °C t2 = temperature of the cooled air, °C t3 = temperature of the saturated air, °C With spray-type coolers, the adiabatic efficiency achieved is 80–85%, whereas with wet pad system it is about 60%. 7.4 Types of EC Systems 7.4.1 Fan and Pad Types In this type of system, the water is allowed to trickle over an excelsior cross-fluted cellulose or plastic coir, or wood fiber pads. A centrifugal pump is used for this purpose (Figure 7.4). The commercial-type evaporative cooler used for cooling warm season fruits or vegetables is shown in Figure 7.5. The arrangement of containers in the cooling chamber should be such that cool air moves all around the containers at a minimum velocity for efficient and uniform cooling. Figure 7.4: Fan and Pad Type Evaporative Cooling. 114 Chapter 7 Figure 7.5: Commercial-Type Evaporative Cooler. The pads are kept moist with water, and the water evaporates as dry air passes through the moist pad absorbing heat from the air. Thus, the air gets cool and enters the chamber where it is circulated among the product. In doing so, the fruits are cooled. The makeup water is controlled by a float in the water tank. Excess water is removed through the drain. Small units of such coolers up to 2,000 m3/min of air are common. 7.4.1.1 Estimation of mass flow rate of air The two general methods of cooling of food materials are refrigerated air-conditioning and EC. Though air-conditioning provides an accurate control over the temperature and humidity of air, the initial cost is more than four times greater and running costs are six to eight times greater than an EC plant. In case of spaces cooled by EC, the circulation of air within the space is on the order 30–60 m/min. If unsaturated air is exposed to free and cooler water in adiabatic conditions, some of the SH of air is transferred to water and is converted to its LH, evaporating some of the water. This additional vapor increases the humidity of the air but its temperature is reduced due to loss of SH. This conversion of SH into LH goes on until the air saturates. This process is known as direct EC. There are limits to the cooling achieved by an adiabatic saturation process. The amount of SH removed can never exceed the LH required to saturate air with the water vapor. Thus, the cooling possibility of air depends upon the RH and WBT of the air. In this process, WBT is the lower temperature that can be achieved by direct EC. Volume of air = 179.5 = 34.7 m 3 /min/ton 30 − 24.9 116 Chapter 7 Figure 7.6: Spray-Type Evaporative Cooler. 7.4.2 Mist or Spray-Type EC This system is provided with one or two banks of mist nozzles (Figure 7.6). The baffles located on the entrance side provide good uniformity of airflow across the face of the cooler. The eliminator on the leaving side prevents moisture carryover. The spray type requires considerably more water, 0.5–1.0 kg/m3 of air than wet pad type (0.1 kg/m3). The three-bank cooler has considerably higher saturation efficiency of 90–95%, whereas single-bank systems give 70–80%. Spray-type coolers are preferred for large-size cooling room. These factors affect the performance of these coolers: 1. 2. 3. 4. Quantity of water sprayed Nozzle spray pressure Velocity of air through the spray Length of spray chamber Air velocities range between 100 m/min and 200 m/min. This unit can be used to supply 600 m3/min and above of cool air. The operating pressure of moist/spray nozzle varies between 20 bar and 40 bar. This type of EC provides cool fresh filtered air to the cooling chamber. 7.4.3 Limitations of Simple EC Systems 1. The lowest possible dry bulb temperature achieved is the WBT of the ambient air. 2. The EC is successful only in those areas where reasonably low WBT (2°C and below) occurs simultaneously with high dry bulb temperature (35°C and above). 3. The humidity of the air cooled by EC is considerably high. Evaporative Cooling Systems for Fruits and Vegetables 117 7.5 Indirect or Modified EC Systems EC is successful in those areas where reasonably low WBT occur simultaneously with high dry bulb temperatures. The maximum dry bulb temperature attainable leaving the evaporative cooler is the WBT of ambient air. To overcome this problem, another method of EC called modified EC has come into use. In modified EC, air is cooled before being sent into the evaporative cooler. The process is represented in Figure 7.7. If the ambient air condition is represented by Point 1 as shown in Figure 7.7, the maximum drop in DBT is t1 – t1′ . This range of drop can be increased by decreasing the initial DBT of the ambient air by sensible cooling with help of some method. This would result in a considerable increase in cooling capacity offered by a simple EC system. In this case, the maximum drop in DBT possible is (t1 – t 2′ ). This type of sensible cooling first and EC afterward is known as modified EC. The modified EC is considered under two types of ambient air conditions: 1. Hot and dry air condition 2. Hot and wet air condition The schematic diagrams representing these two types and their processes on psychrometric chart are explained next. 7.5.1 Modified EC When Outside Air is Hot and Dry The principle of the system is to reduce the WBT of the outdoor air by sensible cooling without the use of a refrigeration system. With a single spray-type EC system, the maximum drop in DBT possible is the difference between DBT of outdoor air and its corresponding WBT. This difference can be increased by Figure 7.7: Modified Evaporative Cooling. 118 Chapter 7 Figure 7.8: (a) Two-Stage Evaporative Cooling with Heat Exchanger. (b) Presentation on Psychrometric Chart. introducing a heat exchanger in the circuit as shown in Figure 7.8(a). For starting the plant, first load is kept off and air is allowed to pass through both the spray chambers. When the air is sufficiently cooled then it is passed through the heat exchanger and after that through the load in the cooled room. The systematic changes of air condition through different equipment are shown in Figure 7.8(b) on a psychrometric chart. a = Condition of the outdoor air ab = Sensible cooling of outdoor air in the heat exchanger bc = Adiabatic cooling through first spray chamber cd = Absorption of SH load from the room de = Adiabatic cooling through second spray chamber ef = Heating of the air at condition e due to the cooling of outdoor air from condition a to b The advantage of this type of system is that the DBT of outdoor air can be reduced below its WBT of outside air shown by Point a in Figure 7.8(b). The maximum possible DBT drop with number of adiabatic chambers in a series is (ta – tg), but due to precooling of the air in the heat exchanger, the maximum possible drop in DBT is (ta – th) as shown in the Figure 7.8(b). The actual drop achieved is (ta – tc). It has been practically observed that the effect of decrease in DBT with one heat exchanger and a two-stage adiabatic spray cooling is more economical. 7.5.2 Modified EC When Outside Air is Hot and Wet The modified EC can also be used in wet and hot weather successfully. The arrangement of the components is as shown in Figure 7.9(a). Evaporative Cooling Systems for Fruits and Vegetables 119 Figure 7.9: (a) Evaporative Cooling Circuit. (b) Presentation on Psychrometric Chart. If the temperature of the ambient air is 40°C and RH is 80%, the air first passes through the drier as shown in Figure 7.9(a) where its RH is reduced considerably. The condition of the air through different equipment is represented on the psychrometric chart as shown in Figure 7.9(b). a = Condition of the ambient air ab = Removing of moisture from the ambient air in a silica gel dehumidifier bc = Sensible cooling in heat exchanger cd = EC in the first evaporative cooler de = Absorption of SH load from the room ef = EC in the second evaporative cooler 120 Chapter 7 fg = Heating of the air passing through heat exchanger and used for initial cooling of the air coming from the silica gel dehumidifier 7.5.2.1 Heat Balance Heat lost during cooling (bc) = Heat gained by passing through heat exchanger (fg) Actual DBT drop is (ta – th), but due to precooling, the maximum possible drop is (ta – td). 7.6 Energy Cube System The modified EC system is also presently known as energy cube system (En3), and it saves energy through three ways. 1. Initial costs are as low as 50% of the conventional refrigeration system. 2. The power goes down by 80%. 3. Conditioned fresh air at no extra cost. 7.7 Design of WBT and Airflow for EC Systems The EC mainly constitutes adiabatic humidification followed by sensible heating of air because of its passing over the produce. During the process, adiabatic humidification gets cooled, and the cooled air absorbs heat from fruits when it enters the produce chamber and is heated again. This is true both for fan and pad systems or spray such as fogging or misting systems of air cooling. The only difference between these two systems is that in the pad system, water evaporates from the pad by absorbing heat from the air and the air thus cooled is not saturated, whereas in the case of spray or foggers, as water is sprayed into the air, the air is both cooled and saturated. For these two systems the psychrometric representation on the chart is given separately in Figure 7.10. Line ab shows the adiabatic humidification and bc represents addition of heat while passing through the produce in the chamber. If the cooling load is h kJ/unit quantity of produce and (hc – hb) is the enthalpy change of air passing through the produce, the rate of airflow Q is given by Q = h/(hc – hb) kg/h unit quantity of produce Because enthalpy of moist air is closely related to the WBT, the value of hb (enthalpy of incoming air) to be used to find the required airflow rate depends on the outside design WBT. As the air passes across the load, heat is added to it and the highest temperature will be reached just as it reaches the outlet. Therefore, (tmax) permitted temperature of air at the outlet of the room limits enthalpy hc of the outgoing air. The figure also shows that the amount of heat that can be picked up by air following path b1c1 without exceeding tmax depends primarily Evaporative Cooling Systems for Fruits and Vegetables Figure 7.10: The Process on the Psychrometirc Chart. 121 Figure 7.11: Psychrometrics for a Spray or Mist System. on how much the air is initially cooled below tmax. If there is insufficient supply of water to adequately cool the air, either the enthalpy change during b1c1 will have to be reduced, otherwise tmax may be exceeded. If the air is cooled a given number of degrees below tmax, the amount of water required increases as the DBT of air increases; this increase is more or less independent of outdoor WBT. To be sure of having enough water, a high-design DBT should be used. 7.7.1 Spray or Mist System When water is sprayed into the air, the process is different and may be like that shown in Figure 7.11. The difference occurs if more water is added to the air than can be evaporated by the SH that is immediately available. If this happens, the air becomes fully saturated and the water droplets are entrained in it. These droplets may fall out or be evaporated by the heat of the produce of the cooling chamber as the air moves across the load. If the temperature is high, the saturated air remains so up to part of its travel in the cool chamber until the entrained droplets are evaporated as shown by b1b2 and then follows the path b2c. 7.8 Ductwork The air distribution system should be low in cost because EC is a low investment means of providing for cooling of fruits or vegetables. Ductwork should be kept short with few branches and no complex turns. An arbitrary rule commonly used in the layout of an EC distribution system is to limit duct length to 15 m as a practical measure for simplification. 122 Chapter 7 7.9 Example Problems on EC Problem 7.1 A fan and pad system of 80% efficiency is used for supplying cool air to a product in a room. The maximum allowable temperature of the product is 28.6°C. The cooling load is 1.25 kw/m2 of the product surface area. The DBT and WBT of the ambient air are 35°C and 16°C, respectively. The SHF of the cooling room is 0.5. The total surface area of the product is 5000 m2. Find the airflow rate and water flow requirement of the system. Solution The psychrometric representation of the cooling process is shown in Figure 7.12(a) and the same process actually drawn on the real psychrometric chart is shown in Figure 7.12(b). Locate Point a on the psychrometric chart as per the outdoor air conditions. Draw a line following the constant enthalpy line. Locate Point b on this line representing 0.8 of the distance ad. From Point b, line bc is drawn representing the SH factor of 0.5. Point c is located at the intersection of the SHF line with tmax of 28.6°C line. The following data are noted from the psychrometric chart. hb = 45 kJ/kg hc = 61 kJ/kg Wb = 0.00950 kg/kg of dry air Wa = 0.00380 kg/kg of dry air Wc = 0.0128 Density of air = 0.845 kg/m3 Total cooling load = 1.25 × 5000 = 6,250 kJ/sec Water evaporated per kg of airflow = 0.00950 – 0.00380 = 0.00575 kg/kg of dry air Heat load The airflow rate ma = hc − hb 390 = 462 m3/sec Airflow rate = (6,250) / (61–45) = 390 kg/sec = 0.845 Total water evaporated = 390 × 0.00575 = 2.24 kg/sec Figure 7.12: (a) Psychrometric Representation of the Cooling Process Problem. Evaporative Cooling Systems for Fruits and Vegetables Figure 7.12: (cont.) (b) Problem 1 Solution on Actual Psychrometric Chart. 123 124 Chapter 7 Problem 7.2 A room is to be cooled with an EC system using foggers. The foggers are controlled by a humidistat set at 90% RH located at the middle of the room. The maximum temperature of the air leaving the cold storage is 31°C. The outdoor design conditions of the air are 40°C DBT and 25°C WBT. The heat load in the cool room is 6000 kJ/hr. Taking SHF of 0.5 for the cool room, find the airflow and water flow rate per second. If the air carries the water particles with it, then assume that the air passing through the cold room remains saturated till all water particles get evaporated. Solution The schematic of the spray chamber and the representation of the process on psychrometric chart are shown in Figures 7.13, 7.14, respectively. Locate Point a on the psychrometric chart at the given outdoor air conditions. As the air is saturated while passing through the foggers, locate Point b on the saturation line. The process on an actual psychrometric chart is shown in Figure 7.15. After cooling with entrained moisture in it, the air enters the cooling chamber. The air follows the saturation line of an indefinite length to account for entrained moisture, but the Point c is not yet located. Location of the path is found by assuming that half the enthalpy change in air has taken place by the time air reaches the humidistat. Therefore, the enthalpy of the air when it reaches the humidistat may be represented by ha = (hb + hd ) / 2 The process proceeds from Point c to some Point d, somewhere on tmax = 32°C DBT line along the SHF line of 0.5. This equation dictates that the line should cross the 90% RH line at Point o such that do = eo, where Point e is the intersection of the extension of lines ab and dc. Thus, with the slope of the line determined by the given SHF and its terminus known to be on the 31°C DBT line, dc can be drawn by trial and error in such a way that do = oe. After locating all the points on the psychrometric chart, the values noted are as follows: ta = 40°C DBT Wa = 0.0138 kg/kg of dry air tmax = 31°C Wb = 0.0202 kg/kg of dry air hb = 77 kJ/kg Wc = 0.0216 kg/kg of dry air hd = 90 kJ/kg Wd = 0.0224 kg/kg of dry air ho = 83.5 kJ/kg Heatload 6000 The airflow (ma ) = = = 461.53 kg /hr ( hd – hb ) 90 – 77.0 The water supplied by the spray cooler (for evaporation and water particles carried) = ma (Wc – Wa) = 461.53 (0.0216 – 0.014) = 3.507 kg/h Evaporative Cooling Systems for Fruits and Vegetables Figure 7.13: Schematic of Problem 2. 125 Figure 7.14: Psychrometric Representation of Problem 2. 7.10 Points to Be Noted in EC The following points should be noted in cases of EC: 1. There is transfer of SH of air into the LH of water; therefore, the total heat in the air remains constant. 2. WBT is constant, DBT decreases, and dew point rises. 3. The initial temperature of water in the evaporative cooler has no effect on the efficiency of the cooler because heat involved in cooling 1 kg of water to WBT is less than 20 kJ, while the heat of evaporation of 1 kg of water is of the order 2260 kJ. Recirculated spray of water adjusts itself to the WBT of the air. If the water enters the cooler at a temperature lower than WBT of the air, then it is first warmed to the WBT and then evaporates. If the water enters the cooler at a temperature higher than WBT of the air, then it is first cooled to the WBT and then evaporates. 7.11 Cost of EC Systems 1. EC systems initially look attractive on a cost basis as compared with untreated outside air as well as refrigerated cooling systems. 2. The investment cost of EC systems runs from US$100–300 per m3/min. The wide variation in cost results from many items that vary from system to system, including length of supply and exhaust air ducts, sophistication of control system, accessibility to equipment location, sound attenuation provision, insulation requirements, and special construction materials such as stainless steel and glass fiber. 3. Operating costs are based on 0.4 to 1.2 kW per 1000 m3/min for the water pump and 3 to 4.5 kW per 1000 m3/min for air handling device. 126 Chapter 7 Figure 7.15: Problem 2 Solution on Actual Psychrometric Chart. Evaporative Cooling Systems for Fruits and Vegetables 127 7.12 Maintenance of EC Systems The maintenance procedure used in EC system is simple: wood excelsior pads must be replaced after every year because they deteriorate. Water spray heads should be cleaned and checked once or twice in course of the cooling season. Even though an evaporative cooler itself will do a sufficient job of removing airborne particulate matter, many installations are more satisfactory with prefilters because this reduce load on pads results in more life to the pads. In a hard water condition, maintenance of washer tank and eliminators is more intense because of the collection of salts that precipitate out and collect on the inside of the unit. Water treatment is often required in addition to bleeding to prevent hard scale formation and algae growth. The growth of algae in an evaporative cooler rapidly plugs the pack and nozzles and also creates undesirable odors and possibly corrosion. For preventing and treating algae, a solution of hypochloride (bleach) can be injected into the water supply line to the pad. This will provide the required 3–5 ppm chlorine in the pad. Some coolers use hydrogen peroxide, which will not raise the pH level. Recently biocides have become available; and Biocide-20 when added once or twice to the water sump will control algae, bacteria, and fungi. It is used 20–47 mL/100 L of water and subsequently at the rate of 40–47 mL/100 L of water. Agribom tablets that contain bromine and lesser amounts of chlorine are also used. 7.13 Design of Cascade EC Systems Large differences in DBT and WBT in the summer, particularly in desert areas, makes the evaporative cooler a useful device to lower the DBT by a simple humidification process. But the condition of the air coming out of the evaporative cooler has high humidity, and therefore some fruits and vegetables sensitive to humidity cannot be stored effectively. If in a heat exchanger, the humidified air at low temperature from the evaporative cooler is utilized to cool another stream of air that is taken from the atmosphere, and the amount of humidified air is large compared to that of outside air, then the DBT of outside air (here after referred to as cooler air) will be reduced up to that of humidified air. Since no moisture is being added to the cool air its humidity remains constant, the cooled air will have lower wet and dry bulb temperatures than that of the original atmospheric air. If this cooled air is further humidified it will attain lower effective temperature than that of the original atmospheric air. Hence, cooled air after humidification will be more effective than the air coming out from an ordinary summer cooler. Because the humidification is done at two places it is named a cascade cooler system. Figure 7.16 shows the schematic of the cascade cooler system. In this the humidification of atmospheric air and the exchange of heat between humidified air and the air to be cooled 128 Chapter 7 Figure 7.16: Heat Exchanger Showing Metal Plate and Wick. 1, Air to be Humidified; 2, Air to be Cooled. take place simultaneously. One stream of air flows over a metal plate on which a wet wick is placed and hence this stream will get humidified. At the same time another stream of air flows below the metal plate and this stream becomes cooler because of heat transfer from it to the interface (i.e., between wick and humidified air) through the metal plate and wick. If the length of the metal plate and the wick is sufficient enough, the RH of the humidified air coming out of the cooler will be 100% and it will follow the path AB on the psychrometric chart (Figure 7.17). Another stream of air that flows below the metal plate will be cooled along the path AC because no moisture is being added to it. If the efficiency of the heat Figure 7.17: A – Condition of Outside Air; B – Theoretical Condition of Humidified Air; C – Theoretical Condition of Cooled Air; D – Actual Condition of Humidified Air; E – Actual Condition of Cooled Air.
