Post Harvest Management of Horticultural Crops. Agrobios, Jodhpur. CHAPTE R 10 Handling and Cold Storage of Vegetables 10.1 Introduction Like fruits, vegetables are highly perishable. The nutritional value as well as therapeutic values of vegetables is well recognized. Most producers and marketers are now aware that “fresh” creates the image that sells the product. The grower who sees profit in fresh, the consumer who prefers to use fresh, and those who pack, move, and distribute vegetables all have a stake in the produce market. Freshness required by retailers and ultimately the consumer can be met by using cold chain and by storing in cold conditions. Each type of vegetable has specific temperature (°C) and relative humidity (RH) requirements for their fresh and prolonged storage. In this chapter, the temperatures and RH recommendations (shown in parentheses) are the optimum levels for maximum storage in the fresh condition. For short storage, higher temperatures may be satisfactory for some commodities. Temperature requirements represent commodity temperature levels that should be maintained. Much of this information is taken from USDA Agricultural Handbook No. 66 (Hardenburg et al., 1986). 10.2 Artichokes, Globe (0°C and 95–100% RH) Globe artichokes are seldom stored, but for temporary holding a temperature of about 0°C is recommended. A high RH (at least 95%) will help prevent wilting. This product should keep for 2 weeks in storage if buds are uninjured and wilting is prevented. Perforated polyethylene liners with 250 holes of 6 mm/m2 holes/m2 help retard moisture loss. Hydrocooling or room cooling to 4°C on the day of harvest reduces deterioration. 10.3 Asparagus (0–2°C and 95–100% RH) Asparagus deteriorates rapidly at temperatures above 2°C and especially at room temperature. It loses sweetness, tenderness, and flavor, and decay develops later. If the storage period is 10 days or less, 0°C is recommended; asparagus is not ordinarily stored except temporarily, but at 2°C with a high RH, it can be kept in salable condition for 3 weeks. However, after a long haul to market, even under refrigeration, it cannot be expected to keep longer than 1–2 weeks. Asparagus should be cooled immediately after cutting. Hydrocooling is the usual method. During transit or storage, the butts of asparagus should be placed on some moist absorbent Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00010-5 165 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 166 Chapter 10 material to prevent loss of moisture and to maintain freshness of the spears. Sometimes asparagus bunches are set in shallow pans of water in storage. 10.3.1 Beans, Green or Snap (4–7°C and 95% RH) Green or snap beans are probably best stored at 4–7°C, where they may keep for about 1 week. Even these recommended temperatures cause some chilling injury, but are best for short storage. When stored at 4°C or below for 3–6 days, surface pitting and russet discoloration may appear in a day or two following removal for marketing. The russeting will be especially noticeable in the centers of the containers where condensed moisture is more prevalent. Contact icing is not recommended. To prevent wilting, the RH should be maintained at 90–95%. Beans for processing can be stored up to 10 days at 4°C. Containers of beans should be stacked to allow abundant air circulation; otherwise, the temperature may rise from the heat of respiration. Beans stored too long or at too high a temperature are subject to such decays as watery soft rot, slimy soft rot, and rhizopus rot. 10.3.2 Beans, Lima (3–5°C and 95% RH) For best quality, lima beans should not be stored. Unshelled lima beans can be stored for about 1 week at 3–5°C. They should be used promptly after removal because the pods discolor rapidly at room temperature. Even with only 1 week of refrigerated storage, the pods may develop rusty brown or brown specks, spots, and larger discolored areas that reduce salability of the beans. The pod discoloration will increase sharply during an additional day at 21°C following storage. 10.3.3 Beets (0°C and 98–100% RH) Topped beets are subject to wilting because of the rapid loss of water when the storage atmosphere is too dry. When stored at 0°C with at least 95% RH, they can be kept for 4–6 months. Before beets are stored, they should be topped and sorted to remove all beets that are diseased and showing mechanical injury. Bunch beets under the same conditions will keep 1–2 weeks. Contact icing is recommended. The containers should be well ventilated and stacked to allow air circulation. 10.3.4 Broccoli (0°C and 95–100% RH) Italian or sprouting broccoli is highly perishable and is usually stored for only a brief period as needed for orderly marketing. Good salable condition, fresh green color, and vitamin C content are best maintained at 0°C. If it is in good condition and is stored with adequate air circulation and spacing between containers to avoid heating, broccoli should keep satisfactorily 10–14 days at 0°C. Longer storage is undesirable because leaves discolor, buds may drop Handling and Cold Storage of Vegetables 167 off, and tissues soften. The respiration rate of freshly harvested broccoli is high comparable to that of asparagus, beans, and sweet corn. This high rate of respiration should be considered when storing broccoli, especially if it is held without package ice. 10.3.5 Brussels Sprouts (0°C and 95–100% RH) Brussels sprouts can be stored in good condition for a maximum of 3–5 weeks at the recommended temperature of 0°C. Deterioration, yellowing of the sprouts, and discoloration of the stem are rapid at temperatures of 10°C and above. Rate of deterioration is twice as fast at 4°C as at 0°C. Loss of moisture through transpiration is rather high even if the RH is kept at the recommended level. Film packaging is useful in preventing moisture loss. As with broccoli, sufficient air circulation and spacing between packages is desirable to allow good cooling and to prevent yellowing and decay. 10.3.6 Cabbage (0°C and 98–100% RH) A large percentage of the late crop of cabbage is stored and sold during the winter and early spring, or until the new crop from southern states appears on the market. If it is stored under proper conditions, late cabbage should keep for 3–4 months. The longest-keeping varieties belong to the Danish class. Early crop cabbage, especially southern grown, has a limited storage life of 3–6 weeks. Cabbage is successfully held in common storage in northern states, where a fairly uniform inside temperature of 0–2°C is maintained. An increasing quantity of cabbage is now held in mechanically refrigerated storage, but in some seasons its value does not justify the expense. Use of controlled atmospheres to supplement refrigeration aids quality retention. An atmosphere with 2.5–5% O2 and 2.5–5% CO2 can extend the storage life of late cabbage. Cabbage should not be stored with fruits emitting ethylene. Concentrations of 10–100 mg/kg of ethylene cause leaf abscission and loss of green color within 5 weeks at 0°C. Pallet bins are used as both field and storage containers, so the cabbage requires no handling from the time of harvest until preparation for shipment. Before the heads are stored, all loose leaves should be trimmed away; only 3–6 tight wrapper leaves should be left on the head. Loose leaves interfere with ventilation between heads, which is essential for successful storage. When removed from storage, the heads should be trimmed again to remove loose and damaged leaves. 10.3.7 Carrots (0°C and 98–100% RH) Carrots are best stored at 0°C with a high RH. Like beets, they are subject to rapid wilting if the humidity is low. For long storage, carrots should be topped and free from cuts and bruises. If they are in good condition when stored and promptly cooled after harvest, matured carrots 168 Chapter 10 should keep 5–9 months. Carrots lose moisture readily and wilting results. Humidity should be kept high, but condensation or dripping on the carrots should be avoided, because this causes decay. Most carrots for the fresh market are not fully mature. Immature carrots are prepackaged in polyethylene bags either at the shipping point or in terminal markets. They are usually moved into marketing channels soon after harvest, but they can be stored for a short period to avoid a market glut. If the carrots are cooled quickly and all traces of leaf growth are removed, they can be held 4–6 weeks at 0°C. In Texas, immature carrots are often stored in clean 23 kg burlap sacks. The sacks of carrots should be stacked in such a manner that at least one surface of each sack is in contact with top ice at all times. Top ice provides some of the necessary refrigeration and prevents dehydration. Bunched carrots may be stored for 10–14 days at 0°C. Contact icing is recommended. Bitterness in carrots, which may develop in storage, is due to abnormal metabolism caused by the ethylene emitted by apples, pears, and some other fruits and vegetables. It can also be caused by other sources such as internal combustion engines. Bitterness can be prevented by storing carrots away from products that give off ethylene. 10.3.8 Cauliflower (0°C and 95% RH) Cauliflower may be stored for 3–4 weeks at 0°C with about 95% RH. Successful storage depends on retarding the aging of the head or curd, preventing decay marked by spotting or water soaking of the white curd, and preventing yellowing and dropping of the leaves. When it is necessary to hold cauliflower temporarily out of cold storage, packing in crushed ice will aid in keeping it from freezing, which causes a grayish brown discoloration, softening of curd, and a water-soaked condition. Affected tissues are rapidly invaded by soft rot bacteria. Much of the cauliflower now marketed has closely trimmed leaves and is prepackaged in perforated cellophane overwraps that are then packed in fiberboard containers. Vacuum cooling is a fairly efficient method of cooling prepackaged cauliflower. In general, use of controlled atmospheres with cauliflower has not been promising. Atmospheres containing 5% CO2 or higher are injurious to cauliflower, although the damage may not be apparent until after cooking. 10.3.9 Celery (0°C and 98–100% RH) Celery is a relatively perishable commodity, and for storage of 1–2 months, it is essential that a commodity temperature of 0°C be maintained. The RH should be high enough to prevent wilting (98–100%). Considerable heat is given off because of respiration, and for this reason the stacks of crates should be separated and dunnage used to allow cold air circulation under and over the crates and between the bottom crates and the floor. Forced-air circulation should Handling and Cold Storage of Vegetables 169 be provided; otherwise there may be a 1–2 K temperature differentials between the top and the bottom of the room. Celery can be cooled by forced-air cooling, hydrocooling, or vacuum cooling. Hydro cooling is the most common cooling method; temperatures should be brought to as near 0°C as possible. In practice, temperatures are reduced to 4–7°C. Vacuum cooling is widely used for celery packed in corrugated cartons for long-distance shipment. 10.3.10 Corn, Sweet (0°C and 95–98% RH) Sweet corn is highly perishable and is seldom stored except to temporarily protect an excess supply. Corn, as it usually arrives on the market, should not be expected to keep for more than 4–8 days even in 0°C storage. The sugar content, which so largely determines quality in corn and decreases rapidly at ordinary temperatures, decreases less rapidly if the corn is kept at about 0°C. The loss of sugar is about four times as rapid at 10°C as it is at 0°C. Sweet corn should be cooled promptly after harvest. Usually, corn is hydrocooled, but vacuum cooling is also satisfactory if the corn is prewetted and top-iced after cooling. Where precooling facilities are not available, corn can be cooled with package and top ice. Sweet corn should not be handled in bulk unless it is copiously iced because of its tendency to heat throughout the pile. Sweet corn ears should be trimmed to remove most shank material before shipment to minimize moisture loss and prevent kernel denting. A loss of 2% moisture from sweet corn can result in objectionable kernel denting. 10.3.11 Cucumbers (10–13°C and 95% RH) Cucumbers can be held only for short periods of 10–14 days at 10–13°C with an RH of 95%. Cucumbers held at 7°C or below for longer periods develop surface pitting or dark-colored watery areas. These blemishes indicate chilling injury. Such areas soon become infected and decay rapidly when the cucumbers are moved to warmer temperatures. Slight chilling may develop in 2 days at 0°C, severe chilling injury within 6 days at 0°C. The susceptibility of cucumbers to chilling injury does not preclude their exposure to temperatures below 10°C for short intervals as long as they are used immediately after removal from cold storage. Chilling symptoms develop rapidly only at higher temperatures. Thus, 2 days at 0°C or 4 days at 4°C are both harmless. Waxing is of some value in reducing loss of mass and in giving a brighter appearance. Shrink wrapping with polyethylene film can also prevent the loss of turgidity. At temperatures of 10°C and above, cucumbers ripen rather rapidly as the green color changes to yellow. Ripening is accelerated if they are stored in the same room with ethyleneproducing crops for more than a few hours. 170 Chapter 10 10.3.12 Eggplants (8–12°C and 90–98% RH) Eggplants are not adapted to long storage. They cannot be kept satisfactorily even at the optimum temperatures of 8–12°C for over a week and still retain good condition during retailing. Eggplants are subject to chilling injury at temperatures below 7°C. Surface scald or bronzing and pitting after and scarring are symptoms of chilling injury. Eggplants that have been chilled are subject to decay by Alternaria when they are removed from storage. Exposure to ethylene for 2 or more days hastens deterioration. 10.3.13 Endive and Escarole (0°C and 95–100% RH) Endive and escarole are leafy vegetables not adapted to long storage. Even at 0°C, which is considered the best storage temperature, they will not keep satisfactorily for more than 2–3 weeks. They should keep somewhat longer if they are stored with cracked ice in or around the packages. Some desirable blanching usually occurs in endive held in storage. 10.3.14 Garlic, Dry (0°C and 95–98% RH) If it is in good condition and is well cured when stored, garlic should keep at 0°C for 6–7 months. Garlic cloves sprout most rapidly at 4–18°C; therefore, prolonged storage at this temperature should be avoided. In California, it is frequently put in common storage, where it can be held 3–4 months or sometimes longer if the building can be kept cool, dry, and well ventilated. 10.3.15 Greens, Leafy (0°C and 95–100% RH) Leafy greens such as collards, chard, and beet and turnip greens are highly perishable and should be held as close to 0°C as possible. At this temperature, they can be held 10–14 days. They are commonly shipped with package and top ice to maintain freshness and are handled like spinach. Kale packed with polyethylene crate liners should keep at least 3 weeks at 0°C or 1 week at 4°C. Vitamin content and quality are retained better when wilting is prevented. 10.3.16 Lettuce (0°C and 95–100% RH) Lettuce is highly perishable. To minimize deterioration, it requires a temperature as close to its freezing point as possible without actually freezing it. Lettuce will keep about twice as long at 0°C as at 3°C. If it is in good condition when stored, lettuce should keep 2–3 weeks at 0°C with a high RH. Most lettuce is packed in cartons and vacuum cooled to about 1–2°C soon after harvest. It should then be immediately loaded into refrigerated cars or trailers for shipment or placed in cold storage rooms for holding prior to shipping. Handling and Cold Storage of Vegetables 171 An increasing quantity of lettuce is shipped in modified atmospheres to aid quality retention. Modified atmospheres are a supplement to proper transit refrigeration but are not a substitute for refrigeration. Head lettuce is not tolerant of CO2 and is injured by concentrations of 2–3% or higher. Romaine is injured by 10% CO2, but not by 5% at 0°C. Leaf lettuce and chopped romaine tolerate 10% CO2, and chopped, shredded iceberg lettuce tolerates 15% CO2 (Gorny, 1997). Excess wrapper leaves are usually trimmed off before sale or use, so it is suggested that lettuce be trimmed to two wrapper leaves before packaging (rather than the usual five or six) to save space and mass. The extra wrapper leaves are not needed to maintain quality. 10.3.17 Melons Persians should keep at 7–10°C for up to 2 weeks; honeydews for 2–3 weeks; and casabas for 4–6 weeks. These melons will definitely be injured in 8 days at temperatures as low as 0°C. Honeydews are usually given an 18–24 h ethylene treatment (5000 mg/kg) to obtain uniform ripening. Pulp temperature should be 21°C or above during treatment. Honeydews must be mature when harvested; immature melons fail to ripen even if treated with ethylene. Cantaloupes harvested at the hard-ripe stage (less than full slip) can be held about 15 days at 2–3°C. Lower temperatures may cause chilling injury. Full-slip hard-ripe cantaloupes can be held for a maximum of 10–14 days at 0–2°C. They are more resistant to chilling injury. Cantaloupes are precooled by hydrocooling or forced-air cooling before loading or by top-icing after loading in railcars or trucks. Watermelons are stored at 10–15°C and should keep for 2–3 weeks. Watermelons decay less at 0°C than at 4°C, but may tend to become pitted and have an objectionable flavor after 1 week at 0°C. At low temperatures, they are subject to various symptoms of chilling injury (loss of flavor and fading of red color). Watermelons should be consumed within 2–3 weeks after harvest, primarily because of the gradual loss of crispness. 10.3.18 Mushrooms (0°C and 95% RH) Mushrooms are usually sold in a retail market within 24–48 h after harvesting. They keep in good salable condition at 0°C for 5 days, at 4°C for 2 days, and at 10°C or above for about 1 day. An RH of 95% is recommended during storage. While being transported or displayed for retail sale, mushrooms should be refrigerated. Deterioration is marked by brown discoloration of the surfaces, elongation of the stalks, and opening of the veils. Black stems and open veils are correlated with dehydration. Controlled atmosphere storage can prolong the shelf life of mushrooms held at 10°C if the O2 concentration in the atmosphere is 9% or the CO2 concentration is 25–50%. Moisture-retentive film overwraps of caps usually help in reducing moisture loss. 172 Chapter 10 10.3.19 Okra (7–10°C and 90–95% RH) Okra deteriorates rapidly and is normally stored only briefly before marketing or processing. It has a high respiration rate at warm temperatures. Okra in good condition can be kept satisfactorily for 7–10 days at 7–10°C. An RH of 90–95% is desirable to prevent wilting. At temperatures below 7°C, okra is subject to chilling injury, which is shown by surface discoloration, pitting, and decay. Holding okra for 3 days at 0°C may cause pitting. Contact or top-icing causes water spotting in 2–3 days at all temperatures. Fresh okra bruises easily; the damaged areas blacken within a few hours. A bleaching injury may also develop when okra is held in hampers for more than 24 h without refrigeration. 10.3.20 Onions (0°C and 65–70% RH) A comparatively low RH is essential in the successful storage of dry onions. However, humidities as high as 85% and forced-air circulation also have given satisfactory results. At higher humidities, at which most other vegetables keep best, onions develop root growth and decay; at too high a temperature, sprouting occurs. Storage at 0°C with 65–70% RH is recommended to keep them dormant. Onions should be adequately cured in the field, in open sheds, or by artificial means before, or in, storage. The most common method of curing is by forced ventilation in storage. Onions are considered cured when the necks are tight and the outer scales are dried until they rustle. If they are not cured, onions are likely to decay in storage. Onions are stored in 23 kg bags, in crates, and in pallet boxes that hold about 450 kg of loose onion. Bags of onions are frequently stored on pallets. Bagged onions should be stacked to allow proper air circulation. In the northern onion-growing states, onions of the globe type are generally held in common storage because average winter temperatures are sufficiently low. They should not be held after early March unless they have been treated with maleic hydrazide in field to reduce sprout growth. Refrigerated storage is often used to hold onions for marketing in late spring. Onions to be held in cold storage should be placed there immediately after curing. A temperature of 0°C will keep onions dormant and reasonably free from decay, provided the onions are sound and well cured when stored. Sprout growth indicates too high a storage temperature, poorly cured bulbs, or immature bulbs. Root growth indicates the RH is too high. Globe onions can be held for 6–8 months at 0°C. Milo or Bermuda types can usually be held at 0°C for only 1–2 months. Spanish onions are often stored; if well matured, they can be held at 0°C at least until January or February. In California, onions of the sweet Spanish type are held at 0°C until April or May. Handling and Cold Storage of Vegetables 173 Onions are damaged by freezing, which appears as water soaking of the scales when cut after thawing. If allowed to thaw slowly and without handling, onions that have been slightly frozen may recover with little perceptible injury. When onions are removed from storage in warm weather, they may sweat due to condensation of moisture. This may favor decay. Warming onions gradually (e.g., to 10°C over 2–3 days) with good air movement should avoid the difficulty. Onions should not be stored with other products that tend to absorb odors. Onion sets require practically the same temperature and humidity conditions as onions, but because they are smaller in size they tend to pack more solidly. They are handled in approximately 11 kg bags and should be stacked to allow the maximum air circulation. Green onions (scallions) and green shallots are usually marketed promptly after harvest. They can be stored 3–4 weeks at 0°C with 95% RH. Crushed ice spread over the onions aids in supplying moisture. Packaging in polyethylene film also aids in preventing moisture loss. Storage life of green onions at 0°C can be extended to 8 weeks by 1. packaging them in perforated polyethylene bags or in waxed cartons and 2. holding them in a controlled atmosphere of 1% O2 with 5% CO2. 10.3.21 Parsley (0°C and 95–100% RH) Parsley should keep 1–2.5 months at 0°C and for a somewhat shorter period at 2–3°C. High humidity is essential to prevent desiccation. Package icing is often beneficial. 10.3.22 Parsnips (0°C and 98–100% RH) Topped parsnips have similar storage requirements to topped carrots and should keep for 2–6 months at 0°C. Parsnips held at 0–1°C for 2 weeks after harvest attain a sweetness and high quality equal to that of roots subjected to frosts for 2 months in the field. Ventilated polyethylene box or basket liners can aid in preventing moisture loss. Parsnips are not injured by slight freezing while in storage, but they should be protected from hard freezing. They should be handled with great care while frozen. The main storage problems with parsnips are decay, surface browning, and their tendency to shrivel. Refrigeration and high RH will retard deterioration. 10.3.23 Peas, Green (0°C and 95–98% RH) Green peas lose part of their sugar rapidly if they are not refrigerated promptly after harvest. They should keep in salable condition for 1–2 weeks at 0°C. Top-icing is beneficial in maintaining freshness. Peas keep better unshelled than shelled. 174 Chapter 10 10.3.24 Peas, Southern (4–5°C and 95% RH) Freshly harvested southern peas at the mature-green stage should have a storage life of 6–8 days at 4–5°C with high RH. Without refrigeration, they remain edible for only about 2 days, the pods yellowing in 3 days and showing extensive decay in 4–6 days. 10.3.25 Peppers, Dry Chili or Hot Chili peppers, after drying to a moisture content of 10–15% are stored in nonrefrigerated warehouses for 6–9 months. The moisture content is usually low enough to prevent fungus growth. An RH of 60–70% is desirable. Polyethylene-lined bags are recommended to prevent changes in moisture content. Manufacturers of chili pepper products hold part of their raw material supply in cold storage at 0–10°C, but they prefer to grind the peppers as soon as possible and to store them in the manufactured form in airtight containers. 10.3.26 Peppers, Sweet (7–13°C and 90–95% RH) Sweet peppers can be stored for a maximum of 2–3 weeks at 7–13°C. They are subjected to chilling injury if they are stored at temperatures below 7°C. The symptoms of this injury are surface pitting and discoloration near the calyx, which develops a few hours after removal from storage. At temperatures of 0–2°C peppers usually develop pitting in a few days. When stored at temperatures above 13°C, ripening (red color) and decay develop rapidly. Rapid cooling of harvested sweet peppers is essential in reducing marketing losses. It can be done by forced-air cooling, hydrocooling, or vacuum cooling. Forced-air cooling is the preferred method. Peppers are often waxed commercially, which reduces in-transit chafing and moisture loss. 10.3.27 Potatoes (90–95% RH) The proper potato storage environment will promote the most rapid healing of bruises and cuts, reduce rot penetration to a minimum, allow the least loss of mass and other storage losses to occur, and reduce to a minimum the deleterious quality changes that might occur during storage. Early-crop potatoes are usually stored only during congested periods. They are more perishable and do not keep as well or as long as late-crop tubers. Refrigerated storage at 4°C, following a curing period of 4–5 days at 21°C, is recommended; they also can be stored for about 2 months at 10°C without curing. If early-crop potatoes are to be used for chipping or French frying, storage at 21°C is recommended. Holding these potatoes in cold storage (even at moderate temperatures of 10–13°C) for only a few days causes excessive accumulation of reducing sugars, which results in production of dark-colored chips. Handling and Cold Storage of Vegetables 175 Late-crop potatoes produced in the northern half of the United States are usually stored. The greater part of the crop is held in nonrefrigerated commercial and farm storage but some potatoes are held in refrigerated storages. Potatoes in nonrefrigerated storage are usually held in bulk bins 2.4–6.1 m deep. Shallower bins are used in milder climates. Some potatoes are stored in pallet boxes. In refrigerated warehouses, potatoes can be stored in sacks, pallet boxes, or bulk. Late-crop potatoes should be cured immediately after harvest by being held at 10–16°C and high RH for about 10–14 days to permit suberization and wound periderm formation (healing of cuts and bruises). If properly cured, they should keep in sound dormant condition at 3–4°C with 95% RH for 5–8 months. A lower temperature is not desirable, except in the case of seed stock for late planting. For this purpose, 3°C is best. At 3°C or below, Irish potatoes tend to becomes sweet. For ordinary table use, potatoes stored at 4°C are satisfactory, but they will probably be unsatisfactory for chipping or French frying unless desugared or conditioned at about 18–21°C for 1–3 weeks before use. However, conditioning may be costly and good results are often uncertain. Potatoes will remain dormant at 10°C for 2–4 months. Because tubers from this temperature are more desirable for both table use and processing than those from 4°C, late-crop potatoes intended for use within 4 months should be stored at 10°C and those for later use at 4°C. All potatoes should be stored in the dark to prevent greening. A storage temperature of 10–13°C is recommended for most cultivars of potatoes intended for chip manufacture. At these temperatures they usually remain in satisfactory condition if their reducing-sugar content is low enough when they are initially stored. Storage at 16–18°C is less desirable because shrinkage, internal and external sprout growth, and decay are greater at these temperatures than at 10–13°C. Russet Burbank potatoes for table stock or for chipping are stored at 7°C with 95% RH. Potatoes usually do not sprout until 2–3 months after harvest even at 10–16°C. However, after 2–3 months of storage, sprouting occurs in potatoes stored at temperatures above 4°C and particularly at temperatures around 16°C. Although limited sprouting does not affect potatoes for food purposes, badly sprouted stock shrivels and is difficult to handle and market. Certain growth-regulating chemicals have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to control or reduce sprouting on potatoes. Potatoes treated with chemical sprout inhibitors should not be stored in the same warehouse with seed potatoes. If 90% RH or slightly higher is maintained, potatoes will have the best quality and the least amount of shrinkage. Cunningham et al. (1971) recommend 95% RH or higher for late-crop potatoes. Condensation on the ceiling and resultant moisture drip is sometimes a problem when high humidity is maintained. 176 Chapter 10 Ventilation or air circulation in potato storage is needed to provide and maintain optimum temperature and RH throughout the storage and the tubers it contains in northern states where average outdoor temperatures during storage are low. Little circulation or ventilation is necessary; shell or perimeter circulation is extensively used in these areas for seed and table stock potatoes. Forced circulation through potatoes is required for higher-temperature storage of processing potatoes and for table and seed stock in the warmer parts of the late-crop area. Rapid air circulation may lower the RH of the air immediately surrounding the potatoes and is conducive to drying and loss of moisture, which may be desirable if there are disease problems but undesirable with round potatoes because of increased shrinkage. For late-crop potatoes, a uniform airflow of 0.0068 L/(s·kg) that does not have to be continuous is recommended with this ventilation. Russet Burbank potatoes stored at 7°C with 95% RH should keep in good condition for 10 months or longer. Potatoes can absorb objectionable flavors from fruits, nuts, eggs, dairy products, and volatile chemicals, consequently they should not be kept in the same room. 10.3.28 Pumpkins and Squash Hard-shell winter squash, such as the Hubbards, can be successfully stored for 6 months or longer at 10–13°C with an RH of 60–75%. Dry storage is needed for quality retention. All specimens should be well-matured, carefully handled, and free from injury or decay when stored. Hubbard and other dark-green skinned squashes should not be stored near apples, because the ethylene from apples may cause squash skin to turn orange-yellow. Most varieties of pumpkins do not keep in storage for as long as the usual storage varieties of squash. Such varieties as Connecticut Field and Cushaw do not keep well and cannot be kept in good condition for more than 2–3 months. Acorn squash can be stored satisfactorily for 5–8 weeks at 10°C. Butternut squash should keep at least 2–3 months at 10°C with 50% RH. Summer squash, such as yellow crookneck and giant straight neck are harvested at an immature stage for best quality. The skin is tender and these varieties are easily wounded and perishable. The storage temperature range for summer squash is 5–10°C with 95% RH. A temperature of 5°C is best for zucchini squash stored up to 2 weeks, because they are sensitive to chilling injury. 10.3.29 Radishes (0°C and 95–100% RH) After harvest, topped spring radishes should be precooled quickly, often by hydrocooling, to 5°C or below. If they are then packaged in polyethylene bags, radishes can usually be held 3–4 weeks at 0°C and for a somewhat shorter time at 4°C. Bunched radishes with tops are more perishable. They can be stored at 0°C and 95–100% RH for 1–2 weeks. Handling and Cold Storage of Vegetables 177 10.3.30 Rhubarb (0°C and 95% RH) Fresh rhubarb stalks will wilt and decay rapidly. Rhubarb in good condition can be stored 2–4 weeks at 0°C with 95% RH or above. Moisture loss during holding or storage can be minimized by using nonsealed polyethylene crate liners or by film wrapping consumer size bunches. Removing and discarding leaf blades at harvest is desirable, because it not only reduces the possibility of decay and loss of mass but also reduces shipping mass and package size by one-third. Rhubarb is usually marketed with about 10 mm of the leaf blade attached to the petiole. Splitting of the petiole is more serious if the entire leaf is removed. Fresh rhubarb cut into 25 mm pieces and packaged in 0.5 kg perforated polyethylene bags can be held 2–3 weeks at 0°C with high RH. Splitting of cut ends and curling of these pieces in film bags may be a problem if marketing is at warm temperatures. 10.3.31 Rutabagas (0°C and 98–100% RH) Rutabagas lose moisture and shrivel readily if they are not stored under high humidity conditions. A hot paraffin wax coating, often given to rutabagas, is effective in preventing wilting and loss of mass; it also slightly improves appearance. Too heavy a wax coating may produce severe injury from internal breakdown caused by suboxidation. Rutabagas in good condition when stored should keep 4–6 months at 0°C. 10.3.32 Spinach (0°C and 95–98% RH) Spinach is highly perishable and can be stored for only short periods of 10–14 days at 0°C with 95–98% RH. It will deteriorate rapidly at higher temperatures. Spinach is commercially vacuum cooled and forced-air cooled. If it is thoroughly cooled, it can be held for 10–14 days at 0°C without the addition of any package ice prior to storage. When precooling facilities are not available, crushed ice should be placed in each package to provide rapid cooling and to take care of the heat of respiration. Top ice is also beneficial. 10.3.33 Sweet Potatoes (13–16°C, 85–90% RH) Most sweet potatoes are stored in nonrefrigerated commercial or farm storage. Preliminary curing at 29°C and 90–95% RH for 4–7 days is essential in the healing of injuries received in harvesting and handling and in preventing the entrance of decay organisms. After curing, the temperature should be reduced to 13–16°C, usually by ventilating the storage, and the RH should be retained at 85–90%. Most varieties will keep satisfactorily for 4–7 months under these conditions. Loss of mass of 2–6% can be expected during curing and about 2% a month during subsequent storage. 178 Chapter 10 Usually, sweet potatoes will not keep satisfactorily if they have been subjected to excessively wet soil conditions just before harvest or chilled before or after harvest by exposure to temperatures of 10°C or below. Short periods at temperatures as low as 10°C need not cause alarm; but after a few days at lower temperatures, sweet potatoes may develop discoloration of the flesh, internal breakdown, increased susceptibility to decay, and off-flavors when cooked. Temperatures above 16°C stimulate development of sprouting (especially at high humidities), pithiness, and internal cork (a virus disease). Refrigeration is frequently used in large sweet potato storages to extend the marketing season into warm weather when ventilation will not maintain low enough temperatures. Sweet potatoes are usually stored in slatted crates or bushel baskets. Palletization of crates and use of pallet boxes facilitate handling. Sweet potatoes are usually washed and graded and are sometimes washed before being shipped to market. They may be treated with a fungicide to reduce decay during marketing. 10.3.34 Tomatoes (Mature green, 13–21°C; Ripe, 10°C; 90–95% RH) Mature green tomatoes cannot be successfully stored at temperatures that greatly delay ripening, even at a temperature of 13°C that is considered to be a nonchilling temperature. Tomatoes held for 2 weeks or longer at 13°C may develop an abnormal amount of decay and fail to reach as intense a red color as tomatoes ripened promptly at 18–21°C. Temperatures of 20–22°C and an RH of 90–95% are probably used most extensively in commercial ripening of mature green tomatoes. At temperatures above 21°C, decay is generally increased. A temperature range of 14–16°C is probably the most desirable for slowing ripening without increasing decay problems. At this temperature the more mature fruit will ripen enough to be packaged for retailing in 7–14 days. Tomatoes should be kept out of cold, wet rooms because, in addition to potential chilling injury, extended refrigeration damages the ability of fruit to develop desirable fresh tomato flavor. Ethylene gas is sometimes used to hasten and give more even ripening to mature green tomatoes. In ripening rooms, a concentration of 1 part ethylene per 5000 parts of air daily for 2–4 days will usually shorten the ripening period by about 2 days at 20–22°C. Some tomatoes are gassed with ethylene in loaded railcars prior to shipping. Adding ethylene has little or no effect on tomatoes just before or after they have started to turn pink. Tomatoes themselves give off considerable ethylene as they ripen. Interest is increasing in the commercial use of low O2 atmospheres of 3–5% during aging or transport to retard ripening and decay. Storage temperatures below 10°C are especially harmful to mature green tomatoes; these chilling temperatures make the fruit susceptible to Alternaria decay during subsequent ripening. Increased decay during ripening occurs following 6 days of exposure to 0°C, or 9 days at 4°C. Handling and Cold Storage of Vegetables 179 Firm ripe tomatoes may be held at 7–10°C with an RH of 85–90% overnight or over a holiday or weekend. Tomatoes showing 50–70% of the surface colored (the ripeness used when packed for retailing) cannot be successfully stored for more than 1 week and be expected to have a normal shelf life during retailing. Such fruits should also be held at 7–10°C and 85–90% RH. A storage temperature of 10–13°C is recommended for pink-red to firm red tomatoes raised in green houses. When it is necessary to hold firm ripe tomatoes for longest possible time, consistent with immediate consumption on removal from storage, such as on board a ship or for an average military base, they can be held at 0–2°C for up to 3 weeks, with some loss in quality. Mature green, or pink tomatoes should be ripened before storage at this low temperature. 10.3.35 Turnips (0°C and 95% RH) Turnips in good condition can be expected to keep 4–5 months at 0°C with 90–95% RH. At higher temperatures (5°C and above) decay will develop much more rapidly than at 0°C. Injured or bruised turnips should not be stored. Store turnips in slatted crates or bins and allow good circulation around containers. Dipping turnips in hot melted paraffin wax gives them a glossy appearance and is of some value in reducing moisture loss during handling. However, waxing is primarily to aid in marketing and is not recommended prior to long-term storage. Turnip greens are usually stored for only short periods (10–14 days). They should keep about as well as spinach at 0°C with crushed ice in the packages. 10.3.36 Beer Because beer in bottles or cans is either pasteurized or filtered to destroy or remove the living yeast cells, it does not require as low a storage temperature as keg beer. Bottled beer may be stored at an ordinary room temperature of 21–24°C, but for convenience, it is often stored with keg beer at a lower temperature of 2–4°C. The bottled product should be protected from strong light, especially direct sunlight. The storage life will vary from 3–6 months depending largely on the method of processing and packaging. Keg beer, usually stored at 2–4 °C, has a storage life of 3–6 weeks. 10.3.37 Canned Foods Canned foods that are heat processed in hermetically sealed containers do not benefit from refrigerated storage if they are to be stored for no longer than 2 or 3 months at temperatures that rarely exceed 24°C. However, seasonal commodities produced to provide an inventory for an entire year or longer do benefit from reduced temperature and humidity storage, which delays 180 Chapter 10 the onset of considerable color, texture, and flavor changes; loss of nutrients; and container corrosion. Notable examples are canned asparagus, cherries, and catsup. Reduced temperature and humidity storage for canned goods is essential in environments where ambient temperatures and humidities regularly exceed 30°C and 70% RH. PAR T I I Cold Storage 181 Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 11 Moist Air and Applied Psychrometry 11.1 Introduction The change of state of moist air is referred to as a psychrometric process. The content of the water vapor in air is wholly responsible for maintaining required conditions in the cold storages. Moist air is a mixture of two gases─one of dry air, which itself is a mixture of number of gases, and the other of water vapor that may exist in a saturated or super-heated state. The dry air part of the moist air is considered the fixed part and the other, solely of water vapor, as variable. The major constituent of dry air is nitrogen, weighing 0.7547 parts, and oxygen, weighing 0.2319 parts, in 1 kg. Both dry air and water vapor can be considered as perfect gases because both exist in the atmosphere at low pressure. Hence, perfect gas laws can be applied to them individually. Gibbs-Dalton laws for nonreactive mixtures of gases can be applied to the dry air part only to obtain its properties as a single pure substance, before establishing the properties of moist air. Fruits and vegetables, or any food material for that matter, require a low temperature and high relative humidity as well as air moving around them at certain velocity to keep their respiration and transpiration at minimum level to prolong their storage period with minimum loss of their original attributes, including freshness, color, and aroma. To manipulate the properties of this working substance (air), we need air-conditioning equipment. The purpose of the air-conditioning equipment is to supply a sufficient volume of clean air containing a specific amount of water vapor and at a temperature capable of maintaining predetermined atmospheric conditions within the selected enclosure. The knowledge of this working substance (moist air) is important for all those involved in the design, operation, and maintenance of cold chain conditions. This chapter focuses attention on the properties of the working substance (moist air) in airconditioning and the various processes that are involved in manipulating the properties of the moist air to make it suitable and economical in conditioning the inside atmosphere of cold storage. These processes are explained and illustrated by using psychrometric formulae and with psychrometric charts. 11.2 Dalton’s Law of Partial Pressures Consider a homogeneous mixture of nonreacting ideal gases 1, 2, etc., at temperature T, pressure P, and occupying volume V as shown in Fig. 12.1. All rights reserved. 184 Chapter 11 Let the number of moles of individual gases be n1, n2,…, and their respective masses be m1, m2,…. Total number of moles n = n1 + n2 + … = ∑ ni (11.1) Total mass m = m1 + m2 + … = ∑ mi (11.2) In the Dalton model, each gas is conceived of as existing separately at the temperature T and total volume V of the mixture as shown in Figure 11.1 (b) and (c). If we are able to measure pressure exerted by individual gases, they would be found to be p1, p2,… less than the total pressure p of the mixture. These are referred to as partial pressures. Considering mixture and each component gas existing separately at T and V, we find the following for a binary mixture: Mixture PV = n RT Component1 PV = n1 RT 1 Component 2 P2V = n2 RT Substitution n1 + n2 = n PV RT PV n1 = 1 RT PV n2 = 2 RT n= (11.3) P = p1 + p2 or P = ∑ i pi Thus, for a mixture of ideal gases, the total pressure P is equal to the sum of the partial pressures, which is known as Dalton’s law of partial pressures. Similarly, Amagat’s law of partial volumes states that the total volume of a given mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial volumes and is given by V = v1 + v2 + … = ∑ i vi where V = total volume of the gas mixture v1, v2 are the partial volumes of individual gases in the gas mixture Figure 11.1: Illustration of Dalton’s Model. Then we have for the internal energy of the mixture. MU = m1u1 + m2 u2 U = internal energy (11.7) 186 Chapter 11 Similarly, the enthalpy and specific heat of the mixture can be written as mh = m1h1 + m2 h2 (11.8) mc = m1c1 + m2 c2 (11.9) where h = enthalpy c = specific heat An equation of the state expressing the relationship between pressure, specific volume, and temperature for a real gas is PV = RT where R is known as the gas constant and its units are Nm/kg. It has been found that the product of molecular weight of any gas and its gas constant are the same for all the gases and are denoted by R , and R is known as universal gas constant R = RM The value of R is 8314 Nm/kg·K = 8314 J/kg·K or 8.314 kJ/(kg.K) The molecular mass of dry air 28.966. The temperature measured by the wick-covered bulb of such a thermometer indicates the 196 Chapter 11 temperature of the liquid water in the wick and is called the wet bulb temperature. It is denoted by symbol t9. The WBT is easily measured with the help of a psychrometer. The WBT is not a thermodynamic property; therefore, no analytical expression can be derived to relate WBT with pv or other thermodynamic properties. The empirical relations exist to obtain the value of pv in terms of t9. They are (a) Modified Apjohn equation Pv = Pv′ − 18 P ( t – t ′ ) 2700 (11.16) (b) Modified Ferral equation  1.8 t  Pv = Pv′ − 0.00066 p ( t – t ′ ) 1 +  1571  (11.17) (c) Carrier equation Pv = Pv′ – ( p – pv′ ) (t – t ′ )(1.8 ) 2800 – 1.3 (1.8 t + 32) (11.18) where all the temperatures are in °C, and pv′ is the saturation pressure at the wet bulb temperature t ′. P is the total pressure, t is the DBT. The pressure P, Pv′, and Pv may be in any consistent units. Another method to determine such properties is by using a psychrometric chart. These charts are available separately for low-temperature and high-temperature process calculation, and the charts are appended. The basic coordinates of the chart are dry bulb temperature (DBT) plotted as the abscissa on the horizontal axis and humidity ratio (specific humidity) as the ordinate on the vertical axis. The constant wet bulb temperatures (WBT), which also coincide with enthalpy lines, are drawn obliquely. The relative humidity (RH) curves swing upward to the right. The saturation curve represents 100% RH. The constant specific volume lines are drawn obliquely but they have a different slope than the WBT line. To use the chart, any two independent psychrometric properties are required. This allows location of a point on the chart. The remaining property values can then be read corresponding to the located point. 11.6.1 Basic Processes in Conditioning of Air Figure 11.2 shows the basic psychrometric processes. These processes are used in single or in combination to condition the moist air for use in the air-conditioning processes. They are: • • • • • • • • Sensible heating – process OA Sensible cooling – process OB Humidifying – process OC Dehumidifying – process OD Heating and humidifying – process OE Cooling and dehumidifying – process OF Cooling and humidifying – process OG Heating and dehumidifying – process OH 202 Chapter 11 Figure 11.2: Basic Psychrometric Processes. The first two processes, sensible heating and cooling, involve only a change in the dry bulb temperature, whereas the processes of humidifying and dehumidifying involve a change in the specific humidity. Thus, when the state of the air moves from O to A or to B, there is no change in the moisture content of the air; if the state changes from O to C or to D, the DBT remains constant. However, most practical moisture-transfer processes involve a change in temperature as well. The last four fundamental processes listed involve both changes in temperature as well as in humidity. The DPT is measured by cooling a bulb in a stream of air until the first dew appears on the bulb. The WBT is measured by rotating the wick-covered bulb of the thermometer at 60–600 rpm in the air. To define the complete thermodynamic state of the air and water vapor, we need to know three properties; usually two of these are the total pressure (barometric pressure) and DBT. The third measurable property is either the dew point temperature or the WBT. 11.6.2 Problems Solved Using the Psychrometric Chart Example 11.11 Heating and Humidifying An air-conditioned plant is to be designed for a small office room for winter conditions. CHAPTE R 12 Preliminaries for the Estimation of Cooling Loads 12.1 Introduction The air circulated in the conditioned room must be adequate to take different types of loads that come in the conditioned room. Some types of loads contribute heat in the form of sensible heat, some in the form latent heat, and some other types contribute in both sensible and latent heat forms. It is necessary for the design engineer to know about heat sources and their nature before designing an air-conditioning system. In this chapter, the nature of heat sources that contribute heat to the air-conditioning systems and their estimates are given. 12.2 Different Heat Sources The air-conditioning systems used for conditioning storage houses have to carry two types of loads known as sensible heat loads and latent heat loads. The sources that contribute to the sensible heat (SH) are: 1. Heat flows through the exterior walls, ceilings, floors, windows, and doors due to the temperature difference between their two sides 2. Loads due to solar radiation (sun load) is divided into two forms: a. Heat transmitted directly by radiation through glass of windows and ventilators b. Heat from sun absorbed by the walls and roof and later on transferred to room by conduction and convection 3. Heat received from the produce 4. Heat received from different equipments commonly used in cold storage 5. Heat received from infiltrated air from outside through cracks in doors, windows, and ventilators and through their frequent openings 6. Miscellaneous heat sources that include the following: a. Heat gain by the ducts carrying the conditioned air and passing through unconditioned space b. Heat transferred through interior partition of rooms in the same building that are not air-conditioned Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00012-9 209 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 210 Chapter 12 The sources that contribute to the latent heat (LH) load (vapor added) are listed here. 1. 2. 3. 4. The latent heat load from the air entering into the air-conditioned space by infiltration The latent heat load from the produce The latent heat load from cooking foods and from stored materials Moisture passing directly into the air-conditioned space through permeable walls where the water vapor pressure is higher These sources add water vapor into the air-conditioned space, which should be removed by absorbing its latent heat by the cooling apparatus. The amount of heat removed in the form of latent heat is known as the latent heat load. The removal of 1 kg of water vapor is considered equivalent to approximately 2400 kJ of heat load on cooling coil. This figure includes some sensible heat in addition to the latent heat because the vapor always remains in superheated condition in air unless the air is not in saturated condition. The SH loads and LH loads add the heat in the air-conditioned room. The total heat load to be removed by the air-conditioning system is the sum of the SH loads and LH loads and extra loads added by the following sources: 1. The fresh air taken from outside adds to the sensible and latent heat loads on the air-­ conditioner and not in the room. 2. Heat gain from the fan work (sensible heat) is added in the fresh air and it is also removed in the air-conditioner, if the fan is installed before the air-conditioner. For finding out the load on air-conditioning system, the previously mentioned loads should be considered in addition to the loads listed under SH loads and LH loads. The details of each load are described in the following paragraphs. 12.3 Heat Flow Due to Conduction The heat transferred by conduction through wall and ceiling to the air-conditioned space is seldom steady. Even if the temperature in the conditioned space is maintained at a constant, the rapid changes in the ambient temperature cause unsteady state heat conduction. The steady-state condition can be assumed if the temperature difference between the ­conditioned space and ambient air is large compared with the variation in ambient temperature. If the steady-state heat flow is considered then the heat flow is given by the equation: Q = UA (to − ti ) watts where to = temperature of outside air ti = temperature of inside conditioned air (12.1) Preliminaries for the Estimation of Cooling Loads 211 Table 12.1: U values for different types of walls Material of the Wall Thickness (cm) U (W/m2 – k) 20 30 40 20 30 40 15 25 40 20 30 20 30 2.45 1.75 1.35 1.45 1.15 1.00 3.15 3.05 2.35 2.55 2.25 1.90 1.80 Brick (plain) Brick (plastered on one side) Concrete (plain) Concrete (plastered on the side) Cinder block (plastered inside) A = area through which heat is transferred U = overall heat transfer coefficient The overall heat transfer coefficient is given by 1 1 1 x x = + 1 + 2 + ..... + hi U ho K1 K 2 n 1  x 1 = + ∑  +  K  hi ho 1 (12.2) where ho = heat transfer coefficient on the outer surface hi = heat transfer coefficient on the inner surface n x ∑  K  = Thermal resistances of the materials used for the construction of the wall 1 The values of U for different types of walls and ceilings are given in Tables 12.1, 12.2, and 12.3. Generally the produce is precooled to remove the field heat and then transported to cold storage for storage at the desired temperature and relative humidity (RH). The produce so loaded into cold storage still respire and transpire, which means that heat and moisture are released from the produce. The respiration heat and latent heat of condensation of moisture are to be removed from the cold storage. The heat of respiration is removed by sensible cooling, and heat of moisture is removed by latent heat of condensation at that temperature. The load of sensible cooling and latent heat of condensation are calculated by the following formulae. Sensible cooling load is given by Qc = mCPm (T1 − T2 )θ c where m = mass of the product cooled, kg/hr CPm = mean specific heat of the product, kJ/kg °C Preliminaries for the Estimation of Cooling Loads 213 Table 12.4: Air changes per hour for cold storages due to infiltration and door openings under normal conditions Volume (m3) Air Changes Per Hour Volume (m3) Air Changes Per Hour 5 10 15 20 25 30 35 40 50 60 70 80 100 1.84 1.23 1.15 1.95 0.75 0.65 0.60 0.575 0.500 0.45 0.415 0.375 0.35 120 150 200 250 375 500 625 750 1000 1250 1850 2500 0.30 0.27 0.23 0.21 0.165 0.145 0.125 0.110 0.095 0.085 0.0665 0.0585 (T1 – T2) = difference in initial and final temperature uc = cooling time, hours Latent heat load QL = m . hfg . θ c m and uc are as given previously hfg = latent heat of condensation, kJ/kg of moisture. The load added by the infiltrated air in the air-conditioned room can be calculated with the help of the psychrometric chart in Figure 12.1. a = condition of outdoor air b = condition of air leaving the air-conditioned room Latent heat load added per kg of dry air infiltrated into the room = ha – hc Sensible heat load added per kg of dry air infiltrated into the room = hc – hb. 12.8 Miscellaneous Heat Sources 12.8.1 Duct Heat Gain The heat gain through the duct is calculated by using the equation   T –T  Q = Ad .U Ta –  i o    2   (12.5) where Ad = area of duct, m2 U = overall heat transfer coefficient, kJ/m2 s, °C Ta = temperature of ambient air, °C Ti = temperature of air entering the duct, °C To = temperature of air leaving the duct, °C The heat gain by the duct running to the air-conditioned room is to be added into the sensible heat load of the room. The heat gain by the return air duct need not be added in the room sensible heat load but it should be added in the total system load and it should be considered in designing the air-conditioner capacity. 216 Chapter 12 12.8.2 Fan Load The power consumed by the fan is converted into heat and given into the air. If the fan is located before the air-conditioner, then the energy is added to the total load. If the fan is located after the air-conditioner, then the heat is added to the room sensible heat load. The heat equivalent of an air-conditioning fan horsepower (HP) is added as the sensible heat to the system. If the fan motor is outside the air stream, the energy lost due to the inefficiency of the motor is not added to the air. There are two types of air supply systems by fans: • • Draw-Through System In the draw-through system, the fan is drawing air through the cooling coil and supplying it to the conditioned space. It is the most common system in which the fan heat is in addition to the supply air heat gain. The heat should, therefore, be added to the room sensible heat. Blow-Through System In the blow-through system, a fan blows air through the cooling coil before being supplied to the conditioned space. In this system, the fan heat is added after the room to the return air. Thus, the fan heat is a load on the cooling coil. The heat should, therefore, be added to the total heat. The fan efficiencies are of the order of 70% for a central air-conditioning plant and about 50% for package air-conditioner fans. The fan HP depends on the quantity of air supplied and the pressure rise, compared to the total pressure developed by the fan. The supply air quantity in turn depends on the dehumidified rise, which is of the order of 8–14°C. The fan total pressure depends on the system pressure loss, which comprises the pressure drop through the duct work, grills, filters, cooling coil, and so on. The approximate values of pressure to be developed by fans are given in Table 12.7. Once the supply air rate and pressure are known, the fan power can be calculated. But these cannot be known until the load calculations have been completed. Hence, the procedure is to initially assume fan heat between 2.5% and 7.5% of the room sensible heat and check the value after the design has been completed. Designers usually take 5% of RSH as fan heat. Table 12.7: Fan pressure for different duct systems Sl. No. Type of Duct Work 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. No duct work (package units) Moderate ductwork, low velocity systems Considerable ductwork, low velocity systems Moderate ductwork, high velocity systems Considerable ductwork, high velocity systems Fan Pressure (cm H2O) 1.25–2.5 1.9–3.75 3.0–5.0 5.0–10.0 7.5–15.0 Preliminaries for the Estimation of Cooling Loads 217 12.9 Moisture Gain Through Permeable Walls and Ceilings In the summer, the vapor pressure of outdoor air is greater than that in air-conditioned space so that water vapor will enter into the conditioned space through walls and ceiling. Water vapor entering into the air-conditioned space adds to the latent heat load in the room. 12.10 Fresh Air Load Fresh air is supplied to the air-conditioned room to reduce the concentration of odors and smoke and simultaneously to maintain the required level of oxygen. Many types of fruits and vegetables remain alive even while stored in cold storage. The oxygen supply is necessary for these types of foods, and circulation of air is necessary to remove the heat generated by these foods. Apples, pears, and bananas fall in this category. The quantity of heat removed by the cooling coil is calculated from the psychrometric chart in Figure 12.2. a = condition of outside air b = condition of air leaving the cooling coil and entering into the room c = condition of air leaving the room Sensible heat removed by the cooling coil from fresh air per kg of dry air = hd = hb Latent heat removed by the cooling coil from air per kg of dry air = ha = hd The total heat removed from the fresh air should not be added to the room load for finding out the room SHR. The amount of heat added in the air after leaving the conditioner and before entering the room should be taken into account for finding out the room SHR value. All heat added in the air after leaving the room and before entering the conditioner should not be added in the room load Figure 12.2: Quantity of Heat Removed by Cooling Coil. 218 Chapter 12 Figure 12.3(a): Heat Flow System for a Room and Air-Conditioner. for finding out room SHR, but all heat of these types should be considered for finding out the capacity of the cooling coil or air-conditioner. 12.11 Design Concept of Air-Conditioning System The heat flow system for a room and air-conditioner is shown in Figure 12.3(a). Consider 1 kg of air entering the coil at a temperature t1. Figure 12.6 shows the process on a psychrometric chart. Out of 1 kg, x kg of air is bypassed and (1 – x) kg will come in contact with the cooling coil. The temperature of the cooling coil surface is ts. In the transfer of heat and water vapor in any conditioning process, the particles of air stream come in contact with the surface. The state of the contacted air is that of the saturated air at the temperature of the coil surface (i.e., ts). The uncontacted air (i.e., bypassed air) remains at the entering state. The end state of the air is the same as that produced by the complex mixing of the contacted and uncontacted particles (i.e., Point 2) as shown in Figure 12.6. 222 Chapter 12 Figure 12.5: Illustration of Bypass Factor. Figure 12.6: Bypass Factor and Leaving Air State. By making heat balance of the process, we can write xCpm t1 + (1 − x ) CPm ts = 1CPm t2 (12.12) where CPm is the mean specific heat of air, kJ/kg °C xt1 + ts − ts x = t2 x (t1 − ts ) = t2 − ts t –t x= 2 s t1 – ts (12.13) Thus, one can define a bypass factor (BPF) of the apparatus representing the fraction of the uncontacted air in terms of states 1, 2, and S. Similarly, by specific humidity balance and enthalpy balance, the bypass factor can also be defined as x= ω 2 – ω s h2 – hs = ω 1 – ω s h1 – hs (12.14) Preliminaries for the Estimation of Cooling Loads 223 Conversely, one can define a contact factor (1 – x) as representing a fraction of the contacted air. In the absence of any specific data, values from all three may be considered to be the same. In Figure 12.6 then, the resulting state 2 divides the line joining 1 to S in the ratio of x and (1 – x). The bypass factor is an important tool for measuring the performance of the heating and cooling coils. The performance of the coil is better with lower bypass factor. 12.12.1 Importance of Bypass Factor If mao is the mass flow rate of outside air (OA) entering, the effect of BPF is such as to add (x)(mao) amount of the outside air directly to the room and to allow only (1 – x)(mao) to pass through the apparatus. Although the room air is also bypassed, this does not affect the breakup of the load as the room air going to the room does not change the load situation. Then, we can say that a part of the ventilation load form a component of the room load. This bypassed outside air load is proportional to the bypass factor, x. It has both sensible and latent heat components. The other part, which is proportional to 1 – x, both sensible and latent and is passed around the apparatus, is added to the equipment load. Thus, the bypassed outside air loads on the room are SH = (OASH) BPF (12.15) LH = (OALH) BPF (12.16) where OASH = outside air, sensible heat OALH = outside air, latent heat These loads are imposed on the room in exactly the same manner as the infiltration load. The heat transfer is given by Qs = ma (hB − hA ) (12.22) = ma Cp (t B − t A ) = ma Cpa (t B − t A ) + maω Cpv (t B − t A ) = [ma (1.005 + 1.88 ω )](t B − t A ) (12.23) where, Cp = specific heat of humid air Figure 12.7: Sensible Heat Process. Preliminaries for the Estimation of Cooling Loads 225 Cpa = specific heat of dry air Cpv = specific heat of water vapor Where Cp is the humid specific heat. This heat, denoted by the subscript S, is called the sensible heat. If a building to be air-conditioned receives or loses heat due to transmission or other reasons, it is supposed to have sensible heat load. Heat gain in buildings will require the conditioning of air to lower temperatures, causing a cooling load on the air-conditioning equipment. However, heat loss in buildings will require the heating of air, causing a heating load on the equipment. In Eq. (12.23), ma denotes the mass flow rate of dry air. Generally the flow rate of air is measured in terms of cubic meters of air per minute (cm m). Then, the mass flow rate of dry air can be calculated from ma = Qv ρ where, Qv = volume flow rate of air ρ = density of air Expressing Qv in Cm m, we have m a = (Cm ⋅m ) ρ kgDa/ s 60 (12.24) For the purpose of calculations, standard air is taken at 20°C and 50% RH. Cooling below this temperature will result in the condensation of moisture. 12.14 Latent Heat Process: Humidification or Dehumidification When the state of air is altered along the t = constant line, such as BC in Figure 12.8, moisture in the form of vapor has to be transferred to change the humidity ratio of the air. This transfer of moisture is given by G = ma (ω C − ω B ) (12.26) 226 Chapter 12 Figure 12.8: Latent Heat Process. Because of this change in the humidity ratio, there is also a change in the specific enthalpy of the air given by (hC – hB) as shown in Figure 12.8. In air-conditioning practice, this change in enthalpy due to the change in the humidity ratio is considered to cause a latent heat transfer given by QL = ma (hC − hB ) = ma (Cp tC + hfg0 ω C ) − (Cp t B + hfg0 ω B ) = ma hfg0 (ω C − ω B ) = Ghfg0 = 2500 G (12.27) hfg0 = latent heat of vaporization at 0°C, kJ/kg In the preceding derivation, Cp has been taken as the same for both B and C. It is evident that though the term latent heat appears to be a misnomer, the quantity QL is proportional to the latent heat of vaporization hfg0. It implies that if water is to be evaporated or condensed at the temperature of air, the required heat transfer would be QL. Accordingly, if a building gains or loses moisture, it is supposed to have a latent heat load. A gain of moisture will require the condensation of moisture for the dehumidification of air in the conditioning apparatus, and hence a cooling load. On the other hand, a loss of moisture will necessitate the evaporation of water for the humidification of air in the apparatus and hence a heating load. Substituting 2,500 for hfg0 in Eq. The process line AC is called the sensible heat factor line, process line, or condition line. It is obvious that a sensible heat factor of unity corresponds to no latent heat transfer, and the SHF line is horizontal on the psychrometric chart. However, a zero SHF line is vertical on the psychrometric chart and implies no sensible heat transfer. An SHF of 0.75–0.8 is quite common in air-conditioning practice in a normal dry climate. Sensible heat factor 12.17 Methods of Drawing the SHF Line on the Psychrometric Chart The following are the ways in which the SHF line can be drawn on the psychrometric chart with these data: 1. Calculate tan u. Then, move vertically a certain distance ∆ω from the initial state, and then horizontally a distance ∆t = ( ∆ω ) (tan θ ) Finally, join the point obtained to the initial state point. However, this method is prone to grave error, because ∆ω is numerically small and tan u tends to a value close to zero. The method is given here only to illustrate the principle involved. It is never used. 2. Move vertically a certain enthalpy change ∆ hL. This is proportional to the latent heat change. Then, move horizontally equivalent to the sensible heat change in terms of enthalpy given by  SHF  ∆hs = ( ∆hL )   1 – SHF  Again, join the final point to the initial point. 3. This method uses a nomographic method with some charts in which a scale is provided for SHF. A given reference point is joined to the appropriate SHF on the scale. Then a line from the initial state point can be drawn parallel to the above line, which will give the required SHF line. 4. The fourth and the best method is by calculation. In the case of cooling and dehumidification of air, we have from Eq. CHAPTE R 13 Air-Conditioning Systems and Estimation of Cooling Load 13.1 Introduction The air circulated in cold storage must be able to take the load from the room. The outlet air conditions of the room air are fixed as per the produce requirements in the room. The condition of the air (dry bulb temperature, DBT) entering the room must be such that it must be able to take the load in the room and follow the path along room the sensible heat ratio (SHR) line. The lower the temperature, less the quantity of air required to be circulated. The minimum temperature of the supply air is determined by the arrangement of the system. Airconditioning installations for summer air-conditioning (cold storage) are commonly designed much below the product storage exit temperature. In this chapter, the calculation of heat loads and air quantities for different types of arrangements of equipment for cold storages and for human comfort air-conditioning are given. Only psychrometric charts are used in these calculations. 13.2 Types of Air-Conditioning Systems for the Cold Storages The different types of arrangements of equipment and the process representation on psychrometric charts are as follows. 13.2.1 All Fresh Air The schematic of the system (Figure 13.1a) and the process representation on the psychrometric chart (Figure 13.1b) using all fresh air c = condition of the outdoor air b = condition of room outlet air Draw the room SHR line through Point b, which cuts the saturation line of psychrometric chart at Point e, or room dew point temperature (DPT). The DPT of the coil is Point d. Join the line cd, which cuts the line be at Point a. Point a is the condition of the air entering in the storage room. The quantity of room circulated and bypassed air is mixed with the air coming out of the conditioner to raise its temperature in such a way that the air will be capable of taking the load in the air-conditioned space. The quantity of bypassed air is decided as per the condition of air leaving the conditioner, which is dependent on its DPT. The lower the DPT, the higher will be the recirculated mass, which is mixed with the air leaving the conditioner. In Figure 13.6b, ad is the conditioner line and be is the room SHR line, which cuts line ad at Point c as shown. Point c represents the condition of the air leaving the conditioner coil. The quality of air at Point c is the fresh air quantity taken into the conditioner. The quantity of air at condition b (room outer air) is mixed with the quantity of air at condition c in such proportion that the resulting condition will be f, which is capable of taking the load of the air-conditioned space. In this arrangement, the quantity of recirculated air required is considerably large (80–85%) compared with the other arrangements. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 14 Evaporators 14.1 Introduction The evaporator is the component of a refrigeration system in which heat is removed from the air, water, or any other body required to be cooled by the evaporating refrigerant. The evaporators are manufactured in different sizes, shapes, and types as per requirements. 14.2 Factors Considered in the Design of Evaporators 14.2.1 Heat Transfer The three heat transfer resistances in evaporators are: 1. Refrigerant side for the transfer of heat from solid surface to the liquid refrigerant 2. Metal wall 3. Cooled-medium side, which could be due to air, water, brine, or any other fluid or a wetted surface on a cooling and dehumidifying coil The heat is carried by the refrigerant from air, water, and brine. The refrigerant boils; therefore, the heat transfer coefficient of the refrigerant side is considerably high compared with heat transfer coefficient of the other side. The heat transfer capacity of the evaporator is given by Q = UA (tf − ts ) (14.1) where Q = heat capacity, kw U = overall heat transfer coefficient, W/m2K A = area of evaporator surface, m2 tf = temperature of fluid to be cooled passing through the evaporator, °C ts = saturation temperature of refrigerant at evaporator pressure, °C Too high (tf – ts) causes excessive dehydration of the product to be cooled and too low (tf – ts) causes (< 8°C) slime on some products like meat and fish if primary refrigerant is used for direct cooling. Some temperature differences for different products to be cooled are listed here. All rights reserved. 246 Chapter 14 Product Eggs and butter Frozen meats Vegetables and fruits Milk and cream Bear Cooling temperature (°C) 0 to –2 –20 to –15 +7 +3 +4.5 Refrigerant temperature (°C) –10 –30 –5 –8 –7 Temperature difference (°C) 8 10 12 11 11.5 14.2.2 Materials The choice of the material used depends upon the refrigerant used. Brass and copper, which are good conductors of heat, are used with all refrigerants except with ammonia. Freon should not be used with aluminum. 14.2.3 Velocity With an increase in velocity of the refrigerant, the heat transfer coefficient also increases, but the increased velocity causes greater pressure loss. There are recommended velocities for different refrigerants, which give high overall heat transfer coefficient (OHTC) with allowable pressure loss. 14.3 Classification of Evaporators D-X chiller: (a) Flooded or Direct Expansion (b) Dry Expansion Evaporators In flooded evaporators, the liquid refrigerant covers the entire heat transfer surface. In dry evaporators, a part of the heat transfer surface is used for superheating the vapor. A float valve is used for the expansion of the refrigerant in the case of a flooded evaporator, whereas a thermostatic expansion valve or a capillary tube (in case of small units) is used in conjunction with a dry evaporator. A distinction can also be made on the basis of the flow of refrigerant inside tubes in dry evaporators and outside tubes in flooded evaporators. A flooded chillertype evaporator is shown in Figure 14.1. The direct-expansion evaporators are also called D-X evaporators. Different types of D-X evaporators include the following: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Direct-expansion chiller Direct-expansion cooling coil for air with forced convection Direct-expansion coil for air blast freezer Natural convection evaporator for freezers of domestic refrigerators Evaporator coils submerged in brine tanks for ice plants 14.3.1 D-X Chiller Figure 14.2 shows a D-X chiller. In it, water flows in the shell across a number of baffles, and refrigerant from the liquid line directly expands inside the tubes and flows through a number of passes simultaneously, absorbing heat from recirculated water. Evaporators 247 Figure 14.1: Flooded Chiller. 14.3.2 D-X Coil-Type Dry Evaporator This type of evaporator (Figure 14.3) with fins on the airside is used in air-conditioning equipment. The coil in Figure 14.3 has four rows of tubing and only one tube circuit. Large D-X evaporators have more than one refrigerant circuit, otherwise the pressure will become too great. The name direct-expansion is derived from the fact that the refrigerant expands directly inside the tubing and evaporates, thus cooling the medium outside. To facilitate the return of oil to the compressor, D-X evaporators are fed from the top by a thermostatic expansion valve. Figure 14.2: Direct-Expansion Chiller. 248 Chapter 14 Figure 14.3: Direct-Expansion Cooling Coil with Thermostatic Expansion Valve. The D-X coil for air-blast freezers is similar in construction except that the refrigerant temperature is much lower (e.g., –35°C to –40°C). As a result, there is frost formation in between the fins; the flowing air therefore gets blocked. The frosting is more at the inlet end. Accordingly, larger fin spacing is provided at the inlet end. The spacing progressively decreases as the air gets dehumidified. 14.3.3 Design Procedure of D-X Chiller Evaporator The example is a basic design of a D-X chiller. Flooded evaporators are used in chillers for water or brine. The pool boiling refrigerant-side heat transfer coefficient in flooded evaporators is very low. The order of magnitude is 396 W/m2K as against 4170 W/m2K for water flowing inside tubes. Accordingly integral fins on the outside of the tubes are provided as shown in Figure 14.4. In any instance when the rate of heat flow from the refrigerant to the inside surface exceeds the rate of heat flow from outside surface to coolant, the capacity of the evaporator is limited by the capacity to dissipate the heat from the outer surface of the evaporator. In such conditions the OHTC – U can be increased by increasing the outside surface heat transfer coefficient, which can be done by providing the fins. The external area provided should be such that h0A0 = hiAi where h0 and hi are outside and inside heat transfer coefficients, and A0 and Ai are outside and inside areas of the evaporator. The finning of an air-cooled evaporator is more economical because h0 (from outer surface to air) is far less than hi (from refrigerant to inner surface of the evaporator). The finning of the Figure 14.4: Integral Fin Tube Construction Showing Tip Areas A1, Base Areas A2, and Fin Surface Areas A3. Evaporators 251 Figure 14.5: Inner Finnings. Figure 14.6: Configuration of Rectangular Fins. refrigerant side also helps to increase the heat transfer rate when the water or brine is used as a coolant at a high velocity (h0 > hi). The inner finning toward the refrigerant side will improve the evaporator capacity in proportion to the increase in amount of interior wetted surface. The two types of interior finning are shown in Figure 14.5. The finning toward the low heat transfer coefficient side is always preferred as compared with high heat transfer coefficient side. Extended surface evaporators, such as Figure 14.6 are extensively used for cooling of air, because the airside heat transfer coefficient is much lower than the boiling coefficient. Coupled with forced convection, high overall heat transfer coefficients can be achieved in D-X coil evaporators. Problems 1. Calculate the overall heat transfer surface area for the chiller. 3. A direct-expansion chiller provides 20 tons of refrigeration for water entering at 20°C and flowing at the rate of 250 g/min. The evaporator is fed through an automatic expansion valve. The evaporator temperature is 2°C. It is now required to use the same chiller for cooling 100 kg/min of water at 30°C.
