CHAPTE R 15 Refrigerant Compressors A compressor is considered the heart of the refrigeration system, because it pumps the refrigerant through the system, similar to the heart that pumps blood in the human body. Three types of compressors are commonly used in industry today: reciprocating compressors, centrifugal compressors, and rotary compressors. 15.1 Thermodynamics of Compression Process The types of compressors that are in common use in the industry are described in the following sections. 15.1.1 Reciprocating Compressors The reciprocating compressor sucks the low pressure and low temperature refrigerant during its suction stroke and delivers at high pressure and high temperature. 15.1.1.1 Work in Reciprocating Compressor (Arora, 2000) The p-v diagram for the machine cycle of a reciprocating compressor is shown in Figure 15.1, along with the skeleton diagram of the cylinder and piston mechanism. When the piston is in the extreme left position of the inner dead center (IDC), the volume occupied by the gas is Vc = V3, called the clearance volume (i.e., the volume between the IDC position of the piston and the cylinder head). As the piston moves outward, the clearance gas expands to 4, where the pressure inside the cylinder is equal to the pressure at the suction flange of the compressor. As the piston moves further, the suction valve S opens and the vapor from the evaporator is sucked in until the extreme right position of outer dead center (ODC) is reached. At this point, the volume occupied by the gas is V1. The stroke or swept volume or piston displacement is Vp = (V1 – V3 ) = π D2 L 4 Where D is the bore or diameter and L is the stroke (i.e., the distance traveled by the piston between IDC and ODC of the cylinder). At 1, the suction valve closes as the piston moves inward and the compression begins. At 2, the pressure in the cylinder is equal to the pressure at the discharge flange of the compressor. A further inward movement of the piston results in the pressure in the cylinder exceeding the condenser pressure. This opens the discharge valve D, and the vapor from the cylinder flows into the condenser until the piston again reaches Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00015-4 253 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 254 Chapter 15 Figure 15.1: Cylinder and Piston Mechanism and p-v Diagram of a Reciprocating Compressor. the IDC position. Gas equal to the clearance volume Vc remains in the cylinder, and the cycle is repeated. The work done for the compression of the machine cycle is given by the cyclic integral of the pressure delivery valve (PDV). The reciprocating compressors are built in sizes ranging from a fraction of horsepower to several hundred horsepower. These are used for refrigeration plants ranging in size from 0.25 tons to 1000 tons. The reciprocating compressors are satisfactorily used with refrigerants such as NH3, SO2, CH3Cl, and most of the Freons, which is preferable for high compression ratio and low specific volume refrigerants. There are two different types of reciprocating compressor in general use. 1. Single-acting vertical compressor 2. Double-acting horizontal compressor There is one delivery of high-pressure refrigerant for every revolution for a single-acting compressor, and two deliveries from both sides of the piston for each revolution of the double-acting compressor. 15.1.2 Multistage Compression When the compression ratio required is considerably high, as in the case of low temperature refrigeration systems, the single-stage compression is highly uneconomical due to the following reasons. Refrigerant Compressors 255 Figure 15.2: (a) Multistage Compression with Perfect Intercooling. (b) Multistage Compression with Perfect Intercooling (p-v Diagram). 1. 2. 3. 4. Very low volumetric efficiency High frictional losses Leakage problems High running cost In multistage compression, the compression of refrigerant from initial pressure to final pressure is carried out in more than one cylinder. A multistage compression with intermediate cooling is generally adopted for economical working. A schematic diagram of multistage compression with perfect intercooling is shown in Figures 15.2a and b. The kW required for multistage compression with intermediate cooling can be calculated with the following equation. n –1 n –1    p3  n n 1   p2  n T1 + T3   – T1 – T3  kW(total) = mR .  n – 1 1000   p1   p2    where m = mass of refrigerant compressed, kg/sec n = index of compression 256 Chapter 15 P2 = delivery pressure of compression, N/m2 P1 = suction pressure of compression, N/m2 T1 = temperature at start of compression T3 = temperature at the end of compression 15.1.2.1 Factors affecting the performance of reciprocating compressors 1. Suction temperature: The compressor capacity decreases with a decrease in suction (evaporator) temperature. The lower the evaporator temperature, the lower is the vaporizing pressure, resulting in lower density of the suction vapor. Thus, the mass of refrigerant circulated per unit time decreases with decrease in suction temperature for a given displacement. 2. Effect on compressor brake power (BP): Keeping the condenser temperature same reduces the evaporator (suction) temperature increase the BP per ton. But total BP is dependent on work of compression and mass flow rate of refrigerant. With decrease in evaporator temperature, the work of compression increases and mass of refrigerant circulated per second decreases. Decrease in mass flow outweighs the increase in compression work per kg. Therefore, the net effect is to decrease the total BP of the compressor. 15.1.3 Capacity Control of Reciprocating Compressors Refrigerating capacity control with reciprocating compressors running at constant speed consists of controlling the quantity of the gas delivered to match the fluctuating load. In an efficient control system, the power consumption of the compressors should be proportional to the amount of gas delivered. Various control methods are discussed here. 15.1.4 On and Off Control A simple on-off or start-stop control in conjunction with a thermostat is used to advantage in small unitary equipment, such as refrigerators, air-conditioners, and water coolers. It is particularly suited to situations in which a sudden large demand is followed by periods of small or no demand on capacity. Switching off is preferable to running at partial load because of the low part-load efficiency of squirrel-cage induction motors employed in refrigerant compressors. 15.1.5 Holding the Valves Open Holding the valves open is the most commonly used method of unloading in multicylinder vertical water–cooled (VW) compressors. It is accomplished by the lifting of suction valves, usually of two cylinders together, by means of depressors or fingers. The gas drawn into the cylinder during the suction stroke is displaced back into the suction Refrigerant Compressors 257 line during the discharge stroke. No work is involved except the frictional work during such idling. The depressor rods are operated by a cam, which is turned either manually or by means of a thermostat or a pressure-stat (for suction pressure). This method is best for capacity control when the condition is of intermittent unloading that requires idling for short periods only. 15.1.6 Hot Gas Bypass In this method, a part of the compressed gas is bypassed back to the suction line through a constant pressure throttle valve. The valve admits hot gas in the suction line as the evaporator pressure tends to drop, thus maintaining constant suction pressure. This method is not efficient because the suction temperature tends to increase as more and more hot gas is bypassed. The compressor work also tends to increase, thus resulting in the loading of the compressor instead of unloading. However, the method is simple and can be used in conjunction with other methods. 15.1.7 Using Multiple Units The use of multiple units of reciprocating compressors is common, especially when unloading is required for long periods. Some units may serve the purpose of stand-by equipment as well, which allows for partial load operation in the case of breakdown or routine maintenance of other units. 15.2 Centrifugal Compressors (Arora and Domukundwar, 2004) A single-stage centrifugal compressor mainly consists of the following four components as shown in Figure 15.3. Figure 15.3: Elements of a Centrifugal Compressor. 258 Chapter 15 1. An inlet casing accelerates the fluid to the impeller inlet. 2. An impeller transfers energy to the fluid in the form of increased static pressure (enthalpy) and kinetic energy. 3. A diffuser converts the kinetic energy at the impeller outlet into enthalpy, resulting in an increase in pressure. 4. A volute casing collects the fluid and further converts the remaining kinetic energy into enthalpy, resulting in further pressure increase. Besides these components in a multistage compressor, intercoolers are generally integrated with the casing. The casing is usually made of cast iron and the impeller of high-speed (chrome-nickel) steel. The maximum stress develops at the root of the blades. The diffuser is normally of the vaneless type, which permits more efficient part load operation and is typical for most air-conditioning plants. A vaned diffuser will certainly cause shock losses if the compressor has to run at reduced capacity and flow (part load). The rise in pressure per stage of centrifugal compressor is smaller compared with single-stage reciprocating compressor, and hence when high compression ratio is required with centrifugal compressor, a multistage system is used. This system is shown in Figure 15.4a with an accompanying p-h chart in Figure 15.4b. In multistage, the impellers are made progressively smaller in size in the direction of vapor flow to compensate with the reduction in volume of the vapor resulting from previous compression. These can be used for temperature ranges of –10°C to –100°C. Centrifugal machines are built for industrial use with NH3 and other refrigerants. These compressors may have up to seven stages. The smallest centrifugal compressor has a capacity of 250 kW. Semihermetic compressors are made up to 7,000 kW and open drive machines up to 21,000 kW. These compressors are preferred above 50 tons load. Some of the commercial centrifugal compressors are shown in Figures 15.5, 15.6, and 15.7. Systems of large size require large-diameter refrigerant suction and discharge pipes to connect the components of the system. As a result, they are built up as liquid cooling, watercooled packages with condenser and evaporator components as part of factory-built assembly as shown in Figures 15.5, 15.6, and 15.7. 15.2.1 Capacity Control of Centrifugal Compressors Centrifugal compressors require high tip speeds (u2) to develop the necessary pressure ratio. The high tip speed is achieved by employing either a large-diameter impeller or high rpm or both. Because of large u2, the velocities in general, including the flow velocity C, are high. Also, there must be a reasonable width of the shrouds to minimize friction and Refrigerant Compressors 259 Figure 15.4: (a) Refrigeration System with Multistage Centrifugal Compressor. (b) p-h Diagram. achieve high efficiency. Thus, because of the sufficiently large flow area (diameter D and width of shrouds b) required and large flow velocity, the satisfactory volume that can be handled by a centrifugal compressor is about 30–60 cubic meters per minute (cmm). A single centrifugal compressor, therefore, can be designed for a minimum capacity approximately of the order of 250 TR with R 11 and 150 TR with R 113 for the purpose of air-conditioning. These two refrigerants are common and have been used with centrifugal compressor in the past. The centrifugal compressors are, therefore, used in large-capacity installations in which the load varies through a wide range and hence, capacity control in them, although simple, is especially important. 260 Chapter 15 Figure 15.5: Centrifugal Compressor (Carrier 19DG). One of the common methods varies the compressor speed through a speed-reduction gear. The decrease in speed results in an operation on a lower head-flow characteristic, giving a lower volume flow rate that corresponds to the same pressure ratio. The use of variable inlet whirl vanes is another method of capacity control frequently employed with a constant-speed drive. The capacity is varied by changing the angle at which the gas enters the impeller. The gas then enters with prerotation, resulting in a decrease in flow. Figure 15.6: Centrifugal Compressor (Trane CVGA). Refrigerant Compressors 261 Figure 15.7: Centrifugal Compressor (York Open Turbopak). Both methods are efficient and the work done remains proportional to the volume handled. 15.3 Screw Compressors The use of screw compressor in refrigeration industry is recent. Following the use of injected oil for cooling, sealing, and lubrication, the versatility, reliability, and compactness of screw compressors have earned them a significant share. Rotary screw compressors also belong to the category of positive displacement compressors. The machine essentially consists of two helically grooved rotors as illustrated in Figure 15.8, which rotate in a housing. Figure 15.8: Sectional and Side Views of a Screw Compressor. 262 Chapter 15 The male rotor consists of lobes and is normally the driving rotor. The female rotor has gullies and is normally the driven rotor. A four-lobe male rotor will drive a six-gully female rotor at two-thirds of its speed. At 3,600 rpm, the number of compressed gas discharges of a four-lobe rotor will be 4 × 3,600 = 14,400 per minute. As in the case of other positive displacement machines, the working cycle involves three basic continuous phases: suction, compression, and discharge. When the male rotor turns clockwise, an interlobe space between a pair and housing, nearest to the suction end, opens and is filled with the gas. Four such pairs are filled during one revolution in a four-lobe rotor, and the suction periods overlap one another. When remeshing starts, the volume decreases and the pressure rises. The charge is moved helically and compressed until the trapped volume reaches the discharge end. The compression ratio is thus fixed. Further rotation simply empties the rotors of the high-pressure gas until the last traces of the gas are squeezed out, irrespective of the pressure in the condenser. On completion of the discharge phase, no residual gas remains in the rotors. As a result, no expansion of clearance gases occurs. The compressor has no suction and discharge valves. There are leakage paths in a screw compressor, mainly across the line of mesh between the rotors and across the clearance between the rotors and the housing. To eliminate leakage, oil is injected in a number of small jets directed toward the mesh. Oil injection also serves the purpose of cooling and lubricating along with that of sealing the leakage paths. Medium-size screw compressors have capacities between 150 kW and 350 kW, working with NH3 and CFCs refrigerants installed in dairies, meat and fish processing plants, and cold storages. By changing built-in step-up gear ratio, different gear ratios are obtained (i.e., four different compressor sizes in the same compressor body). This is an advantage for customer from the point of view of spare parts. The four steps are 100%, 75%, 50%, and 25% of full capacity. This new system gives even better full-load as well as part-load characteristics, due to smaller dead volumes and smaller pressure drop in the bypass channel. A cut view of a commercial screw compressor is shown in Figure 15.9. Volumetric ratio control has two main objectives. For certain applications where the condensing temperature and evaporating temperature vary within wide ranges, the built-in volume ratio should be optimized in relation to the variation in condensing and evaporation temperatures. The reason is to obtain as high an average coil factor as possible. An application of this type is found in refrigerated cargo vessels carrying frozen food stuff in one direction and fruits in the other. The evaporating temperature varies from –40°C during the first voyage to –50°C during the second. By optimizing the built-in volume ratio, a high coefficient of performance (COP) is obtained. Refrigerant Compressors 263 Figure 15.9: Dismantled View of a Screw Compressor (Commercial Type). A slide valve, closely following the shape of the rotors is used for capacity control. At full load, the valve is closed. At part load, the valve opens enabling a return flow passage to be formed so that a part of the gas drawn into the interlobe spaces can flow back to the suction side. The screw compressor combines many advantageous features of both centrifugal and reciprocating compressors, along with some of its own. Because it is a positive displacement machine, high-pressure refrigerants, such as R 22 and ammonia are used in it. Because it is a high-speed rotary machine, it can handle a large volume. It is, therefore, extremely suitable for largecapacity low-temperature applications such as in food refrigeration, and also in large-capacity central air-conditioning plants as an alternative to R 11 (CFC 11) centrifugal compressors. Unlike centrifugal compressors, it has no surging problems. Like reciprocating compressors, it has small pipe dimensions and positive pressures due to the use of high-pressure refrigerants. Like centrifugal compressors, it has high compression efficiency, continuous capacity control, unloaded starting, and no balancing problems. Also, the compressor is suitable for large-capacity installations. 15.4 Rotary Compressors Rotary compressors are positive displacement, direct-drive machines. There are essentially two designs of this compressor: 1. Rolling piston type 2. Rotating vane type 264 Chapter 15 Figure 15.10: Rotary Compressor. (a) Rolling Piston Type. (b) Rotating Vane Type. In the rolling piston type shown in Figure 15.10a, the roller is mounted on an eccentric shaft with a single blade, which is always in contact with the roller by means of a spring. The theoretical piston displacement is Vp = π H ( A2 – B 2 ) 4 where A and B are the diameters of the cylinder and rolling piston, respectively, and H is the height of the cylinder. In the rotating vane type with four vanes shown in Figure 15.10b, the rotor is concentric with the shaft. The vanes slide within the rotor but keep contact with the cylinder. The assembly of rotor and the vanes is off-center with respect to the cylinder. In both designs, the whole assembly is enclosed in a housing (not shown in the figures) that is filled with oil, and it remains submerged in oil. An oil film forms the seal between the high-pressure and the low-pressure sides. When the compressor stops, this seal is lost and the pressure equalizes. Rotary compressors have high volumetric efficiencies due to negligible clearance. They are normally used in a single stage up to a capacity of 5 TR with R 114. Large rotary compressors are used in low-temperature fields, such as in chemical and industrial processing, cold storages, and freezing, as high displacement, low-stage or booster compressors at –90°C to –100°C evaporator temperature with R 12, R 22, and ammonia. They are available in 10–600 hp sizes with 2–120 cmm displacement in one unit. Refrigerant Compressors 265 15.5 Pressure–Enthalpy Charts In vapor compression refrigeration system, the refrigerant changes its phase as it is conveyed through various components of the system. Pressure–enthalpy charts are extensively used to represent thermodynamic properties of the refrigerant. Most commonly used charts depict pressure and enthalpy values on the x axis (log scale) and y axis, respectively. The entire refrigeration cycle comprising evaporator, compressor, condenser, and expansion valve can be conveniently drawn on a pressure–enthalpy chart. Pressure–enthalpy and pressure–entropy charts are available for many refrigerants conforming to the specifications of ASHRAE (1981). The pressure–enthalpy charts for NH3 and R 12 refrigerants are given in the Appendix. The pressure–enthalpy charts are useful in obtaining enthalpy values for each process as H1, H2, H3, and so on. Substituting these values in the mass and energy formulae for each component, the results, such as work done or energy input and mass flow rate in various operations, can be calculated. In the examples shown next in this chapter, only these charts are used. While using these charts, students are advised to remember that for the expansion process in constant enthalpy, evaporation and condensation are isothermal processes (constant temperature) and compression is an isentropic process. 15.6 Worked out Problems Example 15.1 In a catalog of refrigerant compressor data, it is shown that an R 12 compressor delivers 10 tons at –15°C evaporator temperature and 40°C condensing temperature, when the suction temperature of the compressor becomes +15°C. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 16 Condensers 16.1 Introduction The condenser is another important component of a cold storage refrigeration system and needs consideration in design and construction. The condenser removes the heat from the refrigerant that is carried from evaporator as well as heat added by the compressor and converts the vapor refrigerant into liquid refrigerant. It is a heat exchanger in which heat transfer takes place from high-temperature vapor to low-temperature air or water, which is a cooling medium. It is ultimately in the condenser that heat is rejected in a vapor compression refrigeration machine. The vapor at discharge from the compressor is superheated. The superheating of vapor takes place in the discharge line and in the first few coils of the condenser. It is followed by the condensation of the vapor at the saturated discharge temperature or condensing temperature. In some condensers, subcooling may also take place near the bottom where there is only liquid. However, the sensible heat of the superheating and subcooling processes is small as compared to the latent heat of condensation process. 16.2 Heat Rejection Ratio The loading on the condenser per unit of refrigeration is called heat rejection ratio. Because Qk = Q0 + w, the heat rejection ratio is Qk w 1 = 1+ = 1+ Q0 Ec Q0 where (16.1) Qk = heat rejection ratio Q0 Qk = heat removed in the condenser Q0 = heat load from the evaporator W = heat equivalent of work from the compressor Ec = work input of compressor per unit load from evaporator. This ratio depends on the coefficient of performance (COP), which in turn depends on condenser and evaporator temperatures. In actual air-conditioning equipment for R 12 and R 22 operating at ti = 40°C and t0 = 5°C, the heat rejection ratio is approximately 1.25. All rights reserved. 274 Chapter 16 16.3 Types of Condensers The type of condenser is generally characterized by the cooling medium used. Thus, the three types of condensers are air-cooled condensers, water-cooled condensers, and evaporative condensers. A fourth type is dependent on ground-cooling, which is not commonly used. 16.3.1 Air-Cooled Condensers In air-cooled condensers, heat is removed by the air using either natural or forced circulation. The condensers are made of steel, copper, or aluminum tubing provided with fins to improve airside heat transfer. The refrigerant flows inside the tubes and the air outside. Air-cooled condensers are used only in small-capacity machines, such as refrigerators and small water coolers, which use vertical wire and tube or plate-and-tube construction with natural circulation, and in window-type and package air-conditioners, which have tubes with five to seven fins per cm and use forced circulation of air. The current practice in the forcedconvection type is to use 10–15 m2 of the total surface area per ton of refrigeration based on 2–5 m/s face velocity of air over the coil. Air-cooled condensers are seldom made in sizes over 5 TR because of high head pressure, excessive power consumption, and objectionable fan noise. 16.3.2 Water-Cooled Condensers Water-cooled condensers can be of three types: shell and tube, shell and coil, and double tube. The shell and tube type, in which water flows inside tubes and the refrigerant passes outside the tubes and condenses in the shell, is the most commonly used condenser. Figure 16.1 shows the arrangement for a two-pass condenser. A shell and tube condenser also serves the purpose of a receiver, especially for pumping down the refrigerant, because there is sufficient space in the shell. The bottom portion of the condenser serves the purpose of a subcooler as the condensed liquid comes in contact with the entering water at a lower temperature. Thus, we see that shell and tube condensers—and for that matter, all types of condensers—are usually overdesigned. This also keeps the head pressure low and saves power. Further, the outside surface of the shell is available for heat transfer. The shell is made of steel. Copper tubes are used for fluorocarbons and steel tubes for ammonia. The shell and coil condenser consists of an electrically welded closed shell that contains a water coil, sometimes of finned tubing. In the double tube arrangement, the refrigerant condenses in the outer tube and water flows through the inner tube in the opposite direction. Condensers 275 Figure 16.1: Schematic Representation of a Two-Pass Water-Cooled Shell and Tube Condenser. Water-cooled condensers are invariably used in conjunction with cooling towers, spray ponds, and so on. Heated water from the condenser is led to the cooling tower where it is cooled by self-evaporation into a stream of air. After cooling, the water is pumped back to the condenser. 16.3.3 Evaporative Condensers Figure 16.2 shows the schematic diagram of an evaporative condenser. The refrigerant first rejects its heat to water and then water rejects its heat to air, mainly in the form of evaporated water. Air leaves with high humidity as in a cooling tower. Thus, an evaporative condenser combines the functions of a condenser and cooling tower. Evaporative condensers are commonly used on large ammonia plants because they are found to be lower in cost. Such condensers require a large amount of the refrigerant charge due to the longer length of the refrigerant piping. But in the case of ammonia systems, this aspect is immaterial because the refrigerant is quite inexpensive. Figure 16.2: Evaporative Condenser. 276 Chapter 16 Most of the heat given by the refrigerant vapor is carried by air in the form of sensible and latent heat; therefore, the effectiveness of this type of condenser depends upon the wet bulb temperature (WBT) of the incoming air. The capacity of the condenser also depends upon the quantity of air circulated through the condenser, which is limited by the air velocity permitted through the eliminator without carryover of water particles. The quantity of water required for this type of condenser is less than 10% of that required for a water condenser. 16.4 Water-Side Coefficient The water-side coefficient is expressed by the well-known Dittus–Boelter equation, which relates the Nusselts number with Reynolds and Prandtl numbers for forced convection for turbulent flow inside the tubes.  D µρ  hi D = 0.023   µ  K 0.8  Cp µ   K  0.4 (16.2) All the fluid properties are evaluated at the bulk mean temperature of the fluid. 16.4.1 Fouling Factor Condensers should always be designed considering the formation of scales (i.e., fouling inside the tubes). The following fouling factors are recommended. For copper tubes and for R12 and R22 1 = 0.00009 J −1s m 2 K hf (16.3) For steel tubes and ammonia condensers, it is i = 0.0009 J −1 s m 2 K (16.4) 16.5 Air-Side Coefficient In refrigerant condensers with forced convection, air flows outside the tubes in cross-flow to the refrigerant. Average heat transfer coefficient for the forced convection of air across the tube may be calculated from Grimson’s equation. n 1  D µ∞ ρ  hD P3 = C  µ  r K (16.5) Condensers 277 Table 16.1: Constants C and n as evaluated by equation 16.5 Re C n 0.4–4 4–40 40–4,000 4,000–40,000 40,000+ 0.989 0.911 0.683 0.193 0.266 0.33 0.385 0.466 0.618 0.805 where constant C and n are tabulated as a function of the Reynolds’s numbers in Table 16.1. Chato has established the effect of inclining the tubes to the horizontal. He found that the heat transfer coefficient increases by 10–20% at inclination angles of 10–20° as a result of faster drainage of the condensate. 16.6 Condenser Tubes with Integral Fins It is known that the overall heat transfer coefficient (Uo) always has a value lower than the lower of the two film coefficients ho and hi however large the other film coefficient may be. Thus, it is advantageous to decrease the major heat transfer resistance by providing extended surface or fins on the side of the lower heat transfer coefficient. For a shell and tube condenser, the water-side coefficient is 6000 W/m–2 K–1 and on the refrigerant side with ammonia the coefficient is 8000 W/m–2 K–1 and the same for R12, and R22 is 1500 W/m–2 K–1 only. 16.7 Heat Transfer in Condenser The heat transfer in a water-cooled condenser is given by Qk = UA∆t = ∆t R (16.6) where U = overall heat transfer coefficient based on the surface area A of the condenser ∆t = overall temperature difference Figure 16.3 shows the components of the heat transfer resistance in a water-cooled condenser, including the outside refrigerant film, metal wall, scaling on the waterside surface, and inside water film. The overall resistance is obtained by adding all the resistances, which are in series. The preceding equations show that heat transfer coefficient increases with thermal conductivity. For R12 and R22 condensers, it is desirable to use fins on the refrigerant side. In air-cooled condensers, the airside coefficient is much lower than the refrigerant-side coefficient, fins must be provided on the airside. Water enters at 21°C and leaves at 28°C. Air enters at 28°C and 21°C WBT and leaves at 28°C saturated. The suction and condensing temperatures of F12 are –10°C and 40°C, and condensing load per ton of refrigeration is 252 kJ/min. Solution The evaporative condenser with various inputs and outputs is shown in Figure 16.10. Figure 16.10: Evaporative Condenser in Example 16.5. Condensers 293 Figure 16.11: Psychrometric Chart for Example 16.5. It is assumed that the total heat from the refrigerant at the condenser is given only to water, and the same heat is given by the water to the air. This is necessary for steady-state condition. The thermodynamic values of incoming and outgoing streams are shown in Figure 16.11. td1 = DBT of entering air td2 = DBT of leaving air ha1 = total heat of entering air ha2 = total heat of leaving air hw1 = total heat of entering water hw2 = total heat of leaving water w1 = specific humidity of entering air w2 = specific humidity of leaving air mw = mass of water entering ma = mass of air entering hfg = latent heat of vaporization of water content of air Energy balance around the condenser is as follows: Total energy entering = Total energy leaving Total energy entering: mwhw1 + ma(ha1 + w1 hfg1) Total energy leaving: mwhw2 + ma(ha2 + w2 hfg2) mwhw1 – mwhw2 = ma[(ha2 + w2 hfg2) – (ha + w1 hfg1)] mw(hw1 – hw2) = ma[(ha2 – ha1) + (w2 hfg2 – w1 hfg1)] hfg2 and hfg1 are the latent heat of vaporization of moisture of air at incoming and outgoing temperatures of the air. CHAPTE R 17 Expansion Devices 17.1 Introduction An expansion device in a refrigeration system normally serves two purposes. One is the thermodynamic function of expanding the liquid refrigerant from the condenser pressure to the evaporator pressure. The other is the control function, which may involve supply of the liquid to the evaporator at the rate of which it is evaporated. The latter has the important role and determines the efficiency with which the evaporator surface is utilized. The different devices that are used to perform these functions include the following: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. Capillary tube Pressure control or automatic expansion valve Thermostatic expansion valve High-side float valve Low-side float valve Solenoid valve 17.2 Capillary Tube A capillary tube is a fixed restriction–type device. It is a long and narrow tube connecting the condenser to the evaporator. The pressure drop through the capillary tube is due to the follow­ ing two factors. 1. Friction, due to fluid viscosity, resulting in frictional pressure drop. 2. Acceleration due to the flashing of the required refrigerant into vapor, resulting in momentum pressure drop. The cumulative pressure drop must be equal to the difference in pressure at the two ends of the tube. The mass flow through the capillary tube will therefore adjust so that the pressure drop through the tube just equals the difference in pressure between the condenser and the evaporator. For a given state of refrigerant, the pressure drop is directly proportional to the length and inversely proportional to the bore diameter of the tube. The advantage of capillary tube is its simplicity, low cost, and absence of any moving parts. Also its on-off control is advantageous because of its unloading characteristics. Thus, when the compressor stops, it allows high and low pressures to equalize, thereby enabling the compressor motor to restart on no load. Accordingly, smaller low starting torque motors can Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00017-8 297 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 298 Chapter 17 be used. The disadvantage with the capillary tube is that once a capillary tube has been selected, it will be suitable only for the design pressure drop and flow. It cannot satisfy the flow requirements with changing condenser and evaporator pressures. This device is only used for small-capacity units such as domestic refrigerators, water coolers, and small commercial freezers. 17.3 Automatic (Constant Pressure) Expansion Valve An automatic expansion valve works in response to the pressure changes in the evaporator due to either increase or decrease of load. This valve maintains a constant pressure throughout the varying load operation on the evaporator controlling the quantity of refrigerant flowing into the evaporator. The arrangement is shown in Figure 17.1. It consists of a needle valve, a seat, a diaphragm, and a spring. The initial tension of the spring can be adjusted by a screw. In order to maintain the constant pressure, the opening of the valve in the seat is controlled by the two opposing forces: (1) the tension of the spring, and (2) the pressure in the evaporator acting on diaphragm. Once the spring is adjusted for a desired evaporator pressure and given load, the valve then operates automatically with the changing load conditions in the evaporator. It controls the flow of refrigerant into evaporator, maintaining constant pressure in the evaporator as per the change in the load on the evaporator. This process can be further explained with the following example. Assume the spring is adjusted initially to maintain a pressure of 1.5 bar in the evaporator at a given load. If the pressure falls below 1.5 bar due to a decrease in load, the spring pressure Figure 17.1: Automatic or Constant Pressure Expansion Valve. Expansion Devices 299 will exceed the evaporator pressure and cause the valve to open more and increases the flow of refrigerant. The rate of evaporation increases due to increased quantity of refrigerant and builds up the pressure until the equilibrium is reached with the spring tension. If the pressure in the evaporator increases due to a decrease in load above 1.5 bar, the evaporator pressure will exceed the spring tension and the difference in pressure acts to close the valve. This reduces the quantity of refrigerant flowing to the evaporator and further decreases the rate of evaporation in the evaporator, which lowers the evaporator pressure until equilibrium is reached with the spring tension. When the refrigeration system is closed, the evaporation of the refrigerant in the evaporator still continues and increases the pressure in the evaporator above the spring tension, causing the valve to close. The system will be started when the evaporator pressure falls suddenly and the valve opens, allowing the refrigerant to flow into the evaporator to establish an equilibrium between the evaporator pressure and spring tension. The major disadvantage of this device is the poor efficiency of operation (response) compared with other expansion devices. Most commercial and light industrial refrigeration systems employ direct-expansion–type evaporators comprising one continuous circuit of tubing. To obtain maximum heat exchange, it is necessary to control the flow of refrigerant into an evaporator at a rate that matches the prevailing heat load. In doing so, it is also desirable to avoid overfeed, which is wasteful in system performance terms and dangerous from the viewpoint of potential compressor damage. Figure 17.2 shows the events of vapor compression refrigeration on the p-h diagram under different thermodynamic states of refrigerant as it leaves the evaporator and the effect of that state on performance of the system. Figure 17.2: Thermodynamic States of the Refrigerant. 300 Chapter 17 To achieve the preceding parameters, it is necessary to maintain the refrigerant condition at the evaporator outlet in a slightly superheated state (1–3˚C), thereby ensuring that no liquid refrigerant leaves the evaporator. This ensures that all liquid fed into the evaporator is fully used and prevents wasted liquid from slugging back into the compressor. If the amount of superheat at the outlet of evaporator is too large, then the effective heat transfer surface of the evaporator is considerably reduced, resulting in lower overall system performance. Therefore, it is necessary to maintain a careful balance such that the level of superheat maintained is sufficient to avoid flood back, yet is not high enough to cause a loss in evaporator duty. Superheat is the difference in temperature between the actual temperature of refrigerant vapor leaving the evaporator and the saturation temperature of liquid refrigerant at the entry of the evaporator. Therefore, if we monitor the difference in these two temperatures and regulate the refrigerant flow accordingly, a more or less constant superheat value can be maintained. This balance is achieved with a thermostatic expansion valve. 17.4 Thermostatic Expansion Valve The thermostatic expansion valve controls the flow of refrigerant through the evaporator in such a way that the quality of the vapor leaving the evaporator will be always in superheated condition. Its operation is used for maintaining a constant degree of superheat at the evaporator outlet. The arrangement of the system is shown in Figure 17.3. The valve motion to allow the flow of more or less refrigerant to maintain a constant level of superheat at the evaporator outlet is controlled by three pressures: Figure 17.3: Thermostatic Expansion Valve. Expansion Devices 301 Pb = pressure in the bulb Ps = spring tension Pe = pressure in the evaporator Under normal operating condition, the pressure exerted by the vapor in the controlling bulb on the diaphragm is balanced by the spring tension and the pressure in the evaporator. Pb = Ps + Pe This system can be explained with the following example: Say the evaporator temperature maintained is –5˚C so that the pressure in the evaporator is 1.5 bar, which is the saturation pressure corresponding to –5˚C, and the tension of the spring is adjusted to 0.5 bar. The total pressure acting on the diaphragm to close the valve is 1.5 + 0.5 = 2 bar. The pressure in the remote bulb is 2 bar, which corresponds to the saturation temperature of 5˚C. If the vapor leaving the evaporator becomes saturated at Point B (temperature = –5˚C) and absorbs the heat from the surroundings during travel from B to C and becomes superheated to 5˚C, then no heat transfer will occur between the vapor and remote bulb, and the system works in equilibrium condition. If the load on the system increases, then the vapor leaving the evaporator becomes saturated at Point A instead of Point B, and heat absorbed by the vapor from the surroundings during travel from A to C will superheat the vapor to 7˚C, which is 2˚C above the temperature in the remote bulb; therefore, heat will be transferred from the vapor to the bulb and Pb will increase. As Pb > (Ps + Pe), it will try to open the valve to allow more refrigerant to flow to the evaporator. This process will be continued until the pressure equilibrium on the diaphragm is reached. The reverse (closing of the valve) takes place when the load on the evaporator decreases. The degree of superheat of the vapor leaving the evaporator depends on the initial setting of the spring tension. Once the valve is adjusted for a particular superheat, then that superheat will be maintained under all load conditions of the evaporator. This refrigerant control device is used most often due to its high efficiency and its ability to provide effective use of all evaporator surface under all load conditions. These valves have certain disadvantages such as frictional and mechanical losses and fracture of bellows. Low-side float valve and high-side float valve expansion devices are not suitable for automation of the systems and hence not in use for modern cold storage. 302 Chapter 17 Further Readings Arora, S.C., Domkundwar, S., 2002. CHAPTE R 18 Spray Ponds and Cooling Towers 18.1 Spray Pond When the water required for a condenser is inadequate and expensive, then the same water is recooled and used again and again. Spray ponds and cooling towers are commonly used for this purpose. A schematic diagram of a spray pond is shown in Figure 18.1. The pond can be located either on the ground, on a roof, or at certain height above ground level. The water from the condenser is sprayed through the nozzles to expose the maximum surface of water to the air to allow the droplet surface to evaporate and cool the water. Spray ponds are usually surrounded with wooden walls to prevent the loss of water by wind drift. The major disadvantage with this process is that it requires more floor area per kg of water than any other system used for cooling. The efficiency of cooling ponds is about 40–50%. 18.2 Cooling Towers A cooling tower is a means by which the heat from the condenser is dispersed to the atmosphere. Cooling towers are desired when positive control of water temperature is required. Cooling towers are used for big plants as absorption refrigeration systems, steam jet refrigeration systems, and centrifugal units above 100 TR, because at capacity below 100 TR, the adoption of evaporative condensers with reciprocating compressor is found more economical. Proper siting and orientation of a tower are important. The principle of cooling the water in cooling towers is similar to the evaporative condenser. The water goes into the air in the form of vapor, taking its latent heat from the remaining water and causing a reduction in temperature. Theoretically, the water can be cooled to the wet bulb temperature (WBT) of entering air if the air leaving the tower becomes saturated. Generally, the temperature of water coming out from the cooling tower is 3–5°C above the WBT of the entering air. The temperature difference between WBT of incoming air and the temperature of outgoing water is known as cooling tower “approach.” The higher the quantity of water circulated, the lower will be approach of the tower. The quantity of water circulated economically is also limited by the power requirements of the pump. All rights reserved. 304 Chapter 18 Figure 18.1: Spray Pond. 18.3 Classification of Cooling Towers 1. Cooling towers are divided into two main groups: natural draft cooling towers and forced draft cooling towers. 18.3.1 Natural Draft Atmospheric Spray Towers The arrangement of this type of tower is shown in Figure 18.2. This tower should be located in open space or on the roof of the building where the movement of air is best. The capacity of this cooling tower is nearly 30–75 L per square meter of base area, depending upon the air velocity. They work economically for loads under 200 tons capacity. 18.3.2 Natural Draft Deck–Type Tower The construction of this tower is shown in Figure 18.3. Figure 18.2: Spray-Type Cooling Tower. Spray Ponds and Cooling Towers 305 Figure 18.3: Deck-Type Cooling Tower. It is similar to the atmospheric spray tower except that water-distributing troughs are used, which helps to break the water into small droplets. The object of the decks is to provide additional evaporation area. It gives 20–30% greater efficiency than the atmospheric spray tower for the same size and for the same quantity of water flow. 18.3.3 Forced and Induced Draft Cooling Towers The construction of the forced draft tower is shown in Figure 18.4. Figure 18.4: Forced Draft Cooling Tower. 306 Chapter 18 Figure 18.5: Induced Draft Cooling Tower. Water from the condenser is sprayed at the top of the tower and air is forced by the blower from the bottom of the tower as shown in Figure 18.4. The air velocity of 120 m/min is recommended with a flow of 100–130 cmm per min per ton of refrigeration capacity. The construction of induced draft towers is shown in Figure 18.5. The difference lies only in the supply of air. The amount of water usually lost with forced or induced draft cooling tower ranges from 1% to 2% by evaporation and 0.5% to 2% by drift losses. The water for compensating these losses is supplied from external sources. The water must be chemically treated to avoid scale formation of the condenser due to an increase in the concentration of salt in the cooling water. The performance of a cooling tower is measured in terms of its efficiency, which is ­defined as η= twi − twa twi − twha where twi and twa are the inlet and outlet temperature of water and twha is WBT of inlet air. The efficiencies of different types of cooling systems are: Spray ponds Natural draft towers Mechanical draft towers 40–50% 50–70% 60–80% Spray Ponds and Cooling Towers 307 Advantages of Mechanical Draft Towers The mechanical draft (MD) towers offer the following advantages over natural draft towers: 1. It requires less space (m2 and m3) per kg of water cooled. 2. Quantity of water required in condenser is reduced due to more effective cooling. 3. There is full control on the temperature of outlet water from the tower because the quantity of air supply can be controlled. 4. Smaller equipment can be used to handle airflow under fairly well-controlled operating conditions. Advantages of Induced Draft Towers 1. The main advantage of induced draft (ID) towers is that the coldest water comes in contact with the driest air, and the warmest water comes in contact with the most humid air. 2. The recalculation is seldom a problem with the tower because the outlet fan discharges the heated and humid air directly away from the air intakes below the tower. 3. Sizes up to 20 m diameter can be used. 4. Lower first cost, require less space and capable of cooling through a wide range. 5. The power consumption per kg of water cooled is less compared with a forced draft fan system. Advantages of Forced Draft Towers 1. Forced draft (FD) towers are more efficient than ID draft because some of the air velocity is converted into static pressure in the tower and recovered in the form of useful work. 2. The vibration and noise are minimal because mechanical equipment is set on solid ­foundations. 3. Because it handles dry air, problems of blade erosion are avoided. 4. It is safer because it is located on the ground level. Disadvantages of Forced Draft Fans 1. The possibility of recirculation of hot air and humid exhaust coming out from the top of the tower through the low pressure air-intake region can cut efficiency as much as 20%. 2. During cold weather, ice forms on nearby equipment and buildings or in the fan housing itself, which can cause fan blade breakage. 3. Fan size is limited to 4 m. 4. The power requirement of the FD system is approximately double that of the ID system for the same capacity. 18.4 Performance of Cooling Towers The factors that decide the performance of the cooling tower are defined here. The schematic and the process of cooling of water in the cooling tower is represented on the psychometric chart shown in Figures 18.6(a) and (b), respectively. 308 Chapter 18 Figure 18.6: (a) Schematic of a Cooling Tower. (b) Cooling Tower Efficiency (Psychrometric Chart). In the psychrometric chart, Point 1 and Point 2 show the condition of air at the inlet and ­outlet, respectively. twi and two are the inlet and outlet temperature of water passing through the cooling tower (twi > two). twb is the WBT of inlet air. 1. Cooling approach: This is defined as the difference between the water inlet temperature and temperature of the entering air (twi – tab), where tab is the WBT of the inlet air. 2. Cooling range: This is defined as the difference between the inlet (hot) water temperature and outlet (cold) water temperature (twi – two). 3. Cooling tower efficiency: This efficiency is defined as the ratio of actual increase in air temperature (Tao – Tai) to the maximum theoretical drop in air temperature (Tai – Tab), which cannot fall below Tab (its WBT). η= Tao – Tai Tai – Tab where Tao = temperature of the outgoing air, °C Tai = temperature of the incoming air, °C Tab = WBT of the inlet air, °C The desired cooling range (Twi – Two) should be as high as possible, because it reduces the amount of water required in the condenser per kg of refrigerant to be condensed. The factor affecting the cooling range for the cooling tower is mainly the ambient condition. Hotter and drier air will absorb more water vapor and cool the water more effectively. Example 18.3 A cooling tower is to be designed to take the heat load of 200 tons refrigerating plant using F−12 as refrigerant. The heat rejection ratio of the system is 1.2. The rise in temperature allowed in the condenser is 5°C. The atmospheric air condition is 35°C DBT and 25°C WBT. The air leaves the tower at 30°C and 90% RH. Ignoring the heat losses in the system and carryover loss through the cooling tower, find the following: (a) Quantity of air required to pass through a cooling tower per minute. (b) Quantity of makeup water. The temperature of water coming out of the tower is 30°C. Solution The conditions of air at the inlet and outlet of the cooling tower are shown on the psychrometric chart Figure 18.8. The heat carried in the condenser is given by Qc = Heat load of evaporator × Heat rejection ratio = 200 × 3.5 × 1.2 = 840 kJ/sec. The heat carried away in cooling tower must be equal to the heat given out in the condenser. The heat transfer between water and air in the cooling tower is given by the following equation: Qc = mw Cpw (T0 − T1 ) = V ( ha2 – ha1 ) – ( w 2 – w1 ) Cpw T2   Vs1  where Ti and T0 are temperatures of water entering and leaving the cooling tower. ha1 and ha2 are the enthalpies of the air at the inlet and exit of the tower. w2 and w1 are the absolute humidities of air at the inlet and exit of the tower. Routine cooling tower services require visual inspection, mechanical maintenance, and a physical cleaning program that will maintain the system cleanup year round. The importance of cooling tower maintenance is well illustrated by its documented benefits. Power savings are reflected in both electrical demand and consumption, and equipment life is significantly increased through reduced corrosion of metal parts and erosion of system components, including tubes and seals, by abrasive particles. Chemical requirements are reduced as a clean system responds better to water treatment. Failures such as unexpected shutdown and severe freeze damage can be avoided along with their associated costs. CHAPTE R 19 Fans 19.1 Introduction The fan is considered to be the heart of the air distribution system. The successful operation of product precooling chambers, cold storages, and so on depends on proper fan selection and its operational performance under variable load conditions. 19.2 Types of Fans The two primary fan types are axial flow fans and centrifugal fans. Axial flow fans cause the air to flow parallel to the axis of the fan. The axial flow fans are further subdivided into propeller type and disk type. 19.2.1 Propeller Fans In a propeller fan, a twist is given to its blades that project radially outward from the hub. The number of blades varies from two to six. The quantity of air delivered depends upon the number of blades. Generally, axial flow fans are not used for duct air-conditioning systems because they are incapable of developing high pressure. These fans are particularly suitable for handling large volumes of air at relatively low pressure, particularly where noise level considerations are not important. They are therefore used in industrial ventilation and air-conditioning systems. They are inexpensive in initial cost and provide good efficiency. 19.2.2 Centrifugal Fans Centrifugal fans are also known as radial flow fans. The air enters the fan axially and is discharged radially from the fan. Wherever a system has ductwork, centrifugal fans must be used because they can develop considerable pressure compared with axial flow fans. Centrifugal fans have the advantage of quiet and efficient operation at high pressure. The inlet of a centrifugal fan can be connected to larger apparatus suctions and its outlet to smaller supply duct sections. The differences among the three general types of CF fans lie in the curvature of their blades relative to the impeller radius. The three types blades are forward curved, radial, and backward curved as shown in Figure 19.1. Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00019-1 315 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 316 Chapter 19 Figure 19.1: Blade Types for Centrifugal Fans. From the figure, it is clear that the absolute velocity of radial and backward curved blades is less than the absolute velocity of the forward blade for the same speed and diameter of the impeller. Therefore, to obtain the same capacity (flow quantity) under similar pressure conditions, the radial and backward blade fans must be operated at higher speed than the forward blade fans. 19.3 Fan Horsepower and Efficiency The total head developed by a fan is given by Ht = Hp + Hv (19.1) where Ht = total head, cm of water column Hp = static pressure head, cm of water column Hv = velocity pressure head, cm of water column Total brake power (Bp) of the fan is given by Equation 19.2. Bp = where Wa H t kW 1000 Wa = weight of air delivered, kg/min and also Wa = ρa V where ρa = density of air, kg/m3 V = volume in m3/min at standard conditions of temperature and pressure (19.2) Fans 317 19.4 Factors Affecting Fan Selection The following information must be known when selecting a fan. These factors aid in determining the type of fan to be selected and the size. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Quantity of air to be moved per unit of time Estimated system resistance and expected variations Amount of noise permitted Space available for fan Economic implications 19.5 Centrifugal Fan Laws The performance of fans and blowers conforms to certain mathematical laws that have widespread application. These laws may be used to extend the performance data of a specific fan to a geometrically similar fan of a different size or operating at a different speed. Geometric similarity implies that all comparable dimensions of the fans being considered are proportional, and the friction factors do not change appreciably over the range of the Reynolds number, and that the efficiency is constant. These laws apply to the fan only and not to the system to which it is attached. Also they apply to a specific point on the performance curve. Extrapolation of a specific point on a curve will give a new point similarly located on a new set of curves. Fan laws are as follows. 1. For a specific fan with speed varying: The capacity varies directly with the speed (N = revolutions per minute). N 1 /N 2 = q1 /q2 (19.6) The total pressure head varies as the square of the speed, which follows because of the basic relationship between speed and pressure. N 12 /N 22 = H1 H2 (19.7) The power required varies as the cube of the speed. Because power is a product of the rate of mass motion and force or pressure, hp ∝ qH. And because q ∝ N and H ∝ N2, it follows that hp1 /hp2 = N 13 /N 23 (19.8) 2. For a number of geometrically similar fans with constant speed and varying diameter: The capacity varies with the cube of the diameter. The capacity is a direct function of periphery speed and periphery area. Because periphery speed varies directly with the diameter and the area with the square of the diameter, it follows that 318 Chapter 19 D13 / D23 = q1 / q2 (19.9) The head varies with the square of the diameter. The pressure varies with the square of the velocity. The velocity of the fluid leaving the impeller varies with the diameter of the propeller; consequently, D12 / D22 = H1 / H 2 (19.10) The power varies as the fifth power of the diameter. Becuase power is the product of quantity discharge and head, D15 / D25 = hp1 / hp2 (19.11) The fan laws may be combined so that the speed and diameter effect appear in the same equation. q1  N1   D1  = q2  N 2   D2  3 2 H1  N1   D1  = H 2  N 2   D2  3 hp1  N1   D1  = hp2  N 2   D2  (19.12) 2 (19.13) 5 (19.14) By solving Equations (19.10) and (19.11) simultaneously, the following generalized expressions are obtained.  14   12  H q D2 = D1  11   21   2   4  q1   H 2  (19.15)  12   43  q H N 2 = N1  1 3   12   4  2   H1   q2  (19.16) Example 19.1 A fan is to be selected to deliver 340 lpm against a head of 19.8 m, and the basic conditions are Q1 = 718 lpm, H1 = 11 m, D1 = 18 cm, N1 = 1,760 lpm, hp1 = 1.63. Each type of loss, pipe friction, turns, valves, entrances, outlet, process media and so on vary nearly as the square of the velocity. Therefore, the total resistance or static pressure is nearly a square function of the velocity through the system. Figure 19.2 shows the performance curves of a backward-curved centrifugal fan with system characteristics superimpose on it. Curves A, B, and C are system characteristic curves for three different systems. For example, system B requires a static pressure of 3.6 cm of water to deliver 226.56 m3/min of air, but the static head would be only 2 cm of water if 170 m3/min were being delivered. The total pressure, power requirement, and efficiency are located on line bb. 19.7 Fan Selection Fan selection is explained with reference to Figure 19.2. If the factors causing resistance of a system do not change, any variation in the rate of airflow will be accompanied by a change in static pressure and the performance point will always be on the characteristic curve B. The 320 Chapter 19 Figure 19.2: Performance Curves of Backward-Curved CF Fan. operating point on a system characteristic curve will move only if the air-supplying device is varied or changed. If the system resistance is variable and operating speed of the fan remains constant, the performance point will move along the static pressure curve. Suppose an installation with characteristic B contains an air filter that eventually becomes coated with dust, which in turn increases the resistance of the system. The performance point would move along the static pressure curve from line bb to aa, indicating a change in the system characteristic from curve B to curve A. At this instant, the static head is greater, volume flow is less, and efficiency is lower. Suppose system B is a refrigerating system that contains a badly iced heat exchanger. When defrosted, the resistance will decrease and the performance point will shift along the static pressure line to line cc. The rate of flow is frequently controlled by dampers in the system. Drying, air-conditioning, ventilating, burner, draft, and aspirating operations are frequently so controlled. Dampers vary the system resistance and move the point of performance along the static pressure line. Although this control system is usually the most practical one, care must be exercised in design and application to avoid motor overloading on operation in the inefficient region. Tips for Fan Selection 1. A steep static curve is desired so that the variation in rate of flow will be small for a large change in the static head. Fans 321 2. If operating conditions are constant, a fan should be selected to operate at its point of maximum efficiency. 3. If operating conditions vary, selection should be made so that operation is in the most efficient range practicable. 4. Generally, it is inadvisable to operate to the left of the maximum point on the static pressure curve because of possible unstable performance. Velocity pressure added to the static pressure results in total pressure. The velocity pressure indicates the energy needed to accelerate the air from zero to the velocity at the point of air passage through the fan. In most instances, the velocity is lost at discharge so that the power required must be based on the total pressure head. Fan performance data are usually presented by the manufacturer in tabular form. The data represent only the practical operating range of the fan and include only such information as is needed to select a fan for a specific job. 19.8 General Performance For large fans of the same design and similar proportions, the performance may be calculated from tests obtained on fans with a wheel not less than 90 cm (35 inches) in diameter. For fans having wheels less than 90 cm in diameter, the performance may be calculated from tests on fans of the same design and similar proportions and wheel diameter not greater than the rated size. 1 1  4 2  H q D2 = D1  11   21   2   4  q1   H 2  1 (19.17) 3  2  4 q H N 2 = N1  13   12   4 2   H1   q2  (19.18)  D5   N 3  hp2 = hp1  25   23   D1   N1  (19.19) Because all the similar terms are in ratio, the dimensions need to be consistent for all similar terms. The term geometric similarity implies that a performance plot of certain fan will apply to all other geometrically similar fans, axial or centrifugal, simply by changing the abscissa and ordinate values of volume, power, and pressure, with efficiency remaining constant. 322 Chapter 19 In these equations, the subscript 1 values are taken from the performance curve and any one value fixes all the others. In practical terms, it would probably be advisable to use a point to the right of that selected as a base. This choice would yield a larger, slower fan with slightly higher power requirement. Consideration of different type of fan might be advisable. 19.9 Adoption of Fan to the System The resistance along the air-conditioning system consists of the pressure losses in ducts fitting, filters, and air-conditioning equipment. The total resistance of all equipment also increases with an increase in velocity or quantity of air through the system. The resistance curve can be drawn with respect to the flow quantity as shown in Figure 19.5. 326 Chapter 19 For a particular system, there is only one resistance curve, and a fan delivering air throughout the system must operate at the same point on the same resistance curve. Assuming the fan is operating at a speed N1 and delivering air through a system whose resistance is R1, then the point of operation is a as shown in Figure 19.5. The static pressure, the quantity of airflow, and BP required are known from the graph for the operating Point a. If reduction in the flow rate from Qa to Qb is desired, as shown in the figure, then it can be achieved by either of two methods. 1. Increasing the resistance of the system (by partly closing the damper) establishes a new resistance curve R2, which intersects the fan characteristics at Point b, the desired value. The corresponding values of required BP and developed pressure can be determined from the figure. 2. Reducing the fan speed from N1 to N2 changes the fan characteristics and permits the operation of the original system resistance curve. Under this condition, the operating point will be Point c. The corresponding values of required BP and static pressure can be determined from the figure. It is obvious from the figure that the power requirement at Point c is much less than at Point b. The speed reduction is a more economical method for decreasing the volume than changing the system resistance. Therefore, it is necessary to keep the system resistance at a minimum at all times, and volume adjustments should be made by varying the fan speed for maximum operating effectiveness. Figure 19.5: Fan Selection Chart. Fans 327 19.10 Variable Air Volume Method Variable air volume (VAV) method is used for any air-handling system that matches the air volume from a fan to the air-conditioning system as per requirement (per load). Many methods such as variable guide vanes and damper control are used in practice. Extensive maintenance, high installation costs, inefficiency, and inadequate sensing capability have compromised the performance of these traditional VAV methods. Traditional methods of VAV modulate capacity but ignore the fan laws as listed earlier. A better way to provide variable volume of air is by using a variable fan speed with the help of variable speed motor. The most cost-effective method of achieving variable speed fan capacity control is using AC-adjustable frequency fan drives. AC-adjustable frequency controls make any fixed-speed AC motor an adjustable-speed device. N ∝ frequency ∴ Q ∝ frequency as Q ∝ N Adjusting the flow of the fan by controlling the frequency of the AC power to the fan motor reduces the power as per fan laws. Reducing the speed of the fan 50% reduces the flow quantity 50%, but requires only 12.5% of the power required at full capacity, which means a saving of 87.5% power. The method used to provide VAV as per requirements of the air-conditioning system provides the following advantages. 1. Lowest installed cost: AC-adjustable frequency fan drives are ideal for new systems or retrofits due to ease of installation. The control converts any AC fan motor to variable speed. The control, which may be mounted anywhere, simply replaces the motor starter and is as easy to connect. No modification to the motor or mounting configuration is required. 2. Minimum maintenance: AC-adjustable frequency fan drives are totally solid state with no moving parts to wear out. There are no belts, pulleys, or bearings to adjust, lubricate, or maintain. Standard AC motors are used so there are no brushes, commutators, or slip rings to maintain. 3. Fast payback: AC-adjustable frequency fan drives achieve 59% energy savings over the guide vanes method and 69% energy savings over the damper control method. Additional savings are also realized due to reduced use of fuel for heating and cooling, which is accomplished through the precise control of airflow and pressure that AC-adjustable frequency fan drives provide. Payback ranges from 6 months to 2 years. In addition to energy savings, using a variable-speed motor for providing variable flow leads to additional benefits that includes the following: 1. Controlled acceleration lengthens life of belts, pulleys, bearings, and fans. 2. Multifan capacity provides inherent matching of supply and return fans. 328 Chapter 19 3. Soft starting the motor reduces electrical demand charge by eliminating peak starting current. 4. High power factor reduces power factor penalty charges. 5. Operation of motor at slower speed reduces fan noise and vibration. Problems Use the performance curves given in Figure 19.2 to solve the following problems. 1. Air system C is transporting 285 m3/min and is altered so that the resistance is less and the fan delivers 310 m3/min of air. Determine the speed at which the fan must operate to deliver 285 m3/min and the static pressure and horsepower. What is the percentage reduction in power requirement? 2. A fan geometrically similar to that of Figure 19.3 operate at 5.1 cm pressure, 170 m3/min and an efficiency of 75%. Specify the wheel diameter, speed, and power required. 3. Determine the discharge velocity of the fan from the outlet area based on the velocity pressure, both 285 m3/min. Further Readings Arora, C.P., 2000. Refrigeration and Air Conditioning.
