CHAPTE R 20 Transmission and Distribution Systems of Cool Air 20.1 Introduction The objective of air distribution is to create the proper combination of temperature, humidity, and air motion in the product zone of the room. The success of any air-conditioning system is dependent upon optimum circulation of cool air in the storage space. The careful estimation of the pressure losses is necessary for the selection of proper duct size and fan capacity. The ducting cost is 20–30% of the total cost of the equipment, and similarly, the power required by the fan accounts for the substantial part of the running cost. The air handling system consists of: 1. The air distribution system comprising various inlets for recirculated air and the outlets for the supply of air. 2. The duct system including the return duct, supply duct, and air-conditioning apparatus comprising dampers, filters, coils, and air washer. 3. The fan provides the necessary energy to move the air. Figure 20.1 shows air handling in a simple air-conditioning system. A closed loop is formed for the circulation of air. The reference point in this loop is the room itself, which can be considered at atmosphere pressure. The air enters the return duct through the inlets from the room and continues to drop in pressure until it reaches the fan. The fan raises the pressure. Thereafter, the pressure starts dropping again in the supply duct until the air is released to the space. Therefore, the pressure on the suction side of the fan is negative and on the discharge side positive. The pressure in the room is atmospheric (i.e., zero gauge). 20.2 Room Air Distribution The requirement of a good room air distribution system is to create a proper combination of temperature, humidity, and air motion in the food storage zone at all levels of food stacks or crates. The maximum variation in temperature in a single room should not be more than 1°C Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00020-8 329 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 330 Chapter 20 Figure 20.1: Schematic Airflow Diagram for an Air-Conditioning System. and between rooms 2°C. The desirable air velocity varies with the type of product stored and is about 450 mpm. 20.3 Types of Supply Air Outlets The outlet may be classified as high side wall, low side wall, ceiling, and floor outlets, according to their location. There are four basic types of outlets: 1. Grill outlet: The most common type has adjustable bar grills with vertical and horizontal vanes. These are rarely used because they create draft conditions. 2. Slot diffuser outlet: It is an elongated outlet with an aspect ratio of 25:1 and maximum height of 7.5 cm. This type is used inside walls but at higher height or along the perimeter of the floor. It is also not used in ceilings. 3. Ceiling outlet: Mounted in the ceiling, multipassage round, square, or rectangular outlets are most common. They come with adjustable louvers so the amount of air can be changed. 4. Perforated ceiling: In this case, confined space above the ceiling is used as a supply plenum. The air from the plenum is supplied to the space through small holes or slots. The air is supplied at the rate of 0.3–4.5 m3/m2 of floor area. 20.4 Factors Considered in Air Distribution Systems The requirement of a good air distribution system is to provide the proper combination of dry bulb temperature (DBT), relative humidity (RH), and air motion in the cold store. The principle of air distribution involves factors such as draft, drop and distance traveled, entrainment or induction ratio, and spread. Transmission and Distribution Systems of Cool Air 331 Table 20.1: Desired velocity of air Application Velocities from Air Outlets (m/min) Residence and private office General office Store, main floor Store, upper floor 150–225 300–375 600 450 20.4.1 Draft It is defined as a feeling of coolness or warmth due to air motion at the required DBT and RH. The feeling of warmth or coolness of draft is measured above or below the controlled room condition of 1–2°C DBT and moving with 9 m/min. Therefore, to avoid the feeling of draft, proper air distribution in the room is essential. The desired velocity of air, taking into consideration the permissible sound levels, is listed in Table 20.1. Throw or blow: It is the distance travelled by air stream in the horizontal plane on leaving the air outlet and reaching a velocity of 15 m/min at the height of 1.8 m above the floor level. A desirable throw is three-quarters of the distance to the opposite sidewall. Drop: Vertical distance the air moves after it leaves the outlet and reaches the end of throw, which is illustrated in Figure 20.2. Entrainment or Induction Ratio: The air leaving the outlet is known as primary air, and the air entrained by the primary air from the room is known as secondary air. The sum of primary and secondary air is called the total air. The entrainment or induction ration (u) is defined as: ∅= mp + ms Total air m = t = mp Primary air mp where subscripts p and s are used for primary and secondary and t for total. Figure 20.2: Room Air Movement. 332 Chapter 20 Figure 20.3: Spread in a 45° Outlet. This ratio is governed by the following momentum equation: mp Vp + ms Vs = ( mp + ms ) Vt where m stands for mass flow rate. Higher values of entrainment ratio are always desirable for proper air mixing and for maintaining uniform DBT and RH of the room air. Spread: It is defined as the angle of divergence of an air stream after it leaves the outlet. The spread can be maintained in a horizontal plane or vertical plane as required. The spread depends on the type of outlet used. Air outlets can have three types of vanes: straight, converging, or diverging. Outlets with straight vanes produce a spread of 14–24° on the horizontal as well as the vertical plane. Outlets with converging vanes provide the same spread as straight vanes but the throw is 15–20% higher. Outlets with diverging vanes give a fanning effect and have a marked influence on the direction and throw. The spread in a 45° outlet is shown in Figure 20.3. Such an outlet provides a spread of 60° and its throw is 50% of the straight vane outlet. 20.5 Consideration for Selection and Location of Outlet The selection and location of supply air outlets are governed by the following considerations. 1. The amount of air to be delivered by the outlet should be proportional to the load of the area of the space for which it is installed. 2. The selection of the type of outlet is governed by the ceiling height, nature of room occupancy, and related factors. 3. The location of the outlet should be governed by the condition of uniform air distribution and rapid temperature equalization. Transmission and Distribution Systems of Cool Air 333 4. The selection of outlet size can be made from the manufacturers catalog data, according to the air delivery, core velocity, distribution pattern, sound levels, throw, drop spread, and other specifications. The outlet should be located so as to neutralize the concentrated loads, such as those resulting from exterior windows and electronic equipment. In buildings in which the lighting load is heavy (i.e., more than 55 w/m2) and the ceiling height is more than 4.5 m, it is desirable to locate the outlets below the lighting loads. In these and similar cases of concentrated loads, the return grills or inlets can be located adjacent to these loads so that warm air (in the case of cooling) is withdrawn from the source instead being dissipated into the conditioned space. This arrangement is also suitable to remove fumes and pollutants from their sources in the space. Generally speaking, ceiling diffusers can deliver more air to a space than grillers and slot diffusers. Because of their high entrainment, ceiling diffusers may also be used in system with low supply air temperatures. Despite the low supply air temperature, induction will result in rapid temperature equalization. 20.5.1 Location of Return Air Openings The most important considerations involved in the location of inlets are the following: 1. There should not be any short-circuiting of air between the supply outlet and return inlet. The return air opening should be complementary to the flow pattern generated by the supply air. 2. Return air that is either too cool in winter or too warm in summer or contains dirt, gases, or odors should be removed without causing any drafts or stratification in the conditioned space by making the undesirable product move in its natural direction of flow. For example, to remove tobacco smoke, return air openings located high in the room will be most effective. If the air contains lint, as in textile mills, locating returns in the floor is better. 3. The velocity of air decreases rapidly as one moves away from the inlet. Thus, draft conditions near the inlet are rare. However, the recommended velocities are approximately 240 mpm for inlets above the occupied zone and 180 mpm within the occupied zone. 4. The consideration of noise is a little more reverse in case of return inlets because they are normally located near ear level. In that case, the velocity in the return inlet should not exceed 75% of the velocity in the supply air outlet. From the point of view of location, a wall return near the floor is the best. A ceiling return may short circuit the cold air. Floor returns should be avoided because they can act as dust collectors. Also, as stated earlier in the case of concentrated load, the return opening should be located near the load. 334 Chapter 20 20.6 Air Distribution To obtain comfort conditions within a storage zone, standard limits have been established as acceptable effective temperatures. This term comprises air temperature, air motion, RH, and affects the physiology of stored foods. Any variation from accepted standards of one or more of these elements may cause damage to the food in terms of freshness, edibility, and so on. The same effect may be caused by lack of uniformity of conditions within the space or by excessive fluctuations of conditions in the same part of the space. Such discomfort may arise due to excessive room air temperature variations (horizontal, vertical, or both), excessive air motion (draft), failure to deliver or distribute the air according to the load requirements at different locations, or too rapid fluctuations of room temperature or motion. The temperature variations should not be more than 2°C. The desired air movement is 7.5 m/min. The following three points are preferred in air distribution systems. 1. Flow direction of air toward the product such that almost all the surface of the food is exposed. 2. Depending upon the stacking method adopted, the airflow can be downward, upward, or lateral. 3. The temperature of the conditioned air may be above or below the air in the product zone. The proper air distribution calls for entrainment of room air by the primary air stream outside the zone of product in order that air motion and temperature differences are reduced to accepted limits before the air enters the product zone. Several methods of air distribution systems are used for different purposes. 20.7 Systems for Injecting the Conditioned Air 20.7.1 Perforated Ceiling Panels Perforated ceiling panels are currently commonly used in some industrial applications and in some public buildings. The perforated sheets of metal or fiber are fixed below the ceiling of the room, and the space between the perforated sheet and ceiling is supplied with conditioned air. It is possible to deliver large quantities of air through such panels without draft because the diffusing effect of the air stream creates mixes with the room air. The arrangement of the perforated ceiling panels is shown in Figure 20.4. Often, perforated ceiling and perforated floors are used for even better distribution of air. The only disadvantage of this system is its high cost of construction. The perforated floors with inlets and exits to the sidewalls near the upper level are preferable for cooling/heating of the space. Transmission and Distribution Systems of Cool Air 335 Figure 20.4: Perforated Ceiling Panels. 20.7.2 Pan-Type Arrangement The pan-type arrangement of the supply air shown in Figure 20.5 gives uniform discharge around its perimeter. The air distribution in the room is more uniform. 20.7.3 Wall System In cool rooms where the fresh produce is active, air has to pass continuously around the produce. Most of the air has to pass near the floor, which is 10–60 cm above the floor. The distribution pattern is shown in Figure 20.6. Air flows directly across occupied load, removing vapor and odors and maintaining the heat balance. Figure 20.5: Pan-Type Arrangement. 336 Chapter 20 Figure 20.6: Wall System Distribution. Adequate exhaust must be provided for evaporative cooled spaces. The rule of thumb is that 1 sq m2 of exhaust opening (window, door, or vent) must be provided for every 600 m3 of air supplied. In commercial and industrial applications, powered vent fans are often required to provide adequate exhaust. 20.8 Air Distribution Methods The central air distribution system is commonly used for cooling the agricultural produce. The central air distribution system consists of a fan and it operates to blow air from the central air-conditioned system to the air-conditioned space through ducts and inlet openings. The central air-distribution system is further divided into three groups according to the direction of airflow from the air inlet into the room. 20.8.1 Upward Flow System The upward flow-type of air distribution system is shown in Figure 20.7. In this type of air distribution system, the air is brought into the space through the inlets near the floor. The air flows upward as illustrated in Figure 20.7. The exhaust air outlets are located in the sidewalls near the ceiling or in the ceiling itself. This air distribution system is useful in rooms where there is a marked tendency of air heated by the produce to rise and carry with it the vitiating products from the products. The major difficulties associated with this system are to avoid drafts and to provide more uniform cooling in the space. 20.8.2 Downward Flow or Overhead System The downward flow-type of air distribution system is shown in Figure 20.8. This system is generally preferred when the ceiling is not free from obstructions. In this air distribution system, the air is introduced at the ceiling and is removed through the grills located on the main floor. Transmission and Distribution Systems of Cool Air 337 Figure 20.7: Upward Air Distribution System. The downward air distribution system should be designed to spread the incoming air uniformly over the occupied zone to secure uniform conditions within the air-conditioned space. A downward air distribution system is more satisfactory for cool chamber and is much better for summer air-conditioning than the upward air distribution system. 20.8.3 Ejector Air Distribution System The arrangement of the ejector air distribution system is shown in Figure 20.9 and, is generally adopted when the ceiling is free from obstructions. It is also a form of downward air Figure 20.8: Overhead Distribution System. 338 Chapter 20 Figure 20.9: Ejector Distribution System. distribution, but the velocity of air at the inlet is considerably higher than the air velocity in ordinary downward air distribution systems. The air is introduced at a high velocity through specially designed nozzles at the rear of the building and is discharged well above the occupied zone as shown in the figure. The jet action of the incoming air produces considerable aspirating effects, providing better diffusion of the fresh air within the space. The outlets are located over the floor as shown in the figure. With any type of the system used, supplementary supply of air from the wall openings must be provided if the space is large. Return or Exhaust Inlets: The location of return and exhaust inlets does not significantly affect air motion, except possibly in the area near the inlet where velocities may exceed recommended limits. The inlet should be located so that the short-circuiting of the supply is minimized. An exhaust system provides vent-flues or ducts for the exhaust of air. The airflow through exhaust system is produced either by air pressure in the room or by the action of exhaust fan. Exhaust ducts from the various points are connected to an attic space, and then the air from attic space is exhausted by a fan. The trunk system is also used for exhaust where the ducts from the different rooms are connected to the main duct (trunk duct) and it is exhausted by an exhaust fan. The exhaust fan with trunk duct system yields the most positive result. The considerable operating cost of an air-conditioned system is reduced by recirculating part of the air supplied to the air-conditioned spaces. The proportions of fresh and recirculated air mostly range from 20–30% fresh air and 70–80% recirculated air. Further Readings Arora, C.P., 2000. Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, second ed. Tata McGraw-Hill Publishing Co. Ltd, New Delhi. Arora, S.C., Damkundwar, S., 2004. A Course in Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, seventh ed. Dhanpat Rai and Co., New Delhi. CHAPTE R 21 Heat and Water Vapor Transfer in Cold Storage 21.1 Introduction In cold storage structures, walls, doors, windows, roofs, and floors of different and often complex material combinations are used. The effect of ambient atmosphere conditions because of solar heat, wind velocities, and other climate conditions also has significant effect on heat and vapor transfer through the cold storage. In this chapter, the heat transfer and mass transfer (vapor) principles related to cold storage structure are presented. 21.2 Heat Transfer The most important heat gain or loss to be considered in the air-conditioning of cold storage is the heat transfer through walls, roofs, ceiling, and floors (i.e., the entire building structure). The load due to such transfer is often referred to as fabric heat gain or loss. In the case of a sunlit wall or roof, the heat gain of the room will be compared to a shaded one, because the outside surface temperature of the wall or roof will increase above the outside air temperature due to incident solar radiation. The conduction heat transfer through the wall or roof will depend on the thickness and the thermal conductivity of the material. In addition, there will be convection and radiation from both outside and inside surfaces. Hence, the steady-state heat transfer is expressed in terms of an overall heat transfer coefficient U and the overall temperature difference between the outside and inside (∆t) as given by the following equation. Q = U ∆t = ∆t R (21.1) where R is the overall thermal resistance. Where the wall, roof, or floor may consist of composite layers of different materials including insulation, then U is given as 1 1 ∆x 1 1 = R= +Σ +Σ +Σ U fo K C fi Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00021-X 339 (21.2) Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. These values of C are only applicable to the prescribed thickness ∆x. In the Equation (21.2), C has been included equivalent to the value of Also, fo and fi in the equation represent the heat transfer coefficients for combined convection and radiation from the outside and inside wall surfaces, respectively. These terms are also referred to as surface conductance. The properties such as thermal conductivity, conductance, specific heat, and density are given in Table 21.1. The values of fo and fi depend on the velocity of the air. For example, at velocity of 5 m/s inside a cold store, fi varies between 8–10 W/(m2 · K) for vertical walls and 6–9 W/(m2 · K) for horizontal walls. For normal work fi is taken to be 8 W/(m2 · K). Similarly, the value of fo for the outside air is taken to be 29 W/(m2·K). Modern cold stores are generally built using prefabricated insulation panels composed of two galvanized steel, aluminum, or sometimes polyester cladding sheets, each 0.6 mm thick. The space between the sheets is filled by foaming polyurethane or by placing a polystyrene layer there. The most important value in the calculation of insulation heat transfer is that of K, and in this respect the best insulating material is nonmoving dry air or gas. The K value for nonmoving air at 273 K is only 0.024 W/(m · K) and that of R11 is 0.016 W/(m · K). Typical value of U for 22.5 cm brick wall with 1.25 cm plaster on both sides is 2.14 W/(m2 °C). The same for 13.75 cm, reinforced cement concrete (RCC) slab roof with 1.9 cm plaster is 3.7 W/(m2 °C). These values show the need for insulating roofs, particularly, because they are exposed to solar air temperature and not just dry bulb temperature (DBT) of outside air. 21.3 Surface Conductance The heat transfer between the wall surface and the surrounding air is mainly by convection and to some extent by radiation (Arora, 2000). Practical values of the outside and inside wall surface coefficients are given in Table 21.2. 21.4 Solar Air Temperature For calculation of heat transfer through structures, it has been found convenient to combine the effect of the outside air temperature and incident solar radiation intensity into a single quantity. For this purpose, an expression for the rate of heat transfer from the environment to the outside surface of the wall may be written as qo = f o (to − tso ) + aI (21.10) where fo = outside film coefficient of heat transfer, W/(m2 °C) to = temperature of the outside air, °C a = absorptivity of the surface I = total radiation intensity, W/m2 The schematic representation of the preceding parameters is as shown in Figure 21.1. Introducing an equivalent temperature te, we may write for heat transfer rate qo = f o (te − tso ) (21.11) Then, from Equations 21.10 and 21.11 te = to + aI fo (21.12) This temperature te is called the sol-air temperature and can be considered as equivalent to outside air temperature such that the total heat transferred is the same as the combined effect of the incident solar radiation and outside air and the wall temperature difference. 344 Chapter 21 Figure 21.1: Solar Heat Transfer to Outside Wall Surface of a Building. Example 21.1 Calculate the instantaneous solar air temperature for a wall with the following conditions Total of direct and diffuse solar radiation 260 W/m2 Absorptivity of surface = 0.9 Outside surface heat transfer coefficient = 23 W/m2·K Outside air temperature 35°C Solution Solar air temperature: te = to + aI 0.9 × 260 = 35 + = 45.2 oC fo 23 For all purposes of heat transfer through building structures, the solar air temperature may be used instead of the DBT of the outside air and the solar radiation separately. 21.5 Air Spaces Modern insulation materials are based on the principle of creating a material consisting mostly of air or gas, enclosed in cells of material with a low density; the smaller the cells and thinner the cell walls, the closer the value of the material and gas comes to the ideal value of air or gas. Sometimes the construction of storage structures includes an air space between the wall materials. Because air has less thermal conductivity than any other type of insulating material, it acts as a good barrier for heat transfer. The air space may be narrow such as a Heat and Water Vapor Transfer in Cold Storage 345 Figure 21.2: Air Gap in a Wall. cavity of 5 cm or less in a 55 cm thick brick wall, or large such as the air space of a void between a flat ceiling and a pitched roof. Heat transfer is greatly affected by surface emissivity and width and orientation of the air space. The greater natural convection results when the air space is vertical than when horizontal or sloping. When the surfaces are close together, the natural air movement is suppressed and the heat transfer is by conduction alone. With smaller thicknesses the resistance of the gap is low and conductance is high. As the width of the gap increases, the conduction component of the heat transfer decreases rapidly to the extent that it becomes negligible, but convection comes into play and, as a result, the overall conductance of the gap is not significantly decreased. Consider an air gap in a wall as shown in Figure 21.2. The two surfaces of the wall are at temperatures t1 and t2. Let the convective and radiative components of the heat flux between the two surfaces be qc and qR, respectively. Now convection occurs on both the surfaces. Thus, if fc is the convective coefficient for one surface, then the total convective resistance is given by 1 fc + 1 fc = 2 fc (21.13) The reciprocal fc/2 becomes the effective convective coefficient between the two surfaces, and the convective heat flux is given by qc = fc 2 (t1 − t2 ) (21.14) 346 Chapter 21 Considering the surfaces as comprising infinite parallel planes, we have for the radiative flux qR = F12σ (T14 − T24 ) = f R (t1 − t2 ) (21.15) where F12 = 1 1 1 + −1 ε1 ε 2 is the shape factor in which ∈1 and ∈2 are the emissivity of the two wall surfaces. With nonreflecting surfaces, as is usual in building construction, emissivity can be taken as equal to 0.82. Equation 21.15 gives the value of the radiative coefficient fR. Then, by adding Equations 21.14 and 21.15, we obtain for the total heat flux between the wall surfaces. q = qc + qR  f  =  c + f R  (t1 − t2 ) = C (t1 − t2 )  2  (21.16) where C represents the overall conductance between the two wall surfaces. CHAPTE R 22 Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 22.1 Introduction The rapidly escalating cost of fuel in recent years has made everyone aware of the importance of energy conservation, and the desire for better levels of thermal insulation of buildings has become one inevitable consequence. The materials having extremely low thermal conductivities are called insulating materials. The heat flow rates from the air-conditioned buildings can be considerably reduced with the use of insulating materials. Properly applied insulation helps in economic running of cold storage. Insulating materials used for domestic refrigerators, cabinets, brine pipe lines, refrigerant pipe lines, and cold storage rooms as well as the insulating materials used for steam carrying pipes, ducts carrying the hot air, and for boilers are primarily selected by their ability to retard the flow of heat. 22.2 Basic Uses of Insulation Materials Insulating materials generally have four basic uses, all of which govern the selection of the kind and the type to be selected. 1. 2. 3. 4. To retard heat flow To prevent surface condensation To add structural rigidity To control noise and vibration There is a wide variety of insulating materials, some of which are adaptable to all requirements while others cannot be considered as structural members. In cold storage projects, walls, floor, roof, doors, and windows are made of different materials. According to theory of resistance in electrical theory, one can add the heat transmission resistances of the difference layers of the conductors. 22.3 Heat Transfer The heat transfer by conduction through a composite wall, roof, or floor is given under steady-state conditions by the equation Q = UA∆t Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00022-1 355 (22.1) Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 356 Chapter 22 where U is overall heat transfer coefficient, W/m2 °C A is the area through which heat flows, m2 ∆t is the temperature difference between the two sides of the wall, °C The overall heat transfer coefficient in turn is expressed by the following equation. 1 1 ∆x 1 = +∑ + U h1 K h2 (22.2) where h1 = surface heat transfer coefficient from air to the wall on the warm side, W/m2 °C. h2 = surface heat transfer coefficient from air to the wall on the cold side, W/m2 °C ∆x = thickness of any layer in the composite wall, m K = thermal conductivity of any layer of solid material in the wall, W/m2 °C Values of h depend on the velocity of the air. For example, at a velocity of 5 m/s inside a cold store, h2 varies between 8 W/m2 °C and 10 W/m2 °C for vertical walls and 6 and 9 W/m2 °C for horizontal walls. For normal work, h is taken to be 8 W/m2 °C; similarly, the value of h1 for the outside air is taken to be 29 W/m2 °C. Modern cold stores are now generally built using prefabricated insulation panels composed of two galvanized steel, aluminum, or sometimes polyester cladding sheets, each 0.6 mm thick. The space between the sheets is filled by foaming polyurethane or by placing a polystyrene layer there. The most important value in the calculation of insulation heat transfer is that of K, and in this respect the best insulating material is nonmoving dry air or gas. K for nonmoving air at 0°C (273 K) is only 0.024 W/m·K and that of R11, 0.016 W/m·K. Metals have the highest value of K. For instance, copper has a value of 380 W/m · K. For most commonly used construction materials, K varies between 0.58 W/m · K for brick and 2.3 W/m · K for heavy concrete. Until the invention of plastics and their derivatives, cork was the most commonly used insulation material. But in most countries it has been replaced by polystyrene, polyurethane (PUR), foamed glass, glass wool, rock wool, perlite, and other artificial insulation materials. Pure and expanded cork slabs with a density of 120 kg/m3 have a K value of 0.04 W/m · K at 293 K. 22.4 Modern Insulating Materials Modern insulating materials are based on the principle of creating a material consisting mostly of air or gas, enclosed in cells of a material with a low density; the smaller the cells Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 357 and thinner the cell walls, the closer the value of the material and gas comes to the ideal value of air or gas. Standard polystyrene cells filled with air. Steam is used in the production of white polystyrene, and the blue variety is produced by extrusion. Foamed glass cells are filled with H2S. For calculation purpose, the following K values are used Expanded polystyrene: 0.03–0.035 W/m·K (5–10 kg/m3) Extruded polystyrene: 0.029–0.038 W/m·K Polyurethane (PUR): 0.029 W/m·K (40 kg/m3) Polyisocyanurate (PIR): 0.023 W/m·K (40 kg/m3) When the insulation is applied to the cold surfaces, the water vapor from the ambient air tries to pass through insulation toward the cold surface because the water vapor pressure in the air is higher than the vapor pressure near the cold surface. This vapor is condensed when subjected to below-freezing temperature. This increases the heat flow because the conductivity of water is 25 times that for air and conductivity of ice is 100 times that of air. The moisture has another serious effect on the insulation, because the volume of water increases when it freezes and thus rupture the insulation. 22.5 Characteristics of Insulation Materials 1. The K value: This value must be lower than 0.058 W/m·K 2. The coefficient of linear expansion: This value varies from one material to another. It should not be too high; if it is, the space between the cladding sheets will get larger after a certain period of time. When using materials with high linear expansion coefficients, such as expanded polystyrene, it is advisable not to use these materials within 3–6 months after the date of manufacture in order to allow time for the expansion to reach its maximum. 3. Stability: As K and expansion values vary over time, one should select materials that are as stable as possible. 4. Permeability: Some materials absorb water; others do not, such as extruded polystyrene. Most insulation materials are not water-vapor tight and due to varying degrees absorb the water vapor in the air or the gas. It is therefore important to compare the water vapor transmission resistance coefficients. 5. Mechanical strength: This character is of special importance for floor insulation. PUR, cork, and foamed glass have the highest mechanical strength and the extruded polystyrene is stronger than expanded polystyrene. 358 Chapter 22 6. Density: For reason of mechanical strength it is inadvisable to use polystyrene with a density less than 20 kg m3 and PUR with less than 35 kg m3. However, the higher the density, greater the ratio of material/gas volume and higher the value of K. 7. Fireproofness: Foamed glass and glass wool are commonly used insulation materials that are fireproof. All the others may have more or less fire retardant or low fire-transmitting characteristics, but once they start burning, they do so quickly. 8. Attack by rats and termites: Polystyrene is sometimes eaten by rats; foamed glass when broken may release H2S, creating a bad smell. 9. Price: They may be classified from least to most expensive, as follows: a. Glass wood b. Expanded polystyrene c. Extruded polystyrene d. Cork e. PUR f. PIR g. Foamed glass In daily refrigeration practice for cold store tunnels, pipe work, and vessels, the value of K is chosen in such a way that the heat losses by transmission and limited to 8 and 9 W/m·K. This ∆t ⋅ k ⋅ 100 ∆t ⋅ k ⋅ 100 means that ∆ x = cm or cm. 8 9 The insulation thickness for pipe work and vessels is normally calculated based on the prevention of the condensation on the outside surface of the insulation. Note that the U-value for noninsulated concrete floors lies between 1.7 W/m2·K and 2.2 W/m2 · K depending on the K value of the ground underneath. 22.6 Water Vapor Transportation The water vapor difference between the outside and inside air of the cold storage is mainly responsible for transport of vapor and its deposition on the insulation. The properties of the air, such as specific humidity, relative humidity (RH), dry bulb temperature (DBT), wet bulb temperature (WBT), total pressure, and partial pressure play an important role in transportation of this moisture. Understanding these parameters is necessary before going into the full length of this topic. With this intention, a few of these properties and their measurements are given elsewhere. It may be seen that there is no convenient way of measuring specific humidity (w), degree of saturation (m), or the relative humidity (). These are the properties that have to be calculated. The measurable properties are DBT, WBT, and dew point temperature. Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 359 22.7 Types of Insulation Materials The selection of the different types of insulating materials depends on the use for which it is intended. Five basic types of insulation may be used alone or in combination. 1. Flake insulation is composed of small particles that finely divide the air space. Vermiculite or expanded mica are the most common materials. 2. Fibrous insulation is composed of small diameter fibers that finely divide the air space. They may be organic or inorganic and may or may not be bonded. Inorganic fibers such as glass or rock wool are the most common materials. 3. Granular insulation is composed of small nodules that contain voids. It is not considered a true cellular material because gas can be transferred between the individual spaces. Typical materials are magnesia, calcium silicate, diatomaceous earth, and cork. 4. Cellular insulation is composed of small individual cells that finely divide the air space. It is produced from glass, rubber, or plastic. 5. Reflective insulation is composed of parallel thin sheets of foil with high thermal reflectance, spaced to restrict radiant heat transfer across the space. Spacing is designed to reduce heat transfer by conduction and convection. Aluminum and stainless steel foils are usually used. Matching the type of insulation to the job while maintaining cost efficiency is usually a matter of compromise. To match various job requirements, insulation is available in many different forms, including batts, blankets, boards, and blocks. Each product has a combination of properties such as thermal conductivity, temperature limits, fire hazards, dimensional stability, and moisture absorption. All these factors must be considered when insulation is selected. The amount of thermal insulation required depends on four primary factors: (1) project personnel and equipment, (2) control of process (for maintaining the temperature), (3) prevention of condensation, and (4) energy and money savings. 22.7.1 Insulators Made from Natural Materials • Cork board: The bark from the trees is dried and pressed and baked at moderate temperature. During this process, the natural gum melts and spreads, binding together the entire mass. Thickness varies from 0.5 cm to 1.5 cm. It is able to resist the flow of heat because it consists of homogeneous mass of small air cells separated from one another by their one cell walls. Palco bark is loose insulation made from redwood bark and is similar to cork board in thermal properties. 360 • • • • • Chapter 22 Celotex: Celotex, a proprietary material, is an excellent example of a fireproof fiber wall board, in which bagasse (sugarcane after juice is removed) is a principal ingredient. In the manufacture of celotex, the fibers are cooked to dissolve all soluble matter and then waterproofing chemicals are added. The final product is an odorless light material. Kapok: This silky fiber is found within the seedpod of the ceiba tree. The slabs for household refrigerator requirements are made in various sizes depending on the type of cabinet. It is also used in loose form for different purposes. It is so light and fluffy that it settles only due to its weight. Hair felts: A high-grade insulating material is made from cattle hair that has been washed, cleaned, and compressed into matlike sheets. Hair felt may be applied in the form of pads. Insulating papers: Although paper itself is an insulator, it is generally used to protect other insulating materials from moisture. The best insulating papers are those that have been coated with asphalt to give them greater durability and high resistance to moisture absorption. 85% magnesia: It is made from light carbonate of magnesia with approximately 15% asbestos fiber added to give strength. This material, after being molded and baked, can be used at temperatures up to 300°C. It is available in the form of slabs, ropes, pipes, and in powdered form. It is commonly used in heating systems. The natural materials listed here are conveniently used. They are somewhat more expensive than polystyrene, but because of economy of labor in their application, they are the predominantly used as thermal insulants. 22.7.2 Urethane The overwhelming bulk of this material is used for insulation. About 35% is used in refrigeration and 45% in building industry. It is known as super insulation in the air-conditioning industry. Rigid urethane foam is increasingly specified. It is available in a variety of forms as slabs, panels, moldings, pipes, ducts, and liquid that can be poured, sprayed, or frothed on the job side. It provides two to four times the insulating value of other popular insulating materials. Urethane is the only insulating material that can be sprayed as a liquid to reach virtually inaccessible areas. Urethane Product Board Panels Sheet Moldings Foamed in situ Physical Form Sheet with flexible facing attached Foams with attached rigid facings Foam without attachment Special shapes with smooth skins Continuous layers following given counter Typical Application Roof insulation Cold stores Containers Pipe sections Domestic appliances, sprayed roofs Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 361 Urethane foam has high thermal resistance to the heat flow and can lower heating or cooling costs of the buildings, particularly in electrically heated buildings where effective insulation is required to make operation costs competitive with other fuel systems. The important properties to building construction are minimum water absorption, low vapor transmission, self-adherence, and excellent dimensional stability at high and low temperature. All these properties are combined in urethane foam. 22.8 Insulation Applied to Buildings In this case, the vapor barrier must be provided outside the insulation material to prevent the moisture from entering and condensing on the insulation. The water vapor will try to come inside the air-conditioned space because the vapor pressure of the ambient air is higher than the vapor pressure of the room air. The arrangement of the insulating material and water vapor barriers are as shown in Figure 22.1. Two vapor barriers, one inside and one outside of the insulation material, are used when the building is provided with heating in winter and cooling in summer as shown in Figure 22.2. Figure 22.1: Water Vapor Insulation. Figure 22.2: Outer and Inner Vapor Barrier. 362 Chapter 22 22.9 Floor Insulation A particular important function of the cold store floor is its need to carry heavy loads. Except for small commercial cold stores, the floor is almost always insulated in the traditional way and not with prefabricated insulated floor panels of the sandwich design. Here also the vapor barrier is important. A poor barrier can cause serious problems to the foundation of the building. In cold stores, even with insulated floors, there will be more or less 8 w/m2 flux through the floor, which of course may be limited by increasing floor insulation. Owing to relatively large average ground temperature compared with ambient air, there is however, a tendency to provide a thin floor insulation. In case of relatively high cold temperatures, floors are sometimes not insulated at all. 22.10 Low Temperature Cold Storages For low temperature cold stores, depending on the building construction and composition of the ground, the 0°C (273 K) isotherm tends to descend into the ground year after year; in other words, the ground is “frozen-up” as is shown in Figure 22.3. The soil delivers a certain quantity of thermal energy, 1–2.5 W/m2 depending on its composition; however, this is far too small in relation to the 8 W/m2 heat flux created by the conditions in the cold store. Ward and Sewell developed an equation to calculate the penetration p of the 273 K isotherm as follows: Tp − Tm =   2 p2 2 p  p2  1+ 2 − 1 +   r0 r0  r02    2δ K a     1 + r − K   0 i  (T0 − Tm ) Figure 22.3: Lowering of the 270 K Isotherm into the Ground Beneath a Cold Store. (22.3) Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 363 where Tp = minimal temperature at depth p, expressed in feet Tm = average temperature of the ground T0 = cold store temperature d = insulation thickness in feet r0 = radius in feet of the equivalent area of the cold store floor Ka = heat transfer coefficient of the ground K1 = heat transfer coefficient of the insulation Depending on the values of these different coefficients, p can have values of 10 feet after 7 years, as we calculated and measured in –25°C cold store in Ottawa, Canada. The deformation of the floor of this particular store showed an elevation of 27 cm in the middle of the floor. Thus, the development of the situation depends on the composition of the soil. Nonbinding material, such as gravel, freezes as one solid layer. In other typical soil types, layers of ice crystals are formed; however, certain sliding layers are dangerous because their expansion can cause serious damage to the foundations. A first solution in cases where there are doubts about the composition of the soil is to remove a layer of 0.5–1 m and replace it with a nonbinding material. But still there might be the risk of a high water table. Another possible way of avoiding problems is to build a cellar under the cold store floor. Such a construction is expensive because it must be combined with the creation of a loading bay. The best and most frequently used solution is under-floor heating, which can be achieved in several ways: • • • By means of 10 cm diameter asbestos tubes put into the first layer of concrete at distances of about 1 m, connected on both ends to an air duct, preferably placed with one end in a warm environment such as in the machinery room. If necessary, the air circulation can be forced by small centrifugal fans connected to the duct, preferably on the warm side. By means of electrical resistance cables manufactured by specialists and available in mats or rolls placed on the concrete layer. A floor surface of 1000 m2 requires about 25 W/m2 (40 V). By means of a floor heating system consisting of 2 cm diameter plastic tubing at 600 mm distance set in the concrete layer (as shown in Figure 22.4), and through which a water/ glycol solution is pumped. The solution passes over a heat exchanger, acting as a small water-cooled condenser, to recuperate surplus energy from the discharge gas. 364 Chapter 22 Figure 22.4: Section Through a Cold Store Floor Showing Insulation and Underfloor Heating. Where heat is needed when the plant is at standstill, electric heating resistance is provided. Everything is controlled by thermostats, the ground being kept at about + 6°C by circulating the glycol solution at +10°C. Several circuits are available in case one should fail. To illustrate what happens below the surface, some calculations that can be followed in Figure 22.4 are given here. 1 1 ∆x c1 ∆x i ∆x c2 ∆xs 1 = + + + + + U tot h1 K c1 Ki K c2 K s h2 (22.4) where c = concrete layer (1 or 2) i = insulation layer s = soil we know that heat flux q (W/m2) is given by q = Utot. ∆ttot ∆ttot = tsoil – tcold store = 10 – ( – 30) = 40 °C Utot = overall heat transfer coefficient, W/m2 °C h1 = surface heat transfer coefficient from the cold store air to first layer of concrete, W/m2 °C ∆ x c1 = thickness of first concrete layer, m Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials Kc1 = thermal conductivity of first layer of concrete, W/m °C ∆xi = thickness of insulation layer, m Ki = thermal conductivity of the insulation layer, W/m °C ∆ x c2 = thickness of second concrete layer, m Kc2 = thermal conductivity of the second layer of concrete, W/m °C ∆xs = thickness of soil layer, m Ks = thermal conductivity of soil layer, W/m °C h1 = surface heat transfer coefficient from the soil, W/m2 °C which is considered as negligible. h1 = 8 W/m2 °C Kc = 1.5 W/m °C Ki = 0.037 W/m °C Ks = 1.2 W/m °C For calcareous soil with 10–28% water, ks varies between 1.15 W/m °C and 2.3 W/m °C. This soil is rather humid and at this point the situation is rather dangerous because the isotherms have a tendency to descend over the years. If it were required to compensate for this by increasing the insulation thickness, 1 m of insulation is needed. If we want to keep Point 3 above 273 K, then we need to supplement the heat flow q. Considering only the layers above Point 3 and allowing t1 – t3 of 30°C, local q is given by q = U1− 3 × ∆ t 1 1 0.15 0.1 = + + = 2.93(m 2K)/w U1− 3 8 1.5 0.037 U1− 3 = 1 = 0.34 w/(m 2 k) 2.93 Local q = 0.34 × 30 = 10.2 w/m2 We could reduce this by taking the heat flow of the soil into account. However, this flow is rather small and it is safer to neglect it. Taking into account a reasonable safety factor, a floor heating system should be installed with a capacity of 12–15 w/m2 immediately below the insulation layer. The amount of warming for any system can be calculated and is about the same for mediumsized and large refrigerated spaces regardless of ambient conditions. The calculated heat input requirement is the floor insulation leakage based on the temperature difference of 4.4°C between under floor earth and room temperature (e.g., 27.4 K temperature difference for a 23°C storage room). The flow of heat from the earth at about 4.1 w/m2 of floor serves as a safety factor. Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 367 22.11 Protection Against Freezing of the Soil In low temperature stores, it is necessary to protect the soil against risk of freezing with consequent heave of the floor slabs. For this reason, a warming system or guard space is provided under the insulation. Warming: Generally for large stores, warming can be done by these methods. • • • By an electric heater mat at low voltage (a metallic armature) laid on the concrete of the subfoundation and covered with a bed of cement mortar (50 mm) before applying the vapor barrier and the insulation. By a network of rigid plastic pipes in which circulate an aqueous solution of glycol at 5–10°C, often with heat exchange with the condenser. By guard space provided beneath the floor of the building, which needs no maintenance. It is suitable for small stores and regions with warm climate, as long as it is protected from flowing water and risks of erosion and blockage. Guard space can be made by the following methods: • • By burying, under the subfoundation concrete, cement pipes separated by 0.5 m and freely open to the exterior at both ends. By raising the floor of the chamber 60 cm above the natural soil level by a hollow space (Figure 22.5). Figure 22.5: Cold Room on Guard Space. 368 Chapter 22 22.12 Roof Insulation In contrast to the floor situation, roof insulation is subjected to the highest ambient temperature, depending on the aspect of the roof, its construction, and the reflection of the solar energy. This is especially true with prefabricated constructions where the insulation panels are only protected by a thin layer of roofing, or are immediately exposed to solar radiation, so that the surface temperatures of the panels become very high. Often the ceiling panels are protected from direct solar radiation by a roof and an air space that may be ventilated. Even then the surface temperature can reach high levels but not to the extent as in the case of direct exposure. The following calculation illustrates surface temperatures attainable by solar radiation in the roof materials. When using insulation material with relatively high expansion coefficient, one must provide enough space for expansion between the plates, which is filled up with sealer of flexible insulating material. A cold store with an inside temperature of –25°C and in this case the temperature drop across the panel is 51 – (–25) = 76°C. Many insulation materials shrink with time, so the expansion space increases with time and hence sealant must therefore be prepressed. 22.13 Insulation of Pipes and Vessels All those insulating materials mentioned previously can also be used for pipe work and vessels. Prepared segments, mostly of PUR foam, are used or it is injected into a metal sheet casing. When aluminum foil is used as a vapor barrier, care must be taken to finish the joints with silicon sealant. PUC tape can also be used on vapor barriers. For hot gas defrost lines, glass wool is best as the insulation material. Where there are supports in vertical lines, segments of PU of extra high density, 100 kg m–3 are used. Horizontal lines are supported by putting them in steel sheet sleeves. Flexible cellular insulating material is often used for pipe work, especially for smaller plants using copper tubing. It is advisable to use tubes of 2 m length with internal sections corresponding to standard copper pipe sizes. Material with density of 90 kg/m3 has a K value Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 371 of 0.04 w/m·K and permeance coefficient M value of 2.3 × 10–8 g/m·s Pa. The temperature limits range from –75°C to +105°C. The material is also available in slabs. No vapor barrier is necessary. When placed outside, it is necessary to protect the material from infrared rays with a special paint. 22.14 Thickness of Insulation The thickness of insulation is calculated so that condensation cannot occur on the surface. So an insulation of 87 mm thick has to be provided to prevent condensation Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 373 22.15 Gas-Tight Insulation Special insulation techniques are necessary in the case of cold stores that provide a controlled atmosphere as in the storages of fruits and vegetables. The insulation must not only prevent thermal energy leakage and water vapor diffusion, but also gas leakage. Therefore, in addition to a vapor barrier, a gas barrier must also be provided. By using prefabricated sandwich panels of 60–120 mm PIR covered with metal sheets up to a thickness of 0.6 mm, the problem of gas is solved, because metal or polyester sheets are gas-tight. The problems of gas-tightness are confined to joints and to nonprefabricated, traditionally insulated floors. Joints should be carefully filled up with gas-tight silicone kits and a layer of 100 mm fiber glass tape. Every passage of pipe work and cables should also be carefully sealed with silicone. Doors should have special gaskets that can be expanded with compressed air. The floor, which should preferably be insulated with 6 cm foam glass or PUR, should be provided with a gas and vapor barrier of special gas-tight bitumen 110/30 with a thickness of 2.5 mm. In corners connecting with the walls, a gas-tight polyvinyl film of 0.75 mm should be installed up to a sufficient height and finished off with silicone. Afterward the rooms are put under an overpressure of about 1332 Pa. A pressure gauge is then used to measure the time it takes for the pressure to fall to about 933 Pa. If this takes more than 10 minutes, the room can be considered to be gas-tight. Figure 22.7 shows degrees of acceptability for various leakage rates. Sometimes small smoke-bombs are also used for leak detection. A leakage is measured in cm2/100 m3. A leakage of 0.2 cm2/100 m3 is permissible. Figure 22.7: Pressure/Time Testing Curves for CA Storage. 374 Chapter 22 22.16 Application Methods of Insulation Materials Insulation materials for floors include: Extruded polystyrene > 25 kg/m3 density, K = 0.03 W/m·K and mechanical resistance to 0.75 bar PUR ≥ 30 kg/m3 density, K = 0.023 W/m·K and mechanical resistance to 0.35 bar Linear expansion coefficient, for both about 7 × 10–5 cm/cm °C The floor insulation should have adequate mechanical strength and before placing the final concrete slab, the insulation must be covered with a layer of polyethylene film to prevent water from the wet concrete penetrating the insulation. The final concrete slab or finishing slab must have the following characteristics. • • • • • • Mechanical strength to bear static and dynamic loads Suitable expansion joints Nonflammability Slip resistance for safety reasons Durability No smell, no dust, and ease of cleaning for hygienic reasons In small rooms and stores in which the product hangs on rails, as in the case of meat, the floor can be made of a lighter construction, such as stone. On spots where points loads will occur, caused for instance by the use of steel beams, the load must be spread by placing an insulation material locally with a high resistance against pressure. Also, locally reinforced concrete may be used. See Figure 22.8 for a section through a typical floor and the effects of a severe point load. Nowadays, better precautions must be taken, because the loads are becoming greater, with piles of stacked product becoming increasingly high, thereby adding to the load per m2. The insulation must have adequate mechanical strength. Foamed glass, cork, extruded polystyrene, and PUR are the best materials; expanded polystyrene must be of high density or more than normal 25 kg/m3. When using pallets, the load is relatively well spread. When stacking three or four pallets high, loads of up to 0.35 kg/cm2 may occur. In palletized stores of 6 m height, loadings of 2–3 ton/m2 may occur. In addition, we have to take into account the dynamic loading of the forklift and pallet trucks. Forklift trucks may add to these figures an additional loading of 1200–1500 kg per wheel. A forklift truck may have a total weight of 6–8 tons, spread over four wheels, with a small contact area. As the load is transferred to the ground at an angle of 45°, a 2000 kg wheel load imposes a 1.8 bar load on the insulation, as shown in Figure 22.9, when using a concrete slab 12 cm thick. The thicker this slab, the larger is the loaded surface on the insulation. Because 1.8 bar is unacceptable for any kind of insulation, steel Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials Figure 22.8: Constructional Details of an Insulated and Reinforced Floor. Figure 22.9: Dynamic Load Transmission into Insulated Floor. 375 376 Chapter 22 Figure 22.10: Floor Deformation Due to Elastic Support. reinforcement or a thicker concrete slab must be used. There is also the friction load of the wheel to be considered. Because of the movement of the wheels, the insulation is subjected to a wave movement with a small amplitude, resulting in a local bowing of the concrete slab as illustrated in Figure 22.10. In order to obviate this problem, the reinforcement must be set in the upper side of the concrete slab. An insulant with little tendency to wave movement should be used; the maximum deformation allowed is 1–1.5% or 3 mm on 20 cm. This may lead to expensive insulation material, so steel reinforcement of the concrete slab is a less expensive solution. The lower layer of reinforcement should be placed 2 cm above the insulation surface, and the upper layer of reinforcement 2 cm below the concrete slab surface. The upper reinforcement layer is lighter than the lower one. There are also forces due to the settling of the building during start-up. In freezer stores, temperature differences can reach 50°C and may cause the concrete slab to contract quite a few centimeters. Between two slabs of concrete, an expansion joint must be provided every 5 × 5 m. In most cases it is enough to make a joint in the upper layer and only interrupt the upper layer of steel. The edges of the joint must be protected mechanically against damage by the store traffic. The joints must be closed with an elastic product like silicone as shown in Figure 22.11. It is Figure 22.11: Reinforced Floor Showing Expansion Joint and Polyethylene. Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 377 Figure 22.12: Typical Joint Reinforcement Methods for Cold Store Floor. good practice to place a steel plate local to the joint. See Figure 22.12 for this and other methods of reinforcing concrete floor joints. In small rooms the polyethylene film in the top of the insulation provides a means for possible expansion. This can be avoided, if necessary, by adding a layer of a sliding material such as graphite. The final concrete slab must be provided with a thin layer of small metal particles as an antislip protection. Figure 22.13 shows a section through the walls and floor of a typical cold store. 22.17 Wall Insulation After placing the vapor barrier, the first layer of insulation is fixed to the ceiling or wall by means of mechanical devices such as steel pins with galvanized wire and plates. The second and subsequent layers are fixed to the previous layer by means of wooden pegs inserted at an angle using at least 8 pegs per m. A nonclay-based bituminous emulsion is used as the adhesive between the layers. 378 Chapter 22 Figure 22.13: Section Through Wall and Floor of Insulated Cold Room. The ceiling is made of wooden beams placed 50 cm apart, calculated on a sag of 1/500. All insulation can be covered with paint, plaster, aluminum, or other sheets. A one layer brick wall is a very effective but also very expensive method of protection. As a vapor barrier roofing felt, bituminized paper of 3 mm thick or alu-kraft-paper, reinforced with fiber glass, may all be used. Polyethylene film can be used for the floor, but it must have a thickness of at least 0.2 mm. 22.17.1 Prefabricated Construction A steel frame is built to which the prefabricated walls and ceiling panels are fixed. See Figures 22.14, 22.15, and 22.16 for details of the two methods of assembly. The methods of assembly are: 1. Placing the panels outside the steel structure: In this method, the steel structure will be inside the cold room and can be used to fix piping, air coolers, and so on. Solar radiation falls directly on the panel surface, creating great temperature differences across the outside and the inside surfaces of the panels. This method of construction is called the north European method. 2. Placing the panels inside the steel structure: The walls and ceiling inside are smooth; thermal bridges are inevitable if we want to fix supports for the pipework of air coolers, which can be limited to a small nylon bars, passing through the panels. Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 379 Figure 22.14: Typical Joints in Sectional Cold Store Construction. Steel structures inside the store, placed on the floor, may support air coolers and pipework. Outside the store on the steel frame of the building, metal cladding is fixed in order to protect the walls and ceiling from solar energy penetration, cladding that can be chosen to meet local conditions. This construction method is the south European method and advised for warm climates. The south European method has, however, the disadvantage that the frame is subjected to expansion forces, which could be transferred to the insulation panels. There are several dimensions of panels to choose from. With long panels there are more joints but they are more difficult to handle than short ones. When making a choice between the many available types of panels, certain details must be carefully considered. 380 Chapter 22 Figure 22.15: Sectional Cold Store Erected Outside a Supportive Steel-Frame Structure. • • • • The method of fixing them to the steel frame must avoid thermal bridges as much as possible, but still ensure that the panels are firmly held to the frame. The panels must be of adequate mechanical strength and must have a protective layer against corrosion. No wood should be used inside the sandwich panel (Fig. 22.17), for deformation reasons as well as for fire resistance. The interconnection of the panels must be firm and solid. Mechanical systems, such as those using steel or plastic fixing devices together with neoprene joints are the most reliable. The systems must not create thermal bridges; when not using mechanical connection systems, male-female connections should at least be used. Injection of PUR into the joints is not particularly effective because there is no control of the quality of the injection procedure: it could be inspected by means of infrared cameras, but repair work after application is difficult. Thermal and Vapor Insulation Materials 381 Figure 22.16: Inside Weather-Proof Building, Showing Suspension Methods for Wall and Ceiling Panels. Figure 22.17: Final Assembly of Sandwich Panel. FAO Agriculture Service bulletin 19/2 has given the following for insulation of the floor. This is done by insulant panels, in two layers with staggered joints on a concrete subbase and an impermeable barrier of pitch (1 cm). This must be carefully jointed to that of the walls. The panels may be expanded polystyrene or PUR, in cork, or in any other material with good compression resistance (Figure 22.17). A working surface is applied on the insulation; this may consist of concrete slabs or other material that satisfies the requirements given elsewhere in this book. It is good practice to make an abutment along the perimeter to aid the circulation of the air and to avoid spoiling the vertical finish (see Figure 22.18). 382 Chapter 22 Figure 22.18: Insulation of the Floor and Sandwich Walls. 22.18 Pressure Protection When the difference in pressure inside and outside a cold store is 1333 Pa for instance, there is in fact a pressure of 1333 Pa on the walls. Such pressures on the construction must be avoided. In a gas-tight cold store and even in normal prefabricated construction, there are no normal means of equalizing air in order to deal with the difference in air pressure between the inside and outside atmospheres. These pressure differences, especially when starting up the plant, may be quite large. Therefore, when starting up a plant it is necessary to keep the door slightly open at the beginning. If this is not done, the pressure on the walls may exceed the permitted construction tolerances. For normal operation of the plant, sufficient equalizing valves must be installed. Typical examples are shown on Figure 22.19(a), (b), and (c). Electric heaters must be incorporated in valves where the cold store temperature goes below 273 K. Figure 22.19(b) and (c) are the devices used for pressure equalization, with the effect shown on the graph in (d). Example 22.1 The volume of the cold store 8800 m3 at 4°C and 90% RH. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 23 Design of Small-Capacity Cold Storages 23.1 Introduction Perishable horticultural produce is generally precooled in a separate facility called a precooling chamber before the produce is placed in cold storage. In precooling, the product loses its field heat slowly to a temperature just higher than it has to in the cold storage. The precooling avoids cold bite and color change in the product. The design of a precooling facility or cold storage involves mainly the estimation of refrigeration capacity for the selected type of structure. Before proceeding with the design, the inside and outside conditions have to be specified. In many cases, the supply air design conditions have to be fixed as well. Among the many applications of air-conditioning, the important ones can be identified as: • • • Industrial air-conditioning Cold storage for food materials Comfort air-conditioning 23.2 Comfort Air-Conditioning The three parameters governing human comfort are air temperature, humidity, and air velocity in addition to air purity. Effective temperature (ET) is defined as the temperature of the saturated air in which the subject would experience the same feeling of comfort as experienced in the actual unsaturated environment. At lower humidity, the dry bulb temperature (DBT) of air can be higher for the same ET and for the same feeling of comfort. Thus, at higher DBT, the body would lose more heat in the form of latent heat (LH) (i.e., by the evaporation and perspiration). An increase in temperature can also be compensated by an increase in velocity. For example, an increase of 2–3°C in DBT can be compensated by increasing the air velocity from 0.1 m/s to 0.3 m/s. 23.3 Cold Storage Though cold storage is understood to be an application of refrigeration, it is in fact a complete air-conditioning system in which room air is cooled to a much lower temperature over a cooling coil and supplied back to the storage space. The conditions maintained inside the storage depends on the nature of the product stored. In cold storages, a strict control of temperature and relative humidity (RH) is required. The required storage conditions for a number Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00023-3 389 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. All rights reserved. 390 Chapter 23 Table 23.1: Storage condition of fruits and vegetables in cold storage Product Temperature °C RH (%) Approximate Storage Life –1 to 0 14.5 –0.5 10 3–4.5 14–2.1 7–10 85.90 95 85–90 85–90 85–90 85–90 85–90 8–10 days for spring 3–8 weeks (American) 2–3 weeks 5–8 months 2–4 weeks 2–7 days Apples Bananas Grapes Mangoes Potatoes (late crop) Tomatoes (green) Ripe of important food products are given in detail elsewhere in this book; a few of the items are listed in Table 23.1. 23.3.1 Cold Storage Design A cold storage is a structure in which facilities are available to cool produce and maintain it at the desired levels of temperature and RH by circulating cool air at specified velocity. Therefore, a cold storage has mainly three functional components: (1) chamber for stacking the produce, (2) production and conveying cooling air and circulating around the stacks in the chamber; and (3) materials handling facilities, stacking, and for sending out as per the demand in the market. Among these three, the cooling and circulation of air are most important because it involve a complete refrigeration and air-conditioning plant to be installed attached to the storage structure, and it is considered the heart of the cold storage. In fact, cold storage is a low-temperature refrigeration application. To keep the size of the refrigeration unit small and power consumption low, it is necessary to construct the storage facility such that the cooling load is minimized. In this chapter, cooling load estimation for precooling chambers and design of small cold storages are given. 23.3.2 Types of Loads in Cold Storages The load calculation for a cold store is separated into the following main sources of heat for a given 24-hour period. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Transmission load Air change (infiltration) load Miscellaneous loads, such as electric motors, lighting, people, etc. Product load, sensible Product load, respiration Design of Small-Capacity Cold Storages 391 Table 23.2: Heat of respiration of products in J/kg per 24 h Storage Temperature Product Apples Bananas Cabbage Carrots Cauliflower Cherries Grape fruit Grapes, American Grapes, European Lemons Mushrooms Onions Oranges Peaches Pears Peas Plums Potatoes, immature Potatoes, mature Strawberries Tomatoes, green Tomatoes, ripe Turnips 0°C 4.4°C 15.6°C 312–1500 – 1248 2183 – 1352–1871 416–1040 624 312–416 520–936 6446 728–1144 416–1040 936–1456 728–936 8526–8733 416–728 – – 2807–3950 625 1040 1975 625–2810 – 1770 3640 4680 – 730–1350 1250 – 625–1975 – 830 1350–1665 1455–2080 – 13,520–16,635 935–1560 2705 1350–1870 3745–7070 1145 1350 2290 2390–8215 4265 8420 10,500 11,440–13,725 2290–4160 3640 2290–2705 2390–5200 – 2495 3850–5405 7590–9670 9150–13,725 40,860–46,265 2495–2910 3015–7070 1560–7070 16,220–21,105 6445 5820 5510 The average air changes per 24 h for storage rooms above 0°C due to door openings and infiltration may range from 10 for small cold room of 90 m3 volume to 1 for large cold storage of about 900 m3 volume. In the case of cold storages, the enclosures are insulated with at least 10–15 cm thermocole and are almost completely needed. Thus, many of the loads present in buildings for comfort air-conditioning are either absent or lessened in the case of cold storages. However, in addition to the heat that is removed from products at the time of initial loading, there is also the heat produced by the commodities during storage. This heat of respiration forms a sizable product load even at a storage temperature of 0°C. At higher temperature it is more. The approximate rate of evolution of heat respiration by various products at different temperature is given in the Table 23.2. Although most of the load in refrigerated room is due to transpiration, air changes, and product respiration, the loads due to lighting, motors, and people working should not be overlooked. 392 Chapter 23 23.3.3 Product Load The product load consists of three separate components: 1. Sensible: This is the amount of heat that must be removed to bring the product to storage temperature. It depends on specific heat of the product. 2. Latent: This is the amount of heat that must be removed to freeze the product. It depends on latent heat of fusion, and it is applicable in the case of frozen food storage. For example, 2500 kJ/kg of heat is removed for the hardening of ice cream. 3. Respiration: Fresh fruits and vegetables are alive. They undergo changes even when stored at low temperatures, releasing heat of respiration. Typical values of this respiration load are given in Table 23.2. When product load is calculated on a per-hour basis, then a correction factor for taking into account pull-down time other than 24 hours must be applied as follows: = 24 h Pull-down time A safety factor of 10% is also added to allow for any omissions and inaccuracies. When load in kW has been determined, the condensing unit is selected first to give a capacity greater than the cooling-freezing load. The fan coil unit is then selected to balance the capacity of the condensing unit. The nature of the product governs the choice of RH to be maintained in the room. The RH, in turn, determines the choice of refrigeration temperature. The higher the humidity, the higher is the refrigeration temperature. The Table 23.3 gives recommended temperature differences between the air in the storage room and the saturated suction temperature of the refrigerant in the forced convection evaporator, depending on room RH. In cold storage application, it is recommended that load be divided into multiple units to provide for some capacity control, because the refrigeration system has to be selected for the worst conditions that may occur even for 1 day in the year. Table 23.3: Recommended temperature differences Product Type Fruits, vegetables, flowers, etc. General storage, packed products Pharmaceuticals, beer, potatoes, onions, tough-skin fruits, etc. Prep/cutting rooms, candy, etc. RH Temperature Difference 90% 80–85% 65–80% 4–5 C 6 oC 7–9 oC Minimum moisture loss Products require lower RH Products require moderate RH 50–65% 9–12 oC Products not affected by RH o Remarks Design of Small-Capacity Cold Storages 393 Important consideration in the selection and location of fan coil units include the following: • • Air should be directed to move where there is heat gain (e.g., toward walls and ceiling). Total supply of air is about 40–80 air changes per hour, primarily because the dehumidified rise is small. 23.4 Design of a Precooling Chamber for Onions It is desired to cool field cured fall onions to storage temperature of 0°C over a 15-day period. Cooling is begun when the first onions are placed in the storage, and all must be at 0°C, 15 days after start. Estimate the cooling load and tons of refrigeration. Outside ambient average temperature is 10°C 23.4.1 Conditions 1. Average temperature of onions at harvest is 20°C. 2. Pallet boxes are used. Boxes are 100 × 120 × 75 cm. Average net weight of onions is 540 kg per box; empty boxes weight 35 kg. 3. Harvest is at a rate of 18 metric tons per day; 5 days required for filling each 90 metric ton–capacity room. 4. Two-room storage will require 10 days to fill. Room 1 is completely filled before Room 2 is started. 5. Refrigeration is started in both rooms 2 days before onions are placed in either room. 6. Onions in each room must be cooled to 7°C in 5 days and to 0°C in 10 days. 23.4.2 Facilities Storage Building 1. An insulated mechanically refrigerated two-room storage. Each room opens into a common packing shed, but there is no door between the storage rooms. 2. Inside dimensions of each room: 8 × 10 m with a 4.5 m ceiling. Loading Pattern (shown in Figure 23.1) 1. Pallet boxes are placed 7 × 3 to a layer, on each side of a 2 m aisle for fork lift operation. 2. Each layer contains 42 boxes. 3. Boxes are stacked four high for a total height of 3.5 m (box with pallet totals 85 cm 4 × 85 = 3.4 m; but taken as 3.5 m). Space above load is 1 m. 4. Total capacity of each room is 42 × 4 = 168 boxes, approximately 90.8 metric tons (168 × 540/1,000 = 90.8) of onions. Total capacity of storage is 181.6 metric tons (90.8 × 2 = 181.6). 5. A space of 30 cm is maintained along each 10 m room side to permit air flow along the walls. 394 Chapter 23 Figure 23.1: Plan and Sectional View of the Cool Chamber. Refrigeration 1. Each room has three ceiling-mounted blower coil units, evenly spaced along 8 m outside wall in each room as shown in plan view of Figure 23.1. 2. Refrigerant for all blower coil units is supplied from a central compressor condenser system. 3. Each cooling unit has a ½ metric horsepower (hp) fan circulating air. 4. Air is ducted for each unit to a point just beyond work aisle. 5. Air moves over the stacked boxes, down the open space at the far wall, back through boxes and pallet openings, and returns in the open space on the rear wall. Insulation 1. Outside walls are insulated with 8 cm of polyurethane, k = 0.023 W/m °C. Mylar film outside of insulation serves as vapor barrier. 2. The floor has 10 cm slab polystyrene, laid on polyethylene sheets and with 10 cm of reinforced concrete above as a bearing floor. k = 0.029 W/m °C 3. The ceiling has 8 cm of loose mineral wool between the joists. k = 0.039 W/m °C. 4. The solid partition between the rooms has 5 cm fiber glass batts between the 2 × 4 studs of the bearing wall.
