For assurance of sufficient cooling capacity in seasons of unusually high produce and unusually of high ambient temperatures during harvest, 8.5 tons of refrigeration should be provided. Because the refrigeration load is low after initial produce cooling, it would be advisable to have 7-ton unit and 1-ton unit run separately. Both can be operated if needed at peak load. But with decreasing load only the 7-ton unit will be needed and during late fall and winter, the 1-ton unit alone provide ample refrigeration. 23.5 Design of Cold Store for Apples The following shows the formulae and assumptions that are used in some of Northern European countries for estimating heat load for cold storage for fruits. A numerical example illustrating the application of these formulae and assumptions for actual design of a cold storage for apples is also given. Design of Small-Capacity Cold Storages 399 23.5.1 Thermal Transmission The first element of the heat load is the thermal energy entering the room by heat transfer through walls, ceiling, and floor. The applicable equation is Q1 = UA dt where Q1 = heat load, W U = Over all heat transfer coefficient, W/m–2k–1 A = external insulated surface area, m2 dt = to – ti to = outside temperature, °C ti = inside temperature, °C In Northern Europe, it is usual to establish the outside temperature at 25°C and the soil temperature at between 10°C and 15°C. The outside temperature is usually calculated by taking into account the solar heat parameters. The formula for calculating solar air temperature (te) is te = to + aI fo where to = outside air temperature, °C a = absorptivity of wall surface I = direct and diffuse solar radiation, W/m–2 fo = outside surface heat transfer coefficient, W/m–2°C–1 A 15% safety factor is added to Q1 because the insulation quality decreases with time. For all purposes of heat transfer through building structures, the solar air temperature may be used instead of the DBT of the outside air and the solar radiation separately. 23.5.2 Air Infiltration, Q2 Air filtration is an important element of the total heat load. It is most difficult to calculate the extra heat load that results from fresh air entering from the outside. However, for forced fresh air intake, it is a simple matter. The amount of fresh air intake depends on the product stored and varies from one to five times the total room volume per 24 h. In small rooms, where no fan is used, the opening and closing of the doors provide adequate natural air intake. In freezer rooms and gas-tight rooms there is, of course, no forced ventilation. 400 Chapter 23 The outside air can be cooled by a special air cooler, but normally it is done by the normal air coolers. This heat load can be determined using the formula Q2 = mdh (W ) where m is the mass flow rate of the entering air dh is the difference in enthalpy between outside air and air under cold store conditions It is difficult to calculate exactly how much air is entering during the time that the doors are open. Empirical equations are often used as follows: n = 35/V (room volume) for low temperature rooms n = 70/V (room volume) for chilled rooms where n is the number of times the complete air volume of the room is exchanged in 24 h. In cases where intense traffic can be expected, n is multiplied by 2. Some engineers assume for calculation purposes that Q2 is 10% of the total heat load. This can be too small a figure, especially in public cold stores or stores with heavy traffic. Other factors affect this load: whether the doors are hand or automatically operated; whether plastic strip curtains or an air curtain is used; whether a cold lock or a loading bay, refrigerated or not, is part of the layout. It also depends on the ratio between cold store volume and total doorway area. Underestimating Q2, the infiltration heat load, can lead to big variations in heat load calculations being made by different engineers. Q2 = (1 / 3) ρi AV {h(1 − ρo / ρi )dh (kW / s) This has been modified by Fritzsche to:   T  Q2 = t ρ i A  h  1 − i   ∆h ( kW/s )   To   This short-term load applies only when the door is open. The open time can be reduced to 30 s by using automatic doors. In later work, Fritzsche and Lilienblum gave a correction factor k to be applied to the equation: K = 0.48 + 0.004(to − ti ) Q2 actual is Q2 × k where ρi = density of inside air, kg/m3 A = dimensions of the ventilator opening, m2 Design of Small-Capacity Cold Storages 401 h = height of the ventilator opening, m ρo = density of the outside air, kg/m3 dh = enthalpy difference between outside and inside air, kJ/kg. 23.5.3 Moisture Load, Q3 Moisture enters the cold store in different ways before it finally reaches the evaporator coils and freezes there, a process which adds an extra load, a latent heat load, Q3, to the overall heat load. The different entry methods of the moisture are: • • • • Air leakage through the insulation: Little is yet known about this amount. Experiments are in progress at the University of Delft, The Netherlands. Standards will be created, expressing the leakage in a unit called Selo, the specific leakage opening. Not enough information is yet available to take its effect into account in heat load calculations. Humidity entering as a result of water vapor diffusion through the insulation and vapor barrier. In modern prefabricated construction, this is negligible. Using traditional vapor barriers, calculations can be made as discussed previously. Moisture entering as water vapor content of the infiltration air. This quantity is significant enough to be included in the heat load calculation. Moisture coming from the stored goods: Though it is an important factor, few accurate figures are available. Experiments on the subject are still in progress at the Sprenger Institute in Wageningen, The Netherlands. For some products, the values are already available. See Figure 23.2 for data applicable to one variety of apple. In those graphs, the moisture production is shown at different temperatures and RH. For other products, the figures are given according to the difference in water vapor pressure. For example, the value for carrots is 7.1 × 10–10 kg/(kg Pa·s). The driving pressure is calculated as dp = ps – p, where ps is the saturated water vapor pressure and p = φPs. α / β = ocp J / (m 3 K) and mb = β dp / ( RoT ) 1. Estimate the water vapor quantity difference between inside and outside air, kg/kJ of dry air: ∆w = ω i − ω o where wi = mass of water vapor inside air, kg/kg of dry air wo = mass of vapor outside air, kg/kg of dry air 402 Chapter 23 Figure 23.2: Fruit and Vegetable Moisture Production. Q3 = m(∆w) = 333.4 where 333.4 in the latent heat of vaporization of water vapor at the inside pressure of the cold storage. 23.5.4 Product Load, Q4 The goods loaded into storage bring yet another heat load, the product load. This load may consist of one or more of the following: • • • Sensible heat, when the goods only have to be lowered in temperature Latent heat, when crystallization or freezing takes place Respiration heat, when living matter like fruit, plants, and vegetables are involved. In order to calculate the thermal energy to be taken out of the products during chilling or even freezing, we need to know: Mass m (kg) Specific heat above the freezing Point c1 Specific heat below the freezing Point c2 Solidification heat, crystallization heat, or at least the water content of the product, so that we can calculate the solidification heat of the water content of the product, knowing that the solidification heat of water is 333 kJ/kg The initial temperature of the goods t1 when brought into the store The freezing point of the goods tf The final temperature of the goods t2 Then Q = m(c1 (t1 − tt ) + ( x × 333) + c2 (t2 − tf ) is the equation necessary to calculate the heat load for a complete frozen product. See Table 23.4 for typical food values to use in the preceding equation. Respiration of the fruits and vegetables has three elements: 1. Respiration heat: The heat liberated during the process of respiration mainly depends on the temperature to which the food material is exposed. Respiration heat for different food materials at different temperatures are available in the Appendix. 2. Moisture production: During the process of respiration moisture is also produced and it adds to the surrounding atmosphere depending on temperature and RH of the surrounding medium. Moisture liberated by fruits and vegetables at different temperature and RH is available in Figure 23.2. 404 Chapter 23 Table 23.4: Latent heat and specific heat capacity for typical foods Specific Heat Capacity (kJ/kg·K) Food Apples Bananas Pears Beer Butter Eggs Strawberries Fish-lean • Fat • Veal-lean Pork-fat Chicken Carrots Oranges Above Freezing Below Freezing Latent Heat Capacity (kJ/kg) 3.85 3.35 3.85 3.77 2.51–2.68 3.18–385 73.85 3.43 2.85 2.95 2.14 2.93–3.18 3.64 3.85 1.76 281 251 209 301 196 234–300 300 209 234 209 130–153 247 276 285 1.76 1.26 1.67–1.97 1.97 1.80 1.85 1.67 1.34 1.67 1.88 1.84 3. Sensible cooling of fruits and vegetables. This load is calculated by using the formula m ⋅ Cp ⋅ ∆t where m = mass of food material, kg Cp = specific heat of food material, kJ/kg °C ∆t = temperature difference between outside and inside, °C 23.5.5 Miscellaneous Heat Loads, Qs Finally, we must not overlook the additional thermal energy brought into the cold store by the following sources: • • • People Electric motors, such as those in the air cooler fans or secondary fans, or motors in production equipment found in cutting or packing rooms Electric lights whose source (a) involves small quantities of energy since one person gives out only about 350 W; and source (b) can only be estimated at the start of the calculation because at that point the fans have not yet been in operation. Assume a value based on 0.145 W/m3 of cold store volume. Source (c) depends on the intensity of the lighting chosen. Generally, one may assume that roughly 2% of the total heat load comes from these three sources. Design of Small-Capacity Cold Storages 405 Normal lamps have a relatively large thermal energy production; fluorescent tube lamps produce less warmth but their efficiency at low temperatures is not very good. With a 1.5 W fluorescent tube lamp the light capacity is 7100 lumens; the surface temperature is +40°C. With a normal lamp, the light capacity is 1380 lumens; the surface temperature is +200°C. The TL lamp has an operating life at least 10 times that of a normal lamp and gives maximum light after 20 min. A lighting loading of 115 W/50 m2 normally gives satisfactory visibility in cold stores. Special 125 W sodium lamps give out 5600 lumens. 23.5.6 Design Example Estimate the heat load of an apple cold store from the following data: Dimensions: 30 × 20 × 6 m or V = 3600 m3 Quantity of goods: 1000 ton Daily input: 100 ton including packing at +20°C Insulation: Prefabricated sandwich panels with 10 cm PU foam Floor not insulated Above the ceiling is a ventilated space under the roof. Refrigerating capacity required b. Approximate saturated suction temperature of refrigerant c. Number of air changes of supply air Solution Refer to Figure 23.3. Because the inside condition is close to saturation curve, all psychrometric properties are found by calculation rather than by using a psychrometric chart. The supply air condition lies between 2°C and – 0.55°C. It has to be rather close to – 0.55°C, otherwise the supply air quantity will be extremely large. Hence, one has to choose a coil of almost zero bypass factor (BPF). For the purpose, a large number of rows have to be taken, say, from 6 to 12. Let us choose a coil with BPF = 0.03. Supply air temperature: t i – ts = 1 – x = 1 – 0.03 = 0.97 ti – tADP ts = 0.03 ti + 0.97 ADP = 0.03(2) + 0.97 (− 0.55) = − 0.47 °C Design of Small-Capacity Cold Storages 415 Supply air quantity: Qs 0.0204 (ti – ts ) 6.33 = = 125.6 0.0204 (2 + 0.47) cm.m s = Air changes of supply air quantity per hour: = 125.6 × 60 = 71 106.25 The number of air changes of supply air is large in a cold storage application because the room condition at low temperature (2°C) and high humidity (90%) is close to the saturation curve. It implies that the dehumidified rise is very small (2.47°C in this case) even after selecting a coil with large number of rows and low BPF (0.03 in this case). Even then, the number of air changes of 71 is excessive. For vegetables and fruits, it should be 30–60. Air changes in excess of 60 would lead to abnormal moisture loss and deterioration of the product. The supply air quantity, and hence the air changes can be reduced either by decreasing the load, or by decreasing the supply air temperature. The following measures are, therefore, recommended: • • • • Reduce transmission load by applying further insulation. Reduce infiltration load by minimizing door openings. Limit daily loading of product, and hence cooling load. Decrease coil BPF by increasing number of rows. Another alternative is to have jacketed cold store if the supply air quantity is large. The supply air can be made to flow in a jacket all around the store along the walls. Thus, air velocity will not be large near the product to cause undesirable moisture loss. In this example, the apparatus dew point (ADP) is – 0.55°C, below zero. Hence, it is a frosted coil. Not only timely defrosting is necessary, but the coil itself cannot have more than 3 fins/ cm, otherwise the flow will get blocked too soon due to frosting. To maintain the conditions of comfort in the room it is necessary to condition the air and supply to the room generally at lower temperature and moisture content in summer. It is known that the supply air condition lies on the room sensible heat factor (SHF) line. Thus, thermodynamically, there is a wide choice available for the supply air condition. For each supply air condition, there is a supply air rate. Corresponding to the minimum weight of the supply air, the supply condition is at the apparatus dew point for summer, or slightly away from it in the case of a finite bypass factor of the conditioning apparatus. This minimum weight of the 416 Chapter 23 Figure 23.5: Recirculated Room Air Added After the A/C Apparatus. supply air may not be adequate from the point of view of good room air distribution aimed at equalizing both the temperature and humidity throughout the conditioned space, in addition to providing a certain air movement at the load level. In case the minimum weight of the supply air does not meet the air change requirement, it is possible to increase the quantity of the supply air by mixing it with an additional amount of recirculated room air after the A/C apparatus as shown in Figure 23.5. The effect of such mixing is merely to increase the bulk of the supply air and correspondingly change its temperature and moisture content, but in no way does it affect the capacity of this air to meet the room sensible and latent heat loads. In such a case, the conditioned air quantity is  ma i + ma o  but the supply air quantity becomes ( mai )1 + mao + ( mai )2 . Accordingly, the supply air condition changes its position on the psychrometric chart and the dehumidified air rise also changes. In the former case, it is not possible to design a cooling coil that would satisfy the SHF of the room; and in the latter, an extremely uneconomical refrigerating machine would result with a low suction pressure and high power consumption. Such a situation arises when the latent heat load is high in comparison with the total heat load due to humid outdoor design conditions or when high internal latent loads are present. In all such applications, an appropriate apparatus dew Point ts is selected and the air is reheated to the RSHF line after leaving the cooling coil as shown in Figure 23.8. For this purpose, the following procedure is followed. 1. Select a maximum allowable temperature difference (ti – ts) between the room and supply air conditions. 2. Draw the RSHF line. 3. Locate the supply air Point s. 4. Then the leaving air state 2 lies on the horizontal from s. Design of Small-Capacity Cold Storages 423 Figure 23.8: Psychrometric Processes with Reheat. 5. Select a suitable coil with ADP so that 2 lies on this horizontal. 6. Calculate the reheat from t2 to ts. 7. Calculate the air quantity to take up the RSH from ts to ti or the sensible heat including reheat from t2 to ti. There are two other alternative to reheat. They are: 1. Alter the room design condition to a condition of higher humidity. This will make the grand sensible heat factor (GSHF) line intersect the saturation curve. 2. Use a coil of a lower bypass factor so that effective sensible heat factor (ESHF) is increased and a higher ADP is obtained. Even though these methods may not eliminate the need for reheat completely, they can at least reduce the reheat requirement. Thus, these methods can be used simultaneously with reheat. Problems 1. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 24 Dimensions–Layout–Stacking Methods for Cold Storage 24.1 Data Needed for Determining the Dimensions of Cold Storage In order to determine the dimensions of a cold store and choose the type of construction, the following data are needed: • • • • • • • • • The kind of product to be stored (how it will be packed and stacked) How much will be stored The cost of the land to be built on The availability of handling equipment or the availability of manual labor The rotation time for the goods The number and variety of products to be stored (e.g., only frozen products, only icecreams, only fruits; different kinds of products to store, subject to different storage conditions) The standard dimensions of the insulation materials used The type of internal ventilation system required The nature of any special local conditions, such as aesthetic design requirements of rules, fire protection, soil conditions, etc. To determine the dimensions, the data given in Tables 24.1, 24.2, 24.3 may be used to calculate the exact floor area; to this calculation, space for corridors, equipment, and air circulation must be added. Products must stand at least 30 cm from walls and ceilings. The gross volume should be 36% higher than the calculated net volume. Empirical figures that are available for a multipurpose cold store include 200 tons per 1000 m3, using stacks of three pallets of 4.5–5 m height; about 160 tons per 1000 m3 for chilled products only; for frozen products about 300 tons per 1000 m3; and about 225 tons per 1000 m3 for apples and pears in stores with controlled atmosphere of about 6–7 m in height. Once the volume of the cold store is known, we need to determine the dimensions. Because land is expensive everywhere, it might be more practical to build as high as possible rather than a building that spreads over a larger area. The soil should be capable of bearing the loads. A volume of 6400 m3 at 8 m height has a 3560 m2 surface. The same volume at 4 m height results in a 4000 m2 surface. To have a square floor would be most economical but would be difficult for stacking and handling of the product. A height of 15 m is the present economic limit; however, cold stores can be made higher using fully computer-controlled automatic stacking systems. Such systems only apply to volumes of above 75,000 m3, whereas standard volumes are those between 5,000 m3 and 25,000 m3. For pallets, the international standard sizes most frequently used have the dimensions of 100 × 120 mm, 120 × 80 cm, and 200 × 100 cm. Alternative dimensions are 80 × 100 cm and 120 × 120 cm. 100 × 120 cm is the standard-size pallet, which is now being used more and more. The height of goods stacked on a pallet varies between 1 m and 1.77 m for different products. The pallet load also varies for different products and height of stacking, and ranges from 750 to 1000 kg. 24.2 Relationship Among Length, Width, and Height of a Cold Store The height depends on the stacking system. Length mostly depends on the throw of the air stream leaving the air coolers. With modern fans, a throw of 25–80 m can be obtained without using ducts or false ceilings. It is not always necessary to blow air over the whole 430 Chapter 24 length of the store. However, when air is blown over the full width, more air coolers must be used. For a long jet of more than 30 m, a smooth ceiling is necessary, which means a cold store construction with an external steel frame. This construction eliminates obstructions to the air stream. The width is also limited by the maximum economical allowable span between the columns over the width of the steel structure, which is about 30 m, considering that we do not want to use columns in the floor space in the middle of the store. The distances between the columns over the length of the store are normally 5–6 m. 24.2.1 Dimensions of Cold Store • • • Useful volume: Useful volume of a chamber is calculated as a function of maximum mass of produce in the store, at the same time taking into account the densities of storage expressed as net mass of goods per usable m3. Gross volume: Gross volume is equal to the useful volume increased by the volumes necessary to allow for circulation of air and for handing. For a preliminary plan, it is usually assumed that the gross internal volume is twice the useful volume depending on whether the goods are on pallets of standard size 1 × 1.20 m or not, and depending also on an accessibility to the stacks. Internal height: The internal height depends on the means of handling and stacking. In large stores or where stacking is done by lift trucks, the internal height is of the order of 8.5 m for four superimposed pallets, to 1.7–1.9 m and of the order of 10 m if the storage is five pallets high. If the stacking is manual, the maximum height of stacks does not exceed 3 m, which gives an internal height of 3.5–4 m. The plan of the building should be chosen to correspond with the best of local practice and as a function of local materials or those that can be readily imported. 24.3 General Layout of a Cold Store A typical layout for a cold store is shown in Figure 24.1. In this layout, various services needed for a cold store project are shown. Figure 24.2 shows a transverse section of cold storage in which the stacking of produce, cool air circulation, and few constructional details are detailed. 24.4 Installation of Air-Conditioning Machinery The air-conditioning machinery consists of compressors, evaporators, condensers, and controls associated with them for their functioning. The cold room may be as simple as only one room and also may be as complex as having many rooms. The equipment may be centralized or decentralized. Dimensions–Layout–Stacking Methods for Cold Storage 431 Figure 24.1: Layout Plan of a Cold Store. 24.4.1 Centralized or Decentralized Installations If the store has only one cold room, it may be equipped with a machine assembled in a factory. This is especially important in the case of rooms with demountable sandwich insulation because the work of installation is easy and rapid. Figure 24.2: Transverse Section of Cold Storage. 432 Chapter 24 If the store has several rooms at about the same temperature, the high-pressure side of the equipment (compressor and condenser) as well as associated equipment and automatic controls may be common to the whole store. In such an installation, ammonia and flooded operations may be used. A store may have several independent, centralized circuits for storage of chilled or frozen foods. The installation may also be decentralized. Each room is then equipped with one or more independent factory-assembled machines. This machinery may be called self-contained systems or package units. They have a medium output, use halocarbons, and are often dry expansion. Although the total installed power may be greater than with centralized installation, investment may not be necessarily be higher because the package units are mass produced. The description of machinery used for precooling chambers is discussed here briefly. The technical design for this equipment is given elsewhere in this book. 24.4.2 Compressor Unit Raising the pressure of the fluid from that of evaporation to that of condensation is accomplished mechanically by a compressor driven by a motor, usually electric, but in some cases by a gas or diesel engine compressor of the piston, rotary, screw, or centrifugal type. The latter two types are used in large stores with a refrigerating capacity of several hundred or thousands of kW. Rotary compressors are rarely used today. In practice, multicylinder reciprocating types that are open for ammonia are used most often. For halocarbons, the compressor units may be open but hermetically sealed units are typically used. Multicylinder compressors are fitted with capacity reducer, by reduction of number of cylinders—by one third for machine with 3n cylinder, or a quarter for one with 4n cylinders—to allow for adjustment of the capacity to needs of the store at peak. 24.4.3 Evaporators The evaporators may be for cooling liquid or for cooling air. • • Liquid coolers: These are batteries of smooth tubes immersed in a tank of nonfreeze liquid a brine tank for manufacture of ice in molds Figure 24.6 or a tank if iced water. They may also consist of a shell and coil heat exchanger, which in this case does not accumulate ice on its tubes. These coolers are often employed in central air-conditioning installations to provide cold water between 8°C and 12°C. Air coolers: These are also known as unit coolers. The evaporator is enclosed in a compartment that includes the fans, a defrost system, and gutters to take away the defrost water. These are of two types: wall coolers (Figure 24.3) and ceiling coolers (Figure 24.4). Dimensions–Layout–Stacking Methods for Cold Storage 433 Figure 24.3: Plan for Wall-Type Air Coolers. The evaporator is a battery of finned tubes. The fins usually have height equal to the diameter of the tube and are about 1 mm thick, intimately bonded in the tube and separated by 10 mm or more from each other for chilling rooms and 15 mm or more for freezer rooms. The air of the room is drawn into the lower part of the cooler and delivered at ceiling height. Figure 24.4: Diagram of the Principle of Air-Cooling Ceiling Package Unit. 434 Chapter 24 24.5 Feeding the Evaporators Dry expansion and flooding are the two main methods of feeding refrigerant to the evaporators. Flooding is used only in industrial equipment (i.e., with the storage capacity of 100t frozen and 200t chilled). In dry expansion (Figure 24.5), the evaporator receives the fluid in the state resulting from expansion (i.e., already containing a certain portion of vapor). Expansion generally occurs by means of capillary for small domestic machines but generally it is done by a thermostatic expansion valve that is externally equilibrated in commercial and industrial equipment. The rate of supply of fluid is controlled in such a way that the vapor of the refrigerant fluid leaves the evaporator superheated by 2–4°C and is thus free from droplets of liquid refrigerant. If the vapor withdrawn is humid (i.e., contains liquid), there is a risk of liquid slugging and fracture of the suction valves. For this reason, the compressor is protected by an antislugging device and a solenoid valve, situated upstream from the expansion valve that is actuated when the compressor is running. Further, the difference between the temperature of the air in the room and that of the refrigerant is kept at 5–7°C. To do this it is necessary to calculate the surface area of the evaporator. Additionally a pressure-controlled valve is also fitted. Dry expansion is the simplest process. It may be used with all fluids whether they entrain oil or not and with all sorts of machines, even the most powerful. In fact, the heat transfer of the evaporator cannot be maximal because the refrigerant fluid must be totally evaporated during Figure 24.5: Diagram of a Dry Expansion Installation (Halocarbon). Dimensions–Layout–Stacking Methods for Cold Storage 435 Figure 24.6: Diagram of a Flooded Ammonia System. its passage through the evaporator; therefore, dry expansion is usually used only with smallor medium-capacity machines. In the flooding type (Figure 24.6), the expanded fluid is discharged to a vessel, the lowpressure receiver, in which the liquid is separated from the vapor. The vapor is directly drawn into the compressor without passing through evaporator. The pure liquid is sent by gravity or pump to the evaporator, the fluid leaves this as a mixture of liquid and vapor, the former being recycled to complete evaporation. The expansion of fluid is controlled by a low pressure float valve XE “low pressure float valve” and today by an electronic expansion valve, which has the advantage of easy adjustment of liquid level in the separating vessel. The difference in temperature between the air in the cold room and the cooler is kept at 4–5°C. This method of feeding the evaporator is used only with industrial ammonia machines with or without oil, or also with halocarbons on condition that the fluid is free from oil. If oil is present with halocarbon, flooding may be used on condition that a rectifier is installed in lowpressure circuit to ensure the return of oil to the compressor. 436 Chapter 24 24.5.1 Defrosting Defrosting consists of supplying heat to the evaporator of a cooler in order to melt the ice that has formed. There are three methods of defrosting: 1. By water 2. By electricity 3. By hot gas Electric defrosting or hot gas defrosting is suitable to all types of rooms. Water defrosting is only used in rooms for chilled products. 24.6 Condensers Condensers may be cooled by water or by air. Water is widely used because of the excellent heat transfer conditions. Shell and tube condensers are commonly used provided that the quality of water is good and sufficiently available. If water is not sufficiently available or is expensive, the open circuit (“lost water”) condenser may be replaced by a system of recycling or evaporative system. There are two processes for this: 1. Independent cooling tower: Associated with classic shell and tube condenser. 2. Evaporative condenser: The condenser circuit included in the cooling tower. Both processes are efficient, with the choice typically guided by cost and ease of operation. Air is less efficient than water as a heat transfer medium; therefore, the heat transfer areas must be markedly larger and hence fins are used. Air cooling is used when water is not easily available, expensive, or of poor quality. Air condensers are simple and require little servicing. 24.6.1 Estimation of Coolants for the Condenser For an installation of a system with 100 kW refrigeration capacity, the thermal power to be removed by the condenser is nearly 130 kW. With the shell and tube condenser with lost water, if the water temperature increased by 5°C, the water consumption is calculated by the simple relation: Q = m Cp ∆t ; m = Q Cp ∆t 130 / (5 × 4.18) = 6.2 2l / s or 22.4 m 3 / h (4.18 is the specific heat of water, kJ/kg °C) Dimensions–Layout–Stacking Methods for Cold Storage 437 With a recycled water system, the quantity of water evaporated is 130 / 2500 = 0.052 l / s (2500 is the latent heat of evaporation at atmospheric pressure, kJ/kg) If the quantity of purge is three times that of the water evaporated, the consumption of water is then 0.052 (1 + 3) = 0.280 l / s or 0.75 m 3 / h With an air condenser, the rise in temperature of air is of the order of 30°C and the quantity of air is 130 / (3 × 1.25) = 34.7 m 3 / s or 125000 m 3 / h (1.25 is the volumetric heat of dry air, kJ/m3 °C) 24.7 Operation of Cold Rooms Operation of cold rooms depends on knowledge of the following three factors: 1. The storage conditions of the produce 2. The rules for loading cold rooms, their maintenance, and keeping them in good hygienic state XE “hygienic state” 3. The running and maintenance of the refrigerating equipment 24.7.1 Renewal of Air The atmosphere in a room becomes unfit for storage because of the following factors: 1. Odors given off by the produce 2. High levels of CO2, from the respiration of vegetables or fruits 3. Increase in the concentrations of ethylene and aromatic volatiles from fruits that can ripen in the cold (Ethylene and these volatiles even in trace concentration can induce ripening of other still unripe fruits.) The way to limit these undesirable effects is to ventilate frequently. 24.7.2 Air Circulation Generally it will take few days to completely fill the cold room, and it happens more or less frequently that it may be only partly filled. However, the circulation of air must be correct, no matter the state of loading. Proper circulation is essential to ensure transfer of heat toward the 438 Chapter 24 air coolers and to cool the goods that were warm when loaded. The following recommendations should be followed for proper air circulation. 1. The air must be moved by the fans in the air cooler and at all times while the refrigeration machine is running. 2. The circulation of air should be cost-effective and it should flow horizontally below the ceiling. However, it requires that the loading limit be scrupulously respected. In practice, there must be no obstacle in the segment container between the ceiling and a level tangential to the lower outlet of the fans of the cooler. The air returns to the cooler via the spaces reserved between the stacks and the walls and those below the pallets at the floor level (air mechanical handling) or fixed dunnage. The rate of air circulation is an important factor, as much during storage as when cooling the load entering the stores. For this reason, if a room is used for cooling fruits, vegetables, and meat and used for storage, two flow rates are used for the fans, changed manually, usually 24 hours after the entry of the last lot. 3. For a partially filled or loaded room, or one being loaded, the ranges of produce must be perpendicular to the sense of air movement and the first stacks introduced should be those nearest to the cooler. 24.7.3 Air Changes Air changes are only of concern with certain storage rooms used for long periods with chilled produce. An air change replaces the air in the room with clean external air so that the composition inside approximates that of the outside air. The rotation of cleanliness of external air is especially important for dead tissue of fruits or vegetables and also for carcasses of meat, offal, and so on. For getting clear air, the following practical recommendations are made. 1. Take the air from nonpolluted sources. 2. Pass it through filters. 3. Change the air when the external atmosphere is calm and as cool as possible (i.e., at the end of the night). 4. Air should not be changed when it is raining (RH) and windy (dust). 5. Change the air in relatively large rooms and in any case in those of 1000 m3 or greater by using a specific device working by means of fans, driving the fresh air through the cooler, when the refrigerator machine is running. The functioning time of these fans is such that the volume of clean air introduced is equal to 8–10 times the volume V of the storeroom or otherwise the dilution of undesirable constituents (CO2, C2H4 odors) may be incomplete. If V is the gross volume or the room in m3 and d is the flow rate of fans in m3/h, the duration of air change, t, in hours is t= ( 8 to 10 ) × V h d ( ) Dimensions–Layout–Stacking Methods for Cold Storage 439 6. For small-refrigerated spaces, the air may be renewed by natural convection, by a successive of brief (about 10 min) openings of the door, separated by a closure (often up to 3 h), such that the refrigeration machine may restore the temperature to the desired level. 7. The frequency of change should be as seldom as possible, because each period increases the frost deposit on the evaporator and constitutes a disturbance of the storage condition. It is determined experimentally, and it is unusual to exchange air more than once a week. 24.8 Stacking Methods 24.8.1 Block Stacking From a volume or surface point of view, block stacking is the most successful, although the maximum height is about three pallets. Height can be increased using special pallets and precise stacking methods. Block stacking can only be used under the following ­conditions: 1. The same kinds of goods are stored, making corridors unnecessary, and densities of 400 ton/1000 m3 can be achieved. 2. Where only a few different types of goods are to be stored, one or two corridors are sufficient. Goods can be placed in deep rows on both sides of the corridors. 3. The first-in, first-out system is not needed; otherwise, the number of corridors necessary is doubled. 4. Fresh goods are brought in and the stored ones are taken out in one operation. Block stacking, which requires an internal height of about 6 m, is still the most widely used. It can achieve optimum efficiency when using static racking or even drive-through racks as shown in Figure 24.7. If block stacking is not possible for all the stock, it can be used for one part, for which the first-in, first-out method is absolutely necessary. This way, a partial stock rotation is obtained. When using racks, the stacking height can go up to 12 m, which means a store height of 15 m. This, however, demands special forklift trucks, such as turret-trucks, and preferably those able to turn the forks in different directions as shown in Figure 24.8. When using stackercranes, a height of 35 m, 18 pallets, can be reached, but then the investment for cranes, rails, and building is rather high. This system gives little gain in volume, but much gain in floor space. Drive-through racks permit stacking up to 20 rows deep. However, it will often be necessary to provide several corridors in order to be able to reach the different products; in that case the choice should be for forklift trucks using narrow corridors. 440 Chapter 24 Figure 24.7: Drive-Through Racking. Figure 24.8: Turret-Truck. 24.8.2 Equipment for Stacking 24.8.2.1 Forklift A normal forklift needs a corridor of 3.5 m, a so-called reach-truck needs 2.4 m, whereas a tridirectional turret-truck only needs 1.65 m and is able to reach as far as seven pallets high. 24.8.2.2 Truck The truck does not need rails, just a simple system between the racks, and it can work in different corridors. This type of truck is efficient in long corridors (about 15–20 m) and with piles at least 4 m in height. 24.8.2.3 Stacker crane A stacker crane needs a corridor of 1.4 m; it works on rails and is not able to work in different corridors, so each corridor needs its own crane, which makes the system more expensive. The advantage of stacker cranes is that the operator is at the same level as the product, so he sees exactly what he is doing. On turret-trucks, a television camera and monitor are required for that purpose. Dimensions–Layout–Stacking Methods for Cold Storage 441 In order to reduce investment costs, a combination of forklift, reach, and pallet trucks is often a normal practice. For each forklift truck there must be one or two pallet trucks. Another combination is turret-trucks and stacker cranes. 24.8.3 Mobile Rack System A more efficient block system is the mobile rack system, which can utilize 80–90% of the floor surface. This is double the efficiency rate when stationary racks are used, in which case there must be a corridor between every two racks, whereas normally only one corridor is needed for the whole store. The width of the corridor also depends here on the equipment used, and since there is only one corridor we can design it somewhat larger and to make handling easier (Figure 24.9). The racks are placed on rails by means of a framework with wheels, driven by a small electric motor. Normally all racks are placed against each other, forming a block. Generally four pallets are placed on the racks, resulting in a height of about 8 m and a cold store height of 10 m. It is possible, though, to stack more pallets when using special forklifts. If a particular pallet in a row must be reached, a corridor is created by moving the racks, simply by a pressing a button at the beginning of the row concerned. For security reasons, a Figure 24.9: Mobile Rack System. 442 Chapter 24 button must be activated inside the already existing corridor at that particular time. As long as this is not activated, the system is blocked, to prevent accidents involving people between the moving racks. In systems where the buttons are outside the cold store, a photo electric cell is placed at the entrance to the corridors; when people pass this cell, the moving system is automatically blocked. Every rack has a brake system activated by touching the baseboard of the rack. Activating the buttons outside will save time for the truck operator. When the operator is driving in, the racks will be moving to the desired position. The velocity of movement is about 10 cm/s. However, the efficiency of loading and unloading systems depends on a logical organization being built in at the design stage of the store. The floor must be designed after calculating the extra weight and the location of the rail systems, which may involve 10–20% of the investment cost. All the previously mentioned systems can be combined into one cold store to obtain the highest efficiency. A layout of this type is shown in Figure 24.10. The system used in a particular section of the store depends on the product rotation. The openings in the loading bay are provided with special joints, against which the van opening is placed during loading and unloading, in order to save refrigerating energy. Smaller freezer stores can also be equipped with anterooms, of which the outside door has to be closed before the door of the freezer is opened. Air curtains are not especially effective. The best solution is to place a plastic strip curtain in the freezer door opening. Figure 24.10: Cold Store with Different Racking Methods. Dimensions–Layout–Stacking Methods for Cold Storage 443 Figure 24.11: (a) Diagram of Loading of 142 Stacks of Pallets in a Space for Long-Term Storage of a Single Product, (b) Cross-Section of Space (a). 444 Chapter 24 24.8.3.1 Stacking for long-term storage of a single product The stacking diagram for long-term storage of a single product is shown in Figure 24.11. All space in the area is used. Only the space F is left free for the door. The air cooler is mounted above. When access to the stacks is needed, positions 113–142 may be transformed into a central alley, or indeed into two lateral alleys by moving 29–56 and 85–112. Problems 1.
