CHAPTE R 25 Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 25.1 Introduction Perishable products are moved from the location of production to the consumer in a variety of transportation systems, most by refrigerated highway trucks. Most international trade into and out of North America utilizes refrigerated marine containers for ships. Airplanes that do not have temperature control capability are used for limited quantities of high-value commodities. Refrigerated transport is the main link of cold food chain. The goal of transportation is to move perishable products with a minimum loss of quality. Most transportation equipment controls air temperature around the product. Special equipment is sometimes available to produce a modified or controlled atmospheric (gas) composition around the product. Humidity and vibration control equipment are also used on some vehicles. Carrying mixed loads in North America is a common practice, especially with vegetable shipments. Mixed loads can be a serious concern when products’ optimal temperatures are not compatible, for example, when transporting chilling sensitive fruits with commodities that require very low temperature or when ethylene-producing commodities and ethylene-sensitive commodities are transported together. High-ethylene producers (such as ripe bananas, apples, and cantaloupe) can induce physiological diseases and undesirable changes in color, flavor, and texture in ethylene-sensitive commodities such as lettuce, cucumbers, carrots, potatoes, and sweet potatoes. A wide range of pallet covers are available for covering cooled product during handling and transportation. Polyethylene covers are inexpensive and lightweight and protect the pallet load from dust, moisture, and some loss of cold. Lightweight insulated covers can protect the load from heat gain for several hours. Heavy covers are sometimes used to protect tropical products from the cold when shipped during winter. During transport, produce must be stacked in ways that minimize damage, then must be braced and secured. An open-air vehicle can be loaded in such a way that air can pass through the load and provide some cooling of the produce as the vehicle moves. Traveling during night and early morning can reduce the heat load on the vehicle. Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00025-7 445 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 446 Chapter 25 25.2 Types of Transportation 25.2.1 Open Vehicles In some rural areas, refrigerated vehicles are not available and produce is transported in open trucks or carts. Produce must be handled quickly because most products have limited shelf life under these conditions. Heat gain can be minimized by shipping the product during the cool part of the day or at night and covering it to reduce heat gain from the sun. A fabric or plastic cover should be opaque and light-colored to reflect solar radiation. But more importantly, the cover should be supported above the product to allow a small flow of outside air between the cover and the product. Ventilation removes the heat that builds up under the cover. Clean plant material can also be used as a cover. Bulk loads of produce should be carefully loaded so as not to cause mechanical damage. Vehicles can be padded or lined with a thick layer of straw (Figure 25.1). Woven mats or sacks can be used in the beds of small vehicles. Other loads should not be placed on top of the bulk commodity. Cooling of the open load is desirable whenever possible. A truck ventilating device can be constructed for an unrefrigerated open vehicle by covering the load loosely with canvas and fastening a wind catcher made from sheet metal as shown in Figure 25.2. The scoop can be mounted at the front of the bed and should reach somewhat higher than the height of the cab. High transportation speeds and long-distance transport present the risk of excess drying of the crop. 25.2.1.1 System for open vehicles The ventilating system was designed for hauling bulk loads of fresh beans in some countries. The wind catcher and ducts were constructed using wooden crates. After removing their end Figure 25.1: Open Vehicle Transport. Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 447 Figure 25.2: Truck Ventilating Device. panels, the crates were wired together into the pattern as shown in Figure 25.3. Air flows upward through the load during transport, helping to keep the produce from overheating. This system has also been used in pickup trucks and for hauling bulk green beans. The best results are obtained when transporting during the early morning hours, before sunrise. Figure 25.3: Ventilating System. 448 Chapter 25 25.2.2 USDA Portacooler The USDA postharvest cooling program stresses to small growers the need to: • • • Sort and grade produce out of the fields. Package the produce properly for the market. Immediately cool the produce to remove field heat. The portacooler is a cooler that uses a 3.5 kW or 1 ton 220 volt room window air-conditioner to cool air inside the insulated box shown in Figure 25.4. The cool air inside the front of the box is forced through the produce by pressure fan in a second wall inside. The return air passes under a false floor to the front of the box. The portacooler was built by the USDA in Maryland to cool highly perishable berries and other air-cooled produce. Approximate cost is US$1,200, but the cost can be considerably lower if it is built using a repurposed air-conditioning unit. 25.3 Stacking Patterns 25.3.1 Hand-Stacked Bushels that are sturdy, uniformly made, stackable baskets filled with produce can be loaded into a refrigerated trailer using a pattern of alternately inverted baskets that leave plenty of space between rows for air circulation (see Figure 25.5). Produce transported in cartons should also be stacked to allow adequate air circulation throughout the load. Figure 25.6 illustrates cross-wise offset loading of partial telescopic Figure 25.4: USDA Portacooler. Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 449 Figure 25.5: Alternately Inverted Layer Pattern. containers. On the floor of the truck, pallets or other supports should be used to keep the cartons out of direct contact with the floor. When cartons of various sizes must be loaded together, the large, heavier containers should be placed at the bottom of the load. Parallel channels should be left for air to move through the length of the load (see Fig. 25.7). Figure 25.6: Cross-Wise Offset Loading Pattern. 450 Chapter 25 Figure 25.7: Loading Pattern for Cartons of Various Sizes. Often the large containers used for cut flower packaging must be hand-stacked when loaded into a transport vehicle. The best loading pattern for cut flowers is known as the pigeonhole pattern, where boxes are stacked in alternating solid and open layers and channels are left down both side walls (see Figure 25.8). This pattern provides channels for air circulation lengthwise through the load and allows every box to be in direct contact with refrigerated air. 25.3.2 Pallet and Slip Sheet Loads Containers should be loaded so that they are away from the sidewalls and the floor of the transport vehicle in order to minimize the conduction of heat from the outside environment. Figure 25.8: Pigeonhole Pattern. Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 451 Figure 25.9: Loading Pattern on Slip Sheets and Pallets. In Figure 25.9, the number of cartons refers to how many cartons would be in contact with the walls and floor of the truck when fully loaded. Only the load on the bottom right is fully protected from heat transfer. The use of pallets keeps the cartons off the floor, while center-loading leaves an insulating air space between the pallet loads and the outside walls. 25.3.2.1 Stacking Strength When stacking containers, it should be ensured to align them properly. Whenever possible, stack them so that corner matches corner on both the cartons and the pallet. Most of the strength of corrugated fiberboard containers is in their corners, so an overhang of only 1 inch will decrease stacking strength by 15–34% (see Figure 25.10). A well-aligned stack of cartons has the most strength possible. 452 Chapter 25 Figure 25.10: Stacking Strength. 25.3.3 Bracing the Load When stacking containers are used, be sure to align them properly. Well-aligned stack of cartons has the strongest stacking strength possible. Figure 25.10. A void should always be left between the last stack of produce and the back of the transport vehicle. The load should be braced to prevent shifting against the rear door during transit. If the load shifts, it can block air circulation and fallen cartons can present great danger to workers who open the door at a destination market. A sample wooden brace can be constructed and installed to prevent damage during transport as shown in Figure 25.11. Figure 25.11: A Simple Wooden Brace. Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 453 Figure 25.12: Bracing the Load with Plastic Air Bags. Bracing the load can be accomplished using wooden braces, load rails, air pillows (Figure 25.12), or Styrofoam blocks. The key is to immobilize stacked produce to reduce damage during transport. 25.3.4 Other Practices The majority of the heat that the refrigeration unit removes comes from heat conducted across the walls and from air leaking into the trailer. If the product is not center-loaded it will be warmed by contact with the walls. A series of shipments of California strawberries cooled to 1.7°C (35°F) and shipped with thermostats set at that same temperature showed average arrival temperatures in New York at 3.9°C (39°F) for center-loaded fruit and 5°C (41°F) for side-wall-loaded fruit. The warmest center-loaded berries were 5°C (41°F) and 6.7°C (44°F) for sidewall loading. 25.4 Guidelines for Best Use of Refrigerated Transport General Guidelines • Products should be packaged in containers that are: • Strong enough to withstand high humidity and vibration in transport • Not stacked beyond the edge of a pallet • Unitized and secured on a pallet allow vertical air flow in bottom air delivery transport (mostly marine containers and refrigerated ships) 454 • • • • • • • • • • • Chapter 25 Product must be cooled to proper transit temperature before loading. Do not mix products that have different requirements for different temperature, humidity, or incompatibility because of ethylene or odor sensitivity. Ethylene-absorbing materials can reduce ethylene damage if ethylene producers must be mixed with ethylene-sensitive products. Equipment must be in good condition before loading. Check to ensure that • Air delivery chute is in place and has no tears (mostly on trailers) • Door seals are in good condition • Walls and ceiling are in good repair • Floor and floor drains are clean • Inside smells clean Vehicle should be cooled before loading. Turn off refrigeration when doors are open. There should be evidence that the thermostat has been calibrated. Palletized loads should be well stabilized with netting or banding straps. Do not allow product to touch air delivery chute; do not load above upper limit line. Do not block airflow under load with crushed ice or solid load dividers. Do not load product that is sensitive to vibration damage over wheel axels unless they have air ride suspension. Use load bars or rear air bag to prevent rear product from shifting. Place temperature monitor if needed. Guidelines for Highway Trailers Only • • • • Check RTF classification plate to ensure that trailer was originally designed to handle the temperature conditions of the load. A C65 rating is rarely adequate for fruits, vegetables, or flowers. Trailers must have a front bulkhead. Two pallets placed against the front wall can serve as a temporary bulkhead. Do not load product directly on the floor unless trailer has special deep-channel floor. Load away from walls using stabilizing blocks or small inexpensive air bags. Guidelines for Marine Containers and Ships Only • • • Completely cover floor and pallet openings to force air through the load. Produce containers should have bottom and top panel venting to allow vertical airflow. Vents must not be blocked by interior packaging materials or deck board of pallet. Set fresh air exchange vent to prescribed level. Even with these records, cargo is sometimes misdeclared. Consequently, a trailer should always be well cleaned before each load of perishables to avoid contamination by non foodgrade products or food-borne pathogens. Never load a trailer that is visibly unclean or has an odor from a previous load. Some perishable may be handled in trucks or other vehicles that Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 455 are not temperature controlled. For example, products may be shipped directly to the consumer in the mail and flowers are sometimes shipped to florists on bus services. The customer or receiver will get adequate quality only if the product had a good shelf life to begin with and the transport time is relatively short. Many products are packed in closed, insulated containers to protect them from temperature extremes, both freezing and high temperature damage are possible. Ice or gel ice products that have been well sealed in bags are sometimes added to packages to protect the products from high temperatures. Produce should be immediately placed in a temperature-controlled environment after it is received. 25.4.1 Refrigerated Trucks and Trailers These vehicles are refrigerated to maintain temperatures either 1.5–4°C for cold foods or –18°C for frozen foods. The types of refrigeration systems used are described here. • • • Product subcooling: With the use of improved insulating materials, it is possible to drastically cut the transmission load of vehicles. In that case, use may be made of the storage capacity of the product itself by subcooling it to as low a temperature as possible before transporting for short distances. Thus, even after reaching the destination, the temperature of the product is below the temperature of the storage requirement. Examples are tankers for milk, orange juice, etc. Using water ice: The top of the product can be suitably iced. Again, it is a satisfactory method for short distances and for some products only. The refrigerating effect produced by the melting of ice is 335.4 kJ/kg. Water ice in bunker with forced air circulation: Figure 25.13 shows an ice bunker that is fixed in front of an insulated vehicle. Air is sucked over the ice by the blower taking its drive from the engine. A ½ hp blower will add a heat equivalent of 0.37 kW. A mixture of ice and salt can also be used for lower temperature up to –9°C. 25.4.2 Refrigerated Trailers Large refrigerated highway vehicles are usually semitrailers. A powered tractor provides motive power and support for the front of the trailer. Trailers are sometimes placed on rail cars for a portion of the trip and then transported from a central rail location to the final destination with a highway tractor, sometimes referred to as a trailer on flat car (TOFC) shipment system. In North America, refrigerated highway trailers are used for trips lasting about 1–5 days. For optimum transport temperature management, refrigerated trailers need insulation, a highcapacity refrigeration unit, fan, and air delivery duct. Figure 25.14 includes these and other desired features in a top air delivery trailer. The condition of the inside of a refrigerated trailer affects its ability to maintain desired temperature during transport. Handlers should inspect the trailer before loading and check these features shown in Figure 25.14. 456 Chapter 25 Figure 25.13: Ice Bunker in Transport Refrigeration. The trailer has a self-contained engine-driven refrigeration system that provides conditioned air to the insulated space. Most new trailers in the United States have an outside width of 2.6 m (102 in) and can be purchased in exterior lengths of 12.2–16.2 m (40–53 ft). Most new trailers are 16.2 m (53 ft) long. Interior volume ranges from 70 m3 to 100 m3 (2,500– 3,500 ft3). The gross vehicle weight (including tractor) cannot exceed 36,288 kg (80,000 lb) in the United States and individual axles also have weight limit to ensure a fairly uniform weight distribution in the vehicle. Most semitrailers have a load capacity of about 18,100– 20,400 kg (40,000–45,000 lb). Refrigeration capacity of new units is typically 12.3–16.4 kW (3.5–4.7 tons). The unit can provide heat when the trailer is operated in ambient conditions colder than the set point temperature. The refrigeration unit is located on the top front of the trailer and provides refrigerated air to an air chute in the top of the trailer. Product should be loaded and secured to provide air space around the load. This allows the refrigerated air to flow between the load and the walls, underneath the product and finally return to the refrigeration unit through a bulkhead in the front of the trailer. This design allows the refrigerated air to intercept this heat Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 457 Figure 25.14: Checklist for Transport. before it affects product temperature. Top delivery refrigeration systems do not have enough airflow to dependably remove product heat from most commodities and they should be cooled to transit temperature before loading (see Figure 25.15). In the United States, the Refrigerated Transportation Foundation (RTF) has developed a classification system for the combined insulated trailer and refrigeration unit. Vehicles using this Figure 25.15: Refrigeration and Airflow System in a Highway Trailer. 458 Chapter 25 Table 25.1: Ratings for refrigerated trailers Vehicle Rating Rated Minimum Temperature Type of Product Protection C65 C35 F DF 18°C (65°F) 2°C (35°F) –18°C (0°F) –29°C (–20°F) Controlled temperature Fresh fruits, vegetables, flowers Frozen foods Ice cream and frozen foods classification system are rated for their ability to effectively transport products in four temperature categories (see Table 25.1). Metal placards located on the outside and inside of the trailer list the temperature range and other design characteristics of the vehicle. Most perishable fruits, vegetables, and flowers should be shipped in trailers with the least a C35 rating and equipped with an air chute and front bulkhead. 25.5 Refrigerated Transportation Foundation Temperature Limit Relative humidity (RH) is usually not controlled in refrigerated trailers. Some equipment manufacturers offer atomizers to add water to the refrigerated air. However, the added humidity reduces fireboard strength. Acceptable levels of RH are a compromise between minimizing product moisture loss and minimizing damage caused by weakened packages. Product moisture loss can also be reduced by packaging product in plastic liners, bags, or consumersized packages. These reduce moisture loss while allowing the refrigeration system to operate at lower humidity and protect fireboard strength. Atomizers will freeze if air temperature around them is close to 0°C (32°F). This may require that the thermostat be set a little warmer than the optimum for temperature fruits and coolseason vegetables. If products are not particularly sensitive to damage from moisture loss, it may be better to not to use humidifiers and set the thermostat as low as possible. Humidification systems may find their best use with chilling sensitive commodities that are shipped at temperature between 5°C (41°F) and 13°C (55°F). Highway trailers are not airtight to allow their use as gas barrier for modified or controlled atmosphere handling. Modified atmosphere can be provided through the use of semipermeable films used to form consumer packages or pallet wraps. During transit some products can be damaged by the constant vibration caused by the road or by shock caused by the vehicle travelling over a bump or curb. Both of these cause most damage to product loaded directly over axles. Vibration is amplified as it is transmitted through fiberboard boxes, causing most damage to product in topmost boxes on a load. Commercially available air ride suspension systems eliminate most of this damage. They cost more than steel spring suspensions but are becoming more commonly available on trailers. Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 459 Table 25.2: Effects of pallet wraps on temperature rise of strawberries during air transport from San Francisco to several eastern US cities Pallet Cover over Open-Top, Tray-Packed Berries Average Arrival Temperature Corrugated fiberboard sheet on top of pallet Corrugated fiberboard on top and sides of pallet Four mil polyethylene film and corrugated fiberboard on top sides and under bottom boxes 19.4°C (67°F) 12.2°C (54°F) 8.9°C (48°F) Note: Strawberries were originally cooled to 2.7°C (37°F); average transit time was 18 h; average ambient temperature in the planes was 15°C (60°F) and at airports ranged from 17°C (63°F) to 24°C (76°F). Source: Harvey et al., 1966. Air ride suspension also increases tire life and may reduce vibration damage to the trailer itself. Nearly all long-haul tractors in the United States have air ride suspension for driver comfort, so semitrailers usually have air ride suspension for the axles under the front. Vibration-sensitive product should not be loaded directly over axles suspended on steel springs. Vibration damage can also be reduced by packing product so that it is immobilized. More than three quarters of the product that leaves California is shipped in mixed loads. These loads must be set up so that they are compatible. The chart divides common fruits and vegetables into four categories (Table 25.2). Produce in the same vertical section can be safely held at the same temperature range listed, on the top of the section. If produce in different temperature section are mixed, produce quality will be compromised, especially with longer transit times. The greater the difference in recommended temperature between the produce, the greater is the potential for quality loss. Dried vegetables in the top area should not be mixed with any produce below them on the chart. These vegetables should be held in a 50–70 % RH environment to prevent decay development. Most of the vegetables stored at 0–2°C (32–36°F) are sensitive to moisture loss and should be held at more than 90% RH or packaged to minimize water loss. All the rest of the vegetables and fruits should be held at 85–95% RH. Ethylene-sensitive vegetables near the top of the chart should not be mixed with the ethyleneproducing fruits at the bottom of the chart (e.g., luffa and ripe tomatoes). If for some reason they must be mixed, ethylene scrubbers may reduce damage. Produce items in the shaded middle of the chart are neither sensitive to ethylene nor are they ethylene producers and can be mixed with the items above or below them in the same temperature section. Some produce items can exchange odors with other selected produces. Local refrigerated transport from distribution centers to stores or restaurants is nearly always a mixed load. Products may have widely differing temperature requirements and susceptibility to ethylene and odors. Most products survive because the trip is short, allowing products to be in a compromised environment for only a few hours. If frozen product is also part of the load, 460 Chapter 25 then the vehicles often have several compartments. Each compartment is set at a different temperature and each has a separate outside door allowing products to be carried at more ideal temperatures. 25.6 Control Systems in Transport Vehicles Thermostat temperature is set based on a compromise between the relative obvious damage caused by freezing temperatures and the less obvious damage caused by higher than recommended temperature. For products that are not sensitive to chilling, thermostats are usually set below 4.4°C (40°F) but above 1.7°C (35°F). Newer refrigeration units with supply-air temperature sensing can be set lower than this because the control system is designed to ensure that the cold temperature in the load, at the air chute, does not drop below the thermostat set point. Good loading practices and well-cooled product in a supply-air-controlled refrigeration system allow thermostats to be set below 1.7°C (35°F). This is especially true for products with high sugar content that freeze at temperatures significantly below 0°C (32°F) and for products that can withstand several episodes of light freezing conditions. Many newer refrigeration units offer microprocessor-based controllers that automatically monitor refrigeration system operation and alert the driver to malfunctions. These systems can also transmit the information to satellites that forward the information to a company operations center. The company can then monitor vehicle location and system performance and maintain close supervision of all loads en route. This compatibility should allow companies to set thermostat set points closer to optimal conditions with less concern for load freezing. Refrigeration trailers are used to carry a wide variety of products. The return trip to the production area may be a load of furniture, carpet, chemicals, or even pesticides. The truck owner and the company that contracts for transport of perishable foods need to ensure that residues from pervious loads cannot contaminate food products with materials that are not registered food grade materials. The guidelines for best use of refrigerated trailers are at the beginning of Section 25.4. 25.7 Dry Ice Refrigeration Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. Dry ice may be pressed into various sizes and shapes, as blocks or slabs. It changes directly from solid to vapor and does not go into liquid state. At atmospheric pressure, its sublimation temperature is –78°C. Dry ice is usually packed in frozen food cartons either beside or on top of the food packages. Carbon dioxide, as it changes to a vapor, keeps the food frozen. A common method of using dry ice as a frozen food refrigerating device is shown in Figure 25.16 (Arora and Dumkundwar, 2004). Nowadays application of dry ice for freezing food is commonly used in aircraft transportation. Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 461 Figure 25.16: Dry Ice Refrigeration. The refrigeration effect produced by the sublimation of dry ice, which takes place at a temperature of –78°C, is 605.5 kJ/kg. In the use of dry ice, care must be taken to avoid burns due to low temperature and suffocation due to lack of oxygen. 25.8 Liquid Nitrogen or Liquid Carbon Dioxide Spray In the recent times, due to the expansion of the industry for the manufacture of oxygen, by liquefaction of atmospheric air, liquid nitrogen has become available almost as a by-product. It has, therefore, come into use for the transport of frozen foods. It may, however, be noted that liquid nitrogen has a normal boiling point of –195.6°C. This is an extremely low temperature from the point of view of the coefficient of performance (COP) and refrigeration economy. Liquid nitrogen is, therefore, not recommended if it is not available as a by-product. In both liquid nitrogen and liquid carbon dioxide cooling, the refrigerant is introduced into the vehicle through nozzles, the flow being controlled by thermostats and solenoid valves (see Figure 25.17). The storage vessels for the refrigerants are kept within the refrigerated space. Whereas a liquid nitrogen vessel need not be under pressure, a liquid carbon dioxide vessel has to be under a pressure of about 5.2 bar because at atmospheric pressure it cannot exist as a liquid. Spray nozzles for liquid carbon dioxide should, therefore, be designed to avoid blockage due to snow formation during pressure drop. 25.8.1 Refrigeration Using Liquid Gases The use of liquid nitrogen and liquid carbon dioxide for cooling transportation vehicles is rapidly increasing. The basic system using a nontoxic low-temperature liquid refrigerant as a cooling medium is same as any vapor system without using a condensing unit. The cost of the liquid is rather low in that it can be used as a refrigerant and then released to the atmosphere. Expandable refrigerant systems are also used in the cooling of railroad cars transporting perishable items. 462 Chapter 25 Figure 25.17: Liquid Nitrogen Cooling. 25.8.1.1 Cold-Plate Cooling Systems In this system, the liquid refrigerant is pumped into an insulated container in the front of the cargo vehicle. Each unit has a temperature control that allows for setting of –30–20°C. The temperature control is connected to a temperature sensor. As temperature rises, the switch operating the control valve is opened and liquid refrigerant flows into the cold plates. As the liquid refrigerant passes through the plates, it vaporizes. The vapor is forced through the plates by the difference in pressure. When the desired temperature is reached, the refrigerant valve is closed. The used vapor leaves the cargo space at approximately the same temperature as vapor mixed with the air in the truck body. This type of cooling system is shown in Figure 25.18. The expandable refrigerant passes between the inside wall and the insulation. Figure 25.18: Liquid Nitrogen Plate Cooling System. Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 463 Temperatures of –30–20°C are possible without any of the refrigerant entering the storage part of the truck space being refrigerated. 25.9 Mechanical Refrigeration with Independent Engine or Electric Motor The mechanical refrigeration system mounted on a vehicle has an independent engine. Some are also equipped with an electric motor for stand-by operation at the charging station. These units, by far the most common method used, are available in two ranges: 1. 5.86–10.3 kW capacity at 1.5°C 2. 1.76–5.28 kW capacity at –18°C in a 40°C environment 25.9.1 Mechanical Refrigeration Deriving Power from Vehicle Engine or Transmission There are many practical designs available. The refrigeration compressor may be either directly coupled to the engine or may take power through the transmission. In one design, the engine runs an alternator. The AC current is rectified and is used to run DC motors for compressor and fans. The refrigeration is, however, produced only when the vehicle engine is in operation. 25.9.2 Eutectic Plates with Station Charging Eutectic plates forming channels are placed all around the body of the vehicle. They contain an eutectic solution that can be frozen by a refrigerant flowing in a coil immersed in the solution. The coil is connected to a mechanical refrigeration system at the charging station. Cooling is produced by the evaporation of the primary refrigerant in the coil. When the solution is frozen, the truck loaded with the product for delivery is ready for departure. Eutectic plates are made in many sizes varying from 45 cm to 90 cm in width. A typical plate of 76 cm × 168 cm × 6.65 cm has a refrigerating capacity of 17,935 kJ. Standard plates operate at temperature of –51°C to –3.5°C. 25.9.3 Eutectic Plates with Vehicle-Mounted Condensing Unit This system is becoming increasingly popular because of economy as well as reliability for the transport of frozen foods. Eutectic plates are used for maintaining the product at the required temperature. However, when the frozen eutectic has melted, the vehiclemounted condensing unit can be started. Further, the condensing unit has an auxiliary drive mounted on the vehicle when it is in use and an electric motor drive for use at the charging station. 464 Chapter 25 25.10 Marine Refrigeration A special feature of marine transport is the varying climate, ranging from extreme hot to extreme cold, through which the ship has to pass during the course of its journey. The insula­ tion and fittings should be suitable both for warm and cold water routes. Thus, a vapor barrier for moisture should be provided on both sides of the insulation. Corkboard continues to be favored as an insulation because of its many desirable characteristics, such as structural strength, fire-resistant property, and low permeability for moisture. Marine transportation generally uses marine container and refrigerated ships to transport perishables over the ocean. Travel times are often 1–4 weeks. However, their cost is much lower than air flight. 25.10.1 Difference Between Marine Container and Refrigerated Ships The important difference between marine container and refrigerated ships is the cargo-carrying capacity. A container carries about 1000–1500 packages and a refrigerated ship has a capacity of about 350,000 packages. Their large insulated cargo volume and built-in refrigeration allow refrigerated ships to charge less than container systems. However, containers can be transported directly to a refrigerated loading dock at the packing operation, maintaining a container cold chain. Refrigerated ships are loaded normal, open warehouses and allow product to be exposed to outside ambient weather. This factor is especially a problem in ships that use a common refrigeration system for two compartment levels because the refrigeration system is not operated until both compartments are loaded. Bananas, table grapes, apples, and citrus fruits are commonly transported in refrigerated ships. The key differences between refrigerated marine transport systems and refrigerated highway vehicles include the following: 1. Refrigerated ships have bottom delivery airflow system. 2. They can cool slowly the product during transport. 3. They are more gas tight and are allowed to be used for controlled atmosphere conditions in the storage space. Usual outside dimensions of the refrigerated marine container are 12.2 m (40 ft) length, 2.4 m (8 ft) width, and 2.6–2.9 m (8.59.5 ft) height. Interior range is 56.6–65.1 m3 (2000–2300 ft3). Refrigeration capacity range is 8.4–10.2 kW (2.4–2.9 tons) 25.10.2 New Refrigeration Ships Newer ships have a volume of 10,000–15,000 m3 and some large as 22,000 m3. The storage volume is divided into four separate holds, each with two to five cargo compartments. The compartments have standard height of 2.2 m (7.3 ft). Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 465 Ships usually have their own cranes for loading. Automatic temperature control systems can maintain supply-air temperature within ±0.1°C (about 0.2°F) of the set point temperature. In steady-state operating condition, load space temperature variation is less than 2°C (about 4°F). Controlled atmosphere (CA) transport is commercially available with generation units specially built with onboard atmosphere modification system. 25.11 Bottom Air Delivery System The best use of a bottom air delivery system requires loading so that the refrigerated air is forced through and around the packages and not allowed to bypass pallet units (see Figure 25.19) (Saraswathy et al., 2012). Bottom air delivery systems can accomplish slow product cooling. Citrus from California is usually cooled in marine transport. Seven-eighth cooling is achieved in about 100 h. Products that depend on transport cooling should be packed in boxes that have at least 3% venting on top and bottom panels and the venting should align even if boxes are cross-stacked. Interior packaging and pallet deck boards should not block airflow through panel vents. The floor should be completely covered with product to force the refrigerated air around the packages and through the packages. If the product is palletized, open pallet edges should also be covered to block air from travelling horizontally through the pallet openings and escaping into an open vertical channel between pallet loads. Marine containers should not be center loaded as is recommended for highway trailers. Many have corrugated walls that guarantee airflow between the walls and product. Figure 25.19: Bottom Air Delivery Airflow System. 466 Chapter 25 If the floor and pallet openings are not completely covered, refrigerated air will bypass some of the load. Product with poor airflow around it will tend to arrive too warm, especially if it had not been thoroughly cooled prior to transport. Open floor in the front of the container allows the air to flow through it and the product near the center of the container will tend to be warmer because little refrigerated air reaches it. 25.11.1 Refrigeration Equipment Refrigeration is used in ships for cargo and stores of passenger ships. It is also used in trawlers for fishing. In the case of cargo, the refrigeration system should be capable of providing any temperature between –23.5°C and 12.5°C. R 12 with reciprocating compressor is presently used as a refrigerant. R 22 is not recommended because of its problem of critical oil miscibility. Compound compression is employed. Parallel operation is not recommended with R 12 because of a tendency for oil to migrate and flood one compressor while starving another. Accordingly, each evaporator has an independent compressor. This involves the use of a large number of compressors. The system can be made more economical by the use of parallel brine circuits in cooler coils and fewer condensing units. Capacity control is obtained by speed variation or cylinder cutouts and cylinder unloading. Condensers are of the shell and tube type using seawater for cooling. Corrosion-resistant cupronickel material is, therefore, used for tubes and end covers. A receiver capable of holding 20% more in addition to the whole charge is essential. The liquid line should emerge from both ends of the condenser, later joining into one to ensure continuous draining of the liquid during roll or pitch of the ship. 25.11.2 Refrigeration Maintenance and Control in Ships Refrigeration container ships usually have built-in temperature monitoring and automatic control systems. Monitors are generally installed on top or near pallets for convenience. Containers and refrigerated ships use controlled ventilation systems to prevent high CO2 or low O2 concentrations and to reduce C2H4 levels in the load volume. Container venting is usually set at a constant level at loading. Refrigerated ships often have instrumentation to measure gas concentrations and to vary ventilation as needed. Internationally marked fruits may need to be refrigerated to remove insect pests. Refrigerated ships can slowly warm the product to methyl bromide fumigation temperature just before arrival, speeding handling at the portside fumigation facility. Containers and refrigeration ships must also meet quarantine requirements by holding product at low temperature. For example, USDA regulations allow control of Mediterranean fruit fly with fruit pulp temperature of 1.2°C (34°F) for 12 days or 2.2°C (36°F) for 16 days. Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 467 25.12 Refrigerated Railway Cars Most refrigerated railway cars use ice bunkers with water ice or an ice-and-salt mixture. The recharging of ice is required at intermediate stations en route. Nowadays, the mechanical refrigeration system is being increasingly adopted. It is provided with an independent diesel-generator set so that refrigeration is independent of the car movement. The normal generator capacity is 20 kW. Rail cars used primarily for long-haul shipments within in the country. Transportation times range from 6 days to 10 days. They are mostly used to transport potatoes, citrus fruits, onions, carrots, and other less perishable commodities. Rail shipments are often a single commodity. The cars have a storage volume of more than 113 m3 (4,000 ft3) and can carry more than 45 metric tons (100,000 lb) of product. The cars have their own permanently installed engine-driven generator and electric motor– powered refrigeration system (Figure 25.20). The system incorporates a return-air temperature control system. Conditioned air is supplied to a plenum in the ceiling of the car. Air flows past the product and down wall flues and then returns underneath the load to the refrigeration unit. The units have adequate airflow and refrigeration capacity to produce slow cooling of the product if it is not packed too tightly. The cars are airtight when built and can be used for modified atmosphere transportation. Unintended atmosphere modification can occur if drain vents are clogged or water in them freezes in the winter. Loading guidelines and package specifications for rail cars are generally specified by the railroad company or railroad organizations and can be checked with the transportation supplier for details. Tight loads can restrict airflow and prevent air from travelling past the product and may cause the thermostat sensor to detect warm air conditions and supply cold air to the top of the load, causing some frozen product on the top of the load and warm product beneath. If crushed ice is applied uniformly to the top surface of the load, it blocks airflow and can Figure 25.20: Refrigerated Rail Car. 468 Chapter 25 prevent warm product below from being exposed to cooling conditions. If ice is used it should be applied to allow an open center area along the length of the car to permit airflow. Several North American railroad companies offer trainload service for highway trailers that are designed to be fitted with railroad wheels. The trailers look much like conventional highway trailers, but are strengthened (adding about 500 kg [1100 lb] to the vehicle tare weight) and can have special railroad wheels and couplers attached to them. They use regular over-the-road refrigeration equipment and often have air ride suspension. The vehicles can be placed on rails without cranes or lifts needed for trailer-on-flat car or container operations. 25.13 Air Transportation Air shipment is expensive and provides poor temperature control compared with refrigerated land and sea transport methods, but it often provides shorter transit times than competing methods. It is used mainly to transport highly perishable and valuable commodities to distant domestic and export marketers. It is often used for early-season cherries, cut flowers, strawberries, and some tropical fruits. Products are transported in small aluminum containers that are shaped to fit inside the freight area of passenger planes or on net-covered pallets for transport in freight planes (Figure 25.21). To prevent shifting of the load in a cargo container for air transport, a piece of solid foam or folded fiberboard should be placed along the curved or triangular portion of the floor of the container. Cartons stacked on top will be much better supported and be held upright. Water evaporates more rapidly in lower atmospheric pressures than in higher pressure. For every 10% decrease in pressure, water loss will increase by 10%. Thus, the rate of water loss in an air plane will be about 20% more than at sea level due to difference in pressure alone. The lower pressure coupled with lower RH and relatively higher temperature can result in a significant amount of water being lost from produce during air transit. Therefore, during air transportation of fresh fruits and vegetables, appropriate pressurization should be maintained, especially over 1500 m altitude. Figure 25.21: Transport in Freight Planes. Transportation of Fruits, Vegetables, and Flowers 469 Most air transport containers are not refrigerated and provided minimal air circulation. Air temperature in cargo areas of planes is often set to provide safe conditions for live animals and is too warm for most perishables. At high altitudes, air humidity in planes is extremely low, sometimes less than 10% and can cause product dehydration if it is not packaged correctly or placed in a fairly airtight box. A few containers are available with CO2 refrigerant. A battery-powered thermostatically controlled fan moves air from the container past the refrigerant as needed to control temperature. Improved temperature conditions can be obtained by wrapping the product to prevent warm air from flowing past the boxes. The wraps are sometimes made of reflective materials to reduce radiant heat input when product is held on open docks or runways. Wraps should be removed if product warms to near room temperature because wraps may hold in respiration heat and cause product to heat above room temperature. Product is sometimes packed with enclosed ice, dry ice, or eutectic compounds to provide some refrigeration effect during transport. Use of dry ice must be reported to the airline because of the danger CO2 may pose to animals or passengers. Water ice must be well enclosed to prevent water leakage and may require enough absorbent material in the box to contain an accidental leak. Atmospheric pressure drops in flight to about 60% of sea level air pressure. Bagged product should be vented to allow for pressure equalization. Bags for modified atmosphere packaging should be strong enough to withstand the low atmospheric pressure in air transport. Travel time in the air is often in the range of 8–16 h, but staging at departure and destination airports can add significantly to the total transport time. Staging areas of airlines are usually not refrigerated and product can warm quickly, especially in hot, humid tropical climates or it can freeze in winter conditions. Freight forwarding companies are often hired to arrange transport, handle the product at airports, and ensure best possible temperature conditions. Problems 1. CHAPTE R 26 Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 26.1 Process Control The advantages of process control have been universally recognized. Automatic process control is used primarily because it results in economy of operation of cold storage by controlling temperature and relative humidity as per the changes in the atmosphere around the produce. Elimination of human error is another positive contribution of automatic process control. In this chapter, the principles of the instruments used in control of operational parameters of cold storages are given. 26.2 Automatic Control Figure 26.1 shows the schematic of an automatic control loop diagram. The automatic controller determines the value of the controlled variable, compares the actual value to the desired value, determines the deviation, and produces the counteraction necessary to maintain the smallest possible deviation between the desired value and actual value. The method by which the automatic controller produces the counteraction is called the mode of control, or control action. 26.2.1 Basic Hardware Components The basic hardware components of a control loop are the following: 1. Process: The material equipments such as tanks, compressors, evaporators, and condenser, along with the physical or chemical or flow operations that take place in them constitute the process. 2. Measuring system: It constitutes the sensors, including thermocouples, bellows, diaphragms, and orifice devices, along with the activating linkages and levers. 3. Controller: This unit decides how much to change the manipulated variable in order to achieve the desired value (set point). 4. Final control element: This device receives the control signal from the controller and implements it by physically adjusting the value of the manipulated variable. 5. Transmission lines: These lines carry the measurement signal from the sensor to the controller and the control signal from the controller to the final control element. The lines can be either electrical, pneumatic, or hydraulic. Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00026-9 471 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 472 Chapter 26 Figure 26.1: Schematic Diagram of an Automatic Control Loop. Each of these elements should be viewed as part of a physical system with an input and an output. Consequently their behavior can be described by a differential equation or equivalently by a transfer function. 26.2.2 Steps in Control Action 1. Measuring the value of the output (flow, pressure, temperature, liquid level, composition, etc.). Let Cm (or b) be the value indicated by the measuring sensor. 2. Comparison of the indicated value (actual value) to the desired value (CSP) (set point or reference) of the output. Let the deviation be ∈ or e (error), which is (CSP – CM). 3. The value of the deviation or error is supplied to the main controller. The controller in turn changes the value of the manipulated variable in such a way as to reduce the magnitude of the deviation (error) through the final control element (usually a control valve with an actuator). 26.3 Sensing Elements Sensing elements are the devices that have the measuring capability and positioner built into them. The common types of sensing elements are: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. Thermostats Thermocouples and thermesters Bulb and bellow elements Temperature-sensitive electric resistances Electromagnetic devices Humidity-sensitive devices One such elements is a bimetallic transducer, which consists of two strips of dissimilar materials with different coefficients of thermal expansion, joined together and fixed at one end (see Figure 26.2). Any change in temperature results in nonuniform expansion of the two strips and consequently they bend as shown in the figure. The magnitude of the element’s movement depends on Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 473 Figure 26.2: A Bimetallic Transducer. the length of the strips. Therefore, the greater the length, the more sensitive is the device. Two well-known materials used as pair and their coefficient of expansion are as follows: Brass: 17.5 × 10–6 per °C Invar: (36% Ni + Steel) 0.9 × 10–6 per °C Aluminum: 2.5 × 10–5 °C Their property of bending is generally used to close switch contacts or actuate an ON/OFF mechanism when the temperature increases to some appropriate set point. The effect is also used for temperature indicators by means of assemblages, to convert the curvature into dial rotation. Example 26.1 How much will an aluminum rod of 10 m length at 20°C expand when the temperature is changed from 0°C to 100°C? The coefficient of thermal expansion of aluminum 2.5 × 10–5 per °C. Solution First find the length at 0°C and at 100°C, then find the difference by using the equation. l = l0 [1+ r γ T ] (26.1) where ∆T = T0 – T, and g is the coefficient of linear expansion and its value for aluminum is 2.5 × 10–3 per °C. l1 = (10 m) [1 + (2.5 × 10–5/°C) (0°C – 20°C)] = 9.995 m l2 = (10 m) [1 + (2.5 × 10–5) (100 – 20)] = 10.02 m Thus, the expansion is l2 – l1 = 10.020 – 9.995 = 0.025 = 25 mm. Therefore, the magnitude of movement of the element depends on the length of the strip. Hence, a greater length is required for increased sensitivity. 474 Chapter 26 26.3.1 Electric Resistance Element The electric resistance of the elements changes with temperature. The detecting element forms part of the Wheatstone bridge. The simplest and most common bridge circuit is shown in Figure 26.3. This network is used in signal-conditioning applications where a transducer changes resistance with dynamic variable changes. Many modifications of this basic bridge are also employed for other specific applications. In Figure 26.3 the object labeled D is a null detector used to compare the potentials of Points a and b of the network. In most modern applications, the null detector is a high input impedance differential amplifier. In some cases, a highly sensitive galvanometer with a relatively low impedance may be used, especially for calibration or single-measurement instruments. For initial analysis, assume the null detector impedance is infinite, that is, an open circuit. In this case, the potential difference ∆V between Points a and b is simply. ∆V = Va − Vb (26.2) where Va = potential of Point a with respect to ground Vb = potential of Point b with respect to ground The values of Va and Vb can now be found by noting that Va is just the supply voltage, V, divided between R1 and R3. Va = VR3 R1 + R3 Figure 26.3: Wheatstone Bridge for Electric Resistance Elements. (26.3) Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 475 In a similar fashion Vb is a divided voltage given by Vb = VR4 R2 + R4 (26.4) where V = bridge supply voltage R1, R2, R3, R4 = bridge resistors as given in Figure 26.3 If we now combine Equations (26.2), (26.3), and (26.4), the voltage difference or voltage offset can be written ∆V = VR3 VR4 – R1 + R3 R2 + R4 (26.5) After some algebra, the reader can show that this equation reduces to ∆V = V R3 R2 – R1 R4 R + ( 1 R3 ) ⋅ ( R2 + R4 ) (26.6) Equation (26.6) shows how the difference in potential across the detector is a function of the supply voltage and the values of the resistors. Because a difference appears in the numerator of Equation (26.6) it is clear that a particular combination of resistors can be found that will result in zero difference and zero voltage across the detector, that is, a null. Obviously, this combination, from examination of Equation (26.6) is R3 R2 = R1 R4 (26.7) Equation (26.7) indicates that whenever a Wheatstone bridge is assembled and resistors are adjusted for a detector null, the resistor values must satisfy the indicated equality. It does not matter if the supply voltage drifts or changes, the null is maintained. Equations (26.6) and (26.7) underline the application of Wheatstone bridge to process-control applications using high input impedance detectors. Example 26.2 If a Wheatstone bridge as shown in Figure 26.3 nulls with R1 = 1000 Ω, R2 = 842 Ω, and R3 = 500 Ω, find the value R4. Solution R1 R4 = R3 R2 RR ( 500 Ω )( 842 Ω ) = 421 Ω R4 = 3 2 = R1 1000 Ω 476 Chapter 26 Figure 26.4: Bulb and Bellow Element. 26.3.2 Bulb and Bellow Element The bellow and bulb in Figure 26.4 can be either liquid-charged or gas-charged. In the liquidcharged type, the vapor pressure in the element will increase with increasing temperature of the bulb. It may be noted that the vapors tend to condense on the coldest part. Thus, if the bellows are cooler than the bulb, the liquid will accumulate in the bellows and no liquid may remain in the bulb, which will effectively become gas-charged and therefore insensitive to temperature charge. Hence, it is required that the element should have sufficient charge so as to leave some liquid in the bulb even if the bellows and capillary tube are completely filled with the liquid. As stated already, the gas-charged types are the ones with a small liquid charge at low temperature of operation, so that, at higher temperature, the element is completely filled with gas, and the pressure variation is along the constant–volume line. Such elements are used for low-temperature operation. Single bellows are used in low pressure cutouts provided in all condensing units. By regulating the tension of the spring it is possible to select the vapor pressure and hence temperature at which the assembly will activate the switch or valve. 26.3.3 Electromagnetic Elements The magnetic field in a solenoid can be influenced by an iron armature in a coil. By moving the armature up or down as actuated by a sensing element, a change in current will occur, and Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 477 Figure 26.5: Solenoid. by means of an amplifier, this change can be made strong enough to actuate a control device (e.g., liquid level regulating devices). On the other hand, solenoid valves are used as twoposition controls in the liquid lines of refrigerant circuits. A typical construction of a solenoid operating a valve is shown in Figure 26.5. The solenoid falls down by its own weight when not energized. When it is energized, it is lifted up. 26.4 Pneumatic Actuators Pneumatic actuators often translate a control signal into a large force or torque as required to manipulate some type of control element. The pneumatic actuator is most useful for such translation. The principle is based on the pressure per unit area. If a net pressure is applied to a diaphragm of surface area A, then a net force acting on the diaphragm is given by F = ( P1 − P2 ) A (26.8) where P1 – P2 is pressure difference, Pa A = diaphragm area, m2 F = force, N Out of many types of pneumatic actuators available, the most common are those associated with control valves. The action of a direct pneumatic actuator is shown in Figure 26.6. Part (a) shows the condition of the low-signal pressure state where the springs maintain the diaphragm and the connected control shaft in position as shown. Figure 26.6 (b) shows the 478 Chapter 26 Figure 26.6: (a) Direct Actuator in the Low-Pressure State. (b) Direct Actuator in the High-Pressure State. case of a maximum control pressure and maximum travel of the shaft. The pressure and force are linearly related as shown in Equation (26.8), and the compression of a spring is linearly related to the forces acting on it. Then, we see that the shaft position is linearly related to the applied control pressure. A direct pneumatic for converting pressure signals into mechanical shaft motion is linearly related to the applied control pressure. ∆x = A ∆P K (26.9) where ∆x = shaft travel, m ∆P = applied gauge pressure, Pa A = diaphragm area, m2 K = spring constant, N/m Figure 26.7 shows one such real direct actuator along with the control valve. The pressure on the opposite side of the diaphragm is maintained at atmosphere pressure by the open hole H. Increasing the control pressure (gauge pressure) applies a force on the diaphragm forcing the diaphragm and the connected shaft down against the spring force. Figure 26.6(b) shows this in case of maximum control pressure and maximum travel of the shaft. Here the pressure and force are linearly related, and the compression of the spring is linearly related to the force. Therefore, the shaft position is linearly related to the applied pressure. Find the diaphragm area if control gauge pressure of 70 kPa must provide the pressure. Solution The area is calculated from F = A(P1 − P2 ) 400N F A= = = 5.71× 10–3 m2 P1 − P2 70 × 103Pa or about 8.5 cm in diameter. 26.4.1 Hydraulic Actuators Normally electrical actuators are used in nonhazardous areas and when the force or torque required to operate the control valve is moderate. Pneumatic actuators are preferred in hazardous areas, such as chemical process industries, and more force/torque is required. Yet there are many cases when large forces and high speeds are required. In such cases, a hydraulic 480 Chapter 26 Figure 26.8: A Hydraulic Actuator Converts a Small Force F1 into an Amplified Force Fw. actuator may be employed. The basic principle is shown in Figure 26.8. The basic idea is the same as for pneumatic actuators except that an incompressible fluid is used to provide the pressure, which can be made quite large by adjustment of the area of the forcing piston A1. The hydraulic pressure is given by, PH = F1 / A1 (26.10) where PH = hydraulic pressure, Pa F1 = applied piston force, N A1 = forcing piston area, m2 The resulting force on the working piston is Fw = PH A2 (26.11) where Fw = force of working piston, N A2 = working piston area, m2 Thus, the working force is given in terms of the applied force by Fw = F1 A2 A1 Example 26.4 Find the working force resulting from 200 N applied to a 1 cm radius forcing piston. The hydraulic pressure is PH = Fw 7200 N 5 = 2 = 6.4 × 10 Pa A2 π (6 × 10–2 m) 26.5 Pressure and Flow Transducers The measurement and control of fluid pressure and flow are critical elements in many industrial operations. For this reason, a vast variety of transducers has been developed based upon many physical principles. In this section, we enumerate several of the most common types and their principles. Note: 1 N/m2 = 1 Pa; 101.4 kPa = 1 atm = 1.0333 kg/cm2 are all units of pressure, that is force/area. Most pressure transducers used in process control require the pressure transduction of pressure information into a physical displacement. Measurement of a pressure transducer requires techniques for producing the displacement and the means for converting such displacement into a proportional electrical signal. This is not true, however, in the extremely low-pressure region (p < 10–3 atm) where many purely electronic means of pressure measurement may be used. A special and common pressure to displacement conversion is accomplished by a specially constructed bourdon tube, shown in Figure 26.9. If a section of tubing is partially flattened and coiled as shown, then the application of pressure inside the tube causes the tube to uncoil. This then provides a displacement proportional to pressure. 26.5.1 Flow Transducers In any manufacturing process involving fluids, the rate of fluid flow in the process is typically important. Many techniques have been developed for this measurement depending on 482 Chapter 26 Figure 26.9: The Bourdon Tube is a Common Device for Converting a Pressure to a Displacement. the nature of the fluids, flow rates, and other factors. Flow is indicated either as a direct fluid velocity (in m/s), a volume flow rate (in m3/s), or a mass flow rate (in kg/s). 26.5.1.1 Differential Pressure Methods The differential pressure method of flow measurement depends on the principle that a constriction in a pipe with flowing fluid causes a drop in pressure, which is dependent on the flow rate. In Figure 26.10, this effect is shown for a common type of constriction known as a venturi. Measurement of flow is then performed by employing a differential pressure measurement system between the two pressure ports. A diaphragm pressure measurement system is commonly used. Flow is often measured by a proportional pressure difference produced by introducing a constriction in the flow. A differential pressure (D/P) cell is often used to measure the pressure difference. Figure 26.10: Venturi Principle. Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 483 26.5.1.2 Mechanical Methods Mechanical methods of flow measurement generally involve placing an obstruction in the path of the flowing fluid and measuring the mechanical force the fluid exerts on the obstruction; the specific obstruction may be a float, a moving vane, or a turbine propeller. The measurement may be made, for example, by linkages to a potentiometer, strain gauges on the element, or tachometers. Measurement resulting from obstructions has low sensitivity in that they disturb the original condition that existed prior to their placement. They tend to reduce the flow rate, sometimes severely, particularly when the volume or mass flow rate is small. 26.5.1.3 Electronic Methods If the fluid has finite and relatively good electrical conductivity, it is possible to measure the flow rate by a direct electronic means. This is done by measuring the potential developed across the fluid as it flows through a magnetic field. The section of pipe that contains this measurement system must be a nonconductor, thus Teflon or glass lining is often employed. 26.5.1.4 Control Valve Principles Flow rate in process control is usually expressed as volume per unit time. If a mass flow rate is desired, it can be calculated from the particular fluid density. If a given fluid is delivered through a pipe, then the volume flow rate is Q = AV (26.13) where Q = flow rate, m3/s A = pipe area, m2 V = flow velocity, m/s Example 26.5 Alcohol is pumped through a pipe of 10 cm diameter at 2 m/s flow velocity. Find the volume flow rate. Solution A pipe of 10 cm diameter has a cross-sectional area of π D2 π (10 m) A= = 4 4 A = 7.85 × 10−3 m2 –1 Thus, the flow rate is Q = AV = (7.85 × 10–3 m2)(2 m/s) Q = 0.0157 m3/s 2 484 Chapter 26 Figure 26.11: Flow Rate Through a Restriction in a Line is a Function of the Pressure Drop Across the Restriction. A control valve regulates the flow rate in a fluid delivery system. In general, a close relationship exists between the pressure along a pipe and the flow rate such that if the pressure is changed, then the flow rate is also changed. A control valve changes flow rate by changing the pressure in a flow system because it introduces a constriction in the delivery system. In Figure 26.11, we see that the placement of a constriction in a pipe introduces a pressure difference across the pipe. We can show that the flow rate through the constriction is given by Q = K ∆P (26.14) where K = proportionality constant, m3/s/Pa ∆P = P2 – P1 = pressure difference, Pa Example 26.6 A pressure difference of 11 psi occurs across a constriction in a 5 cm diameter pipe. The construction constant is 0.229 m3/s per Pa.
