Figure 26.12 shows one such arrangement using bellow elements. Two thermistors can also be similarly used, coupled into a Wheatstone bridge. Such a device will operate on the basis of increase/decrease in the difference (DBT – WBT) of air for the control of humidity. In addition, hygroscopic elements, such as a strand of hair, can be used for humidity control. A simple arrangement is shown in Figure 26.13. Elongation of the hair due to an increase in Figure 26.12: Using Bellow Elements for Humidity Control. Figure 26.13: Hair as a Humidity-Sensitive Element. 486 Chapter 26 relative humidity results in a clockwise turning of the roller, moving lever to the left, which may operate a switch. Recently, the hygroscopic nature of some salts (e.g., CaCl2, LiCl2, etc.) has also been used in humidity measurement and control devices. It is found that their electric resistance changes with change in humidity. 26.7 Actuating Elements In response to impulses from detecting elements, the actuating elements bring about adjustment in plants. They may operate directly or indirectly. In the latter case, additional transmitting elements are used to transfer the actuating impulse to the regulating unit. The actuating elements can be categorized as follows: 1. 2. 3. 4. Electric switches Relays Solenoids Electric or pneumatic motors There are a variety of electric switches with considerable differences in their mechanical and electrical construction. A relay is a device that, by a weak pilot current from the detecting and measuring element assembly, actuates switches for heavy-duty circuits. An illustration of a single-phase relay is shown in Figure 26.14 in combination with a solenoid. In another construction, the spring is omitted and it becomes a simple solenoid. The solenoid, if in vertical position, falls by its own weight when not energized. When it is energized, it is lifted up. Such a relay is used as starting relay. Figure 26.14: A Single-Phase Relay. Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 487 26.8 Computer-Based Control Modern control system implementations are carried out using digital computers. The measurement, final control operations, the strategy for control, and the modes of controller action are still the same as what we have already seen under analog controllers. But the functions of the controller have been taken over by a computer. The computer inputs measurement data determine the error, solve the controller mode equations to determine the feedback, and transmit this feedback to the final control element. 26.8.1 Digital Computers Digital computers are playing a major role in process control applications in finance, banking, data storing, statistics, and so on. They became popular in industrial applications in the name of process computers. They are used for controlling individual equipment and the complete process of a store from a central place. Distributed digital control systems (DCS), programmable logic controllers (PLC), and data acquisition system (DAS) have come to stay in process industries. In addition, there are many direct applications of digital electronics in process lines. All these digital electronic systems require data to be presented to them in a digital format. In other words, the data are to be digitally conditioned before presenting to them. At the start of the computer era, analog computers mostly assembled with op amps were tried for process control, but as process computers are mostly digital electronic devices nowadays, all the information they work with has to be digitally formatted. For controlling temperature, the temperature signal has to be represented digitally. Hence, the need for digital signal conditioning—to condition process-control signals to be in an appropriate digital format. Digital signal conditioning in process control means finding a way to represent analog process information (as most of the transducers give analog output by nature) in a digital format. Though greater accuracy is not expected in using digital techniques to represent data, they do offer many advantages. Digital data are much more immune from spurious influences that would cause subsequent inaccuracy, such as noise, amplifier gain changes, power supply drifts, and so on. The use of digital computers in process control systems is more valuable because of the following reasons: 1. It is more useful to control various control loops from a centralized control room. Even here the functionwise distribution of control is possible. 2. Mathematical operation such as linearization, scale and bias changes, and unit conversions can be easily achieved. 3. Complicated control equations can be solved easily. Modeling of processes (static as well as dynamic) can be done, all with faster rates. 488 Chapter 26 4. A large industrial complex can be integrated by networking of computers. Even units at far-distance locations can be linked to the corporate computer to have access to some of the critical parameters by CEOs. 26.8.2 Computer-Based Controller The computer-based controller is the most important element in a modern process control system. Measurement data from the plant process, such as temperature, pressure, flow, level, concentration, and density, are inputs to the computer. The computer performs all the calculations for controller modes. The output from the computer is converted into a suitable signal to operate the final control elements in the field. Such an application is historically referred to as direct digital control (DDC). The DDC directly interfaces with the process for data acquisition and control purpose. It has the necessary hardware for directly interfacing (opto-isolator, signal conditioner, ADC, etc.) and reading the data from process. It should also have memory and arithmetic capability to execute required P, PI, and proportional, integral, and derivative (PID) control strategy. At the same time, the interface to control valve (final control element) should also be part of DDC. The functional blocks in combination with microprocessor are shown in Figure 26.15. The multiplexer acts like a switch under microprocessor control. It switches and presents at its output the analog signal from a sensor/transmitter. The analog-to-digital converts the analog signal to digital value. The microprocessor performs the following tasks: 1. It reads the various process variables from different transmitters through multiplexer and ADC. 2. It determines the error for each control loop and executes control strategy for each loop. 3. It outputs the correction value to control valve through DAC. The hardware configurations of this type of system are numerous. The controlling computer could be similar to a microprocessor-based personal computer (PC) mounted in a rack or Figure 26.15: Schematic of a Computer-Based Controller. Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 489 even on a desktop. It could be a microprocessor-based computer on a small printed circuit board mounted inside measurement equipment or even a large computer. In the following section we will explore the hardware and software configuration of a typical process-control computer. 26.8.3 Hardware Configurations A simplified microprocessor-based computer with a standard array of devices is shown in Figure 26.16. Because all the devices are available as small, integrated circuits, they can be mounted on a relatively small printed circuit board (PCB). The ROM (read-only memory), a nonvolatile memory, holds the programs that the processor executes. The RAM (random access memory or read-write memory) is used to hold the transient results of calculations and other results of data processing. The data I/O (input/output) typically consists of ADCs and DACs as well as digital I/O channels. A brief description of data converters only is given here, whereas for all other hardware configuration the reader is required to have sufficient background on digital fundamentals such as binary, octal and hexadecimal numbers, fractional binary numbers, Boolean algebra, digital logic circuits, PLCs, and computer interfaces. 26.8.4 Digital-to-Analog Converters (DACs) Digital-to-analog converters are used to convert digital signals to analog signals. The digital information may be in the form of a binary number with some fixed number of digits. The binary number is called a binary word, and the digits are called bits of the word. A unipolar DAC converts a digital word into an analog voltage by scaling the analog output to be zero when all bits are zero and some maximum value when all bits are one. This can be Figure 26.16: Basic Microprocessor-Based Computer. 490 Chapter 26 mathematically represented by treating the binary number that the word represents as a fractional number. The output of DAC can be defined as a scaling of some reference voltage as shown here. Vout = VR b1 2 –1 + b2 2 –2 + ⋅⋅⋅ + bn 2 – n  (26.15) where VR = reference voltage The minimum V out is zero, and the maximum is determined by the size of the binary word. Thus, a 4-bit word has a maximum of Vmax = VR  2 –1 + 2 –2 + 2 –3 + 2 –4  = 0.9375 VR and an 8-bit word has a maximum of Vmax = VR  2 –1 + 2 –2 + ⋅⋅⋅ + 2 –7 + 2 –8  = 0.9961VR 26.8.5 Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs) With the growing use of digital logic and computers in process control, it is necessary to employ an ADC to provide a digitally encoded signal for the computer. The I/O relation of ADC can be expressed in a similar way to that of the DAC as given in the equation. In this case, however, the interpretation is reversed. The ADC will find a fractional binary number that gives the closest approximation of the fraction formed by the input voltage and reference. b1 2 −1 + b2 2 −2 + b3 2 −3 + + bn 2 − n ≤ Vin VR (26.16) where b1, b2, . . . bn = n – bit digital output Vin = analog input voltage VR = analog reference voltage The inequality sign is used in Equation (26.16) because the fraction on the right can change continuously over all values, but the fraction derived from the binary number on the left can change only in fixed increments of ∆N = 2–n. In other words, the only way the left side can change is if the least significant bit (LSB) changes from 1 to 0 or from 0 to 1. In either case, the fraction changes only by 2–n and nothing in between. Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 491 Therefore, there is an inherent uncertainty in the input voltage producing a given ADC output, and that uncertainty is given by ∆V = VR 2 − n (26.17) 26.9 Controls in Refrigeration Equipment A few common controls are described here. 26.9.1 High- and Low-Pressure Cutouts Refrigerant compressors are provided with high-pressure (HP) and low-pressure (LP) cutouts. Their designs are similar. The high-pressure cutout is merely a safety control. When the head pressure increases beyond a set point, the HP cutout cycles off the compressor in order to ward off possible damage to the compressor. When the head pressure subsequently drops, the circuit is once again closed and the compressor starts. Some cutouts, however, require manual resetting. Because of the possibility of scale formation in condenser tubes, and more importantly, the failure of water supply, HP cutouts are essential in systems with water-cooled condensers. An LP cutout is used both as a safety control as well as temperature controls. Because the suction pressure is governed by the evaporator temperature, an LP cutout actuated by changes in suction pressure can be used to indirectly control the evaporator temperature. It is suitable as a temperature controller in remote installations in which the compressor is located quite some distance away from the evaporator. 26.9.2 Capacity Control of Reciprocating Compressors A commonly used method known as the pump-down cycle method involves the use of both a thermostat and an LP cutout as shown in Figure 26.17. In this cycle, the room thermostat, instead of starting and stopping the compressor, operates a solenoid valve installed in the Figure 26.17: Pump-Down Cycle. 492 Chapter 26 liquid line of the refrigerant. With a rise in the temperature of the room or chilled water, the thermostat closes the circuit, energizing the solenoid valve, which is lifted up, and allows the refrigerant to enter the evaporator. The flow of the refrigerant into the evaporator raises the suction pressure, closes the LP cutout, and starts the compressor. With a drop in the temperature of the controlled medium, the thermostat operates the solenoid valve and stops the flow of the liquid refrigerant to the evaporator. The compressor temperature continues to drop until the LP cutout opens and stops the compressor. There are many advantages of the pump-down cycle. It provides a dual control and eliminates hunting of the compressor. An important advantage is the elimination of crank case oil dilution by the absorption of the refrigerant, which results in inadequate lubrication, excessive carryover of the oil into the discharge line due to foaming at low pressure, and possible damage to the compressor due to the formation of slugs of refrigerant and oil. Large reciprocating compressors have a stepped-capacity control, achieved by the loading and unloading of compressor cylinders by the lifting of suction valves controlled by a thermostat or LP control. 26.9.3 Stepping Motor A stepping motor represents a marriage of digital techniques with electromechanical rotation. In particular, the stepping motor is a device that rotates through some specific angle for each digital pulse (or count) it receives. Thus, if a stepping motor requires 120 pulses for each full revolution (360°) of its shaft, then each pulse causes a shaft rotation of 3°. Also, if this device receives 1200 pulses per second, then the shaft is rotating at 10 revolutions per second (rev/s). The stepping motor must have associated digital circuitry both to drive the electromechanics of the device and interface with incoming signals. Many configurations are possible, including the use of an analog input to set the speed of rotation or even the particular location of the shaft in angle. Digital signals can be used to set speed or location in a more direct sense. Of major importance is that the stepping motor is a discrete device having a specific number of possible shaft positions. Specifications of stepping motors include the number of steps per revolution, the maximum pulse rate or rotational speed, torque versus pulse rate, and holding torque. A stepping motor develops maximum torque at minimum speed for starting large inertia loads. Maximum speed of 20,000 steps per second has been achieved for high-speed slewing operations. Examples of applications include computer peripheral equipment such as tape drives, readers, and so on, and industrial positioning applications, braking, and machine tooling requirements. 26.9.4 Electric Motors In many cases, an AC or DC electronic motor is employed in a process-control system as an actuator. Controlling crystal pulling rate by smooth variations of motor speed, feed rates of Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 493 conveyer systems, and an electric motor for hydraulic pump pressure are examples of controls using electric motors. In general, many types of motors are used, and the appropriate signal conversion is determined by the particular requirements of the motor specifications. Many applications use DC motors because of inherent high torque and ease of employment in process control with DC signals. Speed is easily altered by variation of the armature voltage. A two-phase AC motor is often used, which can provide variable speed operation through control of one field voltage, form an AC amplifier with a reference field permanently connected to an AC supply. 26.10 Controlling Room Conditions at Partial Load An air-conditioning plant is selected for design peak load conditions. But most of the time the plant operates under partial load, either due to change in the outside conditions or a withdrawal of load. The control of room conditions under part load is, therefore, important. For this purpose, one or more of the following methods may be employed: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. On/off control of the air-handling unit of refrigeration unit Controlled bypass of the air-entering apparatus Varying water flow in the chilled-water coil Reheating the supply air Controlling the volume of the supply air 26.10.1 On/Off Control In the on/off control of the air-handling unit or fan coil unit, the fan motor is operated intermittently by the room thermostat, the bulb of which is installed in the return air, and the refrigerant or chilled water continues to flow through the cooling coil. This results in fluctuating room temperature. In the on/off control of the refrigeration unit, the compressor operates intermittently. The air continues to flow over the cooling coil and in the room. This method also causes fluctuations in room conditions but ensures continuous air movement and is quite convenient in small air-conditioners. 26.10.2 Bypass Control Using Face and Bass Amps The bypass control maintains a constant DBT in the room by bypassing a part of the return air entering the cooling coil from the apparatus and thus increasing the supply air temperature. The schematic diagram of a bypass control with a typical direct expansion (DX) coil is shown in Figure 26.18. The method is employed on chilled water coils as well. Its psychrometrics are illustrated in Figure 26.19. Bypass of the air is purposely diverted around the cooling coil. By far, this is the most common method of control adopted by the industry. The method of bypassing the mixture rather than the room air is inferior because in this case the outside air is also bypassed and is introduced into the room, thus causing an increase in 494 Chapter 26 Figure 26.18: Face and Bypass Control. relative humidity of the room. Why the return air alone should be bypassed in preference to the mixture or outside air, is explained next. Refer to Figure 26.19 and let S at ADP of the coil represent the supply air state at full load, assuming the BPF of the coil is zero. Now consider a case when the room sensible heat (RSH) load decreases to 50%, and the room latent heat (RLH) load remains the same. This scenario may coincide with a reduction in the outside air DBT. Assume, therefore, that the outside air condition changes from 0 to 0’. At this reduced 50% RSH load, the condition of i–s = 0.5 . the supply air should be at s as shown in Figure 26.19, where i–S Figure 26.19: Psychrometrics of Bypass Control. Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 495 If we assume that the ADP of the coil is unaffected, a bypass of the mixture at I around the coil would result in a condition of the supply air slightly above s, or at s′ on the line joining 1 to S. Because the change in the condition of the supply air would occur along a new room sensible heat factor (RSHF) line, which is steeper due to the RLH load remaining the same, the condition of the room air achieved by this controlled bypass by a thermostat will be at i′. The space condition will thus be at a higher moisture content than state i. A bypass of the outside air at 0 around the coil would result in the supply air condition little more above s, and at a still higher humidity in the room. If the change in the outside air condition from 0 to 0′ is also considered, then the bypass of the mixture at 1′ would result in a supply air condition at s′′, and the room condition at a further higher humidity at i′′. Thus, when any outside air is bypassed, the effect is to raise the room humidity. Hence, the bypass should be normally that of recirculated room air and should be arranged as shown in Figure 26.20 in preference to the arrangement in Figure 26.18. Even if no outside air is bypassed, entering air state will be above I and the room humidity will again be higher. This leads to a lack of humidity control. However, the decrease in the flow of air over the cooling apparatus decreases the load on the cooling coil. As a result, the ADP drops from S to S1 and the air leaves at a lower temperature. The supply air state, therefore, is closer to s than s′ and s′′ and the changes in the room humidity are not to the extent as shown. Nevertheless, coil icing may result at higher bypass rates. This condition may be eliminated by using a pump-down cycle and installing a solenoid valve. A bypass control can be used in chilled water coils also. The method is conveniently employed in single zone as well as multizone units for the air-conditioning of large spaces. Figure 26.20: Arrangement with Bypass of Return Air Only. 496 Chapter 26 26.10.3 Varying Flow of Water in Chilled-Water (CW) Coil In this case, the room thermostat operates a three-way or straight-through valve, supplying chilled water to the cooling coil through a modulating motor or a two-position control. The valve throttles the water thereby varying the flow rate. The three-way valve mixes fresh chilled water with return chilled water, which varies the entering water temperature (EWT). The temperature of water does not remain constant in CW coil. It is essential in the case of a chilled-water coil, therefore, to have a counterflow arrangement between air and water as shown in Figure 26.21. Because the increase in water temperature will be greater than the design rise due to smaller flow rate, or the mixed water temperature will be higher at part load, the surface temperature of the coil and hence the ADP will normally increase. Thus, dehumidification of air will be reduced, and the supply air state will be above s′ or s′ in Fig. 26.19. Consequently, this method would maintain a higher humidity in the room than the method of controlled bypass of air. Nevertheless, the method is conveniently applied in the air-conditioning of a large number of rooms, each having its individual fan coil unit and chilled-water supply. If it is desired that the relative humidity does not alter, a return air humidistat can control the water flow rate, while the thermostat can control the bypass of air. Such a combination offers the possibility of maintaining both temperature and humidity, simultaneously, in the conditioned space. Figure 26.21: Control by Varying Chilled-Water Flow and/or Temperature. Instrumentation and Climate Management in Cold Storage 497 26.10.4 Reheat Control Any increase in the latent heat load decreases the sensible heat load of the room and can be handled by employing reheat of the supply air. Reheat thus provides an artificial load on the room and maintains a constant DBT, but there is no control of the room RH. The psychrometrics of reheat control is explained in Figure 26.22. The broken lines in the figure represent the processes at part load. The room thermostat senses the temperature of the room air. As soon as the temperature drops below the design value, the thermostat operates the reheat coil. The leaving air at 2 is reheated to s and then supplied to the room along the part-load RSHF lines s-i. This position of the points can be located on the intersection of the horizontal from 2 with the line of minimum RSHF drawn from i. If the plant is operating under part-load conditions, the LH load may also reduce along with the SH load. Then, the resulting room condition will be at 3 and the RSHF line will be s-3. As reheat adds to the requirement of refrigerating capacity, it wastes energy, and is, therefore, not commonly used in air-conditioning except for high latent-load application. 26.10.5 Volume Control The control of the quantity of the supply air to the room essentially provides the same type of control as obtained by bypassing the recirculated room air. A problem encountered with volume control is the nonuniform distribution of air within the conditioned space. It is, therefore, desirable to see that the supply air quantity at partial load is sufficient for satisfactory distribution. Figure 26.22: Psychrometrics of Reheat Control. 498 Chapter 26 Figure 26.23: Induction Unit. 26.10.6 Induction System In the constant-volume induction system, the central plant conditions only fresh air. The supply air is maintained at a constant temperature of about 1–2°C. Constant volume of this primary air is led to the room through an induction unit as shown in Figure 26.23. This mixture can be further treated in the coil installed in the unit. The all-air-constant-volume induction system is particularly suitable for space with a large ratio of the floor area to height, requiring horizontal ductwork and piping. The treated freshair duct in this case is designed as a high-pressure system. Problems 1. Page left intentionally blank PAR T I I I Controlled Atmosphere for Storage (CAS) Horticulture Produce 501 Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 27 Operation, Maintenance, and Energy Conservation in Cold Storages 27.1 Refrigerated Storage Plant Operation 27.1.1 Checking Temperatures and Humidity To maintain top product quality, temperature in cold storage room must be accurately maintained. Variations of 1–1.5 K in the product temperature above or below the desired temperature are too large in most cases. Storage rooms should be equipped either with accurate thermostats or with manual controls that receive frequent attention. In refrigerated storage rooms, thermometers are usually placed at a height of about 1.5 m for convenience in reading. Temperatures should be monitored where they might be undesirably high or low; one or two air temperatures are not enough. A record of both product and air temperatures is necessary to determine performance of the storage plant. A thermometer or recording device of good quality that is periodically calibrated is essential. Temperature in less-accessible storage locations, such as the middle of stacks, can be obtained conveniently with distant-reading thermometer equipment such as thermocouples or electrical-resistance thermometers. Storage instructions or recommendations usually specify a relative humidity (RH) within 3–5% of the desired levels. An ordinary sling psychrometer at temperatures of 0°C or lower cannot be read closely. An error of 0.3 K in reading either the wet bulb or dry bulb thermometer will cause an error of 5% RH. Carefully calibrated thermometers graduated to 0.05 K with a range of –5°C to +5°C are best adapted for this purpose in fruit storage. A convenient device for measuring humidity consists of a pair of these thermometers, mounted in a short length of metal casing attached to a spring or motor-operated fan that draws air past the thermometers at a speed of 0.9 m/s or faster. The thermometers should be placed so that they will not be heated by the fan motor, and they should be read quickly to prevent warming. The advantage of this instrument over the sling psychrometer is that it can be left in the room long enough to get a true wet bulb reading. This may require 15 min or more if ice is formed on the wet bulb. Under these conditions, a thin coating of ice is preferable to a thick one in getting accurate readings. Hair hygrometers are satisfactory if not subjected to sudden large changes in humidity and temperature and if checked regularly with a psychrometer. Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00027-0 503 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 504 Chapter 27 Perhaps a more accurate method of determining the relative humidity is to electrically record the dew point temperature (DPT) of the air and to use a resistance thermometer of suitable sensitivity to record the ambient or dry bulb temperature (DBT). From these temperature records, the relative humidity can be calculated. 27.1.2 Air Circulation Air must be circulated to keep refrigerated storage rooms at an even temperature throughout. Commodity temperatures in a storage room may vary because the air temperature rises as the air passes through the room and absorbs heat from the commodity; also, heat leakage may vary in different parts of storage. In a duct system, the air near the return ducts will be warmer than the air near delivery ducts. In many storage areas, refrigeration units are installed over the center aisle. Air circulates from the center of the rooms outward to the walls, down through the rows of produce, and back up through the center of the room. Rapid air circulation is needed most during removal of field heat. Sometimes this is best done in separate cooling rooms that have more refrigerating and air-moving capacity than regular refrigerated storage rooms. After field heat is removed, a high air velocity is usually undesirable. Air movement is needed only to remove respiratory heat and heat entering the room through exterior surfaces and doorways. Excessive air movement can increase moisture loss from a product, with a resulting loss of both mass and quality. However, some air, circulated by fans or blowers, must be uniformly distributed through all parts of the room. Also, if the air circulation or refrigeration is turned off, some precaution is needed to ensure that the stored product does not become too warm. The type of container and the manner of stacking are important factors that influence cooling performance. An elaborate system for air distribution is useless if poor stacking prevents airflow. If spacing is irregular, the wider spaces will get a greater volume of air than narrower ones. If some spaces are partially blocked, dead air zones will occur with resultant higher temperatures. 27.1.3 Sanitation and Air Purification The refrigerated storage and the product containers must be clean. Fruits and vegetables coming into storage are generally contaminated with mold spores, which can enter through punctures or breaks in the skin of the product. Commodities so contaminated can foster a rapid development of the spores, which are carried by air currents throughout the storage. Removing decaying raw material from the storage and sanitizing the product container will reduce the problem. If mold contamination is excessive, the storage develops a musty or moldy odor that is quickly picked up by the fruits and vegetables, a fault of many apple varieties and other products held for several months in refrigerated storage. This problem can best be controlled by means of special cleaners, sanitizers, and deodorizers. Operation, Maintenance, and Energy Conservation in Cold Storages 505 Table 27.1: Temperature and time requirements for killing moths in storage areas Storage Temperature (°C) All Eggs Dead After, Days All Larvae Dead After, Days All Adults Dead After, Days –18 to –15 –15 to –12 –12 to –9 –9 to –7 –7 to –4 –4 to –1 –1 to +2 1 2 4 – 21 21 – 2 21a – – 67 125b 283c 1 1 1 1 4 7 – 50–95% of larvae may be killed in 2 days. A few larvae survived this period. c Larvae survived this period. Source: Adapted from USDA Publication AMS- 57(1955). a b During several months of storages, even at –0.5°C, molds may grow on the surface of packages and on the walls and ceilings of rooms under high relative humidity conditions. These surface molds generally will not rot fruits and vegetables. However, because surface molds are unsightly, storage warehouses should have a thorough cleaning at least once a year. Good air circulation alone is of considerable value in minimizing growth of surface molds. If floors and walls become moldy, they can be scrubbed with a cleaner containing sodium hypochlorite solutions or by exposing to stream for 2 min. All inspected plants and warehouses operate under regulations with sanitation requirements clearly set forth in inspection service orders. Plants should be constructed to prevent the entrance of insects and rodents. This involves ratproof building construction and adequate screening. For doors frequently opened, special measures must be taken to prevent the entrance of insects. (See Table 27.1 for guidelines for moth control in storage areas.) The frequency of cleanup operations and the detergents and sanitizing agents used should be specified by the quality control leader. A representative from quality control should inspect all areas after cleanup and determine whether a suitable job has been done. Waste and miscellaneous trash accumulation areas must receive special attention around warehouses, because they become breeding places for rodents and insects. In any food warehouse, the successful quality control and sanitation program depends on the cooperation and vigilance of management. Air may be purified in storage rooms where odors or volatiles may contribute to off-flavors and hasten deterioration. Air may be cleaned with trays or canisters containing 6–14 mesh (2–4 mm spacing of mesh) activated coconut shell carbon. Pinewood volatiles are removed by activated carbon air-purifying units. Some produce volatiles are also removed, but ethylene, a ripening gas, is not removed by activated carbon alone. 506 Chapter 27 Air washing with water to remove volatiles does not delay fruit ripening. Air washing may increase the relative humidity and thus aid in maintaining good fruit appearance by reducing mass loss. 27.1.4 Removal of Produce from Storage When produce is removed from storage, undue warming and condensation of moisture, which promote decay and deterioration, must be prevented. Because most storages are built on railroad sidings, canvas tunnels should be installed between the car and the storage through which the produce will be conveyed to minimize warming and condensation of moisture. When produce is removed from storage for distribution to wholesale and retail markets, the storage operator can do little to prevent undesirable condensation. Warming the packages until they are above the dew point of the air would prevent it, but this takes time and space and is seldom practical. Deterioration in flavor and condition proceeds rapidly after long storage periods. Therefore, the produce should be moved to consumers as rapidly as possible. 27.2 Energy Conservation The total amount of energy consumption in air-conditioning is quite substantial. It is known that 1 ton of refrigeration in central air-conditioning (A/C) plants requires approximately 1.25 kW of power. This estimate is based on a roof that is not exposed to the sun, with minimal glass areas in the walls (Arora, 2000). Energy conservation in cold storage can be achieved by adopting the following measures: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. Minimization of solar gain Building design features and thermal properties of construction materials Minimizing infiltration and ventilation load Use of natural ventilation for cooling Equipment selection Plant maintenance Permitting drift in room design conditions 27.2.1 Minimization of Solar Gain Solar radiation accounts for 40–70% of cooling load in many building. Factors that affect the radiation levels include orientation of the building, fenestration, and preventive measures to intercept solar heat. The maximum area of exposed walls and windows should be in a northsouth direction as against an east-west direction. This means the longer side of the building to face north-south. Operation, Maintenance, and Energy Conservation in Cold Storages 507 Table 27.2: Shadow factor of overhangs Latitude Factor 25° 0.37 30° 0.48 35° 0.59 40° 0.71 45° 0.83 50° 1.02 Further, the following design features will considerably decrease the cooling load due to fenestration: 1. Reduction in glass areas on the western side: The west-facing glass adds about 510 W/m2 during the hot afternoon. Thus, 6.9 m2 of unshaded west-facing glass contributes 1 TR. The same glass area on the north side contributes only 1/15 TR. 2. Direct sunlight on west, northwest, and southwest should be avoided: This can be done by suitable sunshades that will permit just enough light but limit direct solar radiation. The amount of overhang can be calculated from Overhang = Factor × Shadow height where the factors recommended for the period of April through September for various latitudes are given in Table 27.2. 27.2.2 Building Design Features and Thermal Properties of Construction Materials The measures include the following: 1. Air is a good insulator. Hollow tiles with air trapped in them are most ideally suited for walls. Similarly, roofs and floors can be cast with a hollow space full of air. A doublewall construction with hollow bricks and an air gap is commonly used in hot desert areas. 2. Roofs exposed to the sun must be insulated with a minimum of 5 cm thick expanded polystyrene or equivalent insulation. This will reduce the roof load from 3 TR to 0.1 TR in case of 100 m2 of concrete slab. 3. Roofs can be painted with aluminum paint to reflect solar radiation. 4. Spraying a roof with water during sun periods is sometimes an option. 5. Use of small surface to volume (A/V) ration. Division of a building into compartments increases the surface area and hence transmission gain. In the same way, it could be seen that buildings of larger aspect ratio will have more transmission heat gain. 6. Wall transmission gains can also be minimized by applying insulation on exposed walls. 27.2.3 Minimizing Infiltration and Ventilation Load Infiltration load is generally heavy. If, however, infiltration cannot be reduced, then no ventilation air need be taken separately with the recirculated room air before the A/C apparatus. It must be noted that every 5 m3 of fresh air requires about 1 TR. 508 Chapter 27 Infiltration is expected to take care of the fresh air requirement when the dampers are closed. An interesting method to conserve energy is to cool the ventilation air regeneratively with the help of exhaust room air using a heat-pipe heat exchanger. 27.2.4 Use of Natural Ventilation for Cooling When the outside WBT is lower than room WBT of 18–20°C corresponding to room design conditions of 25°C DBT and 50% ± 5% RH, the A/C plant can be shut down, and only natural ventilation employed instead. For this purpose, larger fresh air intakes have to be provided at plant inlet. Such a condition occurs for many days during March–April and September–October, and also at night. If it is resorted to, it will result in considerable power savings and longer plant life. 27.2.5 Equipment Selection 27.2.5.1 Selecting High-Efficiency Compressors Power consumption of reciprocating compressor in central A/C plants is in range of 0.75– 1.25 kW/TR. Hence, one with lowest kW/TR should be selected. This could mean a savings of as much as 40 kW for a 100 TR storage A/C plant. Energy saving is thus quite enormous. 27.2.5.2 Capacity Control of Reciprocating Compressors Suction pressure–operated cylinder unloaders enable a reduction in power proportional to capacity at part loads. External controls with solenoid valves and hot gas bypass do not offer any reduction in power consumption. 27.2.5.3 Multistage Compression in Centrifugal Compressor Two-stage compression has a higher efficiency than single-stage compression. It consumes less than 1 kW/TR. For example, we find: Single-stage requires: 0.8 kW/TR approx. Two-stage requires: 0.71 kW/TR approx. Thus, 11.5% saving in power can be achieved with two-stage compression. Still higher efficiency can be achieved by providing an economizer/flash intercooler. In a single 500 TR centrifugal compressor, the savings during the life of the plant would be substantial. 27.2.5.4 Multi evaporators with Individual or Multistage Compressors In large A/C installations, it is possible to consider cooling of air in two stages, first with chilled water at 15.5°C and then with chilled water at 7°C to achieve final supply air temperature of 14–15°C. Power requirements to cool water to 15.5°C are less than that for chilling to 7°C by about 30%. Hence, for a 500 TR A/C plant, the savings is of the order of 55 kW. Operation, Maintenance, and Energy Conservation in Cold Storages 509 27.2.5.5 Optimal Design of Refrigeration and Air-Conditioning Equipment The design of the condenser and particularly the evaporator is crucial. The cost of equipment can be reduced by selecting tubes and augmentation devices to increase heat transfer coefficients. However, these may result in an increased refrigerant-side pressure drop, and hence higher running costs. The two cost factors have to be balanced to obtain total minimum cost. Similarly, chillers should be operated at the highest possible leaving water temperature (LET). Again, the overall cost has to be minimized. Finally, most designers oversize the equipment, which results not only in more capital cost, but also more energy consumption. 27.3 Plant Maintenance The need for proper maintenance of refrigeration and A/C equipment cannot be overemphasized. 27.3.1 Cooling Tower Maintenance One of the most vulnerable parts of a system is the cooling tower. The pipes and nozzles may easily get clogged due to algae, muck, leaves, or dust, resulting in poor cooling of water. If temperature of water returned to the condenser is increased by 1°C, a 6% increase in power consumption is inevitable. And if the amount of water circulated is also reduced, a further increase in energy consumption will result. Proper maintenance of cooling towers, therefore, is an absolute necessity. Performance of existing cooling towers can also be upgraded. A cellular fill is found to be better. PVC pipes could be used in place of galvanized iron. PVC will be noncorrosive. Similarly, ceramic noncorroding nozzles can be used. Location of cooling towers is important. No high temperature flue gases or exhausts from boiler, kitchen, or laundry should be permitted to enter the cooling tower intake. 27.3.2 Removing Fouling from Condenser and Chiller Tubes Fouling, another important source of deterioration of plant performance, results in high condenser and low evaporator pressure, and thus reduced capacity as well as high-energy consumption. Dirty surfaces of air-cooled condensers have the same effect. This overloading may also reduce the life of the plant. Hence, descaling of condensers and chillers must be done at intervals depending upon the hardness of water to reduce temperature gradient across the surface for heat transfer. 510 Chapter 27 Descaling can keep down the energy consumption by approximately 20%. Water treatment may be necessary to prevent scaling and fouling of heat exchangers. 27.3.3 Cleaning of Air Filters Choking of air filters results in reduced airflow through the cooling coil. At the same time, fan power consumption is increased. With less air flowing over the coil, the evaporator pressure continually drops. Once again, the capacity of the air-conditioner is reduced and the power consumption is increased. Even though the evaporator temperature and the temperature of air leaving coil are lowered, there is not enough cooling as the dehumidified air quantity is reduced. Often then, the cause for complaints in room air-conditioners is simply unclean filters, and not the system, which is mostly working satisfactorily. Air filters must, therefore, be frequently cleaned. 27.3.4 Overhauling of Compressors Timely maintenance and overhauling are necessary. Due to wear on valve reeds and piston rings, the volumetric efficiency is considerably reduced, causing a loss of refrigerating capacity. If the friction losses remaining unchanged, power is wasted. Other energy conservation measures include the following: 1. Providing air locks at all major entrances to minimize infiltration. 2. Shading of building by trees blooming in summer. The trees provide shade, and also act as evaporative coolers. 3. Replacing all resistance-type regulators, dimmers, etc., with electronic ones. 4. Installing timers, controls, etc., to automatically switch off lights and air-handling units (AHUs) when the space is not in use. 5. Preferring central A/C plants that employ water-cooled condensers in place of a number of window-type A/Cs that employ air-cooled condensers. Reference Arora, C.P., 2000. CHAPTE R 28 Controlled Atmosphere Storage The principle of storage under high CO2 and low O2 appears to have been applied in ancient times. The earliest use of controlled-modified atmospheric storage may be attributed to the Chinese. Ancient Chinese writings reported that litchi fruits (also known as lychees) were transported from northern China to southern China in sealed clay pots to which fresh leaves and grass were added. It may be surmised that during the 2-week journey, respiration of the fruits, leaves, and grass generated a high-carbon dioxide/low-oxygen atmosphere in the pots, which delayed ripening of the lychees. The first scientific observation of the effects of atmosphere on fruit ripening was made in 1819–1820 by Jacques Berard, a professor of chemistry at Montpelier Institute in France. Several further independent studies of the effect of controlled atmospheres on fruit ripening were made in the United States. One study involved the construction of a primitive controlled atmosphere store by Benjamin Nyce in Cleveland, Ohio, in which apples were successfully stored. However, it was not until the work of Kidd and West at the Low Temperature Research Station at Cambridge, England, that a sound basis of the controlled atmosphere storage of produce was established in 1927. During the past 90 years, the effects of controlled atmosphere and MA and hypobaric storage on fresh fruits and vegetables have been closely studied. Many of the research studies yielded good results indicating that one of the most effective methods of preserving fruits is to store them in a controlled atmosphere with a strictly specified mixture of oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen. The essence of this method lies not in the substitution of refrigeration of fruits by some other method, but in the further improvement of the refrigeration method itself. Fruits preservation in a controlled atmosphere yields good results only if it is done at a specific air temperature, which in turn can be attained only by refrigeration. The immense potential of the conventional refrigeration method of fruit preservation has not yet been fully exploited in most countries of the world, which is the primary reason for the high losses incurred during the refrigeration of fruits. For example, certain varieties of apples are preserved well at –1°C and even –2°C, others at 0°C, and still others at 1–3°C. ­Experiments have shown that the atmospheric conditions necessary for fruit preservation are quite different at –1°C and 0°C, and different still from those at 3°C. Even so, all varieties of apples are often preserved at the same temperature, near 0°C. Refrigeration of fruits is most effective if the temperature of the atmosphere is maintained at a fairly constant level with a fluctuation of not more than ±0.2°C from the desired Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00028-2 511 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 512 Chapter 28 temperature. In practice, however, fluctuations in the temperature of the atmosphere in refrigeration chambers are usually significantly higher, which adversely affects the preservation process. It is well known that in order to prevent fruits from withering, it is necessary to preserve them at high levels of humidity. In refrigerators, if a low and constant temperature is maintained, the vital activity of phytopathogenic microorganisms is suppressed and transpiration slowed in fruits, and thus the humidity of the atmosphere can be raised to 95% without any risk of fruits being infected with disease. But even this advantage of refrigeration is often not utilized. When no special devices for humidifying the air are used in refrigeration chambers, the result is that humidity is often as low or lower than 8%, leading to withering of the fruits. To reduce fruit losses during refrigerated storage, it is important to utilize this method to its maximum advantage in order to suppress the activity of phytopathogenic microorganisms that are always present on the fruit surfaces, to slow the processes connected with postharvest ripening of fruits, and to delay the senescence and collapse of plant tissues. But is most cases, maintaining a definite regime of temperature and humidity alone is not sufficient for prolonging the period for which fruits can be preserved and for reducing fruit losses. A definite gaseous composition of the atmosphere, strictly differentiated for each type of fruit and for different varieties of the same fruit, is also necessary. The first studies regarding fruit preservation in a gaseous medium were carried out in an atmosphere consisting of more carbon dioxide and less oxygen than is normally present in air. Carbon dioxide plays the dominant role, hence the method is called the carbon dioxide preservation method. It was assumed that the better preservation of fruit in this case was due to the suppression of the vital activity of phytopathogenic microorganisms, with the carbon dioxide acting as a strong antiseptic. However, the antiseptic properties of carbon dioxide manifest themselves only at very high concentrations, which the fruits themselves cannot withstand. Thus, when the CO2 content is about 40%, a relatively long delay can be observed in the development of the main pathogens that cause putrefaction of fruits. At the same time, the optimum gas mixture for many apple varieties is only 5% CO2 and 3% O2, because a higher CO2 content causes browning of the fruit tissues. Consequently, the lower infestation of fruits in a controlled atmosphere is due not to the suppression of the vital activity of microorganisms, but to the better maintenance of the natural resistance of fruits. This resistance is attained primarily through slowing down the processes of ripening and expiration of the cells. Many investigations have shown that the basic advantages of fruit preservation in a controlled atmosphere are as follows: 1. The so-called low-temperature diseases encountered in certain varieties of apples and other fruits are prevented during refrigeration. Controlled Atmosphere Storage 513 2. Infestation of fruits by other physiological diseases frequently encountered when fruits are preserved in refrigerators or in conventional fruit storages is reduced. 3. Taste and aroma of fruits are preserved better. 4. Consistency of fruits is maintained for longer periods. 5. Fruit losses in the controlled atmosphere are half to one-third, while the period of preservation is significantly longer than when kept in an uncontrolled atmosphere. However, each type of fruit and even each of its varieties differ in their reaction to changes in the composition of the atmosphere. Therefore, each type of fruit and each of its varieties require a different gaseous regime that depends on their physiological conditions. However, such a method, though effective for some fruits, is not particularly needed for others because of the high cost of equipment. 28.1 Gas Regimes In practice, preservation of fruits in a controlled atmosphere requires a gas regime with different oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen contents. The success of fruit preservation in a controlled atmosphere depends mainly on correct selection of highly specific gas mixture (O2, CO2, and N2) for each type of fruit and for different varieties of the same fruit, based not only on biochemical and physiological properties of the fruits but also on the conditions of their cultivation, harvest, and preservation. 28.2 Normal and Subnormal Regimes In the beginning, the so-called normal mixture of gases was used, with total O2 and CO2 content same as normal air (i.e., 21%). A mixture of gases containing 5–10% CO2, 11–16% O2, and 79% N2 was most widely accepted. However, for some years now, a mixture of gases with total O2 and CO2 content below 21% has been widely used. Such mixtures are now referred to as subnormal mixtures. The most common subnormal mixtures are those with 3–5% O2, 3–5% CO2, and 90–94% N2. The effect of normal mixtures is based primarily on a high concentration of CO2, with a threshold value of the order of 10%. In this case, a concentration of O2 that is reduced minimally to 11% has no appreciable effect on delays of biochemical processes occurring in fruit. Mixtures of this type are less effective than some others and as such are primarily used in countries (England, the Netherlands, etc.) where gas preservation of fruits was introduced earlier than in other countries. The subnormal gas mixtures slow the ripening of fruits by depleting the environment of O2 and enriching it with CO2. Consequently they are effective in slowing the process of ripening of fruits and are suitable for the maintenance of any of the fruit characteristics such as color, 514 Chapter 28 solid consistency, and taste (especially the acidity). In addition, the combined effect of the considerable depletion of O2 (below 5%) and accumulation of CO2 (3–5%) provides a setback of the development of functional disorders that are frequently encountered when normal mixtures of gases are used. The subnormal mixtures, as a matter of fact, employ a temperature slightly above 0°C (2–4°C) and a relative humidity (RH) of 90–95%. The reaction of fruit to CO2 increases with low temperatures and high levels of humidity. The mixture of gases containing the minimum permissible quantity of O2 (2–3%) and little or no CO2 (below 2%) is sometimes used for the preservation of fruits, especially those sensitive to CO2. These mixtures form a separate group and are less effective in slowing the respiration of fruits; they can be used with only a limited number of type and variety of fruits (i.e., those that cannot otherwise be exposed to increased concentrations of CO2). An analysis of different types of gas mixtures supports the view that the concentration of O2 and CO2 has a certain permissible value related to the biochemical characteristics of fruit preservation. These limiting values are 2–16% for O2 and 0–10% for CO2. As pointed out earlier, a reduction in O2 content below 2% is not suitable because of the sudden increase in anaerobic respiration that results. Any increase in CO2 above 10% damages fruit tissue (with core first to turn brown). The conditions adopted for storage of fruits, especially the temperature and RH of the surrounding medium, have a critical influence on the choice of gas regime. A proper correlation among factors such as temperature, RH, and concentration of O2 and CO2 in the surrounding medium plays a vital role in the preservation period. It may be noted that a more effective gas insulation and more complex equipment are needed for the maintenance of subnormal gaseous mixtures compared to the normal ones. A more careful sealing of storage and additional arrangements are needed for the maintenance of a subnormal and normal gaseous mixtures. The conditions for the preservation both in the subnormal and normal gases mixtures are provided here. The recommendations of the international standards organization (ISO) for preservation of a number of varieties of apples are given in Table 28.1. The recommended mixtures need certain modifications to suit local conditions. For example, for Golden Delicious apples, the following optimum compositions of the gas mixture were specified. Temperature (°C) Relative humidity (%) CO2 (%) O2 (%) First Variant 0.5 91 7 Second Variant 3 91 3 2.5 3.5 The first variant helps prolong the preservation period, and the second helps to improve the quality and taste of the fruit. For any given type and variety of fruit, a unique optimum combination of O2 and CO2 concentrations corresponds to an optimum temperature. Because the best results for most apple varieties and also for other types of fruits are obtained at 3% O2 and 5% CO2 at 2–4°C, it is advisable to begin with these parameters while ascertaining the optimum regimes for different varieties. Storage with a controlled mixture consists of different versions of storages with artificial cooling in order to maintain the desired temperature and humidity and also to provide for changing the composition of the gaseous medium. 28.3 Categories of Storages Operated with Controlled Regimes A storages can be divided into the following categories (Metliski et.al., 1974): 1. Storage with high-density enclosure: Because these units are airtight, the gas exchange through the surface of the enclosure is so low that the desired levels of O2 and CO2 can be produced and maintained through the physiological activity of fruits. 2. Storage with medium-density enclosure: In semi airtight units, the desired condition is maintained artificially through the supply of gas mixture of specific composition. 516 Chapter 28 3. Storages with low-density enclosures: In units that are not airtight, fruits are placed in special airtight wares, such as packets and containers. This category is popularly called modified atmosphere package storage. 28.4 Methods to Maintain Desired CO2 to O2 Ratio in the Controlled Atmosphere Chamber The desired CO2 and O2 ratio in the atmosphere of the storage is maintained in the following way. 1. The excess CO2 is removed by passing the air through special devices containing chemical or physical absorbents. 2. The gas exchange between the inside and the outside atmosphere is organized through filters with selective permeability to the components of the gaseous medium during their diffusion. Such filter may be partitions of the storage, may form an integral part of the partitions as padding, and finally may be kept separate from the storage space. In this last case, the gas mixture from the storage is pumped through the filters (Table 28.2). 3. A part of the atmosphere of storage is substituted by the external or a specially prepared mixture. 28.5 Establishment of Gas Regime Through Physiological Activity of the Fruit When establishing an atmosphere through the physiological activity of the produce being preserved, the enclosure of the storage must be airtight. The maximum permissible gas exchange between the air inside the storage chamber and outside depends on several factors. Foremost among these factors are the amount of product loaded into the chamber and the respiration Table 28.2: Effect of temperature and gas composition on the preservation of Williams pears Temperature (°C) Gas Compaction O2(%) CO2(%) Preservation Period (days) 15 0 0 0 21 21 2 2 0 0 4 10 15 90 180 90 0 4 4 15 2 2 5 4 10 120 60 60 4 15 5 30 Fruit Characteristics Normal ripening Surface darkening Ripening slowed, fruit had fine quality Ripening greatly delayed, fruit showed russeting from inside Ripening somewhat delayed, russeting from inside No normal ripening, fruit moldy Ripening somewhat delayed, russeting from inside, moldy Ripening much less delayed, surface darkened and grew mold Controlled Atmosphere Storage 517 intensity of the produce or fruits. In chambers with sufficient airtight sealing of the enclosure, surplus quantities of CO2 are produced and the lower permissible level may reduce the O2 content. This type of stable composition of the gas mixture in the storage chamber is obtained in 2–3 weeks after loading. However, the gas generators bring down the length of this period to 15–20 h. According to some American researchers, fruits are preserved better under the latter condition. The results of preservation of the experimental fruits in chambers with CA and the Controller kept in chambers under artificial cooling are given in Table 28.3. In establishing the regime through the physiological activity of the fruit, the concentration of CO2 was maintained at 5–7% while that of O2 was at 14–16%. In the GK-200 containers (developed by Gipronisel prom) it was 9% and 12%, respectively. When supplying a gas mixture artificially into the containers, the amount of CO2 was maintained at CO2 6, 8% and oxygen at 10, 11, and 7%. If fruits are placed in such a gastight storage chamber, the O2 tension in the store atmosphere will fall as the O2 of the gas is converted by respiratory activity into CO2. General respiration equation shows this: C6 H12 O 6 + 6O 2 + 6CO 2 → 6H 2 O + 2667 KJ of heat As shown by the equation, one volume of O2 will convent to one volume of CO2, and the sum of the percentages by volume of these gases in the store will remain constant at its initial value (i.e., the value for normal air is about 21%). When the CO2 concentration reaches a predetermined value, say x% by volume, a controlled ventilation of the store with air can be used to maintain the atmosphere composition constant throughout subsequent storage. The O2 concentration will thus be automatically maintained at (21 – x)%. Such conditions have been found satisfactory for some varieties of fruits, but others have been found to require lower O2 Table 28.3: Preservation of experimental fruits in a chamber with controlled atmosphere Apple Variety Duration of Preservation (days) Scarlet Pippin 120 Cox’s Orange Pippin 120 Renet Simirenko 220 Composition of Atmosphere (%) CO2 5 Air 5 Air Air 7 Air O2 16 16 12 Results of Preservation (%) Yield of Good Quality Fruits Losses Due to Infection Natural Weight Loss 94.4 92.0 95.8 89.6 92.5 97.4 88.5 3.2 3.9 2.1 6.8 5.0 1.0 7.8 2.4 4.1 2.1 3.6 2.5 1.6 3.7 518 Chapter 28 concentrations than are attained by this method. For such fruits, a system such as a scrubber using fresh hydrated lime bags is used. Storage chambers for controlled atmosphere storage are not large because it is desirable to fill the stores and close them within 7 days to get the full benefit of the artificial atmosphere.
