CHAPTE R 29 Biochemical Considerations of Controlled Atmosphere Storage The controlled atmosphere (CA) storage process is the most important innovation in fruits and vegetables storage since the introduction of mechanical refrigeration. This method, if combined with refrigeration, markedly delays respiratory activity and may delay softening, yellowing, spoilage, and other breakdown processes by maintaining an atmosphere with more CO2 and less O2 than in normal air. Its development illustrated the successful transmission of a scientific concept from laboratory to large-scale commercial use. Today more than half the total holdings of apples in the United States and citrus in Israel are stored under controlled atmosphere conditions. This chapter gives information on important effects and changes that are caused in fruits because of the controlled atmosphere around them. 29.1 Metabolic Effects of a Controlled Atmosphere 29.1.1 Retarded Respiration Early investigations of CA storage recognized that this new type of storage causes changes in the basic metabolic process of the stored fruits or vegetables. Respiration is one of the metabolic processes influenced by CA storage. The CA storage can influence respiration at three levels 1. Aerobic respiration 2. Anaerobic respiration 3. A combination of these two Respiration may proceed aerobically according to the following general equation: C6 H12 O 6 + 6O 2 → 6CO 2 + 6H 2 O + 2870 kJ ↑ As seen from the equation, the respiration depends on the supply of O2. Thus if the rate of diffusion of O2 through the outer layer of fruit is reduced; the number of glucose molecules oxidized per unit time can be reduced. Similarly, increasing the CO2 level in the storage atmosphere will inhibit CO2 produced by respiration from leaving the fruit and therefore interfere with O2 diffusion inward. In general, the effects of CO2 and O2 on respiration rate are considered to be additive. Kader pointed out that CO2 suppression of respiration does not occur below concentrations of 10–20%. It is also documented that at 0°C, the respiration rate Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00029-4 519 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 520 Chapter 29 at 3% O2 is 10–46% of that in air and at 10–20°C it is 20–60% of the air. However, high CO2 concentrations can cause physiological damage if O2 concentrations fall below the threshold of about 2% when the anaerobic respiration process may be initiated, resulting in rapid spoilage. Anaerobic respiration is more commonly known as fermentation and is represented by the following general equation: C6 H12 O 6 → 2C2 H 5 OH + 2CO 2 + 92 kJ ↑ This equation indicates the breakdown of hexose sugars to ethanol and CO2 with the liberation of heat. A point may be reached where a minimum quantity of CO2 is liberated for minimum respiration and thus minimum sugar utilization takes place. However, the metabolic process of fruits is so complicated that neither CO2 nor low O2 is a completely satisfactory method of changing the whole chain of reaction involved in respiration. This complexity is evidenced by the development of off-flavors, failure to soften properly, or even a complete breakdown of tissue before normal ripening processes are completed. CA storage has an effect on the respiration of fruits. The average rate of carbohydrate loss by respiration is between 1.2 and 1.4 times faster in normal air than in 10% O2 and N2, and between 1.35 and 1.55 times faster in the absence of CO2 than in the presence of 10% CO2. Thus, fruits removed from conventionally refrigerated storage exhibit a higher rate of respiration than the CA–stored fruits. The respiration rate of fruits removed from conventionally refrigerated storage increases rapidly for about 8 days. The fruits from CA storage increase in respiration soon after removal from treatment; however, this increase is generally not as accentuated. Production of CO2, C2H4, and other oxidizable volatiles are higher when Bartlett pears are stored in air than in CA. 29.1.2 Acid Accumulation In atmospheres containing 20–90% CO2, succinate and amino butyrate accumulate, while malate, aspartate, and alanine deplete and organic and amino acids generally react in a similar manner in apples and pears with a tendency to accumulate in CA-stored fruits. The pH of CA-stored greenhouse beans increases in 2 weeks, while that of air-stored samples at 45°F remains fairly constant. The titratable and total acid contents increase during air storage at 45°F, but decrease slightly in controlled atmospheres. There is similar increase in pH and decrease in the titratable acidity of CA-stored spinach. The O2 level does not affect the pH. An increase in pH is paralleled by a decrease in titratable acidity. In apricots and peaches, the pH of stored fruits is inversely related, and titratable acidity decreases in 15–60 days of storage. A marked increase in pH parallels a decrease in titratable acidity in asparagus stored in controlled atmospheres. Modifications in conventional atmospheres result in specific Biochemical Considerations of Controlled Atmosphere Storage 521 alterations in metabolism and some of these induced changes appear to reflect in the improved quality of the fruit. The CO2 atmospheres seemed to check the normal decrease in acidity usually experienced in storage. This finding suggests that the possible reasons for acid accumulation during CA storage might be lowered respiratory activity, increased CO2 fixation, or the presence of a less-active enzyme that converts malic acid to pyruvate or oxaloacetate. The CO2 concentrations in the atmosphere are increased; CO2 fixation also increases. 29.1.3 Acetaldehyde Formation Acetaldehyde is formed in large quantities by cells of higher plants in certain mixtures of CO2 and O2. Often high concentrations of it are accompanied by browning of the cells. 29.1.4 Increase in Sugars Many biochemical changes result from the use of controlled atmosphere. By using 2% O2 and 3% CO2, disappearance of starch from Bartlett pears will result during the first month in storage. The CA-stored fruits contain more sugar after ripening. Conventional storage produces relatively no changes or increases in sugars. 29.1.5 Decrease in Alcohol-Soluble Protein N Total alcohol-soluble N decreased at a slower rate in CA-stored fruit, resulting in higher concentrations of alcohol-soluble N at the end of the storage period. Protein N responds the same way (i.e., decreases at a slower rate in fruits stored in CA). 29.1.6 Pectin Changes Pectin changes correlate with changes in the storage atmospheres. Soluble pectins increase in Bartlett and Hardy pears when stored at 45°F (7.2°C), but in Yellow Newton apples, the increase of soluble pectins is slowed by CO2 storage. In Bartlett pears, a significant correlation is found between degree of maturity and content of soluble pectins. The CO2 storage may have an effect on protopectin hydrolysis. The soluble pectin content is much higher where higher temperatures or no CO2 is involved. The rate of pectin degradation is affected by both time and conditions of storage. CA-stored apricots and peaches retain a higher concentration of total pectins than when fruits are stored in conventional refrigerators. 29.1.7 Chlorophyll Degradation Chemical changes and biochemical processes occur in spinach, broccoli, sweet cherries, strawberries, and other fruits and vegetables during storage in air or controlled atmospheres. 522 Chapter 29 The presence of CO2 in the storage atmosphere is an important factor in preventing chlorophyll degradation of green beans at 45°F (7.2°C). Chlorophyll retention is increased in broccoli by a progressive increase in CO2 and decrease in O2. Higher concentrations of CO2 (2.5–10%) slow down the degreening processes in apricots and peaches. CO2 also suppresses chlorophyll destruction in apricot and peach fruits at 34°F. The degradation rate of chlorophyll in asparagus can be delayed by CA storage. Chlorophyll degradation in lettuce cultivar Great Lakes, throughout a 75-day storage period can be inhibited by CA storage conditions consisting of 2.5% CO2 and 2.5% O2 at 1.7°C, with or without prestorage treatment with phalton (1000 ppm) or polyethylene packaging. 29.2 Physiological Effects of O2 Concentration 29.2.1 Varied Ripening Rate Although low O2 invariably delays ripening, O2 levels higher than those found in air may or may not hasten ripening. Conversely, at O2 concentrations lower than in air, climacteric in avocado was delayed and even lacking. A similar ripening delay was reported in other fruits. On the other hand, at O2 concentrations higher than in air, no change is observed in avocados. An increase in O2 content of the atmosphere from 30% to 50% above that of normal air accelerated ripening of bananas. 29.2.2 Increased CO2 Production at Very Low or Very High O2 Tensions The CO2 production of Valencia oranges decreases as O2 levels decline so that CO2 production is kept at a minimum of 2.5–5% O2. However, at O2 levels below 2.5%, CO2 production increases due to fermentation. Obviously, to avoid this, O2 tension for Valencia oranges must be kept higher than 5%. The critical O2 level for minimum CO2 production apparently differs with this type of produce. The critical O2 level for mangoes is 10%. Levels below and above this stimulate CO2 evolution. Supra-atmospheric concentrations of O2 induce a climacteric rise in lemons. Low concentrations of O2 (5%) slow chlorophyll degradation in citrus fruits, and that addition of CO2 reduced the rate of color change of lemons from green to yellow. 29.2.3 Reduced Decay at Low O2 Levels Levels of 5–0% O2 reduce the decay incidence consistently. Growth of fungi may also be hindered at low O2 concentrations, although there seems to be variation in sensitivity of different fungal species (selective effect). The development of some diseases is related to O2 tension. For example, apple scald gradually becomes more severe as O2 percentage increases. Some storage diseases of plums follow a similar trend. Biochemical Considerations of Controlled Atmosphere Storage 523 29.2.4 Fermentation at Low O2 Levels At low O2 concentrations, the CO2/O2 ratio may increase as a result of fermentative reactions, causing the development of off-flavors in many fruits and vegetables. At 1% O2, alcoholic flavor can be detected in apples, bananas, avocados, artichokes, and peppers. It is generally recommended not to use concentrations below 2% O2. 29.3 Temperature and O2–C2H4 Interactions To initiate ripening, the concentration of ethylene (C2H4) in produce tissue must be kept higher than a certain threshold value. Moreover, O2 must also be present because it is necessary for C2H4 synthesis as well as for the many other O2-requiring reactions characteristic of the ripening process. However, ripening temperature should likewise be considered. C2H4 is not active at temperatures close to freezing, but at 70°F (21.1°C) C2H4 cannot induce ripening if the O2 level is low (1%). Even at high temperatures, the presence of C2H4 in CA storage should be avoided. Softening can be induced by C2H4 even if CO2 and O2 are neither too high nor too low, respectively. 29.4 Physiological Effects of CO2 Concentration When the CO2 level increases in the storage atmosphere, the quantity of CO2 dissolves in the cell or combines with some cellular constituents. This phenomenon is reversible. High levels of CO2 within the cell generally lead to the following physiological changes: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. Decrease in the synthetic reactions of ripening (e.g., proteins, pigments) Inhibition of some enzyme activities (e.g., succinodehydrogenase, cytochrome oxidase) Decrease in production of volatiles Disturbed organic acid metabolism, especially the accumulation of succinic acid Slackening in the breakdown of pectic substances Inhibition of chlorophyll synthesis and fruit degreening, particularly after early picking Alteration in the proportion of various sugars (e.g., chestnuts are sweeter after storage at low temperature and high CO2) 29.4.1 Altered Climacteric Pattern High CO2 treatment postpones the induction of climacteric in bananas. However, the avocado exhibits a different response. When the CO2 concentration is 5% and the O2 level is that of air (21%), the preclimacteric increase is affected only slightly. The onset of the increase is delayed by 3 days. However, the peak rate is 40% below that of air and is attained after 21 days, compared to 8 days in the control. When the gas mixture consists of 10% CO2 and 21% O2, the rate of O2 uptake is low and remains constant for more than 3 weeks at 59°F (14°C). 524 Chapter 29 Upon transferring to air, the respiration rate increases, showing that no climacteric occurs before that point. Raising CO2 content to 15% results in some injury. The effect of CO2 in depressing respiration of climacteric fruits is not observed in citrus. The CO2 causes a curious stimulation of respiration in lemons. In general, the life of lemons is still prolonged by CO2, especially at lower levels of O2. 29.4.2 Off-Flavor Production at High CO2 At high CO2 concentrations (15% or more), off-flavor is usually produced in strawberries, bananas, oranges, apples, and other commodities. In some cases, off-flavor may be due to an accumulation of ethanol and ethanal. Concomitant with the development of undesirable flavor, off-color may also be observed. Sometimes anthocyanins are produced in apples. 29.4.3 Increased pH and Reduced Ascorbic Acid Level Bananas in 72% CO2 at 77°F (25°C) showed an increase in pH after 20 h. In green bananas, when exposed to a high CO2 atmosphere, the ascorbic acid content of the fruits showed a decrease but no dehydroascorbic acid was found. Removal of the fruits to a normal atmosphere resulted in rapid recovery of ascorbic acid. 29.4.4 Induction of Some Physiological Disorders High CO2 may induce many kinds of tissue browning in fruits (e.g., core flush of apples, brown heart of apples, and pears) and vegetables. However, CO2 treatment may decrease the severity of apple scald. High CO2 is toxic to bananas; the degree of severity varies with the stage of maturity, duration of treatment, and storage temperature. Harvesting early in the season and long storage periods at high temperatures predispose the fruits to high CO2 injury. In some cases, even low CO2 concentrations (5–10%) may be dangerous if treatment at rather low temperatures is lengthy. 29.4.5 Slowing Fungal Growth Proper concentrations of CO2 delay the germination and growth of some fungi, such as Rhizopus, Botrytis cinerea, and Trichothecium, which occur on stored fruits. Inhibition occurs at 20–50% CO2; however, high concentrations of CO2 may kill cells, thus facilitating the growth of fungi. This effect of CO2 on fungi is an argument in favor of its use in CA storage. In some cases, however, the ensuing toxic effects and off-flavor development due to CO2 nullify this advantage, so it may be better to use atmospheres devoid of CO2 but containing low percentages of O2. Biochemical Considerations of Controlled Atmosphere Storage 525 29.5 C2H4–CO2 Interaction Like O2, the role of CO2 in relation to C2H4 effects is not to be overlooked. High CO2 concentration causes inhibition of the stimulating effect of C2H4 on ripening CO2 postpones the effect of C2H4 in bananas ripening at ordinary temperatures. A concentration of 10% CO2 counteracts with the effect of 100 ppm C2H4. It appears that CO2 competes with C2H4 at the specific location on the receptor site. It is also possible that CO2 inhibits formation of C2H4. 29.6 Combined Effects of CO2, O2, and Temperature The individual effects of favorable temperature, CO2, and O2 levels on delay of ripening and respiration may be additive if any of the factors are combined. The interrelated effects of O2 and CO2 are clearly elucidated. Samples of 150 apples were placed at 32°F in an atmosphere containing 2.4 or 6% CO2 and 1.2, 2.2, or 13.2% O2. These conditions represent nine possible combinations. Weight loss, fruit color, physiological disorders, firmness, total acidity, and organoleptic value of the samples were assessed. Some interactions were as follows: 1. Weight loss decreases when O2 decreases and CO2 increases. 2. The green color is retained at low O2 levels but color is not affected when the CO2 level is raised. 3. Firmness and O2 concentrations are negatively correlated, but CO2 has a counteracting effect. 4. Scald decreases as O2 decreases, but again CO2 tends to reverse the O2 alleviating effect. 29.7 Humidity and C2H4 During Storage In commercial CA storage operations, the typical main concern is the regulation of temperature and O2 and CO2 in the atmosphere. The presence of C2H4 and water vapor should also be given special attention. As stated before, C2H4 stimulates ripening of green fruits. The degree of ripening induction of C2H4 is a function of its concentration, temperature, stage of fruit development, atmospheric composition, and other factors. To obtain maximum delay of ripening, C2H4 should be removed from the storage rooms or sealed packages. Adding KMnO4 (potassium permanganate) is one of the more effective means of absorbing C2H4. Ripening inhibition is controlled by hypobaric storage. The partial pressures of C2H4 and O2 are lower under these conditions. To hasten ripening or degreening after CA storage, C2H4 may be subsequently introduced and O2 concentration simultaneously increased. In airtight CA storage rooms or packages, water can accumulate and condense. Fungi may develop even if CO2 is in excess. Use of fungicides may be recommended under these conditions. An effective fungicide may obviate lowering of humidity during storage. However, humidity close to saturation has some advantages; for example, a saturated atmosphere has a protective effect against chilling of bananas at 54°F (12.2°C) and improves the aroma development of some fruits. 526 Chapter 29 29.8 Postcontrolled Atmosphere Storage Behavior Removal of produce from a controlled atmosphere to air at ordinary temperatures initiates a series of abrupt changes: marked decrease in firmness, increase in respiratory gas exchange, and the appearance of tissue browning particularly after a long storage period. When CA conditions are well chosen, the organoleptic properties of the fruits are frequently better than after common refrigerated storage. 29.8.1 Lengthy Controlled Atmosphere Storage Treatment Injuries may occur even at the recommended O2 and CO2 levels if the length of the CA storage period is unduly prolonged. However, some fruits store well in reasonably good condition for long periods compared to those stored in air. For instance, Navel oranges when held at 40°F in 15% O2 and 2% CO2 keep for 4 months with better result than in air. Conversely clementines behave better in atmospheres with low O2 content (6%) in the presence of 5% CO2. After numerous experiments on apples and pears, various conditions have been recommended to obtain the maximum storage life consistent with retention of good market qualities. The storage life may be 40–60% longer than in air, and sometimes more, according to temperature and variety. Additional tests are needed to determine the best conditions for lengthy CA storage. 29.8.2 Brief Controlled Atmosphere Storage Treatment It may be useful to know the limits of susceptibility of fruits to CO2 and O2 concentrations during brief periods, because it is then possible to use these conditions during transport or as pretreatments prior to processing. As stated before, fruits may withstand high CO2 or very low O2 concentrations for a brief time. 29.8.3 High CO2 Treatments for Short Periods High CO2 concentration in a storage atmosphere may have an inhibitory effect on fungi development, but can change the organoleptic quality of the fruit. A brief treatment (2– 10 days) in an atmosphere containing 30–60% CO2 provides a favorable effect against apple scald. Limits of susceptibility to CO2 vary with the type of produce. In oranges, 10–15% CO2 results in an increase of alcoholic content, but 5% CO2 does not. The alcohol production of grapes is not too high (17 mg/100 g fresh weight) after 30 days at 21% CO2, but increases up to 170 mg/100 g at 25% CO2. An alcoholic flavor develops and dissipates slowly into the air. Interesting results have been observed by using high CO2 concentrations in the transport of bananas, papayas, strawberries, potatoes, peppers, mushrooms, okra, cauliflower, and cantaloupe. Biochemical Considerations of Controlled Atmosphere Storage 527 29.8.4 Brief Treatment with Low O2 Level If an O2 shortage is responsible for fermentation troubles, one may wonder whether exposure of produce over brief periods in such atmospheres may be less dangerous. Several observations show that it is possible to utilize this method, particularly during transport with fruits and vegetables in atmospheres of 100% N2, 99% N2 plus 1% O2, and in air. Ripening of green bananas and tomatoes is delayed in N2 atmospheres at 60°F (15.6°C). After removal to air, fruits previously held in 99% N2 ripen slowly to a marketable condition. The flavor of bananas and tomatoes is not affected for 4 days in 100% N2 or up to 10 days in 97% N2. Although alcohol rose to 40 mg/100 g fresh weight by holding grapes in low O2 at 32°F (0°C) for 6 days, neither quality nor shelf life is affected. Oranges, when held in N2, produce increasing amounts of ethanol, acetaldehyde, and methanol as the duration of the anaerobic treatment is prolonged. It is interesting that high O2 uptake and CO2 production as a result of exposure to N2 may be reversed if low O2 levels are used. The anaerobic CO2 output initiated by lemons in the N2 atmosphere is suppressed by adding either 2% or 5% O2. Apparently, part of the CO2 in the N2 atmosphere accumulates in the rind and is retained there in a nongaseous form. This bound CO2 exerts a carryover effect on O2 uptake upon transfer to air. Oxygen uptake of lemons when held in N2 or 1% O2 for days is high in air compared to the untreated control. Use of liquid N2 and eventually adding 1–2% O2 is gaining interest as a fruit treatment. Liquid N2 is being studied in the transport of grapes and peaches in Italy. All these observations are interesting, but the treatment of produce in N2 even for a brief time should be examined carefully. Marked detrimental effects on quality may result at any time without proper control of other factors. 29.9 Carbon Monoxide For the last several years, carbon monoxide (CO) at 2–3% has been used as a supplement to controlled atmosphere during transit of lettuce as a discoloration inhibitor. Carbon monoxide is a colorless, tasteless, odorless gas that is explosive at 12–74% (by volume) in air. Carbon monoxide, when added to 2–5% atmospheres, inhibits discoloration of bruised leaves and butts of lettuce. A similar effect of CO is noted in conjunction with reduced O2 and increased CO2 to inhibit discoloration, fungi, and insects in other produce. Five to ten percent carbon monoxide can also control fungal decay and insect population. However, further research is needed. Ultimately it can be said that the CA storage has the following benefits and harmful effects Potential benefits 1. Delay of senescence and associated biochemical and physiological changes (i.e., slowing of respiration, ethylene production, softening, and compositional changes) 2. Reduction of fruits sensitivity to ethylene 528 Chapter 29 3. Control of certain physiological disorders (e.g., chilling injury and russeting in lettuce) 4. Control of postharvest diseases and decaying by inhibiting pathogens and insects Potential harmful effects 1. Start or increase of blackheart in potatoes, brown stains on lettuce, and brown heart in apples and pears 2. Irregular ripening of bananas, pears, and tomatoes due to low concentration of O2 3. Development of off-flavors due to low O2 that causes anaerobic respiration 4. Increased susceptibility to decay due to low O2and/or high CO2 5. Stimulation of sprouting and delay in suberization in periderm formation in potatoes 29.10 Produce Considerations in Controlled Atmosphere Storage Controlled-atmosphere storage is one of the means of supplementing refrigeration to minimize deterioration. Inception of pathogens, effects of C2H2 and relative humidity, and occurrence of many physiological disorders during storage should also be of primary concern. One should be aware that no single combination of CO2 and O2 is best for mixed storage of fruits and vegetables. Controlled atmosphere requirements vary within species or even with commodities that may be held at the same temperature and relative humidity. Varying atmosphere requirements are needed for each of the citrus cultivars and other types of fruits. 29.11 The Devaux Effect When plant organs are brought from one gas mixture to another, physical factors come into play. For example, when an apple is transferred from air to pure CO2 at the same pressure and temperature, CO2 will enter the tissues and air will be given off from the fruit at a different rate. Changes in the pressure of gases inside and outside the produce will take place. This process, termed as the Devaux effect, is influenced by characteristics of the tissue, permeability of the cuticle, lenticels or stomata, volume of intercellular spaces, and other anatomical features that change during ripening. CHAPTE R 30 Gas Exchange Mechanisms in Controlled Atmosphere Storage 30.1 Introduction During respiration, fruits undergo a heterotrophic mode of life in which they utilize earlier accumulated nutrient reserves. The only relationship established between the fruit and the surrounding atmosphere is through the so-called gas exchange. The fruit utilizes O2 of the atmosphere to produce CO2, water vapor, essential substances such as C2H4, and number of other substances that together constitute fruit aroma. 30.2 Respiration of Fruits and Vegetables It is well-known fact that fresh fruits and vegetables are highly perishable in their natural untreated form. The process is a continuation of their metabolic activity after harvest. It is said that fruits and vegetables fall into a “sleep” or “hibernation” condition at a certain temperature, near 4°C. This metabolic activity is manifested by respiration. The mixture is generated by combining appropriate quantities of air and N2 and CO2 gases. Of this mixture 100 m3 at 20°C and 1 atm is needed °C per hour. Air contains 21% O2 and 79% N2. All percentages are by volume. No volume changes occur on mixing ideal gases. Because volume percentage is the same as mole percentage, material balance equations may be made on the basis of volume and volume percentages. Material balance: Let x m3/h may be the air needed for supplying 5% O2. 0.21( x) = 0.5 × 100 x = 23.8 m3 / h Figure 30.2: Schematic for Example 30.3. Gas Exchange Mechanisms in Controlled Atmosphere Storage 533 This 23.8 m3/h of air also contain 79% N2 by volume. Therefore, volume of nitrogen supplied with air is 23.8 × 0.79 = 18.80 m3 / h But accurate volume of N2 required in the gas mixture is 90% of 100 m3 of mixture 0.9 × 100 = 90 m3/ h Balance N2 to be supplied is 90 – 18.8 = 71.2 m3/h The CO2 required is 0.05 × 100 = 5 m3/h Total = 23.8 + 71.2 + 5 = 100 m3/h CA storage has been developed as a supplement to refrigeration in prolonging the storage life of actively respiring fruits and vegetables. The reaction involved in respiration is primarily the oxidation of carbohydrates and forms CO2, H2O, and heat as follows: C6H12O6 + 6O2 = 6CO2 + 6H2O + 2667 kJ The respiratory quotient (RQ), defined as the ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed, is 1 for the reaction. Most products show respiratory quotients close to 1. The heat evolved during respiration has also been shown to be related to the quantity of CO2 produced in the same manner as that released during the combustion of glucose (10.7 J/mg CO2). The rate of O2 consumption and CO2 evolution can be calculated from the heat of respiration, and vice versa. CA storage is based on the premise that increasing the CO2 level and decreasing the O2 level in the storage atmosphere will result in a reduction of the rate of respiration. Indeed, calorimetric determination of the heat of respiration of products in continuously flowing CA of the optimum composition for the given product has shown that CA can reduce the respiration rate to approximately one-third of the respiration rate in air at the same temperature. Furthermore, the respiration rate for this particular product is so low that flushing the trailer with N2 and CO2 would have to be done initially to bring the CA to the desired composition within a short period of time. 30.3 Specificity of Fruit Respiration It is well-known that the overall respiration equation of energy C6 H12 O 6 + 6O 2 → 6CO 2 + 6H 2 O + 2821 kJ shows that the respiration substratum (i.e., the substance which produces energy) is essentially glucose. But it does not imply that other substances such as proteins, fat, and organic acids have no role in respiration because the intermediate products formed during certain stages of their conversion play a significant role in the process of oxidation of sugars. The gases involved in respiration have similar volumes (i.e., volume of O2 consumed is equal to that of carbon dioxide produced). Thus, the ratio of volume of carbon dioxide released to the O2 consumed, or the respiration coefficient (RQ), is unity, which is an important aspect of respiration. It is sufficient to be considered the change of volume of one gas alone (e.g., CO2) because the determination of the CO2 content is comparatively easy. The majority of studies on the respiration of fruits are based on such estimates. It was shown that O2 concentration in the intercellular spaces is always lower than that in the atmosphere, whereas it is higher for CO2. An equilibrium between the internal atmosphere of fruits undergoing preservation and the external atmosphere is attained in 24–48 h. The cuticle of fruits exhibits considerable resistance to the diffusion of O2 from air into the intercellular space. The rate at which O2 permeates depends on its partial pressure inside the fruit, this relationship can be represented by the well-known Fick’s law. q = K F ( p1 − p2 )l −1 where q = volume of O2 diffused into the fruit, cc/sec K = diffusion coefficient, cc/cm2 per second F = surface area of fruit through which O2 permeates, cm2 p1 = partial pressure of O2 outside the fruit, atm p2 = partial pressure of O2 inside the fruit, atm l = length of diffusion path (i.e., thickness of cuticle), cm (30.16) 540 Chapter 30 A limitation to this equation is that it is difficult to measure partial pressure of O2 inside the fruit and hence the equation is not practically functional. The same diffusion of O2 into the fruit can be expressed in terms of concentration of O2 inside the fruit, which is easier to measure. Because the thickness of cuticle layer and its composition change during the life cycle of the fruit, the permeability of the surface tissues to O2 and CO2 and other gases also varies accordingly. In green but otherwise well-formed apples, the permeability of epicarp is appreciably higher than in the ripe and larger fruits prior to their picking. Minimum permeability is observed prior to picking of matured fruits. With preservation, the permeability of epicarp gradually decreases. Preservation in a controlled atmosphere causes appreciable changes in the composition of cuticular substances, which has bearing on the permeability of the surface tissues. 30.3.1 Oxygen Uptake in Fruit Tissue The rate at which O2 is consumed by the cells of the fruit pulp mass determine the rate at which it must enter from air/gas to the pulp through the cuticle of the fruit. Many factors influence the respiration rate, such as variety, status of maturity, temperature, and the chemical composition of the pulp. The O2 uptake varies with time. Typically, a specific O2 uptake rate passes through a maximum in early exponential phase. If Qo is the O2 uptake rate per volume of sucrose and qo is the specific O2 uptake rate: Qo = − qo VS where Qo = O2 uptake rate, gm/s qo = specific O2 uptake rate gm/s/unit volume of sucrose VS = volume of sucrose, cm3 30.4 Diffusion Theory Diffusion theory is expressed schematically in Figure 30.5. Assume that mass transfer of molecular component A occurs across area a perpendicular to the direction of diffusion. In single-phase systems, the rate of mass transfer due to molecular diffusion is given by Fick’s law of diffusion, which states that mass flux is proportional to the concentration gradient. J A = N A / a = − DAB (dcA / dy ) where JA = mass flux of component A NA = rate of mass transfer of component A (30.17) Gas Exchange Mechanisms in Controlled Atmosphere Storage 541 Figure 30.5: Concentration Gradient of Component A Inducing Mass Transfer Across Area a. a = area across which mass transfer occurs DAB = binary diffusion coefficient or diffusivity of component A in a mixture of A and B CA = concentration of component A y = distance dcA/dy = concentration gradient or change in concentration of A with distance Therefore, mass flux is defined as the rate of mass transfer per unit area perpendicular to the direction of movement. JA has units g mol/s–1·m–2, corresponding units for NA are g mol/s, for CA g mol/m–3, and for DAB m2·s–1. The negative sign in the preceding equation indicates that the direction of mass transfer is always from higher concentration to lower concentration, opposite of concentration gradient. The diffusion coefficient DAB is a property of materials. DAB reflects the ease with which diffusion takes place. Its value depends on both components of mixture: for example, the diffusivity of CO2 in water will be different from the diffusivity of CO2 in another solvent such as ethanol. Diffusivity of gases varies with pressure. For liquids, there is an approximate linear dependence on concentration. Diffusivity values in liquids are several orders of magnitude smaller than in gases. As example DAB for O2 in air at 0°C and 1 atm is 1.78 × 10–5 m2·s–1. DAB of O2 in water at 25°C and one atmosphere is 2.5 × 10–9 m2·s–1. For glucose in dilute solution in water at 25°C, it is 6.9 × 10–10 m2·s–1. Diffusion of O2 into the fruit mass from outside and similarly the diffusion of CO2 from inside of the fruit mass into the surrounding atmosphere can be considered as mass transfer across phase boundaries (i.e., across different layers in fruit cells and also through the epicarp). The O2 transfer process from outside atmosphere into the fruits mass is shown as 542 Chapter 30 O2 in air → O2 in intercellular space of the cuticle → O2 dissolved into the cells → O2 utilized by respiration At each stage of diffusion, there are different boundaries. Mass transfer of O2 from one phase to other involves transport from the bulk of one phase to the phase boundary or interface and then from the interface to the bulk of the second phase. The process of transport of O2 into the fruit pulp can be explained by film theory analogous to Newton-Rickman law in heat transfer. 30.5 Film Theory The film theory is based on the idea that a fluid film or mass transfer boundary layer forms wherever there is contact between two phases. The two-layer film theory is a useful model for mass transfer between phases. Let us consider mass transfer of component A across the phase interface represented in Figure 30.6. Assume that the phases are two immiscible liquids such as water (aqueous phase) and chloroform (organic phase), and that A is initially at higher concentration in the aqueous phase than in the organic phase. The concentration of A in the bulk aqueous phase is CA1; the concentration of A in bulk organic phase in CA2. According to the film theory, turbulence in each fluid dies out at the phase boundary. A thin film of relatively stagnant fluid exists on either side of the interface (like heat transfer from Figure 30.6: Film Resistance to Mass Transfer Between two Immiscible Liquids. Gas Exchange Mechanisms in Controlled Atmosphere Storage 543 steam to a juice inside an evaporated tube). Mass transfer through this film is affected solely by molecular diffusion. The concentration of A changes near the interface as indicated in Figure 30.6. CA1 is interfacial concentration of A in the aqueous phase; CA2 is the interfacial concentration of A in the organic phase. Most of the resistance to mass transfer resides in the liquid film rather than in the bulk liquid. For all practical purposes, it is generally assumed that there is negative resistance to transport at the interface itself, which is equivalent to assuming the phases are in equilibrium at the plane of contact. The difference between CA1 and CA2 at the interface accounts for the possibility that, at equilibrium, A may be more soluble in one phase than in the other. For example, if A were acetic acid in contact at the interface with both water and chloroform, the equilibrium concentration in water would be greater than in chloroform by a factor between 5 and 10. CA1i would then be significantly higher then CA2 i. 30.6 Liquid–Solid Mass Transfer Mass transfer between a moving liquid and a solid is observed in many biological processes. Adsorption of molecules on to surfaces includes transport of O2 molecules into cuticle of the fruit. CA storage is one of the best examples. Conversely, the process of dissolving a solid into liquid–solid mass transfer is directed away from the solid surface. Let us assume that component A is required at the surface of a solid. The situation at the interface between the liquid containing A and the solid is illustrated in Figure 30.7. Near the interface, the liquid velocity is 0 and thereby forms a boundary layer. As A is consumed by reaction, the local concentration of A at the surface decreases and a concentration gradient is established through the film. The concentration difference between the bulk liquid and the phase interface drives mass transfer of A from the liquid to the solid, allowing the Figure 30.7: Concentration Gradient for Liquid–Solid Mass Transfer. 544 Chapter 30 reaction to start and continue. If the cuticle is nonporous, component A does not penetrate further than the surface. The concentration of A at the phase boundary is CAi, and the concentration of A in the bulk liquid outside the film is CA0. If a is the liquid–solid interface area per unit volume, the volumetric rate of mass transfer can be determined from the following equation. N A = K L a (CAo − CAi ) where KL = liquid-phase mass-transfer coefficient Application of this equation requires knowledge of mass transfer coefficient, interfacial area between the phases, the bulk concentration A, and the concentration of A at the interface. Bulk compositions are generally easy to measure, in simple cases, area a can be determined from the shape and size of the solid. Instead, the value of the mass-transfer coefficient is measured or calculated using published correlation. Estimation of interfacial concentration CAi is more difficult, and measuring composition at phase boundaries is not easy experimentally. To overcome this problem, we must consider the processes in the system that are linked to mass transfer of A. In the example in Fig. 30.7, transport of A is linked to the reaction at the inner surface of the cuticle, so that the value of CAi will depend on the rate of consumption of A at the interface. In practical terms we can therefore calculate the rate of mass transfer of A only if we have information about the rate of reaction at the solid surface. Simultaneous reaction and mass transfer occur in many bioprocesses. Therefore, it is essential that students have basic knowledge of biochemical reactions associated with kinetic rates in fruits stored in CA storage. The biochemical reaction may be homogeneous or heterogeneous. These are discussed in detail in the following section. 30.7 Homogeneous Reactions The respiration and transpiration processes in fruits are biochemical. In many bioprocesses, characteristics of the reaction determine to large extent the feasibility and success of the project. The most interesting in biological systems are catalytic reactions. Enzymes and enzyme complexes perform catalytic roles. A biocatalyst can be of microbial, plant, or animal origin. The performance of catalytic reactions is characterized by the variables such as reaction rate and yield of product from substrate. These parameters must be taken into account when designing and operating CA chambers. In engineering analysis of catalytic reactions, a distinction is made between homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions. A reaction is homogenous if the temperature and all concentrations in the system are uniform. In contrast, a heterogeneous reaction takes place in the presence of concentration or temperature gradients. Analysis of heterogeneous reactions requires Gas Exchange Mechanisms in Controlled Atmosphere Storage 545 application of mass transfer principles in conjunction with reaction theory. This chapter covers the basic aspects of reaction theory, which allows the extent and the speed of homogeneous reaction to be quantified and identifies important factors affecting reaction rate. 30.8 Basic Reaction Theory Reaction theory has two fundamental parts. 1. Reaction thermodynamics 2. Reaction kinetics Reaction thermodynamics is concerned with how far the reaction can proceed, no matter how fast a reaction is, it cannot continue beyond the point of chemical equilibrium. On the other hand, reaction kinetics are concerned with the rate at which the reaction proceeds. 30.8.1 Reaction Thermodynamics Consider a reversible reaction presented by the following equation: A +bB yY +zZ (30.18) A, B, Y, and Z are chemical species. b, y, and z are stoichiometric coefficients. If the components are left in a closed system for an infinite period of time, the reaction proceeds until thermodynamic equilibrium is reached. At equilibrium, there is no net driving force for further change. The reaction has reached the limit of its capacity for chemical transformation in a closed system. Composition of the equilibrium mixture is determined exclusively by the thermodynamic properties of the reactants and products. It is independent of the way the reactions are executed. Equilibrium concentrations are related by the equilibrium constant k. For the preceding reaction: k= C yey.Czez CAe CBe (30.19) where CAe, CBe, Cye, and Cze are equilibrium concentrations of A, B, Y, and Z, respectively. The value of k depends on temperature as follows: ln k = 0 – ∆Grxn RT (30.20) 0 where ∆Grxn is the change in standard free energy per mole of A reacted, R is ideal gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature. Values of R are listed in Table 30.2. The thermodynamics outlined in this section apply only to closed systems. True thermodynamic equilibrium does not exist in living cells that exchange matter with surrounding cells. Metabolic processes in cells are in a dynamic state; products formed are constantly removed or broken down so that reactions are driven forward. Most reactions in a biological system proceed to completion in a finite period of time at a finite rate depending on the supply of reactants (e.g., in CA storage, supply O2 to sucrose, the substrate). If we know that complete conversion will eventually take place, the most useful reaction parameter to know is the rate at which the transformation proceeds. Another important characteristic, especially for systems in which many different reactions take place at the same time, is the proportion of reactant that is converted to desired product. 30.9 Reaction Rate Consider the general irreversible reaction: a A +b B → yY +z X (30.24) The rate of this reaction can be represented by the rate of conversion of compound A. Let us use the symbol RA to denote the rate of reaction with respect to A. RA has the unit of kg·s–1 30.9.1 Measures of Reaction Rate For a general reaction system, the rate of reaction is related to the rate of change of mass in the system by the unsteady mass-balance equation as shown here. dM = M i – M o + RG – RC dt where M = mass t = time Mi = mass flow rate into the system Mo = mass flow rate out of the system RG = mass rate of generation by reaction RC = mass rate of consumption by reaction (30.25) 548 Chapter 30 Let us apply the Equation (30.25) to compound A. Assuming that the reaction is the only reaction taking place that involves A. Rate of consumption RC is equal to RA and RG = 0. The mass balance equation becomes: dM A– dt = MAi – MAo + RA (30.26) Therefore, rate of reaction RA can be determined. If we measure the rate of change in mass of dM A– A (i.e., ) and the rate of flow of A in and out of the system MAi and MAO, respectively, in dt a closed system, where MAi = MAO = 0. Equation 30.26 becomes RA = – dM A dt (30.27) and reaction rate is measured simply by monitoring the change of mass of A in the system. Most measurements of reaction rates are carried out in closed systems so that the rate can be analyzed according to Equation (30.27). dM A is negative when A is consumed by reaction; therefore, the minus sign in Equation 30.27 dt is necessary to make RA a positive quantity. Rate of reaction is sometimes called reaction velocity and can also be measured in terms of component B, Y, or Z in a closed system. RB = – dM B – dM Y dM Z , RY = , RZ = dt dt dt (30.28) where MB, MY, MZ, are masses of B, Y, and Z, respectively. When reporting reaction rate, the reactant being monitored should be specified. Because RY and RZ are based on product accumulation, these reaction rates are called production rates or productivity. Equations 30.27 and 30.28 define the rate of reaction in a closed system. However, reaction rates can be expressed using different measurement bases. 30.9.2 Measurement of Reaction Rate In bioprocess engineering, there are three distinct ways of expressing reaction rates, which can be applied in different situations. 1. Total rate: Total reaction rate is defined in Equations 30.27 and 30.28 and is expressed as either mass or moles per unit time. Total rate is useful for specifying the output of a particular reactor or manufacturing plant. Production rates for factories are often expressed as total rates. For example, the production rate is 105 tons per year. Gas Exchange Mechanisms in Controlled Atmosphere Storage 549 2. Volumetric rate: Because the total mass of reactant converted into a reaction mixture depends on the size of the system, it is often convenient to specify reaction rate as the rate per unit volume. Units of volumetric rate are kg·m–3·s–1. Rate of reaction expressed on volumetric basis is used to account for differences in volume between reaction systems. Therefore, if the reaction mixture in a closed system has volume V. RA –1 dM A = (30.29) V V dt where rA is the volumetric rate of reaction with respect to A. When V is constant, Equation 30.29 can be written as: dCA rA = dt (30.30) rA = where CA is the concentration of A in units of kg·m–3. Volumetric rates are particularly useful for comparing the performance of reactors of different sizes. A common objective in optimizing reaction processes is to maximize volumetric productivity so that desired production rate can be achieved with minimum-size chambers and therefore minimum cost. 3. Specific rate: Biological reactions involve enzyme and substrate catalysts. Because the total rate of conversion depends on the amount of catalyst present, it is sometimes useful to specify reaction rate as the rate per quantity of enzyme or substrate involved in the reaction. In a closed system, a specific reaction rate can be measured as follows rA = – (1 / X or1 / E ) dM A dt (30.31) where rA = specific rate of reaction with respect to A X = quantity of substrate E = quantity of enzyme dM A = rate of change of mass of A in the system dt Because quantity of the substrate is usually expressed as mass, units of specific rate for cellcatalyzed reaction would be, (e.g., kg·s–1 or simply s–1). Enzyme activity is often expressed as units of activity measured under specified conditions. One unit of enzyme is usually taken as the amount that catalyzes conversion of 1 m mole substrate per minute at the optimum temperature, pH, and substrate concentration. Therefore, if Equation (30.28) is expressed as units of enzyme activity, the specific rate of reaction under process conditions could be reported as kg (unit enzyme)·s–1. In a closed system where the volume of reaction mixture remains constant, an alternative expression for specific reaction rate is dC rA = – (1 / x or1 / e ) A (30.32) dt 550 Chapter 30 where x is the substrate concentration and e is the enzyme concentration. Specific rate is the rate achieved per unit catalyst and under usual circumstances; it is not dependent on the size of the system or the amount of catalyst present. Different varieties of fruits could be compared in terms of specific reaction rates. 30.10 Reaction Kinetics As reactions proceed, the concentrations of reactants decrease. In general, rate of reaction depends on reactant concentration, so that the specific rate of conversion decreases simultaneously. Reaction rate also varies with temperature; most reactions speed up considerably as temperature rises. Kinetic reaction refers to the relationship between the rate of reaction and the conditions that affect reaction velocity, such as reactant concentration and temperature. These relationships are conveniently described using kinetic expressions or kinetic equations. Consider again the general irreversible equation: aA +bB → yY +zZ (30.33) Often, but not always, the volumetric rate of the reaction can be expressed as a function of reactant concentration using the following mathematical form: rA = kCAa ⋅ CBb (30.34) where k is the rate constant or rate coefficient for the reaction. By definition, the rate constant is independent of the concentration of the reacting species but is dependent on other variables that influence reaction rate, such as temperature. When the kinetic equation has the form of Equation 30.34, the reaction is said to be of order a with respect to component A and order b with respect to B. The order of the overall reaction is (a + b). It is not usually possible to predict the order of the reactions from stoichiometry. The mechanism of a single reaction and the functional form of the kinetic expression must be determined by experiments. The dimensions and units of K depend on the order of the reaction. Problems 1. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 31 Mass Balance Principles Applied to Controlled Atmosphere Chambers In the later 1960s, the French scientist P Marcellin recognized the possibility of applying membrane technology to the storage of fruits and vegetables. The general idea was to inhibit aerobic respiration and prevent moisture loss simultaneously by creating a storage atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide (CO2) and poor in oxygen (O2). The main characteristic of the membrane he used was more permeability to CO2 than to O2. Thus, while the stored product respires, the level of O2 in the storage enclosure drops at a rate higher than the level diffusing through the membrane from the surroundings, and the respiration itself drops accordingly. The differential permeability leads eventually to a quasi-steady-state in which the CO2 level in the enclosure is higher than ambient and the O2 level is lower than ambient. The reduction in respiration rate shows moisture loss and the breakdown of the organic constituents. It is generally accepted that this approach improves the relative storage life by 100% at room temperature storage (20–25°C) and by about 33% at optional refrigeration temperature. In principle, the controlled atmosphere (CA) concept is clear. The engineering calculations needed to design a membrane enclosure for long-term storage of commodities are not complex. However, there are limitations in the atmosphere compositions that may be achieved for a given commodity’s respiratory activity and a given membrane selectivity. The required physical data (size of enclosure, membrane permeability, amount of stored produce, etc.) are readily available. One of the problems addressed by research is to determine the respiration rate at that composition. This problem has so far been addressed by either trial-and-error methods by experiments aimed at estimating the optimum composition using mathematical analysis. In this chapter, the mass balance principle under unsteady-state conditions that are relevant for predicting composition of gas concentration in general reactor chambers and their application in formulating mathematical equations for estimating gas composition under equilibrium conditions in real CA chambers are illustrated. To evaluate the rate of change of mass in the system, let us start with the general mass balance equation. Species A are involved in the process; M is the mass of A in the system. Let Mi be the mass flow rate of A entering the system, and M0 the mass flow rate of A leaving. RG is the mass rate of generation of species A by chemical reaction; RC is the mass rate of consumption by reaction. The dimensions of M̂ i, M̂ 0 , RG, and RC are MT–1, with units such as g S–1 and kg h–1. All of the variables: M̂ i , M̂ 0, RG, and RC may vary with time (see Figure 31.1). The terms of the general balance equation may be written as follows. Mass in: During period ∆t, the mass of species A transported into the system M̂ i ∆t. Note that the dimensions of M̂ i ∆t are M, with units g, kg, and so on. Mass out: Similarly, the mass of species A transported out during time ∆t is M̂ 0 ∆t. Generation: The mass of A generated during ∆t is RG ∆t. Consumption: The mass of A consumed during ∆t is RC ∆t. Accumulation: Let ∆M be the mass of A accumulated in the system during ∆t. ∆M may be either positive (accumulation) or negative (depletion). Entering these terms into the general mass balance Equation 31.1 with the accumulation term on the left-hand side: ∆M = Mˆ i ∆t − Mˆ 0 ∆t + RG ∆t − RC ∆t (31.2) We can divide both sides of Equation 31.2 by ∆t to give: ∆M = Mˆ i − Mˆ 0 + RG − RC ∆t Figure 31.1: Flow System for an Unsteady-State Mass Balance. (31.3) Mass Balance Principles Applied to Controlled Atmosphere Chambers 555 Equation 31.3 applies when ∆t is infinitesimally small. If we take the limit as ∆t approaches zero (i.e., as t and t + ∆t become virtually the same), Equation 31.3 represents the system at an instant rather than over an interval of time. Mathematical techniques for handling this type of situation are embodied in the rules of calculus. In calculus, the derivative of y with respect to x, dy/dx, is defined as: ∆y dy = lim dx ∆x→ 0 ∆x (31.4) where ∆lim represents the limit as ∆x approaches zero. x→ 0 Because Equation 31.3 is valid for ∆x → 0, we can write: ∆M dM = lim = Mˆ i − Mˆ 0 + RG − RC ∆ x → 0 ∆t dt (31.5) The derivative dM/dt represents the rate of change of mass with time measured at a particular instant. We have thus derived a differential equation for rate of change of M as a function of system variables M̂ i , M̂ 0, RG, and RC: dM = Mˆ i − Mˆ 0 + RG − RC dt (31.6) At steady-state there can be no change in mass of the system, so the rate of change, dM/dt must be zero. Therefore, Equation 31.6 reduces to the familiar steady-state mass balance equation as given here: mass in + mass generated = mass out + mass consumed Unsteady-state mass balance calculations begin with derivation of a differential equation to describe the process. Equation 31.6 was developed on a mass basis and contains parameters such as mass flow rate M̂ and mass rate of reaction R. Another common form of the unsteady-state mass balance is based on volume. The reason for this variation is that reaction rates are usually expressed on a per-volume basis. For example, the rate of a first-order reaction is expressed in terms of the concentration of reactant: rC = k1CA (31.7) where rC is the volumetric rate of consumption of A by reaction with units (e.g., g cm–3 s–1, k1 is the first-order reaction rate constant, and CA is the concentration of reactant A. When rate expressions are used in mass and energy-balance problems, the relationship between mass and volume must enter the analysis. 556 Chapter 31 Figure 31.2: Continuous Reactor Chamber. 31.2 Unsteady-State Mass Balance Applied to a Reactor Chamber A continuous gas chamber is operated as shown in Figure 31.2. The volume of gas in the chamber is V. Gas enters with volumetric flow rate Fi; product leaves with flow rate F0. The concentration of reactant A in the entering gas stream is CAi; the concentration of A in the exit stream is CAO. The density of the feed stream is ρi; the density of the products stream is ρ0. The concentration of A in the chamber is CA and the density of gas in the chamber is ρ. In the reactor (chamber), component A undergoes reaction and is transformed into compound B. The volumetric rate of consumption of A by reaction is given by the expression rC = k1CA. 31.3 Derivation of a Differential Equation Using Unsteady-State Balance Example 31.1 Derivation of a differential equation using unsteady-state balance for: (a) Total mass (b) Mass of component A for the system parameters shown in Figure 31.2 The general unsteady-state mass-balance equation is Equation 31.6 dM ˆ ˆ +R −R = Mi − M G C 0 dt (a) For the balance on total mass: RG and RC are zero because total mass cannot be generated or consumed or unchanged by chemical reaction. In addition, the density of the system is constant so that ρi = ρ0 = ρ. Under these conditions, the terms on the right-hand side of Equation 31.9 cancel. On the left-hand side, because ρ is constant, it can be taken outside of the differential. This means that the volume of the chamber is constant and independent of time. 558 Chapter 31 31.3.2 Mass Balance for One Component (A) If fruits are placed in a gastight storage chamber, the O2 tension in the store atmosphere will fall as the O2 of the gas is converted by respiratory activity into CO2. The general respiration equation shows this: C6 H12 O 6 + 6O 2 → 6CO 2 + 6H 2 O + 2667 kJ of heat From the equation then, because one volume of O2 will convent to one volume of CO2, the sum of the percentages by volume of these gases in the store will remain constant at its initial value (i.e., the value for normal air is about 21%). When the CO2 concentration reaches a predetermined value say x% by volume, a controlled ventilation of the store with air can be used to maintain the atmosphere composition constant throughout subsequent storage. The O2 concentration will thus be automatically maintained at (21 – x)%. Such conditions have been found satisfactory for some varieties of fruits, but other have been found to require lower O2 concentrations than are attained by this method. For such fruits, a system such as a scrubber using fresh hydrated lime bags is used. The unsteady-state massbalance equation for component A: d (VC A ) = i FC A i − F0 C A 0 − k1C AV dt (31.11) From Equation 31.10 the concentration of component A in the chamber at any time can be calculated by determination of reaction constant (K1). The limitation with this equation is that the determination of reaction constant between O2 and glucose of fruit mass is difficult. This problem is solved by measuring the respiration rate in respect to fruits and vegetables. Because the composition of the gas changes continuously with time, unsteady-state material balance principles and equations can be used for expressing the process of gas equilibrium in a CA chamber. The relevant differential equations can be obtained. The solutions for these equations are useful for calculating instantaneous values of gas components at the state of gas equilibrium in the chamber. 31.4 Mass Balance Applied to Real Controlled Atmosphere Chambers The schematic plan for a typical CA chamber is shown in Figure 31.3. Various possible ways through which the gas can be exchanged in the system are shown in this figure. The inflow and outflow of gas components CO2, O2, and nitrogen (N2) and the possible pathways in the chamber for applying mass balance as shown in this figure are as follows. • Exchange through walls, windows, and cracks due to poor airtightness of the structure. The degree of airtightness is characterized by K. Mass Balance Principles Applied to Controlled Atmosphere Chambers 559 Figure 31.3: Schematic Plan of a Typical CA Chamber. • • • • • Direct introduction of gas mixture of desired concentration of components into the chamber involves the scrubber. Introduction through the selectively permeable membranes (silicon membrane) fixed in the structure of the chamber. The surface area and the permeability coefficients are known. Through the process of respiration of the stored product, the respiration coefficient value is to be known. In the respiration process, there is depletion of O2 and evolution of CO2. Those pathways that are in use during actual operation of chamber only are considered. Except the respiration rates all the remaining can be measured by using proper instrumentation arranged in the chamber. The process of gas exchange with the surrounding medium in the storage is divided into two stages. • • First Stage: Initially, the process must be a continuous one in order to establish the gaseous medium of the desired composition in the storage. The composition of atmosphere in the storage changes continuously affecting the qualitative and quantitative aspects of the gas exchange significantly. Second Stage: After the desired atmosphere is established in the storage chambers, the gas exchange becomes stable. The organization of gas equilibrium reflects to a great extent the characteristics of the storage itself. The length for which the desired level of gas composition of the medium is maintained 560 Chapter 31 is of considerable practical significance. It determines the necessity of examining the gas equilibrium in storage during a nonstationary period. The same schematic diagram can also be used for a chamber operating to establish gas regime through the physiological activity of the product. The gas equilibrium in the chamber with CA may be expressed by a system of differential equations that are based on the law of conservation of mass.
