CHAPTE R 32 Gas Generators for Controlled Atmosphere Storage Controlled atmosphere storage indicates removal or addition of gases resulting in an atmosphere around the fruits and vegetables that is different from that of air. Usually this involves the reduction of oxygen (O2) and the elevation of carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration. In this chapter, low-cost and high-cost controlled atmosphere facilities are discussed. 32.1 Low-Cost Methods for Controlled Atmosphere Storage Controlled atmosphere (CA) with low-cost devices is used as a supplement to and not as a substitute for proper temperature and relative humidity (RH) management. Some simple methods for modifying the composition of air in the storage chamber are given here. 32.1.1 CO2 Scrubber The CO2 Scrubber is shown in Figure 32.1. To regulate CO2 levels in a CA room, one of the simplest methods is the hydrated lime (calcium carbonate) Ca(OH)2 “scrubber.” The scrubber is constructed using an insulated and airtight plywood box located outside the CA room. The box should contain enough lime for the entire storage period, but new lime can be added if CO2 absorption drops. The CO2 and hydrated lime react in a 1:1 ratio to form limestone and water. Lime with a smaller particle size (fine mesh) is more efficient at reacting with CO2 than lime with a coarse mesh. The following will maximize the effectiveness of a small scrubber: • • • Lime should be packaged in 25 kg bags that have no polyethylene liner (Figure 32.1). Each bag should be only partially filled (50%) to avoid outer layer hardening and a reduction in efficiency over time. Lime bags should be stacked on a pallet equipped with shelves that allow a 10 cm space between layers to maximize air circulation. Fifty percent of the recommended lime for the anticipated storage period can be placed on pallets on the floor of the storage room, which will consume the initially high CO2 produced by the fruit. Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00032-4 565 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 566 Chapter 32 Figure 32.1: CO2 Scrubber in a CA Room. To keep CO2 below 2%, about 12 kg of lime per metric ton of apples is recommended for 3–4 months of storage. For preventing the buildup of ethylene, a simple scrubber can be constructed and added to the air supply line. 32.2 Low-Cost Controlled Atmosphere Storage for Pallet Loads CA storage of pallet loads of produce is also possible using a semipermanent setup for creating a gas seal. Any number of pallets can be accommodated inside a plastic tent made using 7–8 mil polyethylene sheeting. A better gas barrier at the floor (compared with the traditional tube in trough method) can be obtained by laying a sheet of 4–5 mil polyethylene on the floor and covering it with wood panels. The seal is then made by joining the tent plastic with the floor plastic (using tape). 32.3 Ethylene Control To decrease ethylene, the following are used: • • • Potassium permanganate Activated charcoal Catalytic oxidation Gas Generators for Controlled Atmosphere Storage 567 Figure 32.2: Air Passage Through Pallet. For an ethylene scrubber, place Purafil pellets—potassium permanganate (KMnO4)—in shallow layers on screen trays sealed inside a solid wooden box. Air must flow through three or four trays of pallets for successful removal of ethylene gas (see Figure 32.2). Another simple practice that can be used to store produce under CA conditions involves constructing plastic tents (see Figure 32.3) using 20 mil polyvinylchloride (PVC) sheeting suspended over traditional pallet racks inside a refrigerated cold storage warehouse. Figure 32.4 shows two CA tents. On the left, the top of the tent has been sealed by closing zippers on both sides of the door and immersing the bottom of the door and adjacent floor panel in a trough of water. The trough is made using a 6 in diameter PVC pipe (with one-third of the pipe cut away), which also allows supply and sampling gas lines and temperature probe wiring to pass into the tent. All seams and joints of the tents are heat-welded. On the right, the tent is shown with the door rolled open and one pallet load of produce loaded into the tent (Figure 32.4). 32.4 Low-Cost Controlled Atmosphere Plastic Tent for Bananas A low-cost plastic tent (shown in Figure 32.5) fabricated from clear polyethylene sheeting can be used for CA storage of bunches of green bananas. A small fan serves to circulate the CA storage air (2% O2 and 5% CO2) through a chamber of KMnO4 on aluminum oxide 568 Chapter 32 Figure 32.3: Typical Layout of a CA Tent. (Purafil). Ripening is delayed as ethylene is scrubbed from the storage air. The shelf life of bananas under these conditions is 4–6 weeks at ambient temperatures. 32.5 High-Cost Methods for Controlled Atmosphere Storage The normal water vapor barrier provided for cold storage is insufficient for CA storage, and the required barrier is often provided by metal sheet or foil cladding on the store walls or by multilayer bituminous preparations. Close attention must be paid to sealing doorways. Metal Figure 32.4: Plastic Tents. Gas Generators for Controlled Atmosphere Storage 569 Figure 32.5: Controlled Atmosphere Storage of Bananas in Bunches at Ambient Temperature. gastight covers may be fitted across door openings behind a normal insulated door of the cold store. If fruit is placed in such a gastight storage chamber, the O2 tension in the store atmosphere will fall as this gas is converted by respiratory activity into CO2. Because one volume of O2 will convert to one volume of CO2, the sum of the percentages by volume of these gases in the store will remain constant at its initial value (i.e., the value for normal are about 21%) when the CO2 concentration reaches a predetermined value (say x% by volume) a controlled ventilation of the store with air can be used to maintain the atmosphere composition constant throughout subsequent storage. The O2 concentration will thus be automatically maintained at (21 – x)%. Such conditions have been found satisfactory for some varieties of fruits, but others have been found to require lower O2 concentration than are attained by this method. For such a fruit system, the rate of supply of O2 by ventilation with fresh air is required. The excess CO2 produced by respiration is removed by feeding the storage atmosphere at a controlled rate to a scrubber. In Table 32.1, the diversity of optional storage atmosphere in terms of temperature O2 and CO2 concentration for different fruits is given. 32.6 Controlled Atmosphere Chamber The CA storage process is the most important innovation in fruit and vegetable storage since the introduction of mechanical refrigeration. This method, if combined with refrigeration, markedly slows respiratory activity and may delay softening, yellowing, spoilage, and other breakdown processes by maintaining an atmosphere with CO2 and less O2 than in normal air. Its development illustrates the successful transmission of a scientific concept from laboratory to large-scale commercial use (Figure 32.6). 570 Chapter 32 Table 32.1: Optimal CA storage for different fruits and vegetables Fruit Apple Apricot Avocado Banana Blackberry Blueberry Cherry Cranberry Fig Grape Grapefruit Kiwi fruit Lemon and lime Mango Nectarine Olive Papaya Orange Peach Pear Pineapple Temperature Range (°C) O2 Concentration (%) CO2 Concentration (%) 0–5 0–5 5–13 12–15 0–5 0–5 0–5 2–5 0–5 0–5 10–15 0–5 10–15 10–15 0–5 5–10 10–15 5–10 0–5 0–5 10–15 2–3 2–3 2–5 2–5 5–10 5–10 3–10 1–2 5–10 2–5 3–10 2 5–10 5 1–2 2–5 5 5–10 1–2 2–3 5 1–2 1–2 3–10 2–5 15–20 15–20 10–12 0–5 15–20 1–3 5–10 5 0–10 5 3–5 5–10 10 0–5 5 0–1 10 Figure 32.6: Controlled Atmosphere Chamber. Gas Generators for Controlled Atmosphere Storage 571 Today more than half the total holdings of apples in the United States and citrus in Israel are stored under CA conditions. 32.7 Gas Generators The creation of an artificial gaseous atmosphere in storage is often done with the help of special generators. Gas mixtures obtained in them are the combustion products of fuel gases. Golden Delicious apples can be stored successfully in about 3% O2 and 3–4% CO2. The new varieties, however, demand a lower O2 rate between 1.8% and 2.2%. This level is called ultra low oxygen (ULO) storage. The recommended CO2 percentage for new apple varieties is also quite low, 2% and even lower. CA installations have had to be redesigned to accommodate these lower values for O2 and CO2, necessitating better gastight insulation techniques and computerized control systems. Various types of apparatus are used to control the atmosphere, such as scrubbers, burners, and more recently membrane gas separators and molecular sieve systems. The O2 content in the products of combustion is less than in the atmosphere in which combustion takes place, and the CO2 content is more. A gas mixture having the desired composition and temperature is obtained after cooling and purification of the combustion products for excess CO2 and other gases. Air is the medium for combustion of fuel gases in the generators. 32.7.1 Scrubbers A scrubber is a gas absorber. A good scrubber must be able to: • • • • Bring the concentration of CO2 down to suitable values in a short time after loading the storage room. Maintain the value within tight limits during storage without affecting the O2 concentration. Regulate the atmosphere during the ripening period. Absorb other volatile gases when storing vegetables or citrus fruit. The old system utilizes 25 kg bags of high calcium lime Ca(OH2), which is still practiced in some countries. For each ton of Cox’s apples, five bags of Ca(OH2) are required, while three bags are needed for 10 tons of Boskoop, Winston, Melrose, or Golden Delicious apples. A bag lasts 6–10 weeks. Among all the systems tried to date, the activated carbon scrubber system meets most of these requirements. 32.7.2 Methods for Reducing Percentage of O2 Two methods are used to reduce the O2 percentage. The first method is called natural method in which the fruits consume O2 as part of the natural respiration process. This method is slow and requires about 2–3 weeks to reduce to 2% O2. The second method is by burning fuel, 572 Chapter 32 which can take place either by using conventional burners or catalytic burners. With conventional burners, a gas mixture with 1.5–2% O2 can be obtained, whereas with catalytic burners the combustion products with 1% O2 can be obtained. In conventional cases, the efficiency of the gas generator depends on the free volume of storage and the time it takes to attain the desired gas regime. The second method uses forced burning of O2 by means of special burners. There are three type of burners mainly used today. 1. Catalytic burners 2. NH3 cracker 3. Molecular sieve system In order to reduce the O2 from the original 21% to the desired 3% or to today’s ULO value of less than 2%, the room is connected to the burner by plastic tubes through which air or rather N2 is blown. The original cold store air containing 21% O2 leaves the cold store via an exhaust valve. In modern practice, the burner first reduces the O2 concentration down to 5% and then the fruit itself is allowed to bring the value down to 2% by natural respiration. Air can be a medium of combustion of gases in the generators. In this case, the gas mixture obtained is supplied to the chambers where it replaces the existing atmosphere. Such generators relate to the washing type of devices. When conventional burners are used, the maximum concentration of O2 in them is 2%, but in case of catalytic burners it is 1%. Because it is always necessary to remove excess O2 from the chamber when the generators are working, generators that utilize recirculation have been developed in which not just the outside air, but also the air in the chamber is used for combustion of gases. In generators of this type, special catalytic burners can be used to burn the fuel gas quite thoroughly in the medium with low O2 content. In others generators, both outside air and air of the chamber are used for combustion with partial recirculation of the air of the chamber. Generators of gas mixtures work under two situations: 1. During the initial development of the desired composition of gas mixture in the chamber 2. When the desired composition of gas mixture has been attained and must be maintained with the help of various devices in the chambers during storage In the first case, when the generator first begins functioning, the air in the chamber usually has no CO2, but an O2 content of 0.21. This regime is generally used as the basis for determining the capacity of the generator because the workload of the device is most intensive during the time when the desired gas composition is being created in the chamber. A modern technique of fuel-gas combustion makes it possible, with the help of conventional burners, to obtain combustion products containing not less than 1.5–2.0% O2. While supplying Gas Generators for Controlled Atmosphere Storage 573 these combustion products to the chambers, the quantity of O2 in them can be increased to approximately 3%. 32.7.3 Catalytic Burner System The operation of the catalytic burner systems is shown in Figure 32.7. In this system, a ventilator sucks the air out of the cold store through a plastic tube system and pushes it over an active carbon filter that absorbs the CO2. After some time, which may be Figure 32.7: Catalytic Burner Systems. (a) Scrubbing; (b) Regeneration; (c) Regeneration with Lung. 574 Chapter 32 different for every store and product, the scrubber becomes saturated with CO2 and needs to be regenerated, as shown in Figure 32.7(a). This is done by disconnecting it from the cold store and connecting it to the outside air, as shown in Figure 32.7(b). At the end of the regeneration or desorption process, the scrubber is disconnected from outside air and connected to a “lung” that looks like a large plastic balloon of about 5 m3 or more capacity, depending on the capacity of the plant and on the lung air where the low O2 content is stored, as shown in Figure 32.7(c). The air with low O2 enters into the cold chamber. This process ensures that the cold chamber is filled with air of low O2 content after the regeneration operation. The equalizing values of cold stores for CA storage are also equipped with a small lung, the volume of which is calculated in such a way that it can cope with volume changes of the air in the cold store. The capacity must be adequate to bring the room to the desired percentage within 3 days. 32.7.4 Ammonia Cracker Burner System The schematic diagram of an ammonia (NH3) cracker burner is shown in Figure 32.8. The ammonia is first cracked as follows: 2 NH 3 → N 2 + 3H 2 The mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen is then burned with the O2 of the cold store air. 2 N 2 + 6 H 2 + 3O 2 → 2 N 2 + 6 H 2 O Figure 32.8: Ammonia Cracker Burner System. Gas Generators for Controlled Atmosphere Storage 575 In other generators, both outside air and the air in the chamber are used for combustion with partial recirculation of the air of the chamber. 32.8 Fuels for Gas Preparation Propane, methane, or natural gas is burned using outside air over a catalyst at high temperature without a flame. The air leaving the burner will consist mostly of N2 (86.5%), the remainder being O2 (1.5%) and CO2 (12%), removed by passing it over the scrubber before it enters the cold store. The fuel must contain 95% methane with less than 5% propane or butane. There must be a maximum of 1.5–2% propylene, butadiene, and so on. The sulphur content should not exceed a value between 0.25 g/m3 and 0.3 g/m3. An alternative fuel specification is 95% propane, with 1.5–2% nonsaturated hydrocarbons and 0.25 g/m3 sulphur, the remainder being made up of butane, n-butane, and isobutene. When using propane, it is better to use a tank rather than bottles. In a bottle, the heaviest elements collect at the bottom and the lightest at the top. The resulting gas composition makes it difficult to regulate the burning process. 32.9 Types of Generators A circulating-type generator called “Tectrol,” used in the United States, is shown in Figure 32.9. Another generator widely used in the United States is the recirculating type, “Arcat.” This device is shown in Figure 32.10. Generators of circulation type with direct or catalytic burners and generators of recirculating type with catalytic burners have been manufactured in the United States and Russia. Generators in which the combustion of gases is done in the air are used mainly in the United Figure 32.9: Circulating-Type Gas Generator—Tectrol. 576 Chapter 32 Figure 32.10: Recirculating-Type Gas Generator—Arcat. States, France, and Italy to create low concentration of O2 (up to 2–3%) in the chamber. The use of catalytic burners makes it possible to prevent the danger of emergence of combustion products harmful to fruits, which can be formed when the combustion of gas is carried out in an atmosphere with a low concentration of O2. The Institute of Gas, the Academy of Science of Ukrainian SSR, and the global energy company Gazprom have developed the KGS-3-P generator, which is meant for obtaining the desired gas regime through the combustion of either natural or liquid gas. The schematic diagram of the unit is shown in Figure 32.11. The stages and functioning of the KGS-3-P generator include the following: 1. Combustion of propane gas with coefficient of excess air a = 1.1. 2. Cooling of combustion products up to t = 20°C. 3. Complete or partial removal of CO2 by passing the combustion product through 15% water solution of monoethanolamine (MEA). 4. The MEA solution saturated with CO2 passes to the solution collector, while the gas mixture, free from CO2, is cooled to 20°C by water. Gas Generators for Controlled Atmosphere Storage 577 Figure 32.11: Schematic Diagram of the KGS-3-P Generator. 5. At a temperature of about 20°C, the gas mixture passes into a drop separator where drops of MEA are separated from it. 6. If there is no need to remove the CO2 anymore, the gas mixture is supplied to the storage chamber. The composition of the gas mixture being supplied to the storage chamber: Without absorption: 2% O2, 12% CO2, 86% N2 With absorption: 2% O2, 0–12% CO2, 98–86% N2 The URGS-30 generator is meant for the prolonged storage of vegetable produce. It consists of two independent units: a generator unit and a purification unit. The principal diagram of the URGS-30 gas generator is shown in Figure 32.12 and technical data provided in Table 32.2. In the generator, the gas mixture of the desired composition and temperature is processed. Its composition is determined by the coefficient of excess air, and its temperature is determined by the quantity of water supplied for cooling. In the purification units, the gas mixture absorbs CO2 up to the essential concentrations. This is done by purification up to zero concentration of CO2 of a part of the entire quantity of gas mixture coming from the generator unit or chamber (Table 32.2). The special feature of the URGS-30 is that the generator and purification units may function either individually or simultaneously. This device works on liquid gas that is supplied to it through RV-55 type reductor with two cylinders, each with a capacity of 21 kg. Gas from the cylinders and air from compressor are supplied to the mixing burner and then to the combustion chamber where catalytic flameless combustion takes place. 578 Chapter 32 Figure 32.12: Schematic Diagram of the URGS-30 Generator. Size of purification unit, m L = 1.48, w = 0.78, H = 1.7 Gas Generators for Controlled Atmosphere Storage 579 Partial cooling of the combustion products begins in the combustion chamber, which is provided with a recuperator where the temperature is lowered to 800°C. The supply air to the recuperator is accomplished tangentially by its blower. Heated air coming out of the recuperator is diluted with the surrounding air in the injector, and then supplied to the premise for heating with a low temperature. Combustion products enter the first part of the refrigerator where they come into contact with the cold surface of the coil, and their temperature is reduced from 800°C to 50°C. When dew point is attained (62.5°C), deposition of the condensate begins, which is collected in the condensate collector. Through the condensate collector, the combustion products enter the second part of the refrigerator and are cooled to 10–20°C, while the condensed moisture on the trays of the drop separator returns to the condensate collector. The cooled combustion products are then directed to the first filter of the purification unit through the tube with a tap where, for the first 2 minutes, O2 from the air of the intergranular space is pumped to the spark plug through the solenoid valve. During the subsequent 8 min of the 10-min semicycle, the gas mixture is completely purified of CO2, and then supplied to the fruit storage chamber through the solenoid valve and distributing collector. The second filter of the purification unit is regenerated by the air with the help of a ventilator during the 10 min of the first semicycle. In the second 10-min semicycle, the gas mixture automatically goes to the second filter while the first filter is regenerated by air. Capacity of Chamber (tons) Up to 50 50–100 100–150 150–250 Approximate Efficiency (m3/h) 20 40 60 100 For Catalytic Burners (m3/h) 15 30 45 75 32.10 Efficiency of Generators The efficiency of generators is determined by the following formula: Vm = 3.0 Vc 3 m /h t where Vc is the volume of gas mixture in the container, m3 t is the time taken to attain the desired regime, h (32.1) 580 Chapter 32 Generators can also work with catalytic burners, and the content of O2 in the combustion products can then be kept at 1%. In this case, the following formula applies: V Vm = 2.3 c m 3/h t (32.2) Thus in ordinary cases, the efficiency of the generator depends on the free volume of the store and the time it takes to attain the desired gas regime. As shown by research conducted by R. M. Smock, the optimum length of time for attaining the desired gas regime in the chamber is 20–24 h. For this duration and usual combustion of gas, the required efficiency of generators, depending on the capacity of the chamber, is discussed in the following sections. 32.11 Calculation of Pull-Down Time The pull-down time is the time necessary to bring a room with an O2 concentration of 21% down to a desired percentage. Example 32.1 Let fruit density be 500 kg/m3 Total quantity of fruits = T tons Volume of fruits V2 = T/500 m3 Let the total volume of room = V1 m3 Volume of air in the room V3 = V1 – V2 m3 If the volume after pull-down is V4 m3, this value can be calculated by the law of replacement: V4 = C0V3 ln(C1 / C2 ) Where C0 is a factor dependent on the gastightness of the room, the air circulation rate, and O2 leakage rate. A value of 1.3 for C0 is considered reasonable. C1 is the initial percentage of O2, and C2 is the required percentage of O2. If we know the volume V5 of gas produced by burner per unit time, the time necessary for pull-down is calculated as: Pull-down time = V4/V5 h Gas Generators for Controlled Atmosphere Storage 581 32.12 Factors Affecting Time of Stabilization Experiments have shown that the time to reach stable gas levels takes days to weeks, depending upon the following factors: 1. 2. 3. 4. Commodity respiration Designed gas composition Relative stacking volume (RSV) Airtightness Rapid O2 pull-down is technique that drops the O2 concentration of the storage atmosphere to optimal immediately after sealing the chamber. It can be easily achieved by nitrogen flushing. RSV = Volume of produce Totalstorage volume RSV is the measure of the initial buffering of the membrane-produce interaction by the free air in the storage room. The time of stabilization decreases with RSV. Therefore, it is important to properly plan the stacking geometry of the storage room without affecting the air circulation pattern, and ventilation requirements may have to be increased to prevent condensation. 32.13 Design Gas Levels The closer the design gas levels are to ambient, the more rapidly stabilization will occur. In general, the degree of airtightness affects the O2 stabilization time more than the CO2 stabilization time. Standard free volume (SFV) is ratio of air per unit volume of the produce: SFV = RSV Volume of Produce The SFV is typically 1.5–3.0 for warehouse commodity stacking and depends on room geometry, commodity shape and density, and whether the produce is packed in bulk or crated. 32.14 Air Infiltration Rate Air infiltration rate (AIR) reflects the degree of airtightness of the storage room and is usually defined as the number of air exchanges per day when the room is empty. AIR is mainly due to barometric pressure fluctuation, wind, and temperature gradients between the storage room and the ambient environment, and the cyclical operation of the refrigeration system, room orientation, and warehouse management strategy. 582 Chapter 32 The standard technique for determining the AIR of the room consists of pressuring the in­ terior to 250 kPa and determining the time taken for the pressure to drop to the standard of 125 kPa. If this time is 10 minutes, for example, the room is regarded as a 10-min room, which is roughly equivalent to 0.0333 air changes per day. Further Readings Krishnamurthy, S., 1989. CHAPTE R 33 Equipment for Producing and Regulating Controlled Atmosphere Many different methods and devices are being used for establishing and maintaining a given gas regime in the chambers meant for the preservation of fruits. In all of these, the biggest problem lies in the absorption or release of surplus CO2 and O2. The choice of method and equipment depends on the following factors: • • • • Atmosphere adopted for the purpose Extent of airtightness of the storage Energy-producing resources Economic consideration In this chapter, various devices used for creating and regulating the controlled atmosphere (CA) are discussed. 33.1 Scrubbers In fruit storages in CA, several types of scrubbers are being employed. One group consists of scrubbers in which the absorbent is replaced completely when saturated with CO2. Solution of alkalis such as KOH, NaOH, dry slaked lime, and so on are used in these scrubbers. A scrubber working on dry slaked lime shown in Figure 33.1 consists of an airtight chamber in which bags containing 20–40 kg of dry slaked lime are kept on racks. The gas mixture from the chamber is sent into the scrubber and then under pressure it passes through the base where the lime reacts with CO2 gas. The purified mixture then returns to the chamber. It requires 6–10 kg of slaked lime per ton of fruit to maintain a subnormal gas mixture in the chamber for a period of 1 month. Table 33.1 provides more specific rates for apples and pears. 33.1.1 Scrubbing CO2 with Hydrated Lime In developing countries such as India, Bangladesh, and Pakistan, perhaps the simplest method of controlling CO2 levels is through hydrated lime scrubbers, Ca(OH)2. This scrubber is an insulated and sealed plywood box usually containing between half and the total amount of lime required to remove the CO2 produced during the entire storage Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00033-6 583 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 584 Chapter 33 Figure 33.1: Plan of Scrubber Working on Dry Slaked Lime. Table 33.1: CO2 scrub capacity rates for apples and pears Variety Cox’s Orange Boskoop Golden Delicious Jonah Gold Conference Rate (kg CO2/100 ton·day) 35 29 10 14 10 period. The box is connected to the CA room and airflow to it may be left to natural convection or controlled by forced airflow using blowers and dampers. The choice between natural convection and forced flow depends on the commodity respiration characteristics, the room airtightness, quality, and the relative stacking volume (RSV) or Standard free volume (SFV). The efficiency of the lime bag drops with time as it becomes saturated with CO2. The level of efficiency is thus easily determined by simply weighting the bag. A 22 kg bag of hydrated lime weighs 30 kg at its maximum CO2 holding capacity. It is recommended that bags no heavier than 25 kg be used, because crusting of the outer layer may occur in larger bags, thus reducing the efficiency of CO2 absorption. 33.1.2 Scrubbing CO2 with Water There are two types of water scrubbers for CO2. One type is the brine scrubber in which brine is pumped over evaporator coils, solubilizes CO2, and is pumped to an external reservoir (Figure 33.2) and then to an aerator that causes the CO2 to escape to the atmosphere. Dry evaporator coils are used to prevent corrosion. Equipment for Producing and Regulating Controlled Atmosphere 585 Figure 33.2: Brine-Water CO2 Scrubber. Figure 33.3: Modified Brine-Water CO2 Scrubber Equipped with Two Aerators. Smock and others modified the system in Figure 33.2 using two aerators, one internal and one external, as shown in Figure 33.3. The scrubber should be designed on the basis of the quantity, respiration rate, and CO2 level required by the commodity. In application to apple storage, Pflug recommended a circulation rate of 100 per hour per ton of apples stored, based on a recommended atmosphere of 5% CO2 and 2% O2 and a temperature of 1°C. The scrubbing capacity is 0.02 m3 of CO2 removed per m3 of water circulating through the scrubber. This volume is four times lower than the theoretical scrubbing capacity of water under these conditions: that is, 0.086 m3 CO2 per m3 of water with a CO2 differential of 5%. 33.1.3 Scrubbing CO2 with Activated Charcoal and Other Molecular Sieves Activated charcoal and molecular sieve scrubber units are fitted with the respective absorbers, two blowers, and four timer-controlled valves (Figure 33.4). Air from the CA room is circulated to the scrubber, where CO2 is absorbed. The CO2-depleted air is returned to the storage room. When the absorbent is saturated, outside air is circulated through the scrubber and back to the outside to remove the CO2. If a molecular sieve is used, it is also heated to speed up the 586 Chapter 33 Figure 33.4: Activated Charcoal CO2 Scrubber. reactivation process. These systems have low operating costs, and the absorbent lifetime is about 5 years. 33.2 Ethylene Control System Ethylene may be removed from the storage atmosphere by a heated catalyst system such as that developed by Blanpied and tested in a McIntosh apple storage facility. The unit is shown in Figure 33.5. Storage air is blown through two electrically heated ceramic banks in which the ethylene is oxidized to yield CO2 and water vapor. The air leaving the unit is cooled before being returned to the storage room. It was found that the scrubber removed 87% of the C2H4 produced by the stored apples, but required an airflow of 142 L/s. The ceramic packing configuration could be modified to facilitate airflow and reduce the required fan power (which was 7.5 kW). Figure 33.5: Heated Catalyst System for C2H4 Scrubbing. Equipment for Producing and Regulating Controlled Atmosphere 587 An alternative to the heated catalyst system is the use of an absorbent bead scrubber that contains aluminum silicate spheres mixed with potassium permanganate (KMnO4), which is used as an absorbency indicator. The beads are held in a container through which the storage air is circulated. As the beads become saturated, the KMnO4 turns the beads from purple to brown, thus simplifying maintenance. The number of units required depends on the size of the storage room and the expected C2H4 production from the stored commodity. However, more data are needed to determine the C2H4 production rates in a system with C2H4 removal. It is likely that C2H4 production rates diminish with removal because autocatalysis is reduced. About 280 kg of beads are recommended in two units (each equipped with a 280 L/s fan) for a 360 m3 storage room for McIntosh apples. 33.3 Oxygen Control Systems 33.3.1 External Gas Generators External gas generators operate either on the open-flame (Figure 33.6) or catalytic burnet principle to remove O2 from the incoming air. Heat may be recovered or the exhaust air may be water-spray cooled before being blown into the storage room. The disadvantages of these types of system are that fuel is required and a CO2 scrubber must also be used to remove excess CO2. The advantages of these systems are the flexibility of operation and the rapidity with which O2 is depleted in the initial stages of storage, compared to a membrane-only system. The catalytic system is preferable in ensuring better combustion and fewer plant-toxic or plant-activating combustion products. External burners are recommended for rapid O2 pull-down. Catalytic burners are more expensive to install when used in a recirculating configuration but have lower operating costs. Figure 33.6: External Gas Generator. 588 Chapter 33 However, flushing systems are easier to maintain because they do not require the frequent adjustments characteristic of catalytic burners. If the storage room is well-sealed, relative to the standard free volume and commodity respiration activity, it is often only necessary to operate the burners during the initial O2 reduction stage. Thereafter, infiltrating air combined with commodity respiration and operation of the CO2 scrubber can maintain close to optimal conditions. 33.4 Liquid Nitrogen Atmospheric Generators Flushing the storage room with sprayed liquid nitrogen is an excellent method for establishing the controlled atmosphere condition rapidly. The spraying heads that atomize the liquid N2 are best placed in front of evaporator blowers. An O2 sensor is used to determine whether further spraying is needed. To maintain the recommended O2 level, bags are used to absorb excess CO2. 33.5 Gas Separator Systems The two commercially available gas separator systems are the pressure swing adsorption (PSA) system and the hollow-fiber membrane (HFM) system. Both systems are used primarily for rapid O2 pull-down and can be used in flushing or recirculating modes to control the CO2 level during storage. PSA systems work on the following principle (Figure 33.7): A stream of air is compressed, filtered, and circulated through a molecular sieve that selectively absorbs O2. The Figure 33.7: Pressure Swing Adsorption System. Equipment for Producing and Regulating Controlled Atmosphere 589 air stream leaving the unit consists mainly of N2, and O2 is then released from the sieve by depressurizing the vessel and is vented to the outside. Typically, two units are mounted in parallel such that absorption and desorption may be carried out without affecting the flow of N2-rich air. The opening and closing sequences of the valves are microprocessor-controlled. Depending on the level of pressurization (usually 70 kPa) and the temperature, the purity of the N2 gas is between 90% and 99.9%. According to Bartsch, the energy consumption of the PSA in apple storage applications is 1 kW h/m3 of apples. 33.6 Hollow-Fiber Membrane Systems HFM systems are based on hollow fibers made of semipermeable membranes. Air compressed to about 700 kPa is heated to 38°C, filtered, and forced into the HFM unit. Because the membranes are more permeable to O2 and CO2, these gases pass to the external-flow stream and vent to the atmosphere, while the N2-rich stream continues to the storage room and purges O2 (Figure 33.8). The energy consumption in CA storage of apples is about 1.5 kWh/m3 of apples. 33.7 Hypobaric Storage Low-pressure storage by means of a vacuum pump has the advantages of easy manipulation of the effective O2 concentration and relative humidity (RH) level of the storage enclosure. CO2, C2H4, and other volatiles of metabolism are removed. This system also permits the storage of noncompatible commodities. However, due to the low required pressure (1.3–13 kPa), there are significant costs associated with storage room structure and airtightness quality needed for efficient pump operation. Moreover, commodities requiring high CO2 levels cannot be accommodated, and some quality characteristics can be affected (e.g., flavor). Figure 33.8: Hollow-Fiber Membrane System. 590 Chapter 33 33.8 Diffusion Gas Exchanger (Marcellin System) In fruit storage in a number of countries, a new and original system of controlling the atmosphere of cold storages is being used that does not involve the use of scrubber. This system was developed in France by Professor P. Marcellin. The function of the system is based on the principle of selective permeability of gases through plastic membranous materials. The composition of the gas mixture in the chamber is regulated by a special apparatus known as a diffusion gas exchanger. Its gas exchange surface is made of a silicon rubber membrane that has a greater permeability for CO2 than for O2 and N2, as shown in Figure 33.9. The composition of the head space gas is analyzed to determine whether more bags should be used. Typical recommendations are 50 m2 of membrane surface area for each 100 tons of produce at a bulk density of 200–250 kg/m–3 (standard free volume of 2.9–3.6 m3) to maintain an atmosphere of roughly 3% O2 and 3% CO2. The units can be installed inside or outside the cold room. Walls of the membranes form a number of parallel channels (bags) through which the chamber air circulates with the help of built-in blowers. As a result of diffusion of gases, the excess CO2, C2H4, odorous solid substances, and some nitrogen are removed from the air circulating through the membrane. During the process, the air is enriched with a small amount of O2 from the surrounding atmosphere. Because of the fact that the permeability of the membrane differs for CO2 and O2, the quantity of CO2 in the atmosphere of the chamber is reduced considerably faster than the rate of increase of O2. Therefore, it is possible to maintain in the chamber a subnormal gas regime in which the total content of CO2 and O2 is less than 21%. Figure 33.9: Diffusion Gas Exchanger for Regulation of Atmosphere. Equipment for Producing and Regulating Controlled Atmosphere 591 The working surface of the gas exchanger is chosen according to calculations for maintaining an optimum regime for fruit storage automatically in the chamber. Parts of the surface can be disconnected with the help of clamps mounted on flexible plastic tubes that connect the channels with the distributing air collector. Special intermediate rings restrict the expansion of channels and thus reduce the contact of gas mixture with the membrane. One or more axial blowers positioned above the apparatus create air circulation outside the channels and help in removal of CO2 and other volatile substances from the atmosphere. Special air filters of fine air scrubber prevent the inner walls of the channels from contamination. The air filter is positioned directly in the chamber at the point of air suction in the apparatus. This placement has the advantage of elimination of moisture condensation on the working surface of the filter and increases the efficiency and dependability of its operation. The operation of the gas exchanger is controlled by a differential inclined micrometer and electric signal panel with magnetic stretch of the electric motor of the blowers. 33.8.1 Diffusion Walls Silicon elastomers are the most suitable material for construction of diffusing walls of the gas exchanger. These types of scrubbers are highly permeable by C2H4-scented substances, O2, and CO2. Their permeability to O2 and particularly to CO2 does not depend on temperature, even in the relatively wide range of 0–30°C. No chemical change takes place in the structure of the silicon elastomer, even at temperatures ranging from –30°C to 180°C. Rhone-Poulenc of France produced different specimens of cloth that were coated with silicon elastomers whose permeability by CO2 per unit surface changed according to the weight of silicon per 1 m2 of material and difference of partial pressure (concentrations) of CO2 on either side of the cloth. With silicon weight of 80 g/m2, the permeability of this silicon cloth to CO2 is 250 times higher than that of 0.5 mm thick polythene membrane. The permeability of the silicon cloth by O2 gas is approximately six times less than that of CO2. Diffusion gas exchangers for cold storages with capacities of 50–850 tons are commercially available. 33.8.2 Construction Details of Diffuser Exchanger The main body of the apparatus is made of 2 mm thick forged steel sheets, which are protected with an anticorrosive coating. The distributing and receiving collectors as well as the air tubes connecting the apparatus with chamber are made of plastic tubes and molded parts with various couplings. Airtightness (sealing) of the tube couplings is ensured by rubber linings and sealing mastic. 592 Chapter 33 The diffusion surface of the apparatus is determined according to the temperature of storage and the type and quantity of fruit to be stored. For example at 2°C, the specific surface of diffusion bags comes to 0.43, and at 10–12°C, it is 0.86 m2 per ton of Golden Delicious apple in commercial trail of diffusion chamber. A commercial trail with an airtight cold chamber of about 1,200 m3 capacity (20 m × 8.5 m × 7 m) has stored 250 ton of apples for 185 days. During this trail, temperature of 3°C, humidity of 90–95%, and a gas composition of 2.3– 3.5% O2 and 3.5–4.0% CO2 were maintained. By artificial means, 1200 m3 of nitrogen was supplied to the chamber room after it was loaded and sealed in order to reduce the O2 concentration quickly and to bring the chamber to the desired gas regime. The specific surface of the diffusion walls of the gas exchanger was 0.6 m2; the air circulation through the chamber was 5 L/min per ton of fruit stored. The gas exchange surface of the apparatus was 150 m2, with the permeability of the silicon membrane to CO2 being 1730 L/m2·day·atm, and weight being 80 g/m2. Positive results were obtained in the trial with good performance indices and the reliability of the apparatus being confirmed. 33.8.3 Primary Instructions for Using a Diffusion Chamber Before starting the gas exchanger, all preparatory operations in the chamber should be done well in advance. • • • • Air cooling unit is switched on. Chamber is loaded with fruits. Temperature in the chamber is stable in the range of 2–3°C. Airtightness of the chamber doorways is ensured. (The degree of air tightness of the chamber must correspond to the time of falling pressure from 15–7.5 mm of water column within no less than 15 min). 33.9 Establishment of Gas Regime Gas regime is established by enhancing the process of oxygen reduction so as to reduce the time required for achieving the desired gas regime. This can be done by introducing an artificially prepared gas mixture of N2 and CO2 into the chamber or “burning out” O2 from the atmosphere of the chamber. If these steps are not taken, the gas exchanger is started only after achieving an 8–10% concentration of CO2 in the chamber. In such case, only half of the silicon bags are switched on initially. The remaining bags are disconnected with the help of clamps and are gradually brought to working condition according to subsequent changes in the concentration of O2 and CO2 in the chamber. Equipment for Producing and Regulating Controlled Atmosphere 593 When these enhancing steps are used, the gas exchanger apparatus is switched on the moment the desired gas regime is established in the chamber. In this case, all silicon bags of the apparatus are switched on in the beginning, and then some are switched off as the regime changes and the optimum quantity of working bags is determined. 33.10 Operations Required to Start the Gas Exchanger The following sequence is required to start the gas exchanger: 1. Ventilators are switched on to ensure the circulation of air outside the silicon bags. 2. Ventilators are switched on to circulate the gas mixture of the chamber through the bags. 3. From the micromanometer, the pressure in the bags is established at a level not exceeding 3.5–4.0 mm of water column by regulating the damper built into the distributing and receiving collectors to reduce or increase the velocity of the movement of the gas mixture through the apparatus. 4. According to how the concentration of O2 and CO2 change in the chamber as determined by indices of gas analyses, the optimum working surface of the bags is selected, switching some of them on or off with the help of clamps. The intensity of the circulation of the gas mixture through the gas exchanger corresponds to approximately 1/10 of the volume of the chamber, therefore, at least 10 h of operation are required to arrive at any conclusion regarding the necessity of increasing or decreasing the diffuse surface. Table 33.2 presents the recommendations for regulating the concentration of O2 and CO2 in chambers using a diffusion gas exchanger. Table 33.2: Regulation of contents of O2 and CO2 in cold storage utilizing a diffusion gas exchanger Concentration of Gases Regulation of Gas Mixture in the Chamber O2 CO2 Insufficient Insufficient Increase diffusion surface of gas exchanger. Removal of CO2 is possible without apparatus (through absorption by moist floor, walls, etc.). Insufficient Normal Allow small quantity of external air into the chamber through doors of the latches. Insufficient High Increase diffusion surface of gas exchanger. High Insufficient Reduce diffusion surface of gas exchanger. High Normal Reduce diffusion surface of gas exchanger. Disorder in airtightness of adjoining parts and entry of external air into the chamber possible. High High Reduce diffusion surface of gas exchanger. Increased temperature in the chamber possible. 594 Chapter 33 Figure 33.10: Diffusion Gas Exchanger Disorder Analysis. A 2–3% concentration of O2 is considered to be insufficient. A concentration below 2% is alarming and in such case the chamber should be aerated through hatches. After this, the entire surface of the gas exchanger may be put to work. Figure 33.10 provides a graph for determining the reasons for disorders in the functioning of chambers having a CA equipped with a diffusion gas exchanger. In the graph, area 1 indicates that the surface of diffusion is insufficient. In area 2, the surface of diffusion is too large. Area 3 indicates unsatisfactory airtightness of the chamber. Results in area 4 indicate absorption of CO2 by structural and other materials. And area 5 is the zone of normal functioning of gas exchanger and chamber. For example, if the point corresponding to gas composition attained in the chamber lies between two straight lines A1 and A2 or to the left or right of the hatched field labeled “5,” it means the gas composition mixture is disturbed as a result of poor control of gas exchanger. In this case, it is sufficient to increase or decrease the surface of the apparatus in order to get the desired concentration of O2 and CO2 in the chamber. But if the point is below or above the straight lines A1 and A2 then the disturbance of the gas regime is the result of some disorder of other parts of the device, such as inadequate airtightness of the chamber, absorption of CO2 by structural materials, disorder of the functional regime of the refrigerating unit, or variation in the barometric pressure of the external atmosphere. Advantages of a Diffusion Chamber • • • • • Compact and simple to erect and service Less consumption of energy Longer duration of functioning Possibility of simultaneous removal of harmful smells and C2H4 from the chamber Does not use chemicals, hence no corrosion problem and lower maintenance cost Equipment for Producing and Regulating Controlled Atmosphere 595 Disadvantage of a Diffusion Chamber • It is not possible to control O2 and CO2 as individual gases. 33.11 Pallet Package System The first commercial application of the silicon membrane for long-term storage was the pallet package system. This system consists of a pallet box wrapped in a heavy gauge polyethylene (80–150 mm thick) with silicon membrane windows installed for regulation of gas exchange and a calibrated hole for pressure regulation. The advantages of the system are ease of manipulation, optimal atmospheric composition without building modifications and equipment needed for CA storage, and the possibility to market intermediate quantities of produce without disturbing the atmospheric composition of the rest of the produce. However, the disadvantages are the extra space required to provide adequate ventilation to all pallet packages and the time involved in wrapping and installing the proper area of membrane as well as the extra care needed to avoid damaging the packages. This system was originally developed for the storage of apples and pears and could accommodate other perishables. 33.12 Atmolysair System The atmolysair system (Figure 33.11) consists of a set of gas diffusion panels enclosed in an airtight container with two separate airflow paths and a control panel. The panels are arranged side by side so that the exterior air and the modified air from the storage chamber flow on opposite sides of the membrane without direct mixing. Two centrifugal blowers operated by a timer maintain air circulation. The gas composition is analyzed periodically in order to adjust the time of blower operation. Figure 33.11: Atmolysair System. 596 Chapter 33 The advantages of this system over the Marcellin system are ease of operation, better gas exchange due to control of both air streams from the airflow paths, and the potential for complete automation. 33.13 Automated Controlled Atmosphere Control Systems In recent years, better quality requirements and advances in computer technology have led large modern CA storage facilities to adopt automated control systems. Automation of a CA storage facility provides many advantages. Automation has become essential not only to control the process but also to ensure optimum product quality and efficiency. The difficulty in effectively controlling the environment in a CA storage room is due to its dynamic behavior. Physiological response of the stored produce, CO2 and O2 regulating equipment, building airtightness and integrity, cyclical operation of the refrigeration system, and changes in weather are all major elements affecting the gas balance. For these reasons, the process must be carefully studied before an attempt is made to automate the control process. 33.13.1 Control Strategy Aside from temperature and humidity control, the major challenge resides in achieving and stabilizing the O2 and CO2 levels to the desired concentrations (set points). At regular time intervals, the O2 and CO2 levels are measured and compared to their respective set points. The control system attempts to reduce the difference between set points and the process variables and decides whether to operate the gas regulation equipment. The ability of the control system to effectively decide on the type and magnitude of the interventions is based on the control strategy. A properly designed control system is robust and stable, with adequate response time and proper damping. 33.13.2 Control Devices Typical devices used to control the operation of the gas-regulating equipment in control systems include on/off switches and proportional (P), proportional-integral (PI), or proportional integral derivative (PID) controllers. PID controllers are by far the most popular feedback controllers used in controlling automated industrial processes. More advanced controllers such as adaptive, fuzzy logic, knowledge-based, and artificial intelligence controllers can also be used in CA control systems. Advanced controllers are generally more intelligent and can dynamically optimize the process by a detection process. These self-learning and self-tuning controllers can monitor the CA system and adjust controller parameters automatically. Usually designed to provide dedicated control over one parameter, they are sturdy, reliable, and commercially available in a multitude of configurations. One drawback is their limited ability to exchange information. This could be of concern in CA storage facilities equipped with certain types of regulating equipment. Equipment for Producing and Regulating Controlled Atmosphere 597 Morimoto and Hashimoto propose a new breed of intelligent control systems for the automation of storage processes based on a “speaking fruit” approach (SFA). This approach takes into account the physiological status of the stored commodity to optimize the storage environment. It consists of a fuzzy logic controller and two optimizers. Neural networks identify and describe fruit responses and genetic algorithms determine the optimal set points. These set points are then passed to the fuzzy controller to control the environment. The concept was applied to control the RH level in an orange storage facility and was found superior to a basic on/off control. 33.13.3 PC-Based Systems Personal computer (PC)-based systems can also be used to provide direct online control of the gas levels in CA storage facilities. A PC-based system generally consists of a computer, control software, a data acquisition system (DAQ), communication ports, and switching devices. PC-based systems offer great flexibility because, in addition to controlling the gas levels, the software can be programmed to computer online parameters to manage the interaction between process variables and automatically log valuable information for later retrieval and analysis. It is important to plan for contingencies in cases of power or equipment failure or emergencies in order to minimize downtime and avoid costly spoilage. Also, the software should allow for manual control of all equipment. Alarms should be installed to warn of any critical changes in gas levels in the storage room. Implementation of automatic emergency paging features is highly recommended. 33.13.4 Commercial System Dedicated systems for monitoring and control of the environment in CA storage facilities are now available commercially. Most suppliers provide technical support to assist the storage owner in specifying and installing the most suitable equipment for the particular application. The equipment usually consists of a microprocessor-based controller, a CO2/O2 gas analyzer, temperature sensors, and devices to control the operation of the gas-regulating equipment. Most of these systems can be interfaced with a PC to allow the storage operator to enter the required control parameters and monitor the process. 33.14 Instrumentation for Controlled Atmosphere Chambers Automation of CA storage facilities requires the utilization of online instruments to measure the quality of the environment surrounding the stored produce. Variables that are routinely measured include temperature, relative humidity, and gas concentrations. Vibrations, dust, moisture, and temperature fluctuations affect sensor performance. Therefore, verification of the state and accuracy of the instrument should be made in accordance with manufacturer’s specifications or on an annual basis, if not specified. 598 Chapter 33 33.14.1 Temperature Temperature is the easiest parameter to measure in the storage environment. The most common sensors are the resistance temperature detector (RTD), the thermocouple, the thermistor, and the integrated circuit (IC). All will perform well under CA storage conditions, and the selection of the appropriate sensor should be based on the desired accuracy, precision, and output signal, as well as its temperature range, the installation location, and cost. 33.14.2 Relative Humidity Measurements of RH can be accomplished by several means including sling psychrometers (wet bulb and dry bulb temperatures), synthetic hair hygrometers (changes in length of a moisture sensitive fiber), dew point hygrometers (temperature at which the air becomes saturated and begins to condense), thin film capacitive sensors (changes in capacitance of a polymer film), resistive sensors (changes in resistance of a polymer), and new micromachined RH sensor chips (organic or polymer sensing film with a Wheatstone bridge piezoresistor circuit). These instruments vary widely in performance and cost. Electronic RH sensors are most commonly used in CA storage facilities. It should be remembered that monitoring and controlling RH above 95% in an environment maintained at a temperature close to the freezing point are extremely difficult. 33.14.3 Oxygen Concentration The level of O2 in a CA storage environment can be monitored with either a paramagnetic oxygen analyzer or with an electrochemical fuel cell. With the paramagnetic oxygen analyzer, the level of O2 is determined by measuring the magnetic properties of O2 in the air sample. Although high in cost, this instrument can provide an accuracy of up to 0.1% after calibration. With the electrochemical cell, O2 is converted by the fuel cell into a current proportional to the concentration of O2. The fuel technological improvements have increased the accuracy of these cells tremendously, and they are now frequently used in CA storage facilities. 33.14.4 Carbon Dioxide Concentration Measurement of the CO2 level is normally done by infrared absorption. This spectroscopic method is based on the absorption of nondispersive infrared radiation. The reduction in the radiation is a function of the wavelength and provides a measure of the concentration of CO2 in the air sample. Further Readings Bhatia, S.C., 2001. Handbook of Food Process Technology vol. 1 Atlantic Publishers, New Delhi. Metlitskii, L.V., et al.,1983. Controlled Atmosphere Storage of Fruits. Amerind Publishing Co. Ltd, New Delhi. Toledo, R.T., 2000. Fundamentals of Food Process Engineering. CBS Publishers and Distributors, New Delhi. CHAPTE R 34 Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers Fruits can be stored in a controlled atmosphere most effectively in special chambers. These chambers are equipped with a cooling system, devices for creating the necessary gas composition, and devices for controlling and regulating the temperature, relative humidity, and composition of the gas. The basic constructional, functional, and operational aspects of controlled atmosphere storage chamber are furnished in this chapter. The most outstanding constructional feature is presence of enclosures that are impermeable to gas. 34.1 Volume Planning The volume of a controlled atmosphere (CA) chamber should be such that it provides considerable reduction of volume per unit of produce as specified by the fruit storage technology. The lesser the gas mixture per unit of produce stored in the chamber, the smaller the structure and simpler the maintenance of the required concentrations of O2 and CO2. The requirements pertaining to volume planning decisions of a chamber for fruits with CA stipulated are as follows: • • • • High degree of loading of the chamber with produce Arrangement of features of engineering equipment in the chamber Distribution of temperature and gas in the mass of the produce Geometry and constructional parameters of chamber Volume planning decisions regarding these chambers are made on the basis of the following consideration • • • • The specific volume of the chamber must be 4–5 m3/ton. The size of chamber must correspond to size of boxes and trays with the ratio of 1:1–1:2 with the sides of the chamber. The net height of the chamber must be in the range of 4.8–5.4 m. While arranging the produce in the chamber, the possibility of nonuniform loading must be considered. This factor is important because the chambers are loaded with continuous stacks without space between them. In such cases, the recommended gaps in the chamber are 1–2 cm for boxes (piecemeal loading) and 5–10 cm for trays. The distance between produce stacks and the enclosure wall of the chamber should be 5–10 cm from the walls, 20–30 cm from the cooling appliance, and 30 cm from the ceiling.
