All rights reserved. 600 • • • Chapter 34 The minimum capacity of the chamber with CA storage is 30–50 tons. Modern CA food storages consist of individual chambers with a capacity of 50–150 tons or more. The most common plans for CA storages are chambers measuring 6 m × 6 m, 6 m × 12 m, and 12 m × 12 m, with a net height of 4.8–5.4 m. The arrangement of internal engineering equipment in the chamber must ensure its operational specific volume. 34.2 Hermetic Sealing and Gas Insulation Development of the desired composition of a gas mixture and its maintenance during working of chamber with CA depend to a great extent on the degree of airtightness of the enclosure. Hermetic sealing of chamber, by which we mean increasing compactness of partition walls and filling the products and other elements, can be absolute or relative. Experimental studies found that there is no need for absolute airtightness of chamber because the concentration of CO2 in them should not be more than 10–11% and that of O2 not less than 2%. The cost of insulation of partition walls and outfit of these chambers comprises 3–13% of the total cost of conventional cold storage for fruits, depending on the medium used for cooling. 34.2.1 Selection of Gas Impermeable Materials Selection of any type of gas impermeable materials depends upon number of factors, the main ones being: • • • • • Operating conditions of the chamber Method of laying of gas insulation material (heat insulation from inner or outer side) The technology of production work on gas insulation of partition walls of the chamber Operational peculiarities of the materials Cost of the materials 34.2.2 Qualities of Gas Insulation Materials The layer of gas impermeable insulation material is generally fixed from the inner side of partition walls. The gas insulation materials should be: • • • Resistant to mechanical damages resulting from loading and unloading of materials Chemically resistant to CO2 and other components of gas mixture Free from any harmful effect on stored food material 34.2.3 Gas Insulation Materials The following materials are considered as most reliable gas insulation materials: • • Galvanized iron sheets Aluminum foils covered with asphalt from one or both side Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers • • • • 601 Vinyl-based resins Polyester and epoxy resins Reinforced fiberglass Asphalt mastics with rubber Besides the materials listed, plastic sheets, gas impermeable varnish paints, and related techniques are also used in some cases. Galvanized iron sheet and aluminum foil covered with asphalt are the materials used most extensively for gas insulation of partition walls. Eighty percent of the CA stores in Italy, the United States, and England use these two materials because of the following advantages: • • • • • • • • Impermeability to CO2 and O2 Structure of the material is not affected by variations of temperature and humidity Corrosion resistant Absence of any smell Compactness of fixation on the inner surfaces of the chamber Convenience of sealing the enclosures Relatively low cost Can be used with subnormal mixtures A 50–100 m thick aluminum foil is fixed to the surface of the walls and ceiling of the chambers. The foil is coated with asphalt from one or both sides and is pasted with an overlap of 5–10 cm. Sometimes it is pasted in two crisscross layers. Asphalt requirement for this particular gas insulation is 6 kg/m2 with 2–3 mm thickness of each layer. This type of gas insulation is sometimes used only for walls and floors, while the ceiling is covered with galvanized iron sheets. A promising gas insulation material of this type is foil insulation, which is aluminum foil pasted with a rubber-asphalt mixture (insulation) by a hot press method at the plants. It comes in rolls. Its use reduces the work and increases the reliability of the gas insulation of the chambers. Layers of varnish and mastics of plastic resin on the inner surface of the chambers are quite reliable during their operation, but they have an important drawback; during the settling of buildings in such constructions, cracks may appear through which the gas mixture may escape and external air may enter the chamber. In order to avoid this issue, a wire net is laid on the surface of the plaster. Another modification of this type of gas insulation is the application of polyester and epoxy resins reinforced with fiberglass. The resins are applied directly to the plaster of the walls or on the heat insulation after its processing. For hermetic sealing of the floor, its concrete layer, which is generally 100 mm thick, is covered with a 20 mm thick layer of asphalt, followed by another layer of asphalt 602 Chapter 34 reinforced with jute cloth. Aluminum sheets with a thickness of 80 m are then spread on the asphalt. Butt joints between the sheets are made airtight with the help of gas impermeable mastic and adhesive tape. For the protection of aluminum, its upper surface is fixed with asphalt-felt, and then a concrete floor made of 80 mm thick reinforced concrete tiles is laid on the felt. On the ends of the slabs along perimeters of the chamber, a concrete parapet 100–150 mm wide and 150–200 mm high is prepared to protect the walls from damage when stacking the loads. 34.3 Laying the Gas Insulation Materials Galvanized iron continues to be the principal gas insulation material used in storages with subnormal mixtures. Gas insulation with galvanized iron sheet is done by joining separate sheets with butt joints, or overlapping and fixing them on a wooden frame; otherwise it is done by using separate panels welded to each other and fixing them on the metallic frame. Joining the gas insulation of the walls with floor and ceiling is done with asphalt-coated aluminum foil. For a greater reliability of gas insulation where the walls and floor are joined, a channel 4–5 cm wide and up to 20 cm deep is made throughout the entire perimeter of the chamber. The galvanized iron sheet gas insulation is then placed in this channel to a depth of 10 cm, and the channel is then filled with asphalt mastic (viscous at t = 1–0°C). If ordinary iron sheet is used, then both sides are covered with some kind of protective coating (varnish or asphalt) in order to prevent corrosion during use of the chamber. During recent years, the use of ready-made 1.0–1.2 mm thick metallic panels has become popular in place of separate iron sheets. These panels are fixed to metallic bars that are fixed to the walls of the chamber. The size of the panel is generally 2.0 × 1.0 m. All types of gas insulations mentioned here are placed on the inner side of heat insulation. In such cases, it is necessary to add vapor insulation to the outside of the heat insulation. A special sheet iron is widely used for renovating storages. 34.3.1 Doors and Observation Windows At present, heat-insulated doors with galvanized iron sheet from both inner and outer sides are used. These doors measure 1.6–1.8 m × 2.4–2.8 m. Metallic removable doors are fixed with bolts to the lining of the inner surface of the chamber. This type of door is generally used in chambers with a capacity up to 30 tons. Sealing the door flap is done with the help of soft rubber fixed to the body of the door along its entire perimeter. Inflated rubber linings are sometimes used. The use of porous insulation is becoming popular in Russia. Observation windows are generally made in the body of the door for examining the produce and for taking samples by passing pipes to regulate pressure and for analysis of gas. The size of the observation window is generally 75 × 75 cm or 40 × 80 cm. Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers 603 Airtightness of pipe inlets is accomplished with cast iron or galvanized iron sleeves with a diameter of 50–80 mm and embedded in the linings of the walls. The sleeves from both sides are closed with rubber stoppers through which the electric wires and gas tubes pass. The space inside the cast iron sleeve is filled with asphalt or industrial grade grease under pressure. Such construction makes it possible to carry out repair more easily. 34.3.2 Hermetization of Corners The most difficult places in CA chambers are the joints between walls, ceiling, and floors, filled gaps, and also inlets and outlets of pipelines in the building. Making all of the gaps in the chamber airtight can be challenging. Special attention must be paid to hermetization of corners formed by the walls, floor, and ceiling of the chamber, and also to the exit points of industrial pipelines, electric cables, and other means of communication. Thick aluminum sheets are fixed in the corners, while aluminum plates (flanges) are laid in the outlets for pipes and cables. Edges and butt joints of the sheets and plates are smeared with gas impermeable mastic, and then the mastic is pasted with gas impermeable adhesive tape. Estimates put the cost of heat and gas insulated doors at 11–14% of the total cost of construction of the storage. 34.4 New Methods of Hermetic Sealing: Atmostable Method A new method for hermetic sealing of cold store chamber was developed in France by the firm Sipra. The method is called Atmostable (stable atmosphere) and involves special construction of heat, vapor, and gas insulation panels and special system of mounting them in the chamber. The panels are made in factories of polystyrene foam. Polystyrene foam of thickness 12 mm, 100 mm, and 120 mm are used. Slightly corrugated pure aluminum sheets are fixed to them from one side by the hot-press method. These sheets are 80 m thick and have a protective varnish coating on their outer side. The most common sizes of panels are 2.5 × 1 m and 1.5 × 1 m. The work on heat insulation, vapor protecting, and hermetic sealing of the chamber is done simultaneously during the process of mounting the panels. One such method for hermetic sealing of the cold storage chambers was developed in France by the firm “Sipra.” The method is called “Atmostable” (stable atmosphere). This method involves the special construction of heat, vapor, and gas insulation panels, and a special system of mounting them in the chambers. The panels are made in plants from plates of polystyrene foam having a thickness of 12, 100, and 120 mm. Slightly corrugated pure aluminum sheets are fixed to them from one side by the hot-press method; these sheets are 80 m thick, and have a protective varnish coating on their outer side. The most common size of the panels are 2.5 m × 1 m, and 1.5 m × 1 m. The work on heat insulation vapor protection, and hermetic sealing of the chamber is done simultaneously during the process of mounting the panels. 604 Chapter 34 Figure 34.1: Hermetic Sealing of Cold storage Chamber partition walls According to Atmostable Method. Insulation of the walls and ceiling of the chamber by the Atmostable method is done in the following manner (Figure 34.1). A lattice frame of wooden battens is erected and fastened to the partition walls of the chamber. Then, with the help of galvanized nails, the first vapor and gas insulation layer of panels with 12 mm thick polystyrene foam is fixed to this frame. This provides support to the aluminum sheets and prevents them from becoming deformed. Butt joints of the panels and also the places where nails (heads) were driven are coated with a special gas insulation of organic silicon grease using a pneumatic gun. After leveling the mastic with scrapper, a special adhesive tape is pasted on it. This tape is made of cloth coated with glue, has a thin gas impermeable aluminum foil attached firmly to the cloth. On top of the first vapor and gas impermeable layer of panels, the second heat and gas insulation layer of panels is then laid with 100 mm thick polystyrene foam for the walls and 120 mm for the ceiling. Heat and gas insulation panels on the sides of the slots measure 50 mm × 50 mm. These are meant for fixing adjacent panels to the wooden frame of the chamber and for subsequent hermetic lining of the butt joints. The second layer is fixed over the first layer with the help of special bushes provided with caps having female thread in which brass shanks are screwed; these shanks are provided with galvanized fins and press-nuts that ensure the pressing of panels to the wall at the places of their butt joints (slots). The surface of the bushes on both the inside and outside is smeared with gas impermeable mastic. In the space formed by butt joints, struts made of polystyrene foam are laid and pasted with 80 m thick aluminum foil from the outer side. The width of the struts is determined from their fixing in the butt joints with some force to ensure a compact and fair bearing of the edges of polystyrene foam and reduction of gaps between them. The butt joints between panels and struts are carefully smeared with gas impermeable mastic and covered with wide gas impermeable adhesive tape. Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers 605 34.4.1 Hermetic Sealing of Floors For hermetic sealing of the floor, its concrete layer, which is generally 100 mm thick, is covered with a 20 mm thick layer of asphalt, followed by another layer of asphalt reinforced with jute cloth. Aluminum sheets having a thickness of 80 m are then spread on the asphalt. Butt joints between the sheets are made airtight with the help of gas impermeable mastic and adhesive tape. For the protection of aluminum, its upper surface is fixed with asphalt-felt, and then a concrete floor made of 80 mm thick reinforced concrete tiles is laid on the felt. On the ends of the slabs along perimeters of the chamber, a concrete parapet 100–150 mm wide and 150–200 mm high is prepared to protect the walls from damage when stacking the loads. In spite of some increase in expenditure and labor, this method of hermetization is considered one of the most effective and reliable during operation. A settling in the building or the appearance of various types of cracks in the building structure does not disturb the continuity of the gas insulation layer of the chamber; vapor protection from both sides of the heat insulation is ensured irrespective of the direction of movement of water vapor (in summer or in winter), and the location of the main gas impermeable layer of insulation on the visible side of the chamber permits the detection and removal of any possible disorders in the hermetic sealing easily and quickly. 34.4.2 Multiple CA Chambers In constructing a series of composite chambers with common refrigeration, the chambers are built in the form of separate enclosures that are not structurally linked with the partitioning and conducting structures of the main building, but are located at some distance from its walls. For this reason, access to the outer surface of any chamber is ensured from all sides, which is essential for the maintenance of the pressure sealing. For example, in one cold storage the partitions of the main building served the exclusive purpose of shading, while the cold chambers situated in two rows of four chambers each inside the building were practically self-sufficient. The size of each chamber is 12.65 m × 8.4 m × 6.4 m. They are constructed to be independent of each other and easily accessible for maintenance. During the last few years, efforts have been made in the construction of cold storages with a CA to use special multilayered sandwich panel constructions, which are made in a factory from different vapor and gas impermeable plastic materials with heat insulation placed between the layers. These sandwich panels can be self-sufficient, or they can play the role of providing additional lining material for the main enclosures of cold storage buildings. When they are used, the hermetic sealing of the chambers, as in the previous case, is accomplished by closing the butt joints between the panels. 606 Chapter 34 34.5 Tests for Airtightness of Controlled Atmosphere Storage The determination of the degree of airtightness of CA chambers, which work on the principle of the vital activities of the products, is possible at the design and construction stages if the degree of permeability of the materials used in the partition walls and outer walls is known. With this method, it is necessary to know the precise characteristics of the materials and their compounds with due consideration of their selective gas permeability. For this purpose, certain measures have been developed to test the airtightness of the chambers before putting them into operation. There are two main methods for testing airtightness of CA storage chambers: 1. From the intensity of the leakage of CO2 from the chamber, the CO2 concentration is increased. 2. Excess pressure is developed in the chamber, and airtightness of the chamber is determined from the rate of fall in the pressure. Pressure sealing of CA chambers is marked by a resistance of the partitions to gas exchange because of convection and diffusion. The diffusion of gases through partitions takes place as a result of difference in partial pressures of the components of the gas mixture inside and outside the chamber. Diffusion takes place from higher to lower concentration and its intensity is proportional to the difference between the concentrations. In case of insufficient airtightness of chambers whose atmosphere is marked by a reduced concentration of O2 and an increased concentration of CO2, a constant gas exchange through diffusion occurs through the partition (i.e., O2 from outside air enters the chamber and CO2 escapes from it). In contrast with diffusion, gas exchange due to convection takes place as a result of differences in the internal and external pressure of the gas mixture. Any difference leads to the entry of outside air into the chamber and escape of gas mixture from it. Gas exchange due to convection is generally somewhat higher than that due to the diffusion of gases. Tests for airtightness are conducted in empty and carefully closed chambers with the same air temperature outside and inside the chamber. The refrigeration equipment is closed during the test. 34.6 Determination of Gas Chamber Tightness Gas exchange through diffusion is determined by enriching the chamber air with CO2 up to approximately 10%. The concentration of CO2 in the chamber is measured every day. If we assume that over 24 h, the concentration of CO2 decreases from the initial value Co to a value Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers 607 Ci, then the resistance of the chamber partitions to the gas exchange through diffusion is determined as a ratio of these concentrations ρ = Ci / C0 The chamber is considered airtight if the value of ρ is 0.85–0.9 with normal gas mixture and 0.97–0.98 with subnormal mixture. 34.6.1 Marcellin-Dohkoshi Formula Marcellin-Dohkoshi (1965) formula is used for the theoretical evaluation of the airtightness of chamber with a controlled (gaseous environment). h = h0 e − λ ( T2 − T1 ) where h0 and h are the initial and ultimate pressure, kg/m2 l = coefficient of the fall in pressure in the chamber T1 and T2 are the initial and final times, min where ln h = ln ho − λ (T2 − T1 ) ln h − ln ho = − λ [(T2 − T1 )] or ln ho − ln h = λ[(T2 − T1 )] h ln o = λ ( T2 − T1 ) h ln ho h λ= (T2 – T1 ) It follows from this equation that the value of l can be determined by the formula λ= h ln h0 T2 – T1 (34.1) In the United States, it has been found that fall of excess pressure from 2.5 mm to 2.6 mm of water column during testing should not occur earlier than 25 min. By substituting these values into Equation (34.1), we find that the value of l should not be more than 0.09 for subnormal mixtures. For cold storage using normal mixtures, this value should not be less than 0.14. 608 Chapter 34 Figure 34.2: Evaluation of Quality of Airtightness of Chamber from the Time of Fall of Excess Pressure. In Italy and France, the value of l = 0.003 and 0.015, respectively. Marcellin has recommended the graph (Figure 34.2) for evaluating the quality of the airtightness of chambers from the time it takes for a fall in excess pressure. Experience has shown that the concentration of CO2 and O2, as well as the time for restoration of the gas regime, depends on the degree of airtightness of the chamber. For example, when the value of coefficient of fall in pressure is l = 0.02 – 0.03, a 3–5% concentration of CO2 and 3% concentration of O2 are achieved 20 days after the chamber is closed. At l = 0.009 – 0.01, these concentrations are obtained after only 6 days. The degree of airtightness of CA chamber is also characterized by the coefficient of airtightness k, which is the ratio of the volume of the air escaping the chamber (or outside entering the chamber) to its volume in the chamber. The estimated theoretical value of the coefficient of airtightness is 0.024 of air exchange per day for subnormal mixture; 0.044 for normal gas mixture; and 0.1 per day in the case of artificial supply of air into the chamber by generator. In Russia and abroad, analysis of data on degree of airtightness of chamber k, coefficient of fall of pressure l, and time necessary for attaining the desired atmosphere gave a relationship between these values as follows: k = 0.5 λ This relation holds when the chamber is loaded at the rate of 4 m3/ton, the temperature of storage is 4°C, and the duration of the desired condition is 15 days. Temperature control is accomplished using conventional visual thermometer (0.5–1°C) or by electrothermometer. Pressure can be measured with pressure gauges of bourdon tube type, inclined micromanometers, and v-shaped liquid manometers. Differential manometers with autorecorder can also be used. 610 Chapter 34 Control of CO2 during a test for permeability due to diffusion is accomplished with the help of gas analyzers of the ORS type. Ventilators and compressors are used to create excess pressure in the chambers. The compressors are more convenient to use because, when the compressor is not working, the escape of air from the chamber is stopped. Ventilators are connected to the chamber through a hermetic locking device that closes before the ventilator stops. Detection of Air Leaks in Chambers Air leak points under increased pressure are determined by any of the following methods. • • • • Examining and listening to the partition walls of the chambers Letting visible smoke into the chamber By a flickering of a flame near the leak By adding Freon to the air of chamber and determining the point of escape of Freon from outside the chamber with halogen lamp It is recommended that each test be repeated two or three times. Tests for airtightness of the chambers are conducted after completion of construction of cold storage buildings and before each new season of fruit storage. 34.8 Design and Layouts of Commercial Controlled Atmosphere Chambers Commercial storage of fruits can be accomplished most successfully in special storage buildings (i.e., cold storage buildings coupled with CA capabilities). In these fruit storages, a part or sometimes all of the cold storage building is hermetically sealed and equipped with devices for creating and maintaining the required gas regimes. A combination of gas and conventional cold chambers in fruit storage with CA ensures more flexible and effective operations. The share of gas chamber in the total volume of the fruit storage building is determined by technical and economic calculations on the basis of quantity and varietal peculiarities of the fruits to be kept under prolonged storage, as well as the conditions of their cultivation, storage, and utilization. Depending on the number and capacity of the gas chambers and also on the type of gas mixture and devices used, either centralized or decentralized devices are utilized to ensure the required regimes. The plan and sectional diagrams for a 500-ton capacity cold storage with CA are shown in Figure 34.3. The volume planning of the cold storage with separate chambers for controlling the atmosphere is also shown in the diagram. Another design of cold storage building is meant for the prolonged storage of fruits, especially apples. Its total capacity is 1500 tons, including 800 tons in the CA chamber (Figure 34.4). Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers 611 Figure 34.3: A 500-ton Capacity Storage with Controlled Atmosphere. This cold storage building consists of five chambers with CA and five chambers of conventional cold storage. All chambers are of uniform size and are situated on both sides of the loading corridor, which opens into the dispatch passage. A mezzanine is built above the corridor and equipped with devices for controlling the gas regime, ventilation, and humidity of the air in the chamber. The distributing devices of the chamber and coolers are also housed in the same premises. The design of the storage building is single-story and above ground. The dimensions in the design are 30 m × 30 m. Six chambers for fruit storage under CA each have a capacity of 70 tons. The capacity of the two chambers for storage of fruits under artificial cooling during the period of preliminary cooling is 12.5 tons and during the period of storage is 52.5 tons. The size of room in the design is 6 m × 12 m, and the height up to conductance is 5.4 m. The ceiling in the chamber is smooth. A 6.0 m wide central passage serves as a dispatch aisle. 612 Chapter 34 Figure 34.4: A 1500-ton Capacity Cold Storage with Controlled Atmosphere. The doors of the chambers are hermetically sealed and are provided with observation windows and a hole for taking samples. Gas insulation of the partition walls of the CA chambers is done in two ways. 1. With aluminum foil 50 m thick covered on both sides with type IV asphalt 2. With galvanized iron sheets on a wooden frame with a soldered seams Fruits are stored in the chambers in standard boxes on racks. Maintenance of temperature regime is accomplished by a system of artificial cooling. Creation of normal and subnormal gas mixture is done through the vital activities of the fruits. Maintenance of required temperature, relative humidity, and the composition of the gas mixture in each chamber is automatic. Fruits are stored in the CA chambers at a temperature of 0–4°C and humidity of 90–95%. The gas composition of the chamber is envisaged as follows. CO2 5–9% 5% 0% O2 12–16% 3% 3% Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers 613 Temperature, relative humidity, and gas composition are controlled automatically by using relevant sensors through computers. Selective quality testing of the incoming produce is done in the dispatch room. Here, resorting of fruits is also done as necessary after completion of storage. Advance cooling of fruits is done directly in the chamber. The daily arrival of fruits must be about 7.5 tons if the cold storage is to be loaded within 20 days. All the major loading and unloading operations in the cold storage related to transportation and stacking of boxes of fruits are done with the help of electric loaders and stock trays (flat as well as prop type). The ammonia cooling device works as a single system with direct boiling of ammonia in the flooded vaporizing sections of the air cooler. The required gas composition of the air in the CA chamber is brought about by the natural respiration of fruits. N2 is introduced into a chamber artificially in order to enhance the process of development of the desired gas regime. Excess CO2 that builds up during the process of storage is removed by water in special absorption scrubber tanks with ceramic packing. The absorption capacity of water is increased by cooling it with the help of central cooling device. O2 deficit in the chamber is compensated by pumping the required quantity of outside air into the chamber. The ventilation of a conventional cold storage chamber is accomplished by passing outside air through special aerating columns. This process also ensures control of humidity. The concentration of CO2 and O2 in a CA chamber is controlled automatically by gas analyzers. They control the operation of scrubbers and supply of fresh air into the chamber. The remote control of CO2 and O2 concentrations in the gas mixture of the chamber is done by the same gas analyzers at the central control panel. Automatic defrosting of the air cooler-radiator is done by time relays that control the solenoid valves of the water supply pipes for flooding. The additional capacity required for hermetic sealing and equipment for the creation and control of the gas composition comprises approximately 10–15% of the total cost of construction of cold storage buildings. Additional operational costs are associated with increased expenditure on current repairs of gas insulation, increased consumption of electricity, increased pay to service personnel, increased depreciation, and additional equipment and represent 15–20% of the total operational costs of the cold storage building. Economy of means is obtained because of reduction (on average, about one-third) in the natural damage and spoilage of fruits stored in conventional cold storages. 34.9 Air-Conditioning Equipment for Controlled Atmosphere Chambers The refrigeration system of CA chambers does not require any special machinery and does not differ practically from that used in conventional fruit preservation chambers. The refrigeration efficiency of this equipment under similar size and functional conditions must be the same as for conventional cold storage chambers. 614 Chapter 34 Maintenance of the desired optimum temperature and humidity conditions in CA chambers is ensured by the air cooling system exclusively. This system ensures uniformity of the gas composition, temperature, and humidity of the medium throughout the entire volume of the chamber; good conduction of external and internal heat currents is provided; and the work of pressure sealing the enclosure is made easy. The air system economizes the metal needed for cooling devices considerably, increases the loading capacity of the cold storage chambers, and permits easy automatic maintenance of the cooling units. In addition, only with an air cooling system is it effective and practically possible to make use of automatic equipment for the control of relative humidity in the cold storage chambers. The special requirements of designing air coolers and systems of air distribution in CA chambers are related mainly to the imperative of reliable pressure sealing of the partition walls and installation of various connecting structures. 34.9.1 Overhead Air Coolers Air coolers are often installed directly in the chambers. They may be installed on the floor or overhead. Overhead air coolers of the ceiling or wall type are used mostly for cooling chambers having a great height. They have one shortcoming: it is necessary to determine the place where they are to be fixed well in advance. It is a difficult task if a light ceiling is used, or if conducting insulation partitions used do not have an external frame. Apart from these factors, it is necessary to carry out additional pressure sealing at the places they are fixed. This pressure sealing should not be disturbed by the vibrations produced when the ventilator is working. Access to the ventilators during operation becomes somewhat difficult because of the height of the chamber. 34.9.2 Floor-Type Air Coolers The floor-type air coolers are more convenient to use in 4–5 m high chambers. If the chamber has a greater height, they are provided with supply nozzles for discharging air below the chamber ceiling, or they are mounted on special iron concrete or metallic foundations. In comparison with overhead coolers, the floor-type air cooler is not connected with the partition walls of the chamber and they do not affect the gas insulation layer. 34.9.3 Cool Air Distribution In CA chambers, regardless of the type of air cooler, air distributors without canals are used because the lining and fixation of canals considerably complicate the task of laying gas insulation work. Their vibrations can affect the airtightness of the chamber during its operation. A better distribution of air is thus ensured without canals when supplying cooled air into the upper part of the chamber and removing it from the lower part after aeration of the loaded stacks. Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers 615 34.9.4 Management of the Drying Effect of Cool Air A definite relationship exists between the functioning of the air cooler and air distribution system and the relative humidity of air developed in the chamber. In order to attain increased humidity and a decrease in the desiccation of stored fruits, it is necessary to consider a number of factors that decrease the drying effect of the air cooling system while designing and operating air coolers and air distribution systems. 1. Increase in the average temperature of the cooling surface of the air cooler by means of reducing the difference in temperature between the air and the cooling agent, and by increasing the coefficient of heating through reducing edge pitch to 8–12 mm under conditions of simultaneous and reliable defrosting. 2. Establish the optimum quantity of circulating air in the chamber (frequency of circulation). Reduction of the amount of circulating air leads to a fall in the rate of aeration of the product, but it requires higher temperature gradients at the entrance and exit of the air cooler, which intensifies the desiccating effect of the air cooling system. In this context, there is a definite permissible minimum of circulating air, which is approximately 600– 700 m3/hr for 1000 kcal/hr of cold at gradient of air temperature cooling agent at 5–6°C, and cooling in the air cooler at 2.0–2.5°C. On the other hand, an increase in the quantity of air circulating through the air cooler with a definite cooling surface is favorable for establishing high levels of humidity in the chamber by reducing the difference in temperature when air enters and leaves the air cooler. However, an increase in the air draft enhances the desiccation of stored fruits, and it may even increase the advantage obtainable from reducing temperature differences while increasing the frequency of circulation. Apart from that, an increase in the amount of circulating air is governed by the capacity of the air vents, which in turn is associated with the increase of heat currents into the chamber. As a result, in most cases the maximum quantity of circulating air is within a range of 850–1200 m3/h for 1000 kcal/h of cold at ∆t = 5–6°C, and the optimum frequency of circulation corresponds to 20–30 volumes (of empty chamber) per hour. 3. Capacity to reduce air circulation after completing the cooling of fruits when there is a greater initial heat load (e.g., with the help of two-speed ventilators). In this case, in order to enhance the effect, the use of two-speed ventilators must be coordinated with control of the suction pressure of the air coolers with the help of pressure control valves. 4. Layout of the air distribution system in a way that ensures a uniform circulation and a minimum motion of air at the produce level (with a velocity of not more than 0.1 m/s) at a sufficiently high velocity in the air cooler unit (3–5 m/s). The air must leave the air cooler and enter the space above the loaded produce and then it must descend through convection, thus creating uniform temperature and humidity conditions throughout the volume of the chamber. 616 Chapter 34 While constructing cold storage buildings in the climatic regions of Russia, where chambers require heating during winter, the air distribution system must also be capable of circulating heated air. 5. Ensure regulation of the cold-generating capacity of air coolers based on maximum heat stresses. For large industrial cold storages for fruits, it is not sufficient to have simple two-position on/off switches for the cooling surface of the air cooler. For such chambers it is necessary to foresee the possible need for sectional functioning of the different units of the air cooler and to regulate the suction pressure. 6. Develop an effective automatic defrosting system in the air coolers, with at least partial reversal of humidity in the chamber. The estimated refrigeration efficiency of air coolers for CA chambers, as well as for conventional fruit storage chambers, is approximately 20–30 kcal/h·m3 volume of the empty chamber. 34.9.5 Designing Cooling Surface Area of Air Coolers For determining the essential cooling surface of air coolers, several points are generally considered. The cooling surface area is estimated to give 5–7°C difference in temperature between the chamber air and the cooling agent, 3–4°C difference in temperature between the incoming and outgoing air, and coefficient of heat transfer of 13–14 kcal/m2·h °C (for ammonia-based air coolers). It is recommended that an increased level of humidity in CA chambers (about 95%) be maintained by regulating the difference in temperatures between the air and the cooling agent, or by means of changing the working surface and duration of the air cooler functioning. When there is only one cold user (decentralized cooling), the temperature gradient of the air cooling agent is regulated with the help of pressostats. After appropriate adjustment, this regulation helps to maintain a constant boiling temperature of the freezing agent through changes in the frequency of the working cycle of the refrigeration equipment. When many cold users are connected parallel to one or many compressor agents (centralized cooling), the boiling temperature of the cooling agent and the temperature gradients are regulated by means of a pressure control valve that is mounted at the suction point of each cold user. Temperature gradients of the air cooling agent should not exceed 6–8°C during thermal processing and 4–5°C during fruit storage. Under these conditions, increased RH of the air develops in the chamber, ensuring minimum fruit losses from desiccation. Thus, exceptionally large air cooler surfaces are not required. Regulation of room RH by changing the working surface of chamber cooling devices is done through sectionalization of the radiator units of air coolers. The continuity of the air cooler working cycle increases when the surface of the heat exchanger is reduced and the temperature of the Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers 617 air cooling agent is maintained. For this reason, a large quantity of moisture is deposited on the surface of the radiator (when the cooling surface is frequently defrosted) and a reduction in humidity occurs. On the other hand, when the heat exchange surface is increased and the temperature gradients simultaneously reduced, an increase in RH in the chamber is obtained. Usually water is the source of humidity, sprinkled in the form of a fine mist; water vapor is rarely used for this purpose. During the storage of fruits in a CA, it is necessary to have more precise and reliable devices for artificial humidification of air than are required for conventional cold storages. Because even one drop of water falling on the fruit risks the possibility of carbonic acid formation, causing blight and darkening of the stored fruits. Cooling devices are designed with direct boiling of the cooling agent (ammonia or Freon) in the air coolers throughout the pumping and circulating, or pumpless schemes, of cooling. Here the possibility of the chambers working at one or two temperatures of boiling of the cooling agent is also envisaged. In the latter case, better conditions are ensured for regulating the temperature and humidity conditions in the chamber during the cooling of the fruits and during their subsequent storage than in the former. Usually, the design of cooling devices that provides a possibility of individual regulation of the boiling temperature in each chamber is considered a better option. In conclusion, it is worth mentioning that the widespread use of air cooling in cold storage of fruits, including CA chambers, has been ensured by replacement of individual handmade air coolers with those mass-produced at modern plants. Modern mechanized technology of manufacturing radiators results in unified components, reduction in the weight and cost of air coolers, automation of their operation, and a significant increase in their efficiency. 34.10 Important Features for Successful Operation of Controlled Atmospheres The process of cold storage of fruits in CA chambers consists of four major stages: 1. 2. 3. 4. Loading the chamber and cooling the fruits Hermetic sealing of the chamber Creation of the desired gas regime Storage of fruits in the established regime The fruits meant for storage under CA must be of high quality (without any injury, dents, symptoms of diseases, or decomposition), of average size, and of a level of maturity at the time of picking that is suitable for prolonged storage. It is recommended that fruits of only one pomological variety be stored in each chamber. Loading the chamber and cooling the fruits should be done within the shortest possible time. It is necessary to stack the boxes of fruit so as to enhance the process of cooling, and to ensure 618 Chapter 34 uniform temperature and humidity conditions throughout the entire volume of the chamber. The air temperature required for storage must be established in the chamber by the time it is closed. The hermetic sealing of the chamber involves careful packing of the doors, peephole, water-level valve, and other means of communication that have contact with outside air. At present, no clearcut recommendations for a more appropriate sequence of operations for the cooling of fruits and hermetic sealing of the chamber have been established. A number of researchers recommend that high intensity of respiration of fruits under increased temperature be utilized for establishing the required gas regime and the chamber be hermetically sealed immediately after loading. In case of the formation of gas regimes due to respiration, the fruits are left in an insulated atmosphere after cooling, and the chamber is hermetically sealed until the essential concentration of CO2 (of the required gas regime) develops. The duration of this period depends on the given concentration of the CO2 (the desired gas level), the density of stacking, temperatures of storage, and quality and degree of maturity of the fruits. Experience has shown that with density of loading of 200 kg/m3, when the temperature of the air is 4°C, the air of the chamber is saturated with CO2 at a rate of not less than 1% per day, while at 0°C it is 0.5% per day. Otherwise, it must be concluded that the chamber is not sufficiently hermetically sealed. 34.11 Storage with Normal Gas Mixture In case of storage in a normal gas mixture, the process of establishing the gas regime in the chamber is complete soon after the desired concentration of CO2 is attained. Afterward the gas regime is controlled with the help of simple ventilation (aeration) of the chamber (Figure 34.5), Figure 34.5: Stabilization of Gas Mixture Composition in a CA Chamber. Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers 619 by frequently opening the peepholes or special valves. In such cases, the quantity of O2 that has been absorbed by the fruits should be allowed in to the chamber, and the quantity of CO2 released should be released from the chamber. 34.12 Storage with Subnormal Gas Mixture In case of subnormal gas mixture, after establishing the specified concentration of CO2, a device such as a scrubber or a diffusion gas exchanger is switched on to remove the excess CO2 and to continue to lower the concentration of O2 in the chamber (Figure 34.6). This concentration is established at the desired level 3–4 weeks or longer after closing the chamber. In a number of cases it is necessary to enhance the process in order to reduce danger of physiological diseases such as blights. For this purpose, soon after closing the chamber it is recommended that N2 or CO2 gas may be introduced into it. By introducing N2 equal to the volume of the chamber, it is possible to reduce the initial concentration of O2 from 21% to 5–7% within a few hours. In these cases, the required gas regime for CO2 as well as O2 is established in the chamber quickly (i.e., within 3–4 days). 34.13 N2 Management in the Controlled Atmospheres When using N2, it is not desirable to maintain the O2 in the chamber at its required level. Therefore, the supply of O2 is stopped when its quantity becomes slightly above the desired level. Further control of O2 level is accomplished by virtue of the respiration of the fruit being stored in the chamber. For example, when we want to obtain a 3% concentration of O2, the supply of N2 is stopped when there is 5–6% concentration of O2 in the chamber. For practical Figure 34.6: Stabilization of Gas Mixture Composition (Subnormal Mixture). 620 Chapter 34 purposes, gaseous N2 from cylinders or liquid nitrogen from special cisterns is released through an additional vaporizing device. Nitrogen is supplied through a special pipe that is situated horizontally in the upper part of the chamber and provided with discharge outlets. If such pipe is not provided in the chamber, the supply canal of the scrubber may be used or a temporary pipe may be laid. Holes for the release of air open at some height in the chamber in the side opposite this pipe. If possible, a hydraulic valve is opened fully or a peephole may also be used. The correct position of inlets and outlets in the chamber permits considerable reduction in the consumption of N2. Therefore, it is important that the ventilators of the air cooling device be closed while the chamber is flooded with N2. If these instructions are followed, a layer of N2 develops in the upper part of the chamber, which exerts pressure on the gas below and facilitates the removal of gases from the chamber. This reduces to a bare minimum the possibility of their mixing with N2. Trials have shown that in order to obtain a 5% O2 content in the chamber, the consumption of N2 can be maintained at 1.5 m3 per 1 m3 of the net volume of the chamber (its total volume calculated from volume occupied by the produce). It is also worth mentioning that the consumption of N2, as well as the time it takes to establish the desired regime in the chamber, depends greatly on the rate of release of the gases. When cylinders are used (which are economical only for small chambers), the rate of release is about 70–100 m3/h, but for cisterns with liquid nitrogen these rates vary from 70 m3/h to 1000 m3/h. While supplying N2, it is necessary to control the pressure in the chamber. Care should be taken to prevent its increase. After N2 is filled and before beginning the measurement of the established concentration of O2, it is necessary to switch on the ventilators of the air coolers for not less than 15 min in order to obtain a uniform composition of gas mixture in the chamber. If N2 is introduced correctly, there should be no significant changes in the temperature and humidity conditions of the chamber. 34.14 CO2 Management in Controlled Atmospheres Saturation of the atmosphere with CO2 is generally done from cylinders that are connected to the chamber by special pipes. The required quantity of CO2 is supplied from the lower part. If, for example, it is necessary to increase the concentration of CO2 by 1% in the net volume of the chamber (100 m3), it is essential to introduce 1 m3 of CO2 that corresponds by weight to about 2 kg. The quantity of CO2 being supplied is measured with the help of rotameter by volume, or simply by weighing it. In order to simplify the supply of CO2, it is recommended to resort to preliminary heating with the help of electric or water heaters. Design, Construction, and Operation of Controlled Atmosphere Storage Chambers 621 The time taken to create the desired regime in the chamber can also be reduced by “burning out” O2 from the air mixture with the help of special gas burners or through replacement of chamber air with an artificially prepared gas mixture obtained by combustion of natural gas in gas generators. Use of the last two methods is recommended only when there are many (i.e., not less than three) large-capacity CA chambers in the cold storage building. Failure to obtain the required reduced concentration of O2 is usually due to improper pressure sealing of the chamber. It can also be due to faulty functioning of the atmosphere stabilizer, incorrect regulation of the cooling equipment, defects in the pipe for pressure equilibrium in the chamber, and so on. In many cases, it is difficult to establish the actual cause of the disorder. The level of the hydraulic valve of the chamber should be set at 20–25 mm of the water column by providing a pressure connection of the chamber with the outside air. It is recommended that the water level in the valve be checked periodically because it may be lowered due to transpiration. 34.15 Observations for Successful Controlled Atmosphere Operation When the chamber is set to the required gas regime, constant control of various parameters of the medium is essential during the process of storage. It is also necessary to control the temperature, relative humidity, frequency of recharging of air, and the concentrations of CO2 and O2. The composition of the gas mixture is generally controlled with the help of Ors devices, which take samples periodically from the chambers. In most cases, it is sufficient to take two measurements in a day in order to detect any change in the gaseous environment. In the process of storage, it is also essential to observe changes occurring in the fruits. Besides visual examination, which can easily be done through the observation window of the hermetically sealed door of the chamber, it is emphatically recommended that fruits be examined periodically directly in the chamber. The longer the duration of storage, the more frequent such examinations must be done. After two-thirds of the maximum duration of storage passes, it is necessary to visit the chamber not less than once every 2 weeks. While taking samples, some fruits should be cut in order to detect possible internal changes, and some fruits be kept under normal temperature and humidity conditions to determine their degree of maturity. Timely sampling permits the detection of any changes in the quality of fruits, and thus the determination of further storage. The service personnel who enter the chamber through hatches in the doors must use gas masks. While workers are in the chamber, the hatches should be kept open. After storage is completed, normal air must first be restored. Personnel unloading the fruits are allowed into the chamber when the O2 concentration reaches 18% or more. 622 Chapter 34 Further Readings Metlitskii, E.G., et al., 1983. PA R T I V Modified Atmosphere Storage 623 Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 35 An Overview of Modified Atmosphere Storage 35.1 Modified Atmosphere It is a common technical definition that describes the practice of modifying the composition of the internal atmosphere of a package (commonly food packages, but this technique is also used for drugs) in order to improve the shelf life. The modification process often tries to lower the amount of oxygen (O2) of the atmospheric air moving it from 20% to 0% in order to slow down the growth of aerobic organisms and the speed of oxidation reactions. The removed O2 can be replaced with nitrogen (N2), commonly acknowledged as an inert gas, or carbon dioxide (CO2), which can lower the pH or inhibit the growth of bacteria. Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) can significantly extend the shelf life of food products, thus prolonging the logistic efficiencies and diminishing the need for centralized production. Rebalancing of gases inside packaging can be achieved using active techniques, such as gas flushing and compensated vacuum, or passively by designing “breathable” films known as equilibrium modified atmosphere packaging (EMAP). In either case, the dynamics of the micro atmosphere depends on the produce (weight and respiration rate), the package (thickness and gas permeabilities of the plastic film, free volume, and surface area of the package), and the environment (ambient gas compositions and storage temperature). 35.2 Modified Atmosphere Packaging MAP is a technique used for prolonging the shelf-life period of fresh or minimally processed foods. In this preservation technique, the air surrounding the food in the package is changed to another composition. This way the initial fresh state of the product may be prolonged. It is the shelf life of perishable products such as meat, fish, fruits, and vegetable that will be prolonged with MAP by slowing the natural deterioration of the product. MAP is used with various types of products where the mixture of gases in the package depends on the type of product, packaging materials, and storage temperature. Meat and fish need low gas permeability films; so for nonrespiring products (meat, fish, cheese, etc.) high barrier films are used. Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00035-X 625 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 626 Chapter 35 The initial flushed gas mixture will be maintained inside the MA package. But fruits and vegetables are respiring products where the interaction of the packaging material with the product is important. If the permeability (for O2 and CO2) of the packaging film is adapted to the products respiration, an equilibrium modified atmosphere will establish in the package and the shelf life of the product will increase. 35.3 Equilibrium Modified Atmosphere Packaging Among fresh-cut produce, EMAP is the most commonly used packaging technology. When packaging vegetables and fruits, the gas atmosphere of package is not air (21% O2; 0.038% CO2; 78% N2) but consists usually of a lowered level of O2 and a heightened level of CO2. This kind of package slows down the normal respiration of the product to prolong its shelf life. Of course, other factors such as the size of the product, severity of preparation, maturity of the product, and type of tissue have an effect to the shelf life of an EMA packaged produce. 35.4 Packaging Techniques Two techniques are used in the industry to pack vegetables: gas flushing and compensated vacuum. For its cheapness, gas flushing is more widely used. In gas flushing, the package is flushed with a desired gas mixture; in compensated vacuum, the air is removed totally and the desired gas mixture then inserted. The label “packaged in a protective atmosphere” can refer to either of these processes. An example of a gas mixture used for nonvegetable packaged food (such as crisps) is 99.9% N2, which is inert at the temperature and pressures to which the packaging is subjected. 35.5 MAP Gases The atmosphere in an MA package consists of N2, O2, and CO2. It is the altered ratio of these gases that makes a difference in the prolongation of shelf life. By reducing the O2 level and increasing the CO2 level, ripening of fruits and vegetables can be delayed, respiration and ethylene production rates can be reduced, softening can be delayed, and various compositional changes associated with ripening can be slowed down. Oxygen is essential when packaging fresh fruits and vegetables because they continue to respire after harvesting. The absence of O2 can lead to anaerobic respiration in the package, which accelerates senescence and spoilage. Levels of O2 that are too high do not slow respiration significantly. Respiration rate starts to decrease at about 12% of O2. So O2 is used in low levels (3–5%) for positive effect. When packaging meat and fish, high CO2 levels are effective bacterial and fungal growth inhibitors. In the case of vegetables and fruits, CO2 is not a major factor because CO2 levels above 10% are needed to suppress fungal growth significantly. An Overview of Modified Atmosphere Storage 627 Unfortunately, levels higher than 10% CO2 are phytotoxic for fresh produce. Nitrogen is used as a filler gas because it neither encourages nor discourages bacteria growth. 35.6 Packaging Films When selecting packaging films for EMAP of fruits and vegetables, the main characteristics to consider are gas permeability, water vapor transmission rate, mechanical properties, transparency, type of package, and sealing reliability. Traditionally used packaging films such as low-density polyethylene (LDPE), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA), and oriented polypropylene (OPP) are not permeable enough for highly respiring fresh-cut produce like mushrooms and broccoli. Because fruits and vegetables are respiring products, there is a need to transmit gases to and from the package. Films designed with these properties are called permeable films. Other films, called barrier films, are designed to prevent the exchange of gases and are mainly used with nonrespiring products such as meat and fish. EMAP films developed to control the humidity level as well as the gas composition in the sealed package are beneficial for the prolonged storage of fresh fruits, vegetables, and herbs that are sensitive to moisture. These films are commonly referred to as modified atmosphere/ modified humidity (MA/MH) packaging films. 35.7 Plastic Films for MAP A wide variety of metallized plastic films and paperboard products are used in MAP packaging. Characteristics of the most commonly used materials are given in Jenkins (1991: 35-63). Films employed for gas packaging include PET, CPET, OPP, PP, HDPE, and occasionally LPDE, PVC, and PVDC composed as monolayers, multilayered, laminated, or metallized film stock and trays. Among the critical properties of these major packaging resins, the most important characteristic for the purpose of gas packaging is their relative permeability to O2, CO2, and N2 or argon. The CO2 and O2 gas transmission-rate properties of films are generally well known and can be obtained from the materials specification sheets supplied by the manufacturer. The gas transmission rate may also be measured. 35.8 Packaging Machinery for MAP A large number of gas-packaging machinery types are currently in use around the world, and these may be categorized generally by the basic functional process used to prepare and seal the package. Form and fill machines create usually flexible packages by pulling a twodimensional film along a forming guide and sealing it into a three-dimensional pouch. These machines can be either horizontal or vertical in format, and can produce flexible sacks, bags, cylinders, and square or rectangular pouches. Tray-wrapping and tray-overwrapping machines are similar in that they form a gastight enclosure around or over an input tray. Tray-lidding 628 Chapter 35 machines accept incoming preformed rigid trays and seal a gas-tight film over the tray. Thermoforming machines create a semirigid package by using a heated mold to form a tray or other pack on line, which is sealed after the introduction of the product by imposing a covering film in the case of a tray or heat-sealing the finished pack. Bulk gas packaging machines use large plastic sacks or other forms into which product is introduced in large quantities and heat-sealed. MAP gases can be delivered either as premixtures in cylinders or as bulk gases to be mixed on-site. Bulk gases may be delivered as compressed gases in cylinders, or as cryogenic liquids. N2:CO2:O2 systems may also depend upon membrane-generated gas. A calibrated mixing panel or gas mixer is required to prepare the appropriate MAP mixture for introduction into the gas packaging machine. In addition, valves along with pressure-regulating systems are used to step pressure down as it passes from the source tank, through the mixer, to the point of introduction. Most packaging machines rely on a solenoid valve to control gas timing and mass delivery at point of pack; however, continuous form and fill machinery may use a simple lance with appropriate pressure regulation. 35.9 Development of Argon MAP Argon is an inert gas that has been used in MAP and processing of a variety of foodstuffs (Spencer, 1993; Spencer and Rojak, 1993; Spencer and Steiner, 1997). The use of argon improves food quality for a number of reasons. While both N2 and argon are inert gases, their physical properties differ in significant ways. Because argon displaces and excludes O2 more efficiently than N2, it provides better control against oxidation of flavor and color components of foods. In addition, using argon results in the use of less CO2 to control microbes. Because CO2 is reactive and generally deleterious to product quality, the quality of the product is better with the use of argon rather than N2. In extensive laboratory testing, argon has been found to be superior to the MAP gases used previously. Building upon these results, commercial development of the use of argon gas for MAP has proceeded in Europe for a wide range of food products (Spencer and Humphreys, 2002). Currently, more than 200 products, including a wide range of ready-to-eat packaged foods, are offered at retail in the UK and elsewhere in Europe. The commercial development of argon as a MAP gas has required the reengineering of gas-handling systems, modification of packaging equipment, and building a base of practical knowledge and detailed know-how regarding the practical application of argon in factory environments. Considerable engineering has been necessary to maximize the efficiency of argon use in view of its cost, and to ensure the reliability of the product shelf-life outcome. The deterioration of ready-to-eat foods is caused by enzymatic and oxidative changes over time as well as microbial spoilage. Packaging these products in an inert gas atmosphere An Overview of Modified Atmosphere Storage 629 displaces air and hence O2, and thus, prevents oxidation. Admixing a titer, usually 20–70%, of CO2 to the inert MAP gas reduces the rate of microbial growth. 35.10 Films for Argon MAP A wide range of commonly available gas packaging machinery was used in these example experiments, and all were successfully and easily modified to accommodate argon. A wide range of plastic films and trays were used, and most of these were found to be satisfactory. The key point was to use highly impermeable films and trays. A large array of tests was conducted to determine the best economical fit of plastic packaging for various product constraints. Generally, excellent results were obtained with highly impermeable (O2 transmission rate 0–5 cm3/day·m2·atm SPTRH) CPET/PET trays and either high or medium barrier APET/ PET, EVA/PET, or PP/PET film combinations (O2 transmission rate 75–100 cm3/day·m2·atm SPTRH). The results reported here were produced on a tray-lidding machine using heatsealable, peelable top films. Further Readings Robertson, G.L., 1993. Food Packaging. Principles and Practice. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 36 MAP Technology 36.1 Introduction Fruits and vegetables products are becoming increasingly popular throughout the world as rich sources of nutrients, vitamins, and dietary fiber, and are consumed as integral part of a dietary system. People like to have orchard freshness in fruits and vegetables. One of the major objectives of modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) is the retaining orchard freshness of the packaged produce for longer period. By employing controlled atmosphere (CA) storage technology, the life of fruits and vegetables can be increased two to four times longer than those stored in an ambient environment. In most countries in the world, fruits and vegetables are transported long distances to make them available in retail markets. Construction of airtight storage chambers for controlling air composition makes this technology cost-intensive. Moreover, CA storage is limited to bulk storage under low temperatures and high relative humidity (RH). In MAP technology, the product is sealed in a retail-sized package that has relative permeability to O2, CO2, N2, or argon. The optimum levels of O2 and CO2 are established within the package and result in enhancement of shelf life. No external means are required for establishing optimum air composition. MAP applications have been developed most extensively in Europe for a great range of products, including meats, produce, vegetables and fruits, bakery, and other products. MAP is used not only to confer quality advantages but to ensure food safety without added risk. By packaging foods in an anaerobic MAP environment such as N2, CO2 presents no greater risk than the anaerobiosis that results from temperature abuse of sealed packages. In this chapter, various aspects such as MAP gases, MAP procedures, and MAP materials pertaining to this technology are discussed in greater detail. 36.2 Gases Used in MAP In active MAP, the pack is flushed with a gas or a combination of gases. The common gases used are O2, CO2, and N2, traces of CO, nitrous oxide, ozone, argon, ethanol vapor, and SO2. The effects of important gases used in MAP are described in the following sections. All rights reserved. 632 Chapter 36 36.2.1 Oxygen Minimum O2 levels are used to pack food under MAP because O2 reacts with the food stuff, resulting in oxidative breakdown of foods into their constitutive parts. O2 also combines easily with fats and oils, causing rancidity. Foods deteriorate due to physical, chemical, and microbiological factors. O2 is probably the most important gas being used metabolically by both aerobic spoilage microorganisms and plant tissues and taking part in some enzymatic reactions in food including the compounds such as vitamins and flavors. The exception occurs where O2 is needed for fruit and vegetable respiration, color retention, as in the case of red meat, or to avoid anaerobic conditions in white fish. 36.2.2 Carbon Dioxide CO2 is both water and liquid soluble, and although it is not a bactericide or fungicide, it has bacteria-static and fungi-static properties. The overall effect on microorganisms is an extension of the lag phase of growth and a decrease in the growth rate during the logarithmic growth phase. However, the former effect is greater, and therefore as bacteria move from lag to log phase of growth, the inhibitory effects are reduced. The earlier the product is gas packaged, the more effective the CO2 will be. Yeast, which produces CO2 during growth, is stimulated by high levels of CO2 and thus for some products where these levels are potentially a major cause of spoilage, MAP may not be an advisable option. Also the food-associated pathogens, Clostridium perfringens and Clostridium botulinum, are not affected by the presence of CO2, and their growth is encouraged by anaerobic conditions. In general, CO2 is most effective in foods where the normal spoilage organism consists of aerobic, gram-negative psychotropic bacteria. For maximum antimicrobial effect, the storage temperature of MAP products should be kept as low as possible, because the solubility of CO2 decreases dramatically with increasing temperature. Thus, improper temperature control will usually eliminate the beneficial effects of elevated CO2. The absorption of CO2 is highly dependent on the moisture and fat content of the product. If the product absorbs excess CO2, the total volume inside the package will be reduced, giving a vacuum package look, known as “pack collapse.” Excess CO2 absorption in combination with pack collapse can also reduce the water-holding capacity of the product, resulting in unsightly drip. Some dairy products (e.g., cream) are highly sensitive to CO2 concentrations and will be tainted if packed in MAP with high CO2 levels. Fruits and vegetables can suffer physiological damage due to high CO2 levels. For practical purposes, in most foods, gaseous CO2 is applied to a biological tissue that would exist in the liquid phase of the tissue, primarily as dissolved CO2 gas and carbonic acid (∼2%). MAP Technology 633 36.2.3 Nitrogen N2 is an inert tasteless gas that displays little or no antimicrobial activity on its own. Because of low solubility in water and fat, the presence of N2 in a MAP food can prevent pack collapse that can occur when high concentrations of CO2 are used. In addition, N2, by displacing O2 in the pack, can delay oxidative rancidity and also inhibit the growth of aerobic microorganism in foods such as nuts. Removing O2 to <1% by N2 flushing helps prevent oxidative rancidity of fats. N2 can also indirectly influence the microorganisms in perishable foods by slowing the growth of aerobic spoilage organisms. The next important function of N2 is to act as a filler gas, keeping flexible packages from developing a vacuum. Exactly what combination of gases is to be used depends on type of the product, packaging material, and storage temperature. The packaging system selected must have sufficient headspace to provide enough gas to interact with the entire product. The headspace must contain a reservoir of CO2 to compensate for gas absorbed by the product and lost across the packaging material. Hence, enough headspace should be provided to achieve longer shelf life of the commodities. N2, CO2, and O2 are all accorded generally recognized as safe (GRAS) status and may be used freely, alone, or in mixtures in the United States for food preservation. These gases are also considered safe for use in the European Union and are given EU numbers. They may be used freely providing the package is labelled as a preservative atmosphere. 36.2.4 Carbon Monoxide Because CO is highly toxic, it is not approved by the regulatory authorities owing to possible health hazard to the packaging machine operators. Its use, however, has been sanctioned in the United States to prevent browning in packaged lettuce. CO has little inhibitor effect on microorganisms. 36.2.5 Argon Argon (Ar) is a chemically inert, odorless, and tasteless gas. It is a heavier gas than nitrogen and is used to protect sensitive products such as wine. Argon has the same properties as nitrogen and does not affect microorganisms to any greater degree. It can be used in CA/ MA to replace nitrogen in most applications. Its solubility (twice that of nitrogen) and certain molecular characteristics give it special properties for use with vegetables. Under certain conditions, it slows down metabolic reaction and reduces growth. Argon is also accorded GRAS status, has an EU number, and is approved for use in the EU. Experiments have proved that argon provides significant advantages over N2 in the practical control of oxidation and spoilage as well as microorganism growth. But N2 MAP is a low-cost and economical process. 634 Chapter 36 36.2.6 Other Gases The potential of various other gases such Cl2, ethylene oxide, nitrogen dioxide, ozone, propylene oxide, and SO2 for MAP has been investigated experimentally, but their commercial application for packaging foods is not approved. 36.3 Methods of Creating MA Conditions MA can be created either naturally by the commodity or artificially by active packaging. 36.3.1 Natural or Passive MA In natural modification, the respiring product is placed in a polymeric package and sealed hermetically. Only the respiration of the product and gas permeability of the film influence the change in the gaseous composition of environment surrounding the product. If the products respiration characteristics are properly matched to the film permeability values, then a beneficial MA can be created within the package. If a film of correct intermediary permeability is chosen, then a desirable equilibrium MA is established when the rates of O2 and CO2 transmission through the package equal a product’s respiration rate. 36.3.2 Active MAP By pulling a slight vacuum and replacing the package atmosphere with a desired mixture of CO2, O2, and N2, a beneficial equilibrium atmosphere may be established more quickly than a passively generated equilibrium atmosphere. 36.4 Techniques to Replace Air in MAP Two basic techniques are employed to replace air in MAP. They are gas flushing and compensated vacuum. 36.4.1 Gas Flushing Air is replaced by gas in the gas flush technique, which is normally accomplished on a form fill seal machine. A continuous gas stream dilutes the air in the atmosphere surrounding the food product. The package is then sealed. Because the replacement of air inside the package is accomplished by dilution, there is a limit on the efficiency of this unit. Typical residual O2 levels in gas flushed packs are 2–5%. Therefore, if the food item to be packed is highly O2 sensitive, the gas flush technique is normally not suitable. So when considering a packaging system, it is important to consider the O2 sensitivity of the food product. The great advantage of the gas flush technique is the speed of the machine. Its continuous action allows for a high product rate. MAP Technology 635 36.4.2 Compensated Vacuum Vacuum is first applied to remove the air, and then the desired gas or gas mixture is incorporated. The replacement is accomplished in a two-step process, so the speed of equipment operation is slower than the gas flush technique. However, because the air is removed by vacuum and not simply diluted, the efficiency of the unit with respect to residual air levels is better. Therefore, if the food product is extremely sensitive to O2, a compensated vacuum machine must be used. 36.4.3 Active Packaging Another active packaging technique is the use of O2, CO2, or ethylene scavengers and emitters. Such scavengers/emitters are capable of establishing a rapid equilibrium atmosphere within hermetically sealed produce packages. Sometimes certain additives are incorporated into the polymeric packaging film or within packaging containers to modify the headspace atmosphere. This is referred to as active packaging. This concept of active packaging was developed to rectify the deficiencies in passive packaging. For example, when a film is a good barrier to moisture, but not to O2, the film can still be used along with O2 scavenger to exclude O2 from the pack. Similarly, CO2 absorbers/emitters, ethanol emitters, and ethylene absorbents can be used to control O2 levels inside the MA pack. The appropriate absorbent materials are placed alongside the food. By their activity, they modify the headspace of the package and thereby extend the shelf life of the contents. For example, to reduce O2 content quickly and to increase CO2 content within a package, ferrous carbonate inside a gas-permeable sachet is used. In the presence of moist air, the amorphous material oxidizes according to the following equation: FeCO 3 + O 2 + H 2 O → 4 Fe(OH)3 + CO 2 The quantity of FeCO3 used must be carefully calculated; if too much is present inside the package, anoxic conditions will be established. Relative changes in O2 and CO2 concentrations during passive modification and active modification of packaged horticultural products are shown in Figure 36.1 (Robertson, 2006). The commonly used absorbers/emitters in active packaging are presented in Table 36.1. 36.5 Gas Scavenger and Generator Systems Another strategy for altering the gas environment is to add gas scavengers or generators inside a MAP. This technology is popular in Japan but has yet to be used extensively in other parts of the world. O2-absorbing materials such as iron powder are typically contained in gaspermeable sachets in order to minimize food contamination. With these sachets, O2 can be 636 Chapter 36 Figure 36.1: Relative Changes in O2 and CO2 Concentrations During Passive Modification and Active Modification of Packaged Horticultural Products. reduced to as low as 100 ppm, levels that cannot be obtained by vacuum or gas flush systems. CO2 from packaged coffee can also be absorbed using Ca(OH)2. Simultaneous O2 removal and CO2 generation can be accomplished with a combination of iron carbonate and ascorbic acid. These systems have been shown to be effective with products such as peanuts. Other technologies for the adsorption of ethylene and the generation of ethanol vapor are also available. Scavenging kinetics can be controlled by modifying particle size, controlling moisture, and applying various encapsulation technologies.
