This is largely due to the changing consumer demand where convenience, quality, safety, and impact on environment are of prime considerations. These materials provide a range of permeability to gas and water vapor together with the necessary package integrity needed for MAP. Permeability of most commonly used polymeric film to O2 (PO2) and CO2 (PCO2) at ambient temperature (23˚C) and water vapor at 38˚C and RH of 0% at one side and the other side (high-pressure side) at 95% are also shown in Table 36.2. Many of the films used in MAP singly do not offer all the properties required for a MAP. To provide packaging film with wide range of physical properties, many of the individual films are combined through processes like lamination and coextrusion. 36.8 Polyolefins Plastics with their unique and diverse combination of properties are ideal materials to meet the growing demands of innovation and performance in MAP in a sustainable manner. Among the several groupings in MAP films, polyethylene is most commonly used to provide a hermetic seal and also as a medium of control for characteristics like antifogging abilities, mechanical strength, durability, good gas barrier properties, and integrity of closure (heat sealing). Following are the different materials used. • • • Low-density polyethylene (LDPE): This extremely versatile material accounts for the biggest proportion of plastic materials used for packaging. It is an inert film with low permeability for water vapor but has high gas permeability. Ethylene vinyl acetate, a copolymer of ethylene and vinyl acetate, has superior sealing qualities. Blended polyethylene can be used with different additives to make a peelable seal, which is strong and gives an adequate barrier. When used with other films for lidding, base webs, preformed trays, bulk packaging, or horizontal/vertical form-fill-seal webs, low-density polyethylene can be laminated, extrusion coated, or coextruded. Linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE): This material has better impact strength, tear resistance, higher tensile strength and elongation, greater resistance to environmental stress cracking, and better puncture resistance. Thus, LLDPE can meet certain special requirements but at some financial and technical cost. Variation on a basic LDPE film remains by far the most common film used for MAP. High-density polyethylene: This film has a higher softening point than LDPE and provides barrier properties. It is not suitable as a sealant layer and hence is not used in MAP Technology 639 • • • • • thermoformable base webs but is used as one of the layers in the lidding material in coextruded form. It has better gas-barrier properties than LLDPE but poor clarity. Polypropylene (PP) and oriented polypropylene (OPP): PP is chemically similar to polyethylene and can be extruded or coextruded to provide a sealant layer. OPP provides a high-moisture vapor barrier and gas barrier, 7–10 times higher than that of polyethylene. It also has excellent grease resistance. OPP coated with polyvinylidene in low gauge form provides high barrier to moisture vapor. Coextruded-oriented polypropylene (COPP): This film is mostly used for vertical form fill seal packs. It can be a blown film or a cast and drawn film via a stentered system. It has good moisture vapor barrier and gas barrier properties can be further improved by coating with polyvinylidene. COPP can be laminated as a part of the lidding material. It can be produced by coextrusion with the basic properties or it can be perforated mechanically to provide a reduced resistance to gas flow on respiring products. This film is suitable when gas flow is desired in MAP. It is mainly used as breathable package for fresh produce. Ionomers: The first commercially available ionomer was the polymer of ethylene, Surlyn A. It is similar in properties to polyethylene but has many advantages. For example, it develops a high tack and can seal through a level of surface contamination. Ionomers can be extrusion coated but they are not cost-effective. Vinyl polymers: • Vinyl acetate copolymer: This polymer has high flexibility in sheet form and high permeability to water vapor and gases (in comparison to LDPE). In both lidding and base films, it is mainly used as a component of the sealant layer. • Polyvinyl chloride (PVC): It is most widely used as the thermoformable base for MA packs. PVC provides a good gas barrier and a moderate barrier to moisture vapor. It has excellent oil and grease resistance. Both barrier properties and strength characteristics vary with thickness. PVC film is manufactured in a different way than the blown or stentered techniques used for other MAP films: it is milled and calendered. • Polyvinylidene chloride (PVDC) copolymer: This copolymer of vinylidene chloride with vinyl chloride is used in MAP as a gas barrier coating for lidding films and in film form as a sandwiched barrier layer. It has outstanding barrier properties with low permeability to water vapor and gases. It is mainly used as a coating on polyester and OPP for lidding films. • Ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH): This moisture-sensitive, high gas-barrier material is sandwiched between the main formable and sealant layer to provide protection. It is expensive and hence it is used at the lowest gauge that provides adequate barrier properties for the intended laminate. Styrene polymers • Polystyrene: This clear thermoplastic material has a high tensile strength but a poor barrier to moisture vapor and gases. Polystyrene alone is brittle, but it can be blended (styrene butadiene or polybutadiene) to get required properties. This affects the clarity. 640 Chapter 36 • • • • High-impact polystyrene: This is an opaque, thermoformable, moderately low gas barrier material used as a component of laminate or coextrusion. Polyamides: The commonly used material is Nylon-6. When used in MAP, this film is either laminated or extrusion coated with polyethylene and is used as lidding materials producing physically the strongest material. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET): PET is polyester used in various forms in MAP, as a low-gauge-oriented film of high clarity as lidding material and in crystalline or amorphous form as in-line preformed or thermoformed trays. Other polymers: Other films used for thermoforming are polycarbonate and acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS). No single polymer offers all the properties required for MAP. In addition to barrier properties, machinability/sealability must also be considered. One inherent requirement for all MAP packs is the ability to retain the desired atmosphere as long as possible. This is achieved first by choosing a film or films to provide the required gas and moisture vapor permeability characteristics and second by ensuring seal integrity of the packs. To achieve these goals, different plastic films are either laminated or coextruded. In the case of storage in polymeric packing, increase in CO2 content and reduction in O2 content occur naturally as a result of the respiration of the fruit. Thus, it is not subjected to accurate control. However, the composition in the packing can be changed partially by the type of material selected, capacity of the packing, variety of fruits, and temperature of the storage. In the selection of material, its gas vapor permeability is important and depends on the type and thickness of the material. 36.9 Methods for Storing Fruits in Polymeric Packets At present four methods are used in storing fruits in polymeric packets with selective permeability. 1. 2. 3. 4. In small packing (i.e., polyethylene bags) In boxes with polyethylene lining In containers with polyethylene lining In container bags with permeable packing In the first method, the fruits are packed in small polyethylene bags with a 1–3 kg capacity. After packing the fruits, the packets are hermetically sealed and a vacuum is generally created in them so that the material sticks to the surface of the fruits compactly and forms a sort of second skin around them. In the second method, the fruits are kept in polyethylene packets of size equal to that of standard box for apple packing, which has a capacity of 25–30 kg. Inside these packets a vacuum is also created, but it is considerably less than in packs of small volume. MAP Technology 641 In the third method, the standard container of 500–600 kg capacity is lined with polyethylene; fruits are packed in it directly from the orchard and they remain in the container for subsequent storage. The fourth method is different from the first three in that the fruits are kept in practically gas impermeable polyethylene containers having a capacity of 0.3–1 ton of fruits. Gas exchange in these containers takes place through small diffuse packing pieces made of another synthetic material that has selective permeability for gases. A vacuum is created in such containers also, but to lesser degree than in small bags. The first method is labor-intensive and difficult to use for large-scale commercial storage, whereas the remaining three methods can be used for storage of large quantities of fruits. 36.9.1 Bag and Tray Systems A variety of configurations is available, ranging from plastic bags that are heat sealed (sometimes after gas flushing) to rigid, largely impermeable trays (either thermoformed from PET, PVC, or PS, or made from molded paper pulp with a thermoformed plastic liner) to which is sealed a polymeric film with the desired permeability characteristics so that either an optimum MA is created inside the package at equilibrium or a gas mixture flushed through the package immediately prior to sealing is retained. 36.9.2 Individual Seal Packaging This technique was first developed in the 1960s and has recently been reviewed; it appears to be identical to the system known as UNIPACK. Individual seal packaging (ISP) consists of packaging individual units of fruit in a polymeric film (originally 10 micron HDPE, but now coextruded polyolefin), which is then shrunk by blowing hot air over the package. The fruit may be cooled after passing through the hot air tunnel by rapid ventilation. Equipment for seal packaging has developed rapidly, from hand wrapping, through manual, semi, and fully automatic sealers, to automatic form fill seal machinery capable of operating at 200 fruit per minute. It is also possible to code or brand each individual fruit (Metlitski et al., 1972). ISP appears to function primarily by maintenance of a water saturated atmosphere that extends shelf life by reducing shrinkage and weight loss. It also reduces disease severity by preventing cross-contamination of produce in boxes and permitting easy removal of infected fruit. The modification of respiratory gases within ISP produce is generally not sufficient to cause significant atmosphere modification. A marked reduction in shrinkage and weight loss without a deleterious effect on flavor has been shown to result from ISP. It doubles and at times triples the shelf life of the fruit as measured by appearance, firmness, shrinkage, weight loss, and other quality attributes. ISP 642 Chapter 36 also delays various parameters of physiological deterioration better then cooling to optimal temperature. ISP has been shown to reduce chilling injury in various citrus cultivars, and thus, when combined with cooling, which reduces decay, fruit deterioration is reduced. ISP also contributes to the healing of wounds caused during harvesting and markedly reduces the incidence of blemishes on various fruits. Changes related to senescence, such as deterioration of cell membrane integrity and softening, are also delayed by ISP. Undesirable effects of ISP include germination of seeds inside grapefruit stored for a prolonged time, sprouting of carrots, and rooting of citron fruit. The use of films for ISP that contain gradually released fungicides has been suggested as advantageous because most of the fungicide is in the film and is not measured when toxic residues in fruit are examined. New films that contain substances capable of absorbing ethylene would also be excellent for ISP because reduction of the ethylene concentration around the fruit would extend shelf life by delaying the various reactions leading to senescence. For the degreening of citrus fruit, the application prior to sealing of ethylene-releasing agents ensures that ethylene accumulates to a level suitable for accelerating the degreening process. There are advantages over the conventional degreening techniques in which ethylene gas aggravates the development of various blemishes resulting at times in the loss of more than half the fruit. Despite all the advantages listed here, the commercial adoption of ISP has been slow, possibly due to the lack of availability of high-speed, reasonably priced packaging equipment. However, the technique appears to be used extensively in China and Japan where ISP is performed by hand. 36.10 Modified Humidity Packaging of Fresh Horticultural Produce One of the major differences between CA storage and MAP of horticultural produce is that, despite the gas composition around the produce being almost identical in both cases, the storage life of MAP produce is frequently less than that of produce under CA storage. The limiting factor is the appearance of molds and bacteria in MAP produce as a result of high (near saturation) in-package relative humidity (IPRH), a consequence of the low water vapor transmission rate of the films typically used for MAP. Such a problem is not observed in CA storage where the flow system presumably results in lower relative humidity. Although fungicides have been used in an attempt to control mold development in produce packages they have been only partially effective and, in some cases, have caused problems of their own. The incorporation of fungicides directly into films has not been fully effective either. However, even if fungicides were effective, they do not control bacterial development also associated with high humidity in MAP. MAP Technology 643 The optimum RH for storage of fresh produce has not been well established, and the generally recommended levels of 85–95% represent a compromise between preventing excessive weight loss and providing some control of microbial spoilage. Two possible approaches to controlling IPRH are perforation of the package, which precludes the possibilities of achieving MA conditions within the package, and the use of in-package water-adsorbing compounds that can maintain a target RH. The feasibility of the latter approach to produce predetermined humidity within fresh produce packages has recently been described using predried crystals of compounds possessing a type III adsorption according to the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) classification system. The use of xylitol, potassium chloride, sodium chloride, and sorbitol produced and held the IPRH at 78–79%, 84–85%, 73–76%, and 72–74%, respectively, in a model package containing tomatoes and an LDPE film for gas exchange. No shriveling of the fruit was observed provided that their weight loss was less than 7%. As well, because of the reduced RH and aw inside the packages, microbial growth will occur. Clearly, the use of potassium chloride would not be desirable because at the RH of 0.84–0.85 aw (water activity), most of the tomato fruit pathogens would be capable of growth. In commercial packages, it is suggested that the salts be placed inside sachets of spunbonded olefin films that have small holes to readily permit the movement of water vapor but completely block the movement of liquid water. The critical feature of such a system is to have sufficient salt present such that when the desired quantity of water vapor has been absorbed, the salt remains saturated; for if the salt solution becomes unsaturated; the IPRH will rise. However, if salt absorbs too much water vapor from inside the package, shriveling of the produce will result. It should be possible to design sachets having the quantity of salt that will achieve the optimum results. 36.11 Estimation of Surface Area of Polymeric Film for MAP Many synthetic materials have selective permeability for different gases. For storing fruits in polyethylene packs of 1–3 kg, the selective permeability of material for CO 2 (α CO2 ) is 0.003–0.005 m/day·atm. 36.12 Development of Vacuum in Polyethylene Packing P. Marcellin, the well-known French engineer who worked on storage of fruits in controlled and modified atmospheres, gave the following explanation for the formation of vacuum in the polyethylene packings: Fruits kept in a polyethylene unperforated sheet remain in a favorable atmosphere till maturity. After some time the polyethylene packs come into close contact with the fruit surface as a result of volume difference of gases. The accumulation of CO2 around the fruit is less than the absorption of O2 by it. This difference is explained by the fact that the permeability of the polyethylene to CO2 gas is greater than that of O2. Also the value of coefficient of respiration is not sufficiently high. As 646 Chapter 36 the volume of the packs decreases, the partial pressure of nitrogen increases. Polyethylene is permeable to nitrogen, and therefore it allows nitrogen to pass through until the packet starts adhering to the fruit surface. The vacuum phenomenon was observed during packing apples, pears, cherries, bananas, and kola nuts in polyethylene packs. In the case of peaches and apricots, at certain stage of maturity, a reverse phenomenon was observed (i.e., a bulging of packing due to nitrogen from the outside air entering the packet). It is evident from these observations that gas exchange with atmosphere surrounding the sealed packet containing fruits takes place only due to diffusion of gases through the packing (Robertson, 2006). 36.13 Indices of Failure In designing suitable packaging for foods, it is important first to define the indices of failure (IOFs) of the food, that is, the quality attributes that will indicate that the food is no longer acceptable to the consumer. These may or may not be the same as the indices of deterioration (IODs). An IOF could be the development of rancid flavors in cereals due to oxidation, loss of red color (bloom) in chilled beef due to depletion of O2, reduction of carbonation in bottled soda due to permeation of CO2 through the bottle wall, caking of instant coffee due to moisture ingress, development of microbial taint in chilled poultry, or moisture loss in green vegetables resulting in wilting. Once the IOFs for a particular food have been defined, the next step is to attempt to quantify the magnitude of the particular degradation (e.g., how much moisture or O2 can react with the food before it becomes unacceptable). The final step is to ascertain which (if any) of the IOFs might be influenced by the packaging material, because packaging cannot prevent all deteriorative reactions in foods. If, for example, the IOF of a snack food was loss of crispness, then the packaging material could influence this by the extent to which it permitted the ingress of moisture. Different plastic films for example, have a different water vapor transmission rate (WVTR), and thus the shelf life obtained varies depending on the particular plastic selected. Similar considerations apply to foods for which IOF is oxidation, as different packaging materials have different O2 transmission rates (OTRs). However, it is not just the packaging material itself that can influence shelf life; the method of filling the product into the package is also important. For example, with roasted and ground coffee, vacuum filling into metal cans will remove 95% or more of the O2 from the can compared with inert gas flush packaging in plastic fail laminate pouches, which will remove or displace 80–90% of the O2 in the package. The residual O2 in the package at the time of filling will have a major influence on shelf life regardless of the O2 barrier properties of the package itself. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 37 Gases and Vapor Applied to MA Processing Operations 37.1 Introduction Dissolved gases in foods, such as O2 and CO2, affect their shelf life. Gas mixtures are used to flush packages to eliminate O2 and to prolong shelf life. The term vapor is generally used for the gaseous phase of a substance that exists as a liquid or a solid at ambient conditions. The behavior of gases in the food packages changes with temperature and pressure and has direct effects on the shelf life of the packaged food. The behavior of the gases can be modelled by the state equations. Sometimes ambient air is present in the food packages. Air contains some percentage of moisture in it. When the temperature of the packet is reduced, the moisture can condense on the surface, which may spoil the food. 37.1.1 Equations of State for Ideal and Real Gases Equations of state are expressions for the relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature, and quantity of gases within a given system. The simplest equation of state is the ideal gas equation. The ideal gas equation closely approximates the behavior of gases near ambient temperature and pressure. At high pressure and temperature, most gases deviate from ideal behavior. In this chapter, the ideal gas equations and the most often used equation for real gases (Van der Waals equation) and their use in MAP are given. 37.2 Quantity of Gases The most definitive quantification of gases is by mass or the number of moles (n), which is the quotient of mass and the molecular weight. The unit of mass is prefixed to mole (e.g., kg mole) to indicate the ratio of mass in kg and the molecular weight. The number of molecules in 1 g mole is the Avogadro’s number, 6.023 × 1023 molecules/g mole. At 273 K and 760 mm Hg pressure (101.325 kPa), 1 g mole, kg mole, and lb mole occupy 22.4 L, 22.4 m3, and 359 ft3, respectively. Ideal Gas Equation: Pressure (P), the force of collision between gas molecules and on surface of the container, is directly proportional to the temperature (T) and the number of molecules per unit volume (V). CHAPTE R 38 Shelf Life of Foods 38.1 Definition There is no simple generally accepted definition of shelf life in the food technology literature. The National Food Processors Association in the United States in 1978 recommended the following: “A product is within its shelf life when it is neither misbranded nor adulterated; when the product quality is generally accepted for its purported use by the consumer; and so long as the container retains its integrity with respect to leakage and protection of the contents.” The Institute of Food Technologists in the United States defines shelf life as the period between the manufacture and the retail purchase of the food product, during which time the product is in a state of satisfactory quality in terms of nutritional value, taste, texture, and appearance. An alternative definition is that shelf life is the duration of that period between the packing of a product and its use, for which the quality of the product remains acceptable to the user. For the majority of foods and beverages in which quality decreases with time, it follows that there will be a finite length of time before the product becomes unacceptable. This time from production to unacceptability is referred to as shelf life. Because the consumer can generally only judge the quality of the product at the time of consumption, not at the time of purchase, shelf life actually refers to the time for which a food can remain on both the retailer’s and consumer’s shelf before it becomes unacceptable. Although the shelf lives of foods vary, they are generally determined routinely for each particular product by the manufacturer or processor. Storage studies are an essential part of food product development, in which the manufacturer attempts to provide the longest shelf life practicable consistent with both costs and the patterns of handling and use by distributors, retailers, and consumers. Inadequate shelf life will often lead to consumer dissatisfaction and complaints. At best, such dissatisfaction will eventually affect the acceptance and sales of brand name products, while at worst it can lead to malnutrition or even illness. Therefore, food processors give considerable attention to determining the shelf lives of their products. Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00038-5 661 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 662 Chapter 38 38.2 Shelf Life Dating It has been standard practice in almost all food manufacturing and processing establishments to put a “closed” code (so called because only those with knowledge of the coding system can interpret the code) on the packaged product. The code is sometimes placed on the primary package but frequently on the secondary package. Generally this code indicates the time of processing and packaging (e.g., day and year). For many canned foods, it has long been mandatory to include such information on the end of the container in an embossed form together with a code for the product itself to aid identification of unlabeled cans in the factory. The advent of the consumer movement in the early 1970s and the push for the consumer’s “right to know” led to an open date system for the package in an easily readable form. This system was adopted with the purpose of informing the consumer about the shelf life of the product. Several types of dates can be used. The commonly used dates are: • • • • • Pack date: The date on which the product was packed into the primary package (i.e., the immediate container in which it is sold). It does not provide any specific information as to the quality of the product when purchased or how long it will retain its quality after purchase. Display date: The date on which the product was placed on the shelf by the retailer. Pull date or sell by date: The last date on which the product should be sold in order to allow the consumer a reasonable length of time in which to use it. Best before or best if used by date: The last date of maximum high quality. Use by date or expiration date: The date after which the product is no longer at an acceptable level of quality. There is no uniform or universally accepted open dating system used for foods throughout the world. In some countries it is mandatory to put an open date of all perishable and sometimes semiperishable foods, while in other countries such requirements are voluntary. However, the quantity of open dated food on sale has increased throughout the world, a trend that is likely to continue. The European Community (EC) adopted a “minimum durability date.” It indicates the length of time for which the product may be stored—the storage conditions may be specified (e.g., temperature not to exceed 7°C)—before its quality has deteriorated to such an extent that it would be regarded as unacceptable by the manufacturer or the consumer. This concept (basically equivalent to the “best before” date) allows the processor to set the quality standard of the food, given that the product would still be acceptable to many consumers after the “best before” date had passed. Shelf Life of Foods 663 38.3 Factors Controlling Shelf Life Product shelf life is controlled by three factors: 1. Product characteristics 2. The environment to which the product is exposed during distribution 3. The properties of the package The shelf life of the product will be altered by changing any one of these factors. 38.3.1 Product Perishability Based on the nature of the changes that can occur during storage, foods may be divided into three categories: perishable, semiperishable, and nonperishable or shelf stable. These labels translate into very short shelf life products, short-to-medium shelf life products, and mediumto-long shelf life products. Perishable foods: Those that must be held at chill or freezer temperatures (i.e., 0–7°C or –12°C to –18°C, respectively) if they are to be kept for more than a short period. Examples of such foods include milk, fresh flesh foods, poultry, and fish, and many fresh fruits and vegetables. Semiperishable foods: Semiperishable foods are those that contain natural inhibitors (e.g., some cheeses, root vegetables, and eggs) or those that have received some type of mild preservation treatment (e.g., pasteurization of milk, smoking of hams, and pickling of vegetables) that produces greater tolerance to environmental conditions and abuse during distribution and handling. Nonperishable: Shelf stable foods are considered nonperishable at room temperatures. Many unprocessed foods that are unaffected by microorganisms because of their low moisture content (e.g., cereal, grains, and nuts and some confectionery products). Processed food products can be shelf stable if they are preserved by heat sterilization (e.g., canned foods), contain preservatives (e.g., soft drinks), are formulated as dry mixes (e.g., cake mixes), or are processed to reduce their water content (e.g., raisins or crackers). However, shelf stable foods only retain this status if the integrity of the package containing them remains intact. Even then, their shelf life is finite due to deteriorative chemical reactions that occur at room temperature independently of the nature of the packaging and the permeation of gases, odors, and water vapor through high-barrier polymer packaging. 38.3.2 Bulk Density The free space volume of a package (V) is directly related to the bulk density (ρb) and the true density (ρp) of the product as follows: V = Vt − VP = W W – ρp ρ b (38.1) 664 Chapter 38 where V = free space volume of the package Vt = total volume of the package VP = volume of the product W = weight of the product Thus, packages of similar shape, equal weights of products, or different bulk densities will have different free space volume, and as a consequence, package areas and package behavior will differ. This has important implications when changes are made in package size for the same product or alterations are made to the process, resulting in changes to the product bulk density. Even though the true density of the food depends largely on its composition and cannot be changed significantly, bulk density of food powders can be affected by processing. Some food powders (e.g., milk and coffee) are instantized by treating the powder so that it forms into free flowing agglomerates or aggregates in which there are relatively few points of contact, making the surface of each particle more easily wetted when the powder is rehydrated. Instantization results in a reduction of bulk density. For example, the bulk density of milk powder changes from 0.64 g mL–1 to 0.55 g mL–1. A wide range of bulk densities is encountered in food products from about 0.056 g mL–1 for potato chips to 0.96 g mL–1 for granulated salt. The free space volume has an important influence on the rate of oxidation of foods, for if a food is packaged in air, a large free space volume is undesirable because it constitutes a large O2 reservoir. Conversely, if the product is packed in an inert gas, the large free space volume acts as a large “sink” to minimize the effects of O2 transferred through the film. It follows that a large package area and a low bulk density results in greater O2 transmission. Package void volume also is a key design parameter, and it has been shown to significantly affect both unsteady-state behavior and the final gas partial pressures in produce MAP. 38.3.3 Package Configuration MAP systems have taken on a wide range of shapes and sizes, but the most common forms are plastic bags and thermoformed trays (Greengrass, 1998). The package surface-to-volume (S/V) ratio is an important design parameter that determines the amount of active surface for gas transport. For barrier systems where gas permeation is minimized, a more cubic shape with a lower S/V would be preferable, whereas with MAP produce, a flatter shape with a higher S/V is desirable. However, one is often limited by the shape of the product being packaged (e.g., sliced meat). Scaling up of MAP, particularly with packaged produce, can be a challenge because, for a fixed geometry, the S/V decreases with increasing size. Therefore, in order to obtain the same system performance in larger packages, the film permeability must be increased, the produce loading decreased, or the geometry altered. Shelf Life of Foods 665 Table 38.1: Surface areas of different package shapes, with a volume of ∼450 mL Shape Sphere Cylinder Cube Tetrahedron Rectangular pack Thin rectangular pack Dimensions (cm) Diameter 9.52 Diameter 7.3 Height 10.8 Sides 7.67 Sides 15.65 Height 3 Length 15 Width 10 Height 1 Length 20 Width 22.5 Surface Area (cm2) (m2) Increase (%) Surface Area– Volume Ratio 285 331 0.0285 0.0331 0 16 0.63 0.73 353 424 450 0.0353 0.0424 0.0450 24 49 58 0.78 0.94 1.0 985 0.0985 246 2.18 38.3.4 Surface Area–Volume Ratio The dimensions of the package for a given weight of food can have a significant influence on shelf life. Although a spherical shape will minimize the surface area of the package (and thus the quantity of moisture or O2 that will permeate the package wall), it is not a practical shape for commercial use in practice, most packages tend to be rectangular or cylindrical. Table 38.1 gives the surface area range of different shapes with the same volume (450 mL). From the table it can be seen that when compared with the surface area of a sphere, the surface of a cylinder is 16% greater, a cube 24% greater, a tetrahedron 49% greater, a rectangular shape 58% greater, and a thin rectangular shape 246% greater. Extremely thin packages have a much greater surface area–volume ratio and thus require a plastic with better barrier properties to get the same shelf life than if the same quantity of product was packaged in a thicker format. For different quantities of the same product packaged in different-sized packages using the same plastic material, the smallest package will have the shortest shelf life as it inevitably has a greater surface area per unit volume. Many food companies still seem unaware of this fact as they continue to launch smaller packages without changing the packaging material and then wonder why the shelf life is shorter for the smaller package. Example 38.1 A food powder with a density of 1 is to be packaged in a plastic film that has a water vapor transfer rate (WVTR) of 2.1 g/m2·per day at 25°C and 75% RH. The initial moisture content of the powder is 3%; the critical moisture content is 7%. Assuming that each pack will contain 450 g of powder and will be exposed to an external environment at 25°C and 75% RH, 666 Chapter 38 calculate the shelf life if the shapes of the packs are the same as those listed in Table 38.1. For simplicity, assume that the driving force for WVT remains constant and that there are no moisture gradients in the powder. Take dry matter balance: 450(1− 0.03) = x (1− 0.07) where x is the weight of dried product: x= 450 × 0.97 = 469.3 g 0.93 Mass of water permeating into powder = 469.3 − 450 = 19.5 g For a spherical-shaped package: Quantity of water permeating into package per day WVTR (g/m2·per day) × surface area (m2) 0.0285 × 2.1 = 0.05985g per day Therefore, shelf life θ s = 19.35 = 323 days 0.05985 For the other shapes of the package, the shelf life as calculated well: Cylinder :θs = 278 days Cube :θ s = 261days Tetrahedron :θ s = 217 days Rectangle1:θ s = 204 days Rectangle2:θ s = 93.5 days 38.3.5 Concentration Effects It is known that the deteriorative reactions in packaged food and the factors affecting the rate of these reactions can be quantified with the aid of simple chemical kinetic expressions. The progress of deteriorative reaction can be monitored by following the change in concentration of some key component. However, in many foods such as those containing whole tissue components or where the reacting species are partially bound as in membranes, structural proteins, or carbohydrates, the concentration varies from one point to another, even at zero times. The point to be taken made here is that for many foods, it may be difficult to obtain kinetic data useful for predictive purposes. In such situations, use of sensory panels to determine the acceptability of the food is the recommended procedure. Shelf Life of Foods 667 38.4 Distribution Environment 38.4.1 Climate The deterioration of product quality of packaged foods is often closely related to the transfer of mass and heat through the package. Packaged foods may lose or gain moisture, and they will reflect the temperature of their environment since few food packages are good insulators. Thus, the climatic conditions (i.e., temperature and humidity) of the distribution environment have an important influence on the rate of reaction of packaged foods. 38.4.2 Mass Transfer In the case of mass transfer, it is the exchange of vapor and gases with the surrounding atmosphere that is of primary concern. Transmission rates of moisture vapor, O2, volatile aromas, N2, and CO2 have to be taken into account in packages where the concentration of these gases inside the package has been modified from ambient to inhibit or slow down deteriorative reactions in the food. Generally the difference in partial pressure across the package barrier will control the rate and extent of permeation, although transfer can also occur due to presence of pin holes in the material, channels in seals and closures, or cracks that result from flexing of the packaging material during filling and subsequent handling. Because the gaseous composition of the Earth’s atmosphere is essentially constant at sea level, the partial pressure difference of gases across the package barrier will depend on the internal atmosphere of the package at the time the package was sealed. The changes in temperature and relative humidity because of diurnal and seasonal solar radiation intensity can be normalized to a standard cycle and are to be considered in shelf life study. 38.4.3 Heat Transfer Food products are exposed to fluctuating temperature environments during the time from production to consumption. It is important that the nature and extent of these temperature fluctuations are known. If the major deteriorative reaction causing the end of shelf life is known, simple expressions can be derived to predict the extent of deterioration as a function of available time–temperature storage conditions. These reactions and their rates can be analyzed in relation to product shelf life. Fundamental to such an analysis is that the particular food under consideration follows the laws of “additivity and commutativity.” Additivity implies that the total extent of the degradation reaction in the food produced by successive exposures at various temperatures is the simple sum of the separate amounts of degradation, regardless of the number or spacing of each time–temperature combination. Commutativity means that the total extent of the degradation reaction in the food is independent of the order of presentation of the various time–temperatures experiences. 668 Chapter 38 38.5 Shelf Life Plots A useful approach to quantify the effect of temperature on food quality (especially when less data are available to get rate constants or when only the time to reach a certain level of quality change has been determined) is to construct shelf life plots. Several models are in use to represent the relationship between a rate of reaction (or the reciprocal of the rate, which can be time for a specified loss in quality or shelf life) and temperature. The two most used are Arrhenius model and linear model, both of which are discussed here. 38.5.1 Arrhenius Model Arrhenius model in its general form is as follows: θs = θ 0e − Ea RT ln θ s = ln θ o − EA RT E ln θ s − ln θ o = − A RT ( lnθ 0 − ln θ s ) T = − (38.2) EA R ( lnθ o − lnθ s ) = − EA 1 R T lnθ s − lnθ o EA = 1 R T (38.3) The graphical representation of Equation 38.3, shown in Figure 38.1, yields a straight line with the slope EA/R. θ  Figure 38.1: Arrhenius Plot of ln Shelf Life Ratio  s  Versus Reciprocal of the Absolute  θo  Temperature (K) Showing a Slope of EA/R. CHAPTE R 39 Kinetics of Food Deteriorative Reactions 39.1 Introduction The storage climate inside buildings such as warehouses and supermarkets is related to the external climate and climatic variations in temperature and humidity. They differ as much between different buildings and between seasons. Knowledge of influence of season and type of premises on monthly mean temperatures and humidity are essential to predict shelf life. There is little point in carefully controlling the processing conditions inside the factory and releasing the product into the distribution and retail system without some knowledge of the conditions it will experience in that system. Such knowledge is essential in the case of products containing a “best before” or “use by” date. If the major deteriorative reaction causing end of shelf life is known, simple expressions can be derived to the extent of degradation as a function of available time and storage conditions. The basic types of deteriorative reactions of foods are presented in the subsequent paragraphs. It is important that modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) not be considered in isolation from food processing, packaging, and preservation or indeed from food marketing and distribution. All interact in a complex way, and concentrating on only one aspect to the detriment of the others is a surefire recipe for commercial failure. Many chemical reactions occurring in foods can lead to deterioration in food quality, both nutritional and sensory, or the impairment of food safety. The rates of these chemical reactions depend on a variety of factors amenable to control by oxygen (O2) concentration, temperature, water activity, light, and suitable packaging material. More important classes of these deteriorative reactions are listed in Table 39.1. Undesirable changes that can occur in foods are presented in Table 39.2. 39.2 Sensory Quality The two major chemical changes that occur during the processing and storage of foods and lead to a deterioration in sensory quality are lipid oxidation and nonenzymatic browning. Chemical reactions are also responsible for changes in the color and flavor of foods during processing and storage. Once the nature of the reactions is understood, a knowledge of the factors that control the rates of these reactions is necessary in order to fully control the changes occurring in food during storage. Table 39.2: Classification of undesirable changes that can occur in foods Attribute Undesirable Change Texture • Loss of solubility • Loss of water-holding capacity • Toughening • Softening Development of • Rancidity (hydrolytic or oxidative) • Cooked or caramel flavors • Other off-flavors • Darkening • Bleaching • Development of other off-colors • Nonuniformity of particle size Loss or degradation of • Vitamins • Minerals • Proteins • Lipids Flavor Color Nutritive value Source: Fennama and Tannenbaum, 1985. Most fruits and vegetables are classified as perishable unless they have been processed in some way. Often, the only form of processing fruits and vegetables receive is to be packaged with modified atmosphere and kept under controlled temperature conditions. The species of microorganisms that cause spoilage of particular foods are influenced by two factors: the nature of the food and their surroundings. These factors are referred to as intrinsic and extrinsic parameters and are listed in Table 39.3. The minimum water activity (aw) value reported for growth of some microorganisms in food is presented in Table 39.4 Kinetics of Food Deteriorative Reactions 673 Table 39.3: Intrinsic and extrinsic parameters influencing spoilage of foods Intrinsic Factors Extrinsic Factors pH aw: water activity Eh oxidation reduction potential, nutrient content Antimicrobial constituents Biological structures Storage temperature Relative humidity of environment Presence and concentration of gases in the environment Table 39.4: Minimum water activity (aw) value reported microorganism growth in food Minimum aw Organisms Most spoilage bacteria Most spoilage yeasts Most spoilage molds Halophilic bacteria Xerophilic molds Osmophilic yeasts 0.91 0.88 0.80 0.75 0.65 0.60 39.3 Rates of Deteriorative Reactions In foods a number of deteriorative chemical, biochemical, and microbiological reactions can occur. The rates of these reactions depend on both intrinsic (compositional) and extrinsic (environmental factors). It is important to know the rates of these deteriorative reactions so that they can be controlled. Control of deteriorative reactions requires a qualitative analysis based on knowledge of the kinetics of food deterioration. A measurable index of deterioration is necessary for quantitative analysis of deteriorative reactions. The measurable index can be a chemical, physical, or sensory measurement. For quantitative analysis of quality changes, the index must be expressed as a function of the conditions existing during processing and storage so that the changes can be predicted or simulated. Thus, calculation of quality losses requires a mathematical model that expresses the effect of intrinsic and extrinsic factors on the deterioration index.The general equation describing quality loss may written as –dc = f ( I i , EJ ) dt (39.1) where –dc = rate of change of some index of deterioration C with time; (a negative sign is used dt if the concentration of C decreases with time) Ii = Intrinsic factors (i = 1 ... m) EJ = Extrinsic factors (J = 1 ... n) 674 Chapter 39 Because the quality of foods and the rate of quality changes during processing and storage depend on intrinsic factors, it is possible in many cases to correlate quality losses with the loss of particular component such as a vitamin or pigment. The conversion of a single component or quality factor A to an end product B (e.g., conversion of chlorophyll to pheophytin or conversion of ascorbic acid to brown pigments) may be written as A → Intermediate products → B The absolute concentrations of A or B need not be measured. Thus, the production of light brown pigments in foods is often measured as the increase in absorbance of light at 420 Nm of an alcoholic extract of the food, and the change in absorbance is used as an indicator of the extent of the reaction. Such quality loss can be represented as being proportional to the power of the concentration of the reactant or product: or –dA dt ∝ A n (39.2) and dB dt ∝ kB n (39.3) where A and B = concentration of quality factor measured u = time k = rate constant (dependent on extrinsic factors) n = a power factor called the order of the reaction, which defines whether the rate is dependent on the concentration of A. The value of n can be a fraction or a whole number. dA/dt and dB/dt = change in concentration of A or B with time Equation 39.3 implies that extrinsic parameters such as temperature, water activity, and light intensity are held constant; if they are not, then their influence on the rate constant k must be taken into account in evaluating the equation. For most quality changes in foods, the reaction order n has generally been shown to be either 0 or 1. From a shelf life point of view, it is often useful to know the concentration of I or I at which the product is no longer acceptable, such as when the concentration of a vitamin or pigment has fallen to below some level (e.g., 50% reduction in concentration) or the concentration of some undesirable brown color has risen above some level. In these situations, the shelf life of the food (us) is the time for the concentration of A (or B) to reach an undesirable level (Ae or Be). Kinetics of Food Deteriorative Reactions 675 39.4 Zero-Order Reactions When n = 0, the reaction is said to be pseudo-zero-order with respect to A. Equation 39.3 can then be simplified to: − dA dt = k ( A ) ° or − dA dt = k since A° = 1 (39.4) Equation 39.4 implies that the rate of loss of A is constant with time and independent of the concentration of A. Rearranging and integrating Equation 39.4 between A0, the concentration of A at u = 0, and Ae, the concentration of A at time u = ts: A θ A0 0 ∫ dA = – k ∫ dt A − A0 = − k[t − 0] A − A0 = − kt A = A0 − kt or Ae = A0 − kts (39.5) where Ae = value of A at end of shelf life ts = shelf life in days, months, years, etc. For a zero-order reaction, a plot of the amount of A remaining versus time yields a straight line (Figure 39.1) with the slope equal to the rate constant k in units of concentration per unit time. In other words, the loss of quality per day is constant when all extrinsic factors are held constant. In Equation 39.3, there is no sign before dA dt as it is in Equation 39.1, because the concentration of B is increasing: dB = K (B )° dt dB =k dt dB = kdt ∫ B Bo t dB = k ∫ dt o (B − Bo ) = k (t − o) B – Bo k= t (39.6) 676 Chapter 39 Figure 39.1: Change in Quality Versus Time Showing the Effect of the Order of the Reaction on Extent of Change. Typical pseudo-zero-order deteriorative reactions include nonenzymatic browning (e.g., in dry cereals and powdered dairy products); lipid oxidation (e.g., development of rancidity in snacks foods, dry foods, and frozen foods); and enzymatic degradation (e.g., in fresh fruits and vegetables, some frozen foods, and some refrigerated doughs). It is important to appreciate that the order of the reaction (i.e., n) is strictly an empirical concept. Thus, a pseudo-zero-order reaction does not imply that the mechanism is a monomolecular breakdown independent of the concentration of the reacting species. On the contrary, pseudo-zero-order reactions are always an indication that a complex reaction is occurring involving a number of steps. The step that determines the rate is visualized as an equilibriumtype surface-dependent reaction that is relatively slow and independent of reaction concentration, hence the zero-order. Kinetics of Food Deteriorative Reactions 679 Typical pseudo-first-order deteriorative reactions include nonenzymatic browning (e.g., loss of protein quality in dry foods), lipid oxidation (e.g., development of rancidity in salad oils and dry vegetables), vitamin loss in canned and dry foods, and microbial production of offflavors and slime in flesh foods. One difficulty with much of the food literature for food deterioration is that the reaction order is usually impossible to establish from the data, because many studies present data determined by endpoint analysis (i.e., the time to some fractional loss or loss at some single time during storage). As a consequence, much of these data remain food- and process-specific. However, as Labuza has noted, for less than 50% of the total change possible in the parameter of interest (e.g., concentration of a vitamin in a food), little or no difference may be noted between zero- and first-order plots of the data. A linear plot is obtained if 1 A is plotted against time. Second-order bimolecular reactions may also follow the following rate equation: − dA = k AB dt where A and B are the reactants. The differential equation may be integrated by holding B constant to give  A ln   = − k 1t  Ao  k1 is pseudo-first-order rate constant, k1 = kB A second-order bimolecular reaction yields a plot of the concentration of the reactant against time similar to that of first-order unimolecular reaction, but the reaction rate constant varies with different concentrations of the second reactant. Oxygen is a reactant, and a family of pseudo-first-order plots is obtained when ascorbic acid degradation is studied at different levels of oxygen availability. 39.7 nth–Order Reactions − dA = k An ; n > 1 dt A1− n − A01− n = − (1 − n ) kt Evaluations of reaction order is a trial-and-error process that involves assuming various values for n and determining which value would result in the best fit with the nth-order equation. Kinetics of Food Deteriorative Reactions 681 39.8 Reactions Where Product Concentration is Rate Limiting These types of reactions are usually followed not in terms of the concentration of the reactant, but by some manifestation of the completion of the reaction in terms of a physical property change. Examples are protein gelation, measured as an increase in the strength of the gel; the nonenzymatic browning reaction in solid foods; textural changes during cooking; and sensory flavor scores during storage. The magnitude of the attribute measured usually levels off not because of depletion of the reactants but because the measuring technique can no longer detect any further increase in intensity. Reactions of this type can be fitted to the following equation: C  ln  1 – *  = ± kt  C  where C* is the value of the measured attribute when it remains constant over long reaction times, and C is the value at any time during the transient stage of the process. Kinetics of Food Deteriorative Reactions 683 39.9 Relation Between k and D In chemical kinetics, the reaction rate constant is used to express the time dependence of reaction at a constant temperature and is denoted with letter k. In food industry, the reciprocal of the thermal death time, denoted as 1 D, is used to express the rate of food deterioration or microbial destruction at constant temperature and D is defined as the time required for 90% reduction (one log cycle reduction) in some kind of food quality parameter or microbial population. Therefore, in its more general form it can be written as k ∝1 D This method of representing the rate constant for a reaction had its origins in thermobacteriology, where the inactivation of microorganisms during heating at constant temperature is expressed as decimal reduction time. This approach was later applied to biochemical and enzymatic reactions so that the similar computational scheme could be used to determine nutritional degradation or quality degradation during thermal process or sterilization of foods. The D value is defined as D= tf − t0 log C0 − log Cf 1 C C 1 or = or log 0 f = log C0 − log Cf tf − t0 D tf − t0 D (39.11) where tf = time at the end of the process/reaction t0 = time at the start of the process/reaction C0 = initial concentration of the reactant or microbial number Cf = final concentration of the reactant or microbial number From first-order reaction in deteriorative chemical reactions it can be shown that ln A0 − ln Af = k ( t f − t 0 ) where A0 and Af are concentrations at the start and end of the reactions k = reaction rate constant k= ln A0 − ln Af A = ln 0 Af (tf − t0 ) (tf − t0 ) or   A  k = ln (10 )  log  0  ( t f − t 0 )     Af   A0  k log   ( t f − t 0 ) = ln (10 )  Af  (39.12) 684 Chapter 39 Because k in food deteriorative reactions is equivalent to 1 D of microbial reactions: k 1 = ln10 D D= ln10 2.303 = k k 39.10 Temperature Dependence of Reaction Rates It is well-known fact that raising the temperature increases the reaction rate. Quantitatively, this relationship between process’s rate of reaction and its temperature is determined by the Arrhenius equation: k = A0 e− EA RT (39.13) where EA = activation energy, J/mole R = ideal gas constant, its value being 8.314 J/mole/k T = absolute temperature, K A0 = rate constant, independent of temperature, also known as collision or frequency factor The activation energy can be found algebraically by substituting two rate constants (k1, k2) at the two corresponding reaction temperatures (T1, T2) into the Arrhenius equation, Equation 39.13. ln k1 = − EA + ln A0 RT1 (39.14) ln k2 = − EA + ln A0 RT2 (39.15) Subtracting Equations 39.15 from 39.14 results in − EA  1 1  k − ln 1 = k2 R  T2 T1  Equation 39.16 is the equation for straight line with slope EA/R and or EA ln k1 − ln k2 = 1 1 R − T2 T1  ln k1 − ln k2     T1 − T2 T2 × T1  (39.16) Kinetics of Food Deteriorative Reactions 685 Table 39.5: Typical activation energies for reactions in food deterioration Activation Energy Ea (kJ/mole) Reaction Diffusion controlled reaction Lipid oxidation Flavor degradation in dry vegetables Enzymatic reactions Vitamin degradation Color degradation in dry vegetables Nonenzymatic browning 0–34 42–105 42–105 42–126 84–126 67–147 105–210 Rearranging Equation 39.16 and solving for EA yield EA = RT1T2 k ln 1 (T1 − T2 ) k2 (39.17) The integrated form of the Arrhenius equation, Equation 39.13, is obtained from the inherent assumption that the EA and collision factor/frequency factor do not change with temperature. Although this assumption is generally true, it is not universally so, and predictions based on this model sometimes fail when applied over a temperature span of greater than about 40°C. Furthermore, when the reaction mechanism changes with temperature, the activation energy may vary substantially. The value of EA is a measure of the temperature sensitivity of the reaction (i.e., how much faster the reaction will proceed if the temperature is raised). Typical EA values for reactions important in food deterioration are listed in Table 39.5. The EA is 1 generally derived from the slope of the plot of ln k versus and depends on factors such as T aw, moisture content, solids concentration, and pH. 39.11 Half-Life Expressions for half-life or half-time of reactions is t1 2 in terms of D and k. The initial concentration of a reactant or number of microorganisms decreases exponentially with time. Kinetics of Food Deteriorative Reactions 687 Example 39.4 Ascorbic acid in canned orange juice has a half-life of 30 weeks. If the concentration just after canning is 60 mg/100 mL, calculate the concentration after 10 weeks. At t = 10 weeks, a point on the line shows a concentration of 47.5 mg/100 mL. Thus, a concentration of 0.9(47.5), or 42.9 mg/100 mL, would be the maximum that can be declared on the label. If Q reflects the change in rate for 10°C range in temperature, it is than called Q10. If reaction rate doubles with a 10°C change in temperature Q10 = 2. For reactions such as enzymatically induced color or flavor change in foods, degradation of natural pigments, nonenzymatic browning, and microbial growth rate, Q10 is usually around 2. Thus, the rule of thumb in food storage is that a 10°C reduction in storage temperature will increase the shelf life by a factor of 2. 39.12.1 Relationship Between the Q10 and EA The relationship between the Q10 value and the activation energy is derived as follows. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 40 Water Activity and Shelf Life 40.1 Introduction Water may influence chemical reactivity in different ways. It may act as a reactant (e.g., sucrose hydrolysis) or as solvent where it may exert a dilution effect on the substrates, thus decreasing the reaction rate. Water may also change the mobility of the reactants by affecting the viscosity of the food systems and form hydrogen bonds or complexes with the reacting species. Thus, an important practical aspect of water activity aw is to control undesirable chemical and enzymatic reactions that reduce the shelf life of foods. Rates of changes in food properties can be minimized or accelerated over widely different values of aw. Small changes in aw can result in large changes in reaction rates. The effect of water activity on shelf life of food is discussed in this chapter. 40.2 Definitions of Water Activity The parameter water activity (abbreviated aw) is defined as the ratio of the water vapor pressure of a material to the vapor pressure of pure water at the same temperature. Mathematically: aw = p / po (40.1) where p = vapor pressure of water exerted by the food po = saturated vapor pressure of pure water at the same temperature This concept is related to equilibrium relative humidity (ERH) in that ERH = 100 × aw. However, while aw is an intrinsic property of the food, ERH is a property of the atmosphere in equilibrium with the food. The aw of most fresh foods is above 0.99. At subfreezing temperatures, aw is defined as the vapor pressure of ice divided by the vapor pressure of the supercooled water at the same temperature. Thus, the aw of frozen foods depends only on their temperature; and the values of aw are, for example, at –15°C, aw = 0.864; at –10°C, 0.907, and at –5°C, 0.953. As mentioned in the definition of aw, the temperature must be specified because aw values are temperature dependent. The temperature dependence of aw can be described by a modified form of a Clausius-Clapeyron equation: Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00040-3 699 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. R = gas constant (8.314 J/mole · k) Thus, from Equation 40.2, a plot of ln aw versus 1/T at constant moisture content should be linear. But such plots are not always linear over wide temperature ranges, and they exhibit sharp breaks with the onset of ice formation. Due to permeation of water vapor and oxygen through the packaging material, food undergoes changes in water activity and other physicochemical properties. Water activity is a measure of the condition in which water exists in food. Water Activity and Shelf Life 701 Water is the major deteriorative agent for most types of food, and a “critical water activity” corresponds to critical moisture content. When water activity or moisture content becomes higher or lower than the critical value, some foods become unacceptable from the standpoint of quality, safety, and consumer preference. The period during which critical water activity or critical moisture content is reached is called the shelf life of the food. For example, pathogens in dry food would grow when water activity becomes greater than about 0.75; crispy food would become soft and lose consumer preference when its water activity, depending on the type of food, increases more than about 0.35–0.5. For dry foods containing lactose, such as skim milk powder, caking becomes severe in the 0.35–0.5 range of water activity. In tea and spice mix, caking appears to begin at water activity as low as 0.32 and becomes severe at 0.66. When pasta products are dried to low moisture contents such that their water activity becomes less than 0.4, breakage occurs. For some semimoist bakery and confectionary products, lowering of moisture for attaining water activity in the range of 0.5–0.8 would cause hardening and consumer unacceptance. Rate of nonenzymatic browning of food is generally highest at 0.65 water activity. Moisture content of food corresponding to these water activities is the critical moisture content. Due to the presence of low molecular weight, some substances, especially water, sucrose, glucose, fructose and acids, and fruit juice powders, exhibit stickiness and caking, even at room temperature. Moisture content at which stickiness occurs can be designated as the critical moisture content of the powder. Stickiness is related to glass transition temperature, TG (°C) and is a property exhibited by the material when it is in amorphous state. At this temperature, molecular mobility of low molecular weight substances composing the food increases and stickiness develops. The rate of water vapor permeation through packaging material depends on its thickness, surface area, and water vapor permeability. Water vapor pressure differences across the material between food and environment and the moisture sorption behavior of food affect the permeation rate. Storage stability of foods will be high when its moisture content is reduced below this value. Values of equilibrium moisture content of foods kept in different relative humidity environment are generally obtained from experiment. It must be mentioned here that at equilibrium, relative humidity of the environment is equal to the water activity of the food. Moisture sorption behavior of food is normally expressed by equations relating water activity (fraction) and equilibrium moisture content X (kg water kg dry solid–1) at constant temperature. When aw is plotted on abscissa and X on ordinate, a sigmoid-shaped curve is generally observed. Several mathematical equations can describe the aw – X relationship. Some of these model equations are described in subsequent paragraphs. 702 Chapter 40 40.3 Sorption Isotherms The food sorption isotherm describes the thermodynamic relationship between water activity and the equilibrium of the moisture content of a food product at constant temperature and pressure. The knowledge and understanding of sorption isotherms is highly important in food science and technology for the design and optimization of drying equipment, design of packages, predictions of quality, stability, and the shelf life of food products by lowering the availability of water to microorganisms and inhibiting some chemical reactions. The typical shape of an isotherm reflects the way in which the water binds the system. Weaker water molecule interactions generate a greater water activity, thus, the product becomes more unstable. Water activity depends on the composition, temperature, and physical state of the compounds. Sorption isotherms can be generated from an adsorption process or a desorption process; the difference between these curves is defined as hysteresis, as it is shown in Figure 40.1. Water adsorption by food products is a process in which water molecules progressively and reversibly mix together with food solids via chemisorption, physical adsorption, and multilayer condensation. An isotherm can be typically divided into three regions; the water in region A represents strongly bound water, and the enthalpy of vaporization is considerably higher than the one of pure water. The bound water includes structural water (H-bonded water) and monolayer water, which is adsorbed by the hydrophilic and polar groups of food components (polysaccharides, proteins, etc.). Bound water is unfreezable and it is not available for chemical reactions or as a plasticizer. In region B, water molecules bind less firmly than in the first zone, and they usually present in small capillaries. The vaporization enthalpy is slightly higher than the one of pure water. This class of constituent water can be looked upon as the continuous transition from bound to free water. The properties of water in region C are similar to those of the free water that is held in voids, large capillaries, and crevices; and the water in this region loosely binds to food materials. Moreover, hysteresis is related to the nature and state of the components of food, reflecting their potential for structural and conformational Figure 40.1: Sorption Isotherm for a Typical Food Product, Showing the Hysteresis. Water Activity and Shelf Life 703 rearrangements, which alters the accessibility of energetically favorable polar sites. The presence of capillaries in food results in considerable decrease in water activity. Moisture sorption isotherms prepared by the addition of water to a dry sample (resorption) will not necessarily be super imposable with an isotherm prepared by removal of water (desorption). This lack of impossibility is referred to as hysteresis. 40.4 Classification of Sorption Isotherms Brunauer et al. classified sorption isotherms according to their shape and processes, establishing five different types, as shown in Figure 40.2. • • Type I : Langmuir and/or similar isotherms that present a characteristic increase in water activity related to the increasing moisture content; the first derivative of this plot increases with moisture content and the curves are convex upward. This type of sorption isotherm is typically applicable in the process of filling the water monomolecular layer at the interval surface of a material. Type II: These sigmoidal sorption isotherms, in which the curves are concave upward, take into account the existence of multilayers at the internal surface of a material. Figure 40.2: Types of isotherms described by Brunauer. (Source: Mathlouthi and Roge, 2003) 704 • • • Chapter 40 Type III: Known as the Flory-Huggins isotherm, it accounts for a solvent or plasticizer such as glycerol above the glass transition temperature. Type IV: It describes the adsorption of an expandable hydrophilic solid until a maximum of site hydration is reached. Type V: The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) multilayer adsorption isotherm is the one observed in the adsorption of water vapor on charcoal and it is related to the isotherms types II and III. The two isotherms most frequently found in food products are types II and IV. 40.5 Measurement of Sorption Isotherm For food products, the sorption isotherm can be measured by means of three different measuring techniques; gravimetric, manometric, or hygrometric, according to Iglesias and Chirife. In the gravimetric methods, the weight of the sample is measured with a balance. In the manometric methods, the vapor pressure of water is measured when it is in equilibrium with a sample at a given moisture content. In the hygrometric methods, the equilibrium relative humidity with a sample at a given moisture content is measured. Two examples of more modern techniques to measure the concentration in a sample are the impedance spectroscopy technique and the light reflection and/or attenuation technique, such as the infrared spectroscopy. 40.6 Mathematical Models of Sorption Isotherms Aiming to mathematically express the relation between the water activity of food and its moisture content, diverse models have been developed such as nonlinear and linear regression models, constituted in their parameters by two, three, four, and six partial regression coefficients, which explain each one of the three zones that the isotherm of sorption of humidity conforms. In many cases, the model that is suitable for certain food product is not suitable for a different one. What is more, the model only exhibits a suitable predictive ability for certain moisture activity ranges. Several mathematical models have been proposed to describe sorption isotherms. Some of them were developed with a theoretical basis to describe adsorption mechanisms; whereas, the others are just empirical or a simplification of more elaborate models. In some ranges of water activity, sorption isotherms can be approximated to linear equations. Some semiempirical equations with two or three fitting parameters are used to describe moisture sorption isotherms. The most common equations are the Langmuir equation, the BET equation, the Oswin model, the Smith model, the Halsey model, the Henderson model, the Iglesias-Chirife equation, the GAB model, and the Peleg model. Water Activity and Shelf Life 705 40.6.1 Langmuir Equation Langmuir proposed the following physical adsorption model on the basis of unimolecular layers with identical and independent sorption sites, and expressed as follows:  1 1  1 aw  − =   Mw Mo  C Mo (40.4) where Mw is the equilibrium moisture content (kg water/kg dry matter) Mo is the monolayer sorbate content (kg water/kg dry matter) C is a constant. The value of the monolayer (Mo) is of particular importance because it indicates the amount of water that is strongly adsorbed in specific sites, and it is considered to be the value at which a food product is the most stable. Langmuir’s isotherm is the most crucial equation among the theoretical models, and it is based on the forces acting between the product surface and the water condensed from the vapor as a monomolecular layer. The extensions of the Langmuir’s underpinning idea on multimolecular layers result in the BET and GAB isotherms, which are able to describe sigmoidal-shaped isotherms commonly observed in the case of food and other materials of biological origin. Values of the various coefficients and regression coefficient (R2) for Langmuir equation are presented in Table 40.1. 40.6.2 Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) Equation The BET equation, given in Equation 40.5, is the most widely used model in food systems and was first proposed by Brunauer, Emmett, and Teller. It represents a fundamental milestone in the interpretation of multilayer sorption isotherms, particularly types II and III. It is also an effective method for estimating the amount of bound water in specific polar sites of dehydrated food systems. Almost in all cases, the deviation of the linearity of these graphs indicates that, at high vapor pressures, the amount adsorbed by the sorbent is lower than the one predicted by the isotherm. The BET equation represents a basis in the interpretation of isothermal sorption multilayers, and it has been applied in gas adsorption and porous steam in surfaces and solids, as well as in water, especially in steam absorption, by homogenous polymers and other materials. Nevertheless, the considerable success of the isotherm is rather qualitative than quantitative. If we considered the linearized forms of the equations of isotherms as the estimation of the applicability rank that they own in its linear sections, it can be observed that, in almost all cases, BET graphs are linear only in a limited range of water activity from 0.05 to 0.45. This difficulty in the process of fitting the experimental data on the totality of the range of relative pressure application determined that the main application of the BET equation is the one related to the estimation of surface areas (29). The BET equation can be considered to be the most useful for determining the optimum moisture conditions for good storage stability, especially for dehydrated food products. The parameters of the BET equation for different food products are listed on Table 40.2. 40.6.3 Oswin Model Oswin developed an empirical model that consists of a series expansion for sigmoid-shaped curves (1946). The Oswin equation was used to relate the moisture content of fat-free dry milk and freeze dried tea up to a water activity of 0.5, as well as for various foods (Table 40.3). 40.6.4 Smith Model In 1947, Smith developed an empirical model to describe the final curved portion of water sorption isotherm of high molecular weight biopolymers. He theorized that two fractions of water are sorbed onto a dry surface; the first fraction exhibits a higher condensation heat than the normal and would be expected to follow the Langmuir model. Smith based his model on the second fraction, which only can be formed after the first fraction has been sorbed. He considered that the second fraction consists of multilayers of condensed water molecules, which effectively prevent any possible evaporation of the initial layer. He theorized that the moisture content in the second fraction was proportional to the logarithm of the difference between the aw of the sample and pure water. This model can be written as: M w = C1 + C2 ln (1 − aw ) (40.7) where, C1 is the quantity of water in the first sorbed fraction and C2 is the quantity of water in the multilayer moisture fraction. This equation could be used in the water activity range from 0.5 to 0.95 in the case of wheat desorption and for various products, as shown in Table 40.4. 708 Chapter 40 Table 40.4: Constants of the Smith model for some food products Product Temp. This equation is a good representation of adsorption data regarding isotherms Type I, II, or III. Moreover, this equation described the sorption behavior of food products that contain starch. This model postulates that the state of sorbate molecules in the second layer is identical to the one in superior layers, but different from those of the liquid state. These authors introduced a second sorption stage of the molecules of a sorbate that was differentiated as a good sorbate. This isotherm necessarily contains a third constant, k, which measures the difference of the chemical potential standard between the molecules of this second stage and those of the pure liquid state. The GAB model is expressed as: Mw = M o CKaw (1 − kaw )(1 − kaw + CKaw ) (40.12) where Mo is the monolayer moisture content; C and K are the adsorption constants, which are related to the energies of interaction between the first and the further sorbed molecules at the individual sorption sites. They can be theoretically expressed as  H − Hn  C = co exp  o  RT  (40.13)  H − Ht  K = ko exp  n  RT  (40.14) where co and ko are the entropic accommodation factors; Ho, Hn, and Ht are the molar sorption enthalpies of the monolayer, the multilayers on top of the monolayer, and the bulk liquid, respectively. R is the ideal gas constant and T is the absolute temperature. Note that when K is 1, the GAB model becomes the BET equation. The GAB model is divided into two additive terms, the first one describes the classical monomolecular layer expression in Langmuir’s adsorption isotherms, and the second term describes the multilayer adsorption corresponding to Raoult’s law: Mw (C − 1) kaw + kaw = M o (1 − kaw + CKaw ) (1 − kaw ) (40.15) Water Activity and Shelf Life 711 Table 40.8: Estimated parameters of the GAB model for various food products Product Temp. The GAB model has been used due to its theoretical bases; it describes the sorption behavior in a wide range of aw (0–0.9). Thus, it was found to be suitable for analyzing more than 50% of fruits, meat, and vegetables, as shown in Table 40.8. Furthermore, the use of the GAB equation has been recommended by the European COST90 project. The major advantages of the GAB model are the following: • • • • It has a viable theoretical background because it is a further refinement of Langmuir and BET theories of physical adsorption. It provides a good description of the sorption behavior of almost every food product (aw < 0.9). Its parameters (co, ko, Ho, Hn, and H1) have a physical meaning in terms of the sorption processes. It describes most of the temperature effect on isotherms by means of Arrhenius-type equations. The GAB model underestimates the moisture content values at high water activity levels (aw > 0.93). The discrepancy underlines two facts: this type of model is unsuitable for a high humidity range, and the saturated salt solution method does not provide sufficient information to get a complete sorption curve. 40.6.9 Peleg Model This model is a purely empirical equation without a theoretical background. It presents the same or even a better suitability than the GAB model. It is a four-parameter model: M w = C1awc3 + C2 awc4 (40.16) where C1, C2, C3, and C4 are constants; C3 < 1 and C4 > 1. The model does not have a monolayer incorporated in it. 712 Chapter 40 Table 40.9: Constants of the Peleg model for various food products Product Yam Instant green tea Green tea granules Dried potato Walnut kernels Walnut kernels Pistachio nut Pistachio nut Temp.
