The assumptions for the analysis include the following: 1. P X is constant. 2. External environment is at constant temperature and RH, but the external conditions will not remain constant during storage, distribution, and retailing of packaged food. Therefore, P X will not be constant. However, using the water vapor transfer rate (WVTR) determined at 38°C/90% RH gives a worst-case analysis, but if the food is being sold in markets in temperate climates, use of WVTR determined at 25 °C/75% RH would be Water Activity and Shelf Life 713 more appropriate. The WVRT can be converted into permeance by dividing with ∆P (vapor pressure difference). 3. P2, the vapor pressure of water in the food, follows some simple function of the moisture content of the food. 4. The moisture gradient inside the package is negligible (i.e., the package should be the major resistance to vapor transport). This is the case whenever P X is less than about 10 g/m2·day1 (cm/Hg), which is the case for most films. The critical point about Equation 40.17 is that the internal vapor pressure is not constant but varies with the moisture content of the food at any time. Thus, the rate of gain or loss of moisture is not constant but falls as ∆P gets smaller. Therefore, some function of P2, the internal vapor pressure as a function of the moisture content, must be inserted into the equation to be able to make proper predictions. If a constant rate is assumed, the product will be overprotected. In low and intermediate moisture foods, the internal vapor pressure is determined solely by the water absorption isotherm of the food. Several functions are available to describe a sorption isotherm, including the BET (Brunauer-Emmett-Teller) isotherm and the GAB (Guggenheim-Anderson-De Boer) isotherms. But the preferred one is the GAB mode. This model requires numerical evaluation using computational technique. In Figure 40.3, mi = initial moisture content; mc = critical moisture content; and me = equilibrium moisture content. The point on the curve up to which remains almost constant is the point ∆aw (mc) and the moisture content at this point is the critical moisture content and aw is the critical water activity at that particular temperature. The slope of the curve beyond mc does not remain constant and increases with increase in aw as ∆P goes on decreasing, and at me the ∆P becomes equal to zero. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 41 Effect of Logistics Environment on Shelf Life After processing and manufacture, the food product leaves the factory and usually moves into the company’s warehouse. It is then transported by rail, ship, plane, or truck to different countries and from there to distribution centers. From these centers the product may be taken to the retail outlet where it might be stored or placed on display racks for some period of time. Regardless of the distribution pattern, transportation damage may be incurred by the product. The extent of such damage will be a function of not only the packaging (primary, secondary, and tertiary) but also the nature of the distribution environment and the method of transportation. Most secondary packages are stacked on pallets, which may or may not be shrink or stretch wrapped. In warehouses, pallets may be stacked four high. Thus, the forces acting on the top tier of a four pallet stack will be quite different from those acting on the bottom tier of the same stack. The longer the time the product spends in the distribution chain, the more significant are the effects arising from pallet stacking height. These effects usually directly relate to the shelf life of the product. A point to be made from all this is that a knowledge of the distribution environment, both climate and physical, is essential before a meaningful shelf life test can be designed. Taking a product from the production line and conducting a shelf life test on it while ignoring possible distribution environment hazards will almost certainly lead to an overestimation of shelf life. In practice, many products are exposed to a sequential regularly fluctuating temperature profile, especially if held in trucks, rail wagons, and uninsulated warehouses. It has been found that many of these patterns can be assumed to follow either a square or sine wave form. It has been shown that the extent of a reaction after a period of time will be the same as it would have been if the food was held at a certain steady “effective” temperature for same length of time. This effective temperature will be higher than the arithmetic mean temperature. Comparison for losses in a theoretical distribution temperature showed that for less than 50% degradation, the losses were about the same for zero and first-order at any time, and thus the determination of the reaction order is not critical. However, the temperature sensitivity Q10 of the reaction is very important in making predictions. All rights reserved. 730 Chapter 41 Major deteriorative reactions causing end of shelf life are known; these deteriorative reactions that foods undergo were discussed in Chapter 38. These reactions and their rates under varied time–temperature conditions will now be analyzed in order to predict product shelf life. Fundamental to such an analysis is that the particular food under consideration follows the laws of “additivity” and “commutativity.” Additivity implies that the total extent of the degradation reaction in the food produced by a succession of exposures of various temperatures is the simple sum of the separate amounts of degradation, regardless of the number or spacing of each time–temperature combination. Commutativity means that the total extent of the degradation reaction in the food is independent of the order of presentation of the various time–temperature experiences. 41.1 Shelf Life Plots A useful approach to quantify the effect of temperature on food quality, especially when little data are available to get rate constant or when only the time to reach a certain level of quality change has been determined, is to construct shelf life plots. Several models are in use to represent the relationship between the rate of reaction or the reciprocal of the rate that can be time for a specified loss in quality or shelf life and temperature. The most-used models are the Arrhenius plot and a linear plot, which are shown in Figure 41.1. 41.1.1 Arrhenius Plot The Arrhenius equation in its general form is θ s = θ 0 e – E A RT ln θ s = ln θ 0 – (41.1) EA RT ln θ s – ln θ 0 = – EA RT E ( ln θ s – ln θ 0 ) T = – RA ln θ s – ln θ 0 E =– A 1T R ln θ 0 – ln θ s EA = = slope 1T R (41.2) Effect of Logistics Environment on Shelf Life Figure 41.1: Arrhenius Plot of Log Shelf Life us and reciprocal of the absolute temperature 1/T (K). 731 Figure 41.2: Linear Plot of Log Shelf Life Versus Temperature (0c). where u0 = shelf life at temperature T0 us = shelf life at temperature Ts The Arrhenius equation is used in the following form: θs = θ 0e  1 1 EA R  −   Ts T0  41.1.2 Linear Plot For a given extent of deterioration and reaction order, the rate constant is inversely proportional to the time to reach some degree of quality loss. The rate constant for that period is then calculated from the shelf life plot using a zero-order reaction. The rate constant is multiplied by the time interval ui, and the sum of the increments of kiui gives the total amount lost at any time. Alternatively, instead of calculating actual rate constants, the time for the product to become unacceptable (i.e., for A to become Ae) can be measured, and Equation 41.9 modified to give: fc = fraction of shelf life consumed = change in A divided by total possible change in A = Ao − A Ao − Ae (41.10) = ∑ ( ki t i ) ∑ ( ki ts ) (41.11) ∑ ki t i ki ts t  ∑ i   ts Ti (41.12) A similar approach to that described earlier is employed. The temperature history is divided into suitable time periods and the average temperature Ti at each time period evaluated. The time held at that temperature ui is then divided by the shelf life us for that particular temperature, and the fractional values summed up to give the fraction of shelf life consumed. There is similarity between this method and the graphical method used to determine the lethality of a thermal process. Both are concerned with summing the effect of various temperatures on the rates of reactions. The shelf life can also be expressed in terms of the fraction of shelf life remaining fr: fr = 1 − fc (41.13) Effect of Logistics Environment on Shelf Life 737 Thus, for any temperature Ts: frθ s = (1 − fc )θ s = shelf life left at temperature Ts (41.14) In other words, the shelf life kept at any temperature is the fraction of shelf life remaining times the shelf life at that temperature. 41.4 Practical Shelf Life (PSL) Example 41.3 A frozen food (ground beef packaged in polyethylene film) has a practical storage life (PSL) at various temperatures as follows: Temperature (°C) PSL (days) –8 –12 –15 –18 –20 –23 –25 120 180 230 300 350 420 480 Calculate the total loss of PSL along the freezer chain from the processor to the consumer given the time and temperature history. Marcel Dekker, Inc., New York. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 42 Shelf Life Testing Generally, shelf life testing (SLT) of food products falls into one of three categories: 1. Experiments designed to determine the shelf life (SL) of existing product. 2. Experiments designed to study the effect of specific factors and combination of factors such as storage temperature, packaging materials, or food additives on product SL. 3. Tests designed to determine the SL of prototype or newly developed food products. 42.1 Basic Approach to Determine Shelf Life of Food Products • • • • Literature study: The SL of an analogues product is obtained from the published literature or in-house company files. Turn over time: The average length of time that a product spends on the retail shelf is found by monitoring sales from retail outlets and from these data the required SL is estimated. The result does not give the “true” shelf life of the product but rather the “required” SL, it being implicitly assumed that the product is still acceptable for some time after the average period on the retail shelf. End point study: Random samples of the product are purchased from retail outlets and then tested in the laboratory to determine their quality. From these data a reasonable estimate of SL can be obtained because the product has been exposed to actual environmental stress encountered during warehousing and retailing. Accelerated SL testing (ASLT): Laboratory studies are undertaken during which the environmental conditions are accelerated by a known factor so that the product deteriorates at a faster rate than normal rate. This method requires that the effects of environmental conditions on product SL can be quantified. Human judgement is the ultimate arbiter of food acceptability; therefore, it is essential that the results of shelf life obtained from instrumental and chemical analysis correlate closely with the sensory judgments for which they are to substitute. A sample failure (SF) can be defined as the condition of the product that exhibits physical, chemical, microbiological, or sensory characteristics unacceptable to the consumer. The time required for the product to exhibit such conditions is the SL of the product. For the best method of estimation of SL, knowledge of the statistical distribution of SL failure is required together with an appropriate model for data analysis. Five statistical Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00042-7 745 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 746 Chapter 42 models—normal, log-normal, exponential, Weibull, and extreme value distributions—were fitted to failure data. One problem with SL testing is developing experimental designs that minimize the number of samples required, thus minimizing the cost of testing while still providing reliable and statistically valid answers. Three experimental designs for use in SL testing of foods are partially staggered and completely staggered. 42.2 Accelerated SL Testing (ASLT) The basic assumption underlying ASLT is that the principles of chemical kinetics can be applied to quantify the effects that extrinsic factors such as temperature, relative humidity, gas atmosphere, and light have on the rate of deteriorative reactions. By subjecting the food to controlled environments in which one or more of the extrinsic factors is maintained at a higher than normal level, the rates of the deterioration will be speeded up or accelerated, resulting in a shorter than normal time for product failure. Because the effects of extrinsic factors on deterioration can be quantified, the magnitude of the acceleration can be calculated and the “true” shelf life of the product under normal conditions can be determined. Because other decisions (e.g., construct a new factory, order new equipment, or arrange contract for the supply of new packaging material) need lead times of months or years, some way for speeding up the time required to determine the shelf life of the product is necessary, and ASLT has been developed for that reason. The need for ASLT is simple because many foods have SL of at least 1 year. The effect on SL of a change in the product might result from any of the following: • • • A new antioxidant or thickener The process: different time–temperature sterilization regime Packaging: a new polymer film would require SL trials lasting at least as long as the required SL of the product Companies cannot afford to wait for such long periods before receiving information indicating whether the new product/process/packing will give an adequate SL. Some ways for speeding up the ASLT have been developed for that reason. It is known that quality loss for most food follows either a zero-order or first-order reaction. The following curves show the relationship between logarithm of SL versus T (linear relation) and inverse of T (1 T ) (Arrhenius). If only a small range of temperature is considered, the former SL plot generally fits the data for food products. This aspect was discussed in earlier and is given again in Figure 42.1. Shelf Life Testing 747 Figure 42.1: Arrhenius and Linear Plots for Food Quality Loss. 42.3 Temperature Quotient Temperature quotient is another term used to describe the response of biological systems to temperature change. The Q value is a quotient indicating how much more rapidly the reaction proceeds at temperature T2 than at lower temperature T1. If Q reflects the change in rate for a 10°C rise in temperature, it is then called Q10. Mathematically: Q10 = K T +10 KT For a given extent of deterioration and reaction order, the rate constant is inversely proportional to the time to reach some degree of quality loss. Thus, by taking the ratio of the shelf life between any two temperatures 10°C apart, the Q10 of the reaction can be found Q10 = QST QST +10 where QST = shelf life at temperature T°C QS(T+10) = shelf life at temperature (T + 10)°C Therefore, it can be expressed as Q10 = QS T K T + 10 = KT QS(T +10 ) 748 Chapter 42 42.4 Effect of Q10 on Shelf Life The effect of Q10 on shelf life is shown in the following numerical example. Example 42.1 For a certain product, it is arbitrarily set that the shelf life is 2 weeks at 50°C. Estimate shelf life at different Q10 values and at temperatures as shown in Table 42.1. The shelf life at other temperatures is calculated in a similar way. The results are shown under the respective columns in Table 42.1. The calculated values illustrate the importance of accurately estimating Q10 values when making shelf life predictions. For example, if a product has a shelf life of 2 weeks at 50°C and a Q10 of 2, it has a shelf life of 16 weeks at 20°C. However, if the Q10 values were 2.5 rather than 2, the shelf life at 20°C would be almost twice as long (31 weeks). Thus, a small error in the value of Q10 can lead to huge differences in the predicted shelf life of the product. Typical Q10 values for foods have been reported as 1.1–4 for canned products, 1.5–10 for dehydrated products, and 3–40 for frozen products. 750 Chapter 42 42.5 Hypothetical Shelf Life Plot Figure 42.2 depicts a hypothetical shelf life plot for a product that has at least 18 months shelf life at 23°C. The shelf life plots for other u10 values are drawn and are shown in Figure 42.2. 42.6 ASLT Procedure The following procedure should be adopted in designing a shelf life test for a food product • • • • • Determine the microbiological safety and quality parameter for the product. Select the key deteriorative reaction(s) that will cause quality loss and thus consumer unacceptability in the product, and decide what tests (sensory and/or instrumental) should be performed on the product during the trial. Select the package to be used; often a range of packaging materials will be tested so that the most cost-effective material can be selected. Select the extrinsic factors that are to be accelerated. Typical storage conditions used for ASLT procedures are shown in Table 42.2, and it is usually necessary to select at least two. Using a plot similar to that shown in Figure 42.2, determine how long the product must be held at each test temperature. If no Q10 values are known, then an open-ended ASLT will have to be conducted. 752 Chapter 42 Table 42.2: Recommended storage conditions for ASLT • Frozen Foods Dry and IMF Foods Canned Foods –40°C –15°C –10°C –5°C 0°C (control) 23°C (room temperature) 30°C 35°C 40°C 45°C 5°C (control) 23°C (room temp.) 30°C 35°C 40°C Determine the frequency of the tests. A good rule of thumb is that the time interval between tests at any temperature below the highest temperature should be no longer than: f2 = f1Q10∆ /10 (42.1) where, f1 = the time between tests (e.g., days, weeks) at the highest test temperature T1 f2 = the time between tests at any lower temperature T2 ∆ = the difference in degrees Celsius between T1 and T2 Thus, if a product is held at 40°C and tested once a month, then at 30°C with a Q10 of 3, the product should be tested at least every f2 = 1 × 3(10 /10) = 3 months As Labuza has pointed out, more frequent testing is desirable, especially if the Q10 is not accurately known. Also, at least six data points are needed to minimize statistical errors, otherwise the confidence in uS is significantly diminished. In summary: • • • Calculate the number of samples that must be stored at each test condition, including those samples that will be held as controls. Begin the ASLTs, plotting the data as they become available so that, if necessary, the frequency of sampling can be increased or decreased as appropriate. From each test storage condition, estimate k or us and construct appropriate shelf life plots from which to estimate the potential shelf life of the product under normal storage conditions. If the shelf life plots indicate that the product shelf life is at least as long as that desired by the company, then the product has a chance of performing satisfactorily in the marketplace. Shelf Life Testing 753 42.7 Examples of ASLT Procedures ASLT for different processed foods is given in the following sections. 42.7.1 Dehydrated Products In dehydrated vegetables, lipid and hydrolytic oxidation, together with nonenzymatic browning and (in the case of green vegetables) chlorophyll degradation, are the major modes of deterioration. In dehydrated fruit, the major mode of deterioration is nonenzymatic browning. An experimental study was conducted at temperatures 30°C and 40°C to accelerate deterioration in sliced green beans and onion flakes. The study found that at 40°C, the shelf life of onions was 11 times shorter and at 30°C, 3.5 times shorter than at 20°C when the aw was 0.56. 42.7.2 Canned Foods It is generally assumed that if good manufacturing practices are followed, microbial deterioration of canned foods will not be a problem. Thermophilic spoilage when canned foods are stored at elevated temperatures, however, is more than likely due to inadequate cooling of the cans following thermal processing. Microbial spoilage at ambient temperatures is generally the result of “leakage” spoilage, so-called because the microorganisms are drawn into the can during cooling. Chlorination of cooling water according to good manufacturing practice will alleviate this problem. Thus, deteriorative reactions in canned foods will normally be limited to organoleptic changes such as loss of color, development of undesirable flavors, and nutrient degradation. Tests by a processor of a canned meat products found that the major mode of deterioration is hydrogen gas production resulting from internal corrosion of the can. Samples were stored at 37.8°C to accelerate this deterioration; the shelf life at 37.8°C was considered to be 40% of the shelf life at 4.4°C, corresponding to Q10 of 1.3. 42.8 Problems in the Use of ASLT Procedures The potential problems and theoretical errors that can arise in the use of ASLT procedures are described here. • • • Error in analytical or sensory evaluation: Generally any analytical measure should be done with a variability less than ±10% to minimize prediction errors. As temperature rises, phase changes may occur (e.g., solid fat becomes liquid), which can accelerate certain reactions. At the lower temperature, then, the actual shelf life will be shorter than predicted. Carbohydrates in the amorphous state may crystallize out at higher temperatures, resulting in a predicted shelf life that is shorter than the actual shelf life at ambient conditions. 754 • • • • • • Chapter 42 Freezing “control” samples can result in reactants being concentrated in the unfrozen liquid and creating a higher rate at certain temperatures that is accounted for in the measured k value. If two reactions with different Q10 values cause quality loss in a food, the reaction with the higher Q10 may predominate at higher temperatures, while at normal storage temperatures, the reaction with the lower Q10 may predominate, thus confounding the prediction. The aw of dry foods can increase with temperature, causing an increase in reaction rate for products of low aw in sealed packages. The result is an overprediction of true shelf life at the lower temperature. The solubility of gases (especially oxygen in fat or water) decreases by almost 25% for each 10°C rise in temperature. Thus, an oxidative reaction, such as loss of vitamin C or linoleic acid, can decrease in rate if oxygen availability is the limiting factor. Therefore, at the higher temperature, the rate will be less than theoretical, which in turn will result in an underprediction of true shelf life at the normal storage temperature. If the product is not placed in a totally impermeable pouch, storage in high-temperature low-humidity environments will generally enhance moisture loss, decreasing the rate of quality loss compared to no moisture change. The result is a shorter predicted shelf life at the lower temperature. If high enough temperatures are used, proteins may become denatured, resulting in both increases or decreases in the reaction of certain amino acid side chains, leading to either under- or overprediction of true shelf life. Therefore, in light of these points, the use of ASLT to predict actual shelf life can be severely limited except in the case of simple chemical reactions. Consequently, food packaging technologists should always confirm the ASLT results for a particular food product by conducting shelf life tests under actual environmental conditions. Once a relationship between ASLT and actual shelf life has been established for a particular product, then ASLT can be used for that product when process or package variables are to be evaluated. CHAPTE R 43 MAP Modeling 43.1 Introduction Respiration involves the oxidation of energy-rich organic substrates normally present in cells, such as starch and organic acids, to simpler molecules (CO2 and H2O) with the concurrent production of energy and to other molecules that can be used by the cell for synthetic reactions. The greatest yield of energy is obtained when the process takes place in the presence of molecular oxygen. Respiration is then said to be aerobic. If hexose sugar is used as the substrate, the overall equation can be written as follows: C6 H12 O 6 + 6O 2 → 6CO 2 + 6H 2 O + energy (43.1) This transformation actually takes place in a large number of individual stages with the participation of many different enzyme systems. The water (H2O) produced remains within the tissue, but the carbon dioxide (CO2) escapes and accounts for part of the weight loss of harvested fruits and vegetables. A range of 3–5% of weight loss is generally ascribed to respiration. When one mole of hexose sugar is oxidized, 36 moles of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) are produced, each possessing 35 kJ of useful change, with the remainder being dissipated as heat. Rapid removal of this heat is usually desirable, and it is important that the packaging assists rather than impedes this process. The rate of respiration is often a good index to the storage life of horticultural products: the higher the rate, the shorter the life; and the lower the rate, the longer the life. From measurements of CO2 and oxygen (O2), it is possible to evaluate the nature of the respiratory process. The ratio of the volume of CO2 released to the volume of O2 absorbed in respiration is termed the respiratory quotient (RQ). Values of RQ range from 0.7 to 1.3 for aerobic respiration, depending on the substrate being oxidized: for carbohydrates, RQ = 1; for lipids RQ < 1; for organic acids RQ > 1. Anaerobic respiration (sometimes called fermentation) involves the incomplete oxidation of compounds in the absence of O2 and the accumulation of ethanol, acetaldehyde, and CO2. Much lower amounts of energy (2 moles of ATP) and CO2 are produced from 1 mole of hexose sugar than that produced under aerobic conditions. In addition, little heat energy (approximately 5%) is produced for a given amount of carbohydrate oxidation in anaerobic respiration compared to anaerobic respiration. The oxygen concentration at which a shift from aerobic to Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00043-9 755 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 756 Chapter 43 anaerobic respiration occurs varies among tissues and is known as extinction point. High RQ values (7.13) indicate anaerobic respiration. 43.2 MAP Modeling The selection of suitable packaging materials, along with evaluation of modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) for fresh fruits and vegetables, remains a largely empirical, trial-and-error exercise that is time-consuming, subjective, and often without unifying principles to guide the research and development efforts. This empirical approach can lead to long testing times, high development costs, costly overpackaging, and the absence of a mechanism to fine-tune a packaging system once it has been developed. In an attempt to put the design of MAP on an analytical basis, a number of research groups have endeavored to model the interactions between respiring produce and package atmosphere. In order to predict what the equilibrium gas concentrations will be and how long it will take to achieve equilibrium, a model should take into account the following factors: • • • • • • • • The effects of changing O2 and CO2 concentrations on the respiration rate The possibility that the RQ is not equal to 1 The permeability of the film to O2 and CO2 The effect of temperature on film permeability The surface area and head space of the package The resistance of the commodity to diffusion of gases through it The optimal atmosphere for the commodity of interest The gas concentrations that are likely to be deleterious to the commodity, and whether they are likely to be reached before or after equilibrium Yet none of the models are comprehensive enough to include all of the salient variables. The key part of any model is the relationship between the rate of respiration by the commodity and the permeation rate of respiratory gases through the package. As the O2 supply within the plant cells begins to decrease as a result of respiration, the partial pressure of O2 between the cells and the package interior and exterior atmosphere become unbalanced, causing some O2 to diffuse into the package. When the rate of O2 consumption exceeds the rate of permeation into the package, the O2 concentration in the package decreases. This, in turn, further slows the respiration rate to the point where the rate of O2 consumed equals the rate of O2 permeation through the package film. True equilibrium in the package would be reached when the gas flux due to respiration equaled the gas flux due to permeation (i.e., O2 is consumed at the same rate at which it is entering the package, and CO2 is produced at the same rate at which it is leaving the package). MAP Modeling 757 However, unless the package is held under closely controlled temperature conditions, it is doubtful whether true equilibrium is ever achieved. Furthermore, because no polymeric film has the same permeability to O2 as to CO2, and because anoxic conditions and the resultant anaerobic respiration are to be avoided at all costs, steady-state conditions inside a package are generally taken to be when the rate of O2 consumption equals the rate of O2 permeability through the film. In such situation, the concentration of CO2 inside the package will increase over time because the partial pressure difference of CO2 across the package film will, at least in the early stages, be so low as to result in negligible gas flux to the external atmosphere. The real challenge in designing and developing MA packages for fresh produce is to determine the O2 consumption and CO2 evolution rates under the variable atmosphere conditions existing in the package. These values can be found in the literature for many products under normal atmosphere but not under abnormal atmosphere conditions. Three methods can be employed to determine or estimate these values experimentally: 1. A flow-through system in which the produce is kept in an airtight chamber under constant temperature, a gas mixture of the desired composition fed into the chamber, and the effluent gas concentrations monitored over time 2. A closed system in which the produce is kept in an airtight chamber under constant temperature and the gas atmosphere in the chamber sampled over time 3. A permeable system that is identical to the closed system except that part of the chamber is made of a polymeric film with known gas permeations constants A modification of the closed system adopted by some workers involves the addition of a CO2 absorber inside the container; however, this approach to determining the rate of O2 consumption assumes that the CO2 concentration has no effect on the respiration rate, a point on which there is far from total agreement. In examining the relevant factors, several important aspects must be remembered. The standard approach to measuring the gas permeability of films uses Fick’s law with some simplifying assumptions, the most salient in the present context being a constant partial pressure difference across the film of the gas under consideration. Clearly in MAP, this is not the case until (if ever) equilibrium is reached. Thus, the use of traditional film permeability (if it is available at the temperature of interest) to calculate likely gas fluxes will require accurate data on the pressure gradients across the package at any particular time. A helpful approach to selecting the required ratio of CO2 to O2 gas permeability of a polymeric film has been presented. The required ratio of gas permeability can be expressed by the following equation: PC Poo − POi = PO PCi − PCO (43.2) 758 Chapter 43 where PC and PO = the permeability coefficients of CO2 and O2, respectively Poo = partial pressure of O2 outside the package (0.21 atm) POi = partial pressure of O2 inside the package PCi = partial pressure of CO2 inside the package PCo = partial pressure of CO2 outside the package (essentially zero) If air surrounds the package for which POo is 0.21 atm and PCo is essentially zero, Equation 43.2 can be simplified to: PC 0.21 − POi = PO PCi (43.3) If the film has similar permeability coefficients to both O2 and CO2 (i.e., the LHS of equation is unity), the sum of the partial pressures of O2 and CO2 inside the package will equal 0.21 atm. However, because in reality the permeability coefficients of commercial films differ and PC is typically two to five times PO, this sum will be less than 0.21 atm, the partial pressure of O2 in the air. Although the partial pressure of CO2 inside the package increases and the partial pressure of O2 decreases, the total pressure of these two gases will be less than 0.21 atm. Because, according to the gas laws, the total pressure times if the volume is constant, the volume of the package will decrease. As the volume of the package decreases, the partial pressure of nitrogen (N2) inside the package will exceed the partial pressure of N2 outside. This result is permeation of N2 through the package to the outside and, in certain situations, the reduction in package volume such that the film adheres to the surface of the fruit. In other situations, such as the onset of anaerobic respiration with a rapid buildup of CO2, the total pressure inside the package may increase, causing the package to bulge. This would cause the partial pressure of both O2 and N2 inside the package to decrease and favor permeation of these gases into the package. Equation 43.3 can also be used to calculate the ratio of the CO2 to O2 permeability coefficients to determine a desired gas atmosphere inside the package. Therefore, if a film with a CO2 permeability coefficient 3.2 times its O2 permeability at the temperature of the storage is selected, an atmosphere containing 2% O2 and 6% CO2 could develop. Another approach suitable for engineering modeling involves the use of gas-permeable films as the primary packaging material and enclosing the packages in a larger high-barrier bag filled with the desired gaseous mixtures. The gas mixture composition and the package film permeability are balanced to achieve the desired constant MA inside the package. This area in MAP research continues to grow rapidly. MAP Modeling 759 43.3 Estimation of Surface Area of Permeable Film Another important variable can be the free or headspace volume of the package. In converting concentration measurements into volume of gases, it is usually assumed that the total pressure in the enclosed system is constant over time. However, this assumption is true only when the RQ of the produce is unity, which is certainly not always the case in MAP of fresh produce. It is evident that gas exchange with the atmosphere surrounding the sealed pack of fruits takes place only due to diffusion of gases through the packing. The flux of O2 into the fruit is a function of respiration rate (RRo), which in turn is a function of O2 (and possibly CO2) concentration within the package. Qf = RRo·w(43.13) where Qf = flux into fruit per unit time RRo = respiration rate of O2 uptake of the fruit, mL/kg·h w = weight of fruit in package, kg. The O2 flux through the polymeric film is given by Qo = Po × A × Poo − Poi X ( ) (43.14) where Qo = diffusive flux of O2 though the package in unit time Po = oxygen permeability coefficient of the package at the temperature of storage, cm3 (STP) cm cm–2 s–1 Pa–1 A = surface area of the film, m2 x = thickness of film, m Poo = partial pressure of O2 outside the package (0.21 atm) Poi = partial pressure of O2 inside the package, atm At equilibrium Po A × Poo − Poi = R × Ro × w X ( ) 764 Chapter 43 Rearranging Po A RRo × w = X Poo − Poi (43.15) Equation 43.15 enables the prediction of O2 permeability requirements provided RRo, the relationship between the respiration rate and O2 concentration, is known. Inspection of Equation 43.15 indicates that the equilibrium concentration of O2 (Po ) is independent of time. This is understandable because the time of equilibrium will be dependent on the free or headspace volume of the package. Figure 43.1 shows the schematic of the MAP for fruits. i A graphical relationship of the respiration rate of apples and the diffusion rates through LDPE film pack of thickness 1.5 mil and 2.0 mil is shown in Figure 43.2. The respiration curve in the graph shows the relationship between O2 consumption (cm3/bag day) on the y-axis and partial pressure of O2 inside the package Po Po on the x-axis. i i The diffusion curves for both types of film show a similar trend, but the film of higher thickness has lower rates. The difference between Po and Po is higher in the beginning, but this difference gradually decreases and hence the curves show a declining trend. i O The respiration curve and diffusion curves intersect at the point of equilibrium. Therefore, the film with diffusion rates that correspond to the intersecting parts of the respiration curve should be selected. The design parameters to be selected are w, A, x, and Po. The last two parameters are determined when a film of given thickness is selected, leaving w and A. If the w is also known, then the only unknown parameter A can be calculated. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 44 Principles of Enzyme Kinetics 44.1 Introduction Many chemical changes that occur in living tissues are mediated by enzymes. Apart from the predominant part they play in controlling the composition of living tissues both before and after harvest, if they are not inactivated or controlled at some stage in a processing or preservation treatment, they can also cause marked changes in the quality of stored products. Oxidoreductase such as peroxidase, catalase, cytochromes, and dehydrogenases are present universally in plant tissues. Pectolytic enzymes produce marked changes in texture. Lipoxidase has been implicated in the oxidation of carotenoid pigments, which leads to loss of color and provitamin A activity. A substance that increases the rate of chemical reaction without modifying the overall standard Gibbs energy change in the reaction is known as an enzyme and hence does not appear in the stoichiometric expression of the complete reaction. A substance that reduces the rate of chemical reaction by binding to the enzyme is known as an enzyme inhibitor, and the process is called inhibition. The respiration of produce is a complicated and difficult process to model. If all factors involved in enzymatic reactions were considered in a respiration model, it would become so complex that it would be of limited value. Cameron et al. used a trial-and-error approach to curve fit O2 consumption of tomato with an exponential type function that consisted of four coefficients. Yang and Chinnan used a quadratic function with nine parameters to correlate respiration rates of tomato with O2 and CO2 concentrations and storage time. Yang and ­Chinnan also suggested that the Michaelis–Menten type of enzyme kinetics might be appropriate for modeling respiration of produce. The Michaelis–Menten equation has also been used to describe the respiration of microorganisms (Bailey and Ollis) and diffusion-controlled reactions. Based on this literature information, Lee et al. speculated that the Michaelis–Menten equation was useful, and they developed a respiration model based on the underlying principles of enzyme kinetics for predicting respiration rates of fresh produce as a function of both O2 and CO2 concentrations. In this chapter, the basics of Michaelis–Menten kinetics are presented. All rights reserved. 768 Chapter 44 44.2 Michaelis–Menten Kinetics (Doran, 1995) The kinetics of most enzyme reactions are reasonably well represented by the Michaelis– Menten equation: Vmax CA K m + CA rA = (44.1) where rA = volumetric rate of reaction CA = concentration of reactant A Vmax = maximum rate of reaction at infinite reactant concentration and having the dimensions kg/mol·m–3s Km = Michaelis constant for reactant A, kg/mol·m–3 If we adopt conventional symbols for biological reactions and call reactant A the substrate, Equation 44.1 can be written as: ν= Vmax S Km + S (44.2) where ν = volumetric rate of reaction S = substrate concentration For respiration of fruits and vegetables, the Michaelis–Menten equation is written as: rO 2 = Vmax [ O 2 ] K m + [ O2 ] (44.3) where rO 2 = respiration rate [O2] = oxygen concentration This equation can also be expressed as: rO 2 = Vmax PO 2 K m + PO 2 Vmax = K mol/kg·sec PO 2 = partial pressure of oxygen, Pa Km = Michaelis constant 44.3 Determination of Enzyme Kinetic Constants for Batch Data To fully specify the kinetics of Michaelis–Menten reactions, two rate constants Vmax and Km must be evaluated. Graphical methods are available for finding these constants. The first step in kinetic analysis of enzyme reactions is to obtain data for the rate of reaction r as a function of substrate concentrations [O2]. Initial rates and corresponding initial substrate Principles of Enzyme Kinetics 769 Figure 44.1: Michaelis–Menten Plot. concentrations are used as (r, O2) pairs that can then be plotted in various ways for determination of Vmax and Km. Initial rate data are preferred for enzyme reactions, because experimental conditions such as enzyme and substrate concentrations are known most accurately at the start of the reaction. Creating a Michaelis–Menten plot is a simple procedure that involves plotting (r, O2) values directly as shown in Figure 44.1. Vmax and Km can be estimated roughly from the graph: Vmax is the rate as O2 → ∞ and Km is the value of O2 at r = rmax 2. The accuracy of this method is usually poor because of the difficulty of the extrapolating to rmax. To overcome this limitation, the Michaelis–Menten equation is rearranged in a number of ways to give convenient graphical representations including the following: • • • • • • Briggs–Haldane modifications of the Michaelis–Menten equation Lineweaver–Burk plot Eadie–Hofstee and Hanes plots Langmuir plot Direct linear plot Eisenthal and Cornish–Bowden plot The most commonly used of these plots are described in the following sections. 44.4 Lineweaver–Burk Plot They took the Michaelis–Menten (M–M) equation as follows. ro = Vmax [ O 2 ]o [O ] + K 2 o m (44.4) 770 Chapter 44 The reciprocal of the equation is: 1 [ O 2 ]o + K m = ro Vmax [ O 2 ]o [O2 ]o + K m 1 = ro Vmax [ O 2 ]o (Vmax ) [ O 2 ]o Km 1 1 = + ro Vmax (Vmax ) [ O 2 ]o Km 1 1 1 = + × ro Vmax (Vmax ) ( O 2 )o 1 Km 1 1 = + – ro Vmax ( O 2 )o Vmax (44.5) Equation 44.5 is known as the Lineweaver–Burk equation and is in the form of y = mx + c type (i.e., straight line). Hence, a plot of 1 ro versus 1 ( O 2 )o known as Lineweaver–Burk plot, which obeys the Michaelis–Menten equation, is shown in Figure 44.2. Thus, a plot 1 ro against 1 ( O 2 )0 provides a straight line with a slope K m Vmax and intercept –1 K m . The Lineweaver–Burk plot was antagonized on several factors, the first of which fact is that the extrapolated graph across the y-axis sometimes reaches the edge of the paper that makes the estimation of −1 K m across x-axis more difficult. The second fact is that this treatment gives undue importance to the data obtained at low-substrate concentration, which are likely to give inaccurate results. The third fact is that the linearity is less obvious compared to other treatments. Principles of Enzyme Kinetics 777 Figure 44.7: Type of Inhibition by Eadie–Hofstee Plot. 44.8 Noncompetitive Inhibition Enzyme inhibition: Substance that tends to decrease the rate of enzyme-catalyzed reaction by acting either on the enzyme or on the cofactor is known as inhibitor. Competitive inhibition: If the apparent value of Km is reduced by the inhibitor, then the inhibition is known to have a competitive component, and if the inhibitor has no effect on the apparent value of Vmax the inhibition is said to be competitive. A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate in some respect, and it inhibits its reaction by competing with the active site of the enzyme because of its structural similarity with the substrate. This enzyme-bound inhibitor lacks either appropriate reacting group or other potential substrate for a reaction to take place, resulting in dead-end complex, which requires replacement by particular substrate before a reaction can take place by that enzyme molecule. Noncompetitive inhibitor: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds to a site other than that meant for the substrate on the enzyme to form a dead-end complex, regardless of whether the substrate is bound. On binding to a site other than the catalytic site of the enzyme, the noncompetitive inhibition changes the confirmation structure of the catalytic site of the enzyme in such a way that enzyme loses its ability to convert substrate to product even after substrate is able to bind to the active site of the enzyme. The equation takes the form of a Michaelis–Menten equation with Vmax divided by a factor of 1 + [ I o ] K i  . From this equation, it is clear that the Vmax value is altered, but the Km value is unchanged for simple linear noncompetitive inhibition. CHAPTE R 45 Enzyme Kinetics Applied to MAP 45.1 Introduction Enzymes are complex, globular proteins that have three important characteristics. They can act as catalysts, accelerating the rate of chemical reactions by factors of 1012–1020 over that of uncatalyzed reactions. A second characteristic is their specificity, which enables them to selectively modify individual food components and not affect others. Finally, they can have a regulatory role, controlling the biochemical processes associated with various membranous components of a tissue, which has a profound effect on the regulation of life processes and defining the quality of foods during postharvest or postmortem processing and storage. An understanding of the biological mechanisms for controlling enzymatic activities and the biochemical mechanisms of enzyme action can provide the means of effectively exploiting enzymes in food processing and preservation. From the food packaging point of view, knowledge of enzyme action is essential to understanding more fully the implications of one form of packaging over another. Enzymes endogenous to plant or animal tissues or biological fluids can have undesirable or desirable consequences in foods. Examples are the senescence and spoilage of fruits and vegetables. Examples involving endogenous enzymes include oxidation of phenolic substances in plant tissues by phenolase (leading to browning). Starch–sugar conversion in plant tissue by amylases, invertase and invertase inhibitor, and postharvest demethylation of pectic substances leads to softening of plant tissues during ripening and firming of plant tissues during processing. Aerobic respiration involves a series of enzymatic reactions that take place through the metabolic pathways of glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and the associated electron transport systems (Kader, 1987). In fruits and vegetables, enzymatically generated compounds derived from long-chain fatty acids play an extremely important role in the formation of characteristic flavors. Enzymeinduced oxidative breakdown of unsaturated fatty acids occurs extensively in plant tissues and yields the characteristic aroma associated with same ripening fruits and disrupted tissues. If all factors involved in enzymatic reactions were considered in a respiration model it will become so complex that it would be of limited value. Yang and Chinnan (1988) suggested that the principles of enzyme kinetics might be applied for modeling respiration of produce. All rights reserved. 782 Chapter 45 Lee et al. (1991) gave a respiration model for predicting respiration rates of fresh produce as a function of both O2 and CO2 concentrations of atmosphere surrounding the stored produce in a pack, based on the underlying principles of enzyme kinetics. Published respiration data show a similarity between fresh produce respiration and microbial respiration. The Michaelis–Menten equation is used to describe the respiration rate of microorganisms in industrial aerobic fermentation and also in diffusion-controlled reactions. In this chapter, the same methodology as given by Lee et al., 1991: applying the Michaelis–Menten equation for prediction of respiration rates of selected fruits and vegetables. 45.2 Respiration Model A similarity between fresh produce respiration and microbial respiration allows for reasonable speculation that the Michaelis–Menten equation may be used to describe the respiration of produce. 45.2.1 Respiration Rate as a Function of O2 Concentration When CO2 is absent, the dependence of respiration on O2 concentration can be described with the following equation: r= Vm [ O 2 ] K m + [O2 ] (45.1) where r = respiration rate, mL/kg·h or mg/kgh Vm = maximum respiration rate, mL/kgh or mg/kgh [O2] = concentration of oxygen, % O2 Km = Michaelis–Menten constant, % O2 45.2.2 Respiration Rate as Function of CO2 Concentration The dependence of respiration on CO2 concentration was modelled based on the uncompetitive inhibition, which has been used exclusively for product inhibition in reactions involving several substrates and products (Cornish-Bowden, 1979). For the respiration process, the uncompetitive inhibition mechanism due to CO2 is expressed as: r= Vm [ O 2 ]  CO 2  Km + 1 + [O ] K i  2  where r, Vm, Km, and [O2] are same as those given Equation 45.1 Ki = inhibition constant, % CO2 [CO2] = concentration of CO2 % (45.2) Enzyme Kinetics Applied to MAP 783 Equation 45.2 is assumed to be valid as long as the produce undergoes aerobic respiration (i.e., sufficient O2 is available to act as substrate). 45.2.3 Testing of Models Using Published Data To examine the effect of O2, respiration rate data as a function of O2 in the presence of little or no CO2 were collected and analyzed. Equation 45.1 was linearized for this purpose of fitting the data. The linearized equation is as follows: [O ] = K + [O ] or [O ] + K 2 m 2 2 m r Vm Vm Vm Vm (45.3) Equation 45.3 is similar to the linear regression equation of the form y = mx + c. The estimated values of the parameters of the model are Vm = 11.11 mL O2/kg·h, Km = 3.33% O2, and Ki = 27.27% CO2. Using these parameters for package material properties and package conditions reported by Jurin and Karel (1963), the respiration model was used to simulate the gas composition in a polyethylene bag containing apples. The schematic representation of gaseous exchange in modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) is shown in Figure 45.3. These models can be employed for predicting package air composition at any point in time during transient period. The model can also be used for predicting equilibrium time and the composition of package air at equilibrium. Conversely, it can be employed for optimizing various package parameters and determining required rate of gas permeability for the packaging film, to enable the package attain equilibrium in the desired manner. The equilibrium O2 and CO2 obtained from Figure 45.4 are 8.7% O2 and 3.15% CO2, and it occurred after a time lapse of nearly 3–8 days. 45.5 Conclusions A simple semiempirical respiration model based on enzyme kinetics principles adequately described the respiration of fresh produce in terms of O2 consumption rate and CO2 evolution rate as functions of O2 and CO2 concentrations. In the package atmosphere, the model was confirmed with published data for a wide variety of commodities and with experimental data. The model could be used in designing MAP systems for fresh fruits and vegetables provided that the CO2 concentration is below the tolerance limit of the commodity and sufficient O2 is available to support aerobic respiration. The model is particularly useful for predicting the transient respiration compositions where temperature fluctuations are encountered during passive modification of a MAP package and in similar situations. Page left intentionally blank CHAPTE R 46 MAP Design with O2 Modeling (Experiments on Tomato Fruit) 46.1 Introduction A general definition of food stored in a modified atmosphere (MA) environment is one in which the product is stored in something other than air. Aerobic bacteria and oxidative reactions (leading to rancidity) are the two major spoilage agents of foods. Both these phenomena require oxygen. If oxygen (O2) is reduced or eliminated, spoilage is inhibited. Minimum oxygen levels are used to pack foods under MA in order to inhibit the growth of aerobic spoilage microorganisms and reduce the rate of oxidation. This gas is needed for fruits and vegetables to respire. The presence of oxygen inhibits the growth of anaerobic microorganisms. The objective of the study is to modify and refine the O2 depletion method to measure the relationship between the rate of O2 uptake and O2 concentration for tomato fruit at different stages of ripening. The procedure developed by Cameron et al. (1989) for estimation of O2 consumption as a function of O2 concentration around the fruits is used. Equations given by them to estimate time for initial equilibrium O2 establishment as affected by void volume were also used. 46.1.1 Test Particulars The tomato of variety Lycopersicon esculentum Mill. (cv. Tropic) was grown in a greenhouse at three different stages of its growth—breaker, pink, and red stages of ripeness were used. A test jar was submerged in a water bath at 25°C during a test run to ensure both constant temperature and no gas leakage occurred. Duration of the test varied from 28.5 h to 60 h, and during that period, O2 depletion was from 0.21 atm to ∼ 0 atm. They used 4.3 g of magnesium oxide (MgO) as carbon dioxide (CO2) absorbent. An O2 probe calibrated to known O2 partial pressure was monitored with a strip chart recorder at 5-min intervals with a data logger for data analysis. Assumptions included a constant temperature and no influence of CO2 concentration. Measured O2 takedown in packaged fruit matched the modeled timecourse closely (results not shown). The predicted curves shown in Figures 46.3 and 46.4, and the associated Equation 46.10 are unique in the field of MAP technology. One interesting feature is a relatively wide degree of flexibility for systems optimized to low O2 equilibrium levels. For instance, if it is desired to keep the package atmosphere at 0.02–0.04 atm, the weight of fruit packaged can range almost twofold for a given film with a fixed permeability characteristic (Figure 46.4). This implies that O2 can be maintained within the desired limits even with minor variations in fruit weight. This unexpected prediction arises from the fact that the additional O2 uptake by the small increase in fruit weight is nearly offset by the net decrease in total O2 uptake caused by the small decline in O2 concentration.
