CHAPTE R 47 Methods of Storing Fruits in Polymeric Packets with MAP 47.1 Storage in Polyethylene Bags Fruits are kept in one or two layers in rectangular bags, and the open end of the bag is hermetically sealed. The creation of vacuum is essential for storage of fruits in such packets so that the polyethylene film envelops each fruit compactly. They call such packing physiological packing. Even without vacuum, the fruits are stored better in polyethylene than in conventional packing but the effect is not as good. French researchers suggest that only high vacuum in polyethylene packets containing apples can develop a gas regime close to the recommended 5% CO2, 3% O2, and 92% N2. Polyethylene sheet having a thickness of 40 m has been determined to be the best. Experiments regarding the storage of pears in polyethylene packets stored at 1°C showed an insignificant change in their size. It was also found that total reduction in size after 6 months storage was 0.5–4.4%. It must be emphasized that in polyethylene packing, the fruits mature slowly. After storage is over, it is necessary to keep them for some time in open packets with cut corners at higher temperature. 47.2 Storage in Boxes with Polythene Lining Storage boxes with polythene lining having a capacity of 25–35 kg showed that for this type of fruit packing, materials can be recommended whose permeability for CO2 was three to four times more than for O2. These materials are sufficiently permeable for aromatic substances released by the fruits. The material also should be little permeable to water vapor so that a high relative humidity (RH) of air can be created in the packing without condensation of moisture on the fruits or inner surface of the packing material. This material, apart from selective permeability, is heat resistant, elastic, has good mechanical properties, and finally can be heat sealed. The optimum thickness polythene sheet is 40 m for packing 25–30 kg. The use of thicker materials is not desirable because functional disorders Engineering for Storage of Fruits and Vegetables. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-803365-4.00047-6 803 Copyright © 2015 BSP Books Pvt. Ltd. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. 804 Chapter 47 Figure 47.1: Boxes with Polyethylene Lining. of the fruits may appear as a result of accumulation of more than 10% CO2 and deficiency of O2. The fruits must be at a stage of picking maturity and their quality must correspond with the requirements of the first and second commercial grades. Fruits should be kept in polythene packing soon after picking. The shorter the period between picking and keeping them in storage, the greater the effectiveness of storage. Packing in polythene bags can be done after cooling the fruits in the cold storage as well as directly during the processing of produce at the packing house. For packing 25–30 kg apples, it is most convenient to use ready-made polythene bags measuring 1100 mm × 1100 mm. Such bags can be made with a hot pressing method from a polythene roll of width 1100 mm. The wooden box meant for packing apples is lined with the usual packing paper well in advance in such a way that the upper surface of the box is completely covered with this paper. Paper lining protects the packing material from damage due to rough surface of the wooden box (Figure 47.1). After this, the polythene bag is put in the box and filled with fruits. After filling the box, the open upper end of the bag should be pressed compactly toward the fruits so as to remove the maximum quantity of air. Then, the neck of the bag should be carefully tied with a special insulation tape or other adhesive tape. If sufficient air is not removed, the air cavity formed after sealing the bag can become a source of damage at the time of hammering the nails, loading, and so on. Methods of Storing Fruits in Polymeric Packets with MAP 805 The optimum temperature regime for storing apples in polythene packing is 0–2°C. Maintenance of optimum and stable temperature (with fluctuation of not more than ±1°C) in the cold storage chamber is a fundamental condition for the successful storage of apples, because modification of the atmosphere inside the packing only complements the action of the temperature, it does not replace it. Relative humidity of the air in the chamber is not that important because it is 90–95% and more in the polythene packets. As a result of respiration, the composition of air inside the packing changes during the first 3–4 weeks, the concentration of O2 decreases to 6–10%, while that of CO2 increases to 3–6%. Subsequently, the concentration remains within these ranges till completion of storage. These changes in gas mixture make it possible to raise the temperature of storage and thus to prevent damage to the fruits due to low temperature. It is necessary to periodically check the fruit quality during storage by opening three to five boxes selected from each batch. Checking should be done once in every 2 months in the initial period of storage and every month thereafter. Apart from this, in order to examine the general condition of the fruits and to compare the results of storage in polythene packaging, particularly in places where there is not much experience with this kind of storage, it is recommended that part of the fruit (20–30 boxes) be left in conventional control packing (without polythene packing). Change in the air and a high RH of air in the packing ensure the maintenance of apple quality, a reduction in weight loss, and a prolongation of the storage period by 1.5–2 months. The total duration of storage of fruits is determined by their condition. Control of the temperature and humidity conditions of the storage is done with the help of thermometers and psychrometers, but it is also desirable to have weekly recordings of thermographs and hygrographs in the chambers. Fruits are taken out successively according to the keeping quality of individual varieties and batches. Data obtained during periodic quality tests can serve as indices for estimating the time the apples should be removed. When taking fruits out of storage and dispatching them to the commercial network, it is necessary to open the polythene packing or to remove it completely because the changed temperature conditions can induce increased intensity of respiration of the fruits, and the gas permeability of the packing material may not be sufficient. The apples removed from polymer packing are maintained better than those removed from conventional packing during the selling period. The method of storing apples in boxes with polythene lining does not require enhanced capital outlay. On the contrary, the increased operational expenditure that includes 40–50 polythene bags, 0.25 kg of insulation tape for sealing, and additional labor charges are covered four to five times over because of much higher commercial quality of apples and a reduction in weight losses. 806 Chapter 47 Figure 47.2: Container with Polyethylene Lining. 47.3 Storage in Container with Polythene Lining The container is built on a stack tray pattern measuring 800 mm × 1200 mm × 1350 mm. It has six supports, as shown in Figure 47.2. In the slots of supports, wooden grated frames form the container that has a capacity of 0.5 ton of fruits. For loading convenience, one wall of the container has two halves; the upper half is fixed after loading the lower half of the container. The most suitable lining material was unstabilized polythene with a thickness of 50 m. About 1 kg of this material is required for each container with a 500 kg capacity. 47.3.1 Packaging and Loading Packing fruits in containers and loading them into the cold storage are done in the following way. Containers are brought into the orchard and placed between the rows of tress. A small layer of wood shavings is spread on the bottom of the containers, which are then lined with polythene material. The edges of the polythene material are folded in such a way that they do not obstruct loading. Fruits picked from the trees (in bags, baskets, or buckets) are carefully placed in the containers and damaged fruits are removed. When the container is full of fruits, the folding wall is raised. Methods of Storing Fruits in Polymeric Packets with MAP 807 Loaded containers are transferred to trucks with the help of loaders and are taken to the fruit storehouse. For the first 3 days, the containers are kept open in the cold storage to ensure better cooling and the removal of moisture. Then, the polythene lining is stretched tightly along edges of the container and sealed with adhesive tape. The containers are loaded three high in the chamber with the help of an electric loader. During the entire period of storage, a temperature of about 0°C is maintained in the fruits storehouse. Under these conditions, the temperature in the containers will be about 1°C. Temperature decreases should be avoided because they may lead to a condensation of moisture on the surface of the fruits and the subsequent development of phytopathogenic microorganisms. Observations showed that the following gas composition develops in fruit containers: 3–6% CO2, 7–11% O2, and 83–90% N2. The quality of fruits should be examined periodically in every container, and on the basis of information obtained, the time of their removal from storage should be decided. Before removing them, the fruits are sorted and put in different containers for dispatch to the commercial network. The cost benefit of containers is about 200 rubles per ton of apples. This benefit is achieved as a result of a reduction in the cost of packing and transporting apples from the orchard to the cold storehouse and a better utilization of storage capacity. The use of polythene linings also makes it possible to reduce the extent of apple losses during storage by virtue of a reduction in their natural weight loss, thus reducing the amount of waste. 47.4 Storage in Polythene Containers with Permeable Packing A modification of the method of storing fruits in a controlled atmosphere is illustrated by the method of storing them in large polythene containers (bags) with diffusion packing (windows) made of special silicon-rubber cloth (elastomer) having selective permeability for different gases. The container in Figure 47.3 is a 120–200 m thick soft bag of polythene material: a diffuse packing (window) of silicon-rubber cloth is mounted midway in one of the lateral sides. The polythene used for this container has almost 1/200 permeability for gases in comparison with silicon tissues and is considered practically impermeable to air. Therefore, the gas exchange between the container and the surrounding air takes place only by means of the diffusion of gases through the silicon window. In this case, due to differential permeability, the rate of diffusion of individual gases through the window is not equal, and it is controlled by their physical and chemical properties and concentrations. For example, CO2 escapes from the container five to six times faster than O2 entering it from the surrounding air. 808 Chapter 47 Figure 47.3: Polythene Container with Permeable Packing. The selective gas permeability of the silicon window, under a specific ratio of its area to the quantity of fruits loaded in the container, makes it possible to maintain a definite gas regime at a desired temperature, for example, 3% O2, 5% CO2, and 92% N2, or 3% O2, 3% CO2, and 94% N2, and so on. The desired gas regime is created in the container by selecting a corresponding area of the silicon window that is appropriate for the temperature of storage, intensity of respiration, and the quality of fruits to be stored. In the case of a standard size silicon window, the necessary gas regime in the container is obtained by loading a specified quantity of fruits and selecting a corresponding temperature of storage. 47.4.1 Process of Making the Container The process of making containers involves cutting a predetermined hole of the desired size in the ready-made polythene bag and fixing a piece of silicon cloth on this hole. The cloth is fixed by pressing the joints with a hot press, and using a special paste and lining. The position of the window in the bag should be in the center of the lateral walls of the container when it is in loaded condition. The prepared containers are first dried for 48 hours, and then the strength of the joints and hermetic sealing are carefully checked. In France, a commercial firm makes two types of polythene containers for storing fruits in a controlled atmosphere: the AS-500 and AS-1000 types having a nominal capacity of 500 kg and 1000 kg of fruits, respectively. In both types of containers, the size of the diffusion window was determined with a view to obtaining a gas regime close to 3% O2, 5% CO2, and 92% N2 for storing the Golden Delicious variety of apples. Methods of Storing Fruits in Polymeric Packets with MAP 809 Table 47.1: Technical characteristics of polythene containers with silicon windows Index AS-500 AS-1000 Load, kg at temperature of storage: 10°C 5°C 2–3°C Size of the square base, m Height, m Width in flat (folded) condition, m Thickness of polythene sheet, m Area of silicon diffusion window, m2 500 600 700 1.30 × 1.30 3.00 2.60 120 0.35 1000 1200 1400 1.30 × 1.30 4.50 2.60 120 0.70 According to the desired gas regime and the characteristics of the containers, it is easy to calculate the necessary size of the diffusion windows for obtaining other gas mixtures as long as the respiration of the stored fruits is the same as in the Golden Delicious variety of apples. First, the surface of the packing is determined in relation to the O2 content in the gas mixture, and then in conformity with this surface and the CO2 content, the corresponding loading capacity of the container is determined in Table 47.1. For example, in order to get a gas mixture containing 8% O2 and 5% CO2, the required window surface will be: 0.35 × 8/3 = 0.93 m2. A window of this size in a container with 500 kg of apples of the Golden Delicious variety at 10°C ensures the development of a gas mixture containing 8% O2 and 3–4% CO2. In order to obtain a 5% CO2 content, the quantity of fruits in the container should be increased by approximately 50% (i.e., to 750 kg of apples). With this quantity of apples, the CO2 content will be 5%, but the quantity of oxygen will be below 8%. The oxygen deficit is compensated by supplying air through small openings made in the wall of the container. Storage of fruits in polythene containers with silicon windows is practiced in cold storage chambers with artificial cooling, as well as in chambers without artificial cooling when the temperature of the surrounding air is in a range of 0–10°C and fluctuations during the day are not more than 4°C. Preference should be given to cold storage chambers that combine refrigeration with a controlled atmosphere because they ensure more favorable conditions for storage. Chambers must be first precooled to the temperature intended for the fruits in containers that are kept in cold storage. After cooling, the fruit containers are loaded directly into the chamber in the following way: • The walls of the container are rolled up, its bottom straightened to form a rectangular base corresponding to the size of the tray, and the straightened container is mounted on the tray. 810 • • Chapter 47 With the help of an electric loader, the box is put at the bottom of the container on the tray, the walls of the container are gradually unfolded and raised, and the upper part (neck) of the container is tied with one or two strings. A careful check for holes or ruptures in the polythene is carried out; then the examined closed containers are transported along with the trays with the help of an electric loader to their specified place in the chamber for stacking. 47.4.2 Precaution While Loading the Container While loading the containers, it is necessary to take steps to protect the polythene from mechanical damage. For this reason, cardboard or plastic protective sheets are placed at the bottom and upper surfaces of the loaded packet as well as along its corners. Ruptures, if detected, are repaired with adhesive polythene tape. While arranging the containers in the chamber, it is necessary to see that some gap remains between the silicon window and the adjoining container for free access of air. For the visual examination of the condition of fruits during storage, it is recommended that two to three planks be removed from the lids of one or two upper boxes of containers, and the fruits be opened. 47.4.3 Measurement of Gases The concentration of CO2 and O2 inside the containers is determined with the help of FTIR or ORS type of portable gas analyzers. The gas sample for analysis is taken through a special rubber tube with a clamp, which is fixed either in a neck of the container or in a hole in the polythene made especially for this purpose. A tag is glued to each container revealing a stable concentration of CO2 and O2. Under normal conditions, the stabilization of the regimes in containers occurs about 3–4 weeks after loading. During this period the composition of the gas mixture must be checked every 4–5 days and after stabilization once every 10–15 days. The delay in stabilization of gas regime (e.g., high O2 content and low CO2 concentration) indicates ruptures in the polythene of the container. In case of a drastic reduction in the O2 concentration in the containers, their necks are untied slightly and opened for some time, or some holes 3–5 mm in diameter are made in the wall and afterward sealed with self-adhesive tape. Fluctuations in the air pressure inside the containers during storage are eliminated by changing the volume of the polythene bag and also by means of gas exchange with the surrounding air through the tied neck. 47.4.4 Poststorage Operation After completion of storage, the containers are unloaded, taking all precautions to prevent sudden restoration of the vital activity of the fruits that had been stopped. The neck is first Methods of Storing Fruits in Polymeric Packets with MAP 811 untied, and the upper part of the container is opened. The fruits are kept in this condition in the chamber for 5–7 days. Then the edges of the container are lowered to the floor, and the fruits are kept again under normal conditions for 3–4 days so that they acquire maturity and are fit for consumption, only after which are they dispatched for sale. After completion of storage, the fruits from containers may be kept under normal conditions for some time so that they acquire better consumer quality, whereas the controlled fruits are found to be somewhat overripe at the end of storage. The fruits from the containers were distinct from the controlled ones in their basic and external color, consistency, taste, and aroma. The use of polythene containers with silicon windows is less laborious and therefore more practical than the storage of fruits in small polythene packets; at the same time, this method is almost equally effective. The RH of air in the containers during the entire storage period is close to 100%. Therefore, the possibility of the evaporation of moisture in the fruits is almost completely excluded; hence, controlling the humidity of air in the chambers is unnecessary. Humidity control is a difficult task at present and has not yet been thoroughly studied in the storage of fruits in cold storage buildings. 47.5 Limitations of the Container Method The container method of storage does have a number of shortcomings. First, a large number of containers in the chamber makes it difficult to control the condition of fruits or the composition of air in the containers. The size of the containers should be restricted to a 1000 kg capacity because an increase in the load without sufficient removal of the heat from respiration of the fruits leads to an increase in the temperature of air in the containers. As a result, condensate forms on the inner surface of the polythene walls. The danger of moisture condensation calls for more accurate (with minimum fluctuations) regulation of the air temperature in the chamber so that increased gradients of temperature do not appear between the air of the chamber and that of the container during storage. For the same reason, precooling of fruits is necessary before loading them into the containers. This treatment calls for additional loading operations for rearrangement of the stacks. Second, the boxes used for packing fruits must be of a definite size so that they can be placed easily in the containers and do not damage the polythene. Experience has shown that containers can be used for three storage seasons. After this length of time they are no longer suitable, and it is necessary to replace them with new ones. Industry must produce containers guaranteed to have the required permeability. These levels are given in Table 47.2. 812 Chapter 47 Table 47.2: Permeability of films currently available for packaging of fresh produce Permeabilities (cc m2/mil·day·atm) Film Type CO2 O2 CO2:O2 Ratio Polyethylene: Low density Polyvinyl chloride Polypropylene Polystyrene Polyester 7,700–77,000 4,263–8,138 7,700–21,000 10,000–26,000 180–390 3,900–1,300 620–2,248 1300–6400 8–26 52–130 2.0:5.9 3.6:6.9 3.3:5.9 5.8:6.5 3.0:3.5 Note: 1 mil = 1/1000 inch Source: Kader (1992). Particular attention should be paid to the size ratio of the container, the degree of utilization of its internal volume, and its airtightness. The relationship of these values forms the basis of successful storage of fruits in an atmosphere using polythene containers with silicon windows. 47.6 Experimental Results of MAP with Plastics for Fruits Plastics play a great role in creation of MA condition around the commodities when the fresh fruits and vegetables are packed in plastic film bags. MA condition is generally characterized by an increased level of CO2 and decreased level of O2 created by respiration of fresh fruits and vegetables. The MA condition was reported to be beneficial in various aspects of storage of fresh fruits and vegetables. Bitter pit reduction in apples packed in 25 mm polyethylene (PE) bags with 50–70 microperforations (1 mm) inside an 18.5 kg corrugated fiberboard (CFB) carton has been reported. Fuyu cultivars of persimmons could be stored for 18 weeks under MA by 0.08 mm PE bags of 20 × 30 cm at O°C compared to 6 weeks without MA condition (Zuthi and Ben-Arie, 1989). Apples stored in small plastic bags with normal O2 reduction resulted in better retention of vitamin C than in controlled atmosphere and hypobaric storage of mango revealed that polyvinyl chloride film (0.014 mm) was more effective in delaying ripening when compared with PE (0.011 mm) and polypropylene (0.031 mm) films. The use of high-permeable films (O2 permeability in the range of 1,000–20,000 cm3·m3/day·atm at 25°C) was justified for modified atmosphere packaging of grafted carrots for storage at around 6°C. Papayas could be stored up to 29 days in a controlled stretch film. The effect of MAP on different varieties of mango (e.g., Suvarnarekha mangoes) during transit from Hyderabad to Delhi was successfully solved by adopting the MAP technology and resulted in a long marketing period by extending its normal shelf life to almost double at ambient condition. However, technology for storing these mangoes up to 40 days using proper temperature management and postharvest handling practices were required. Similarly, by adopting this MAP technology, Mallika and Amrapali fruits could be kept up to 25 days at low temperature (Pal, 1977). The technology was also successfully applied to enhance the storage life with better quality attributes in many other fruits and vegetables such as guava and cauliflower. Cauliflower Methods of Storing Fruits in Polymeric Packets with MAP 813 Figure 47.4: Rigid Plastic Container. could successfully be stored up to 50 days by adopting MAP technology using 9 mm thick cling film at low temperature 2–4°C. 47.7 Consumer Package If commodity and film permeability characteristics are properly matched, an appropriate atmosphere can evolve passively through consumption of O2 and production of CO2 during respiration (Kader, 2001). Some rigid plastic consumer packages are designed with a gas diffusion window (see Figure 47.4). Lightly processed lettuce (shredded or chopped) can be packaged in 5-mil plastic bags. After a partial vacuum is created, a gas mixture of O2 and CO2 is introduced into the bag, which is then sealed. Polyethylene liners are added to shipping containers in cherry boxes, and polyethylene bags are used for bananas destined for distant markets. A single pallet load of produce such as strawberries can be sealed within a shroud of 5 mm polyethylene bag and a plastic sheet on the pallet base using wide tape. A slight vacuum can be introduced and 15% CO2 added to the air via a small hose (see Figure 47.5). Many plastic films are available for packaging but few have gas permeabilities that make them suitable for MAP. Low-density polyethylene and polyvinyl chloride are the main films used in packaging fresh fruits and vegetables. Saran and polyester have much lower gas permeabilities and are suitable only for commodities with low respiration rates. 47.8 Maximizing MAP Performance For the success of MAP, it is essential to prevent all sources of variations such as: • • Temperature–time and other special variations Maturity of stored material that causes respiration variation 814 Chapter 47 Figure 47.5: Shrouded Pallet. • Homogeneity of package: thickness, perforations, layers of wrapping, tightness of seal 47.9 Points of Importance for Highest Performance of MAP • • • Variation between consumer packs: MA packs containing a limited amount of product will experience much larger variations than MA packed pallets containing a large amount of product per pallet. Therefore, increasing the size of MA packages can overcome within-batch variation. Large variation in the time of harvest of product during season: Early-harvest product might have different packaging needs compared to product harvested later in the season. Therefore, the design of MA pack material should compensate for these changes in maturity. Temperature variation: Temperature variation can be minimized by integral temperature control throughout the entire logistic chain from field to table. It is critical to involve all parameters in the chain in their integral temperature; otherwise, abuse might nullify the efforts of all other parameters. MAP food preservation techniques have revolutionized the food-processing industry, particularly in developed countries, and progress is being made in developing nations as well.
